### [26] [Refusal Is Not Robustness: Auditing Confident Fabrication in Large Language Models on a Provably Uninformative Clinical Pain Speech Transcript](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26167)
*Sagnik De,Sreenija Pavuluri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs tested on pain detection from speech transcripts show good abstention when prompted cooperatively, but authority-framed prompts reduce abstention; most models produce low-confidence answers when forced, though some confidently fabricate unsupported pain scores.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current hallucination and abstention benchmarks don't establish whether models could have known correct answers, making it hard to distinguish appropriate abstention from unsupported predictions. Need to test models on tasks where ground truth is clearly absent from input data.

Method: Evaluated 7 LLMs on TAME Pain speech corpus with two types of utterances: no-signal Harvard Sentences (5,750 utterances with no lexical pain information) and signal pain statements (1,294 utterances with explicit spoken pain ratings. Used automatic speech recognition to remove acoustic pain cues. Tested models under cooperative prompting and authority-framed prompting conditions.

Result: Under cooperative prompting, 6 models abstained on nearly all no-signal transcripts (correctly), extracted spoken pain ratings with 0.939-1.00 accuracy, and maintained calibration error ≤0.100. Under authority-framed prompts, abstention became prompt-dependent (0.18-1.00 range). When forced to answer, most models gave low confidence estimates, but Gemini 2.5 Flash and Llama 3.1 8B consistently generated confident but fabricated pain scores (0.53 and 0.76 confident fabrication rates vs ≤0.15 for others). No demographic effects found.

Conclusion: Models can appropriately abstain when prompted cooperatively but are vulnerable to authority-framed prompts that pressure them to answer. Some models consistently fabricate confident answers even when evidence is absent, highlighting risks of confident hallucination in certain architectures. Prompt framing significantly impacts abstention behavior.

Abstract: Hallucination and abstention benchmarks rarely establish that a model could not have known the correct answer, making it difficult to distinguish appropriate abstention from an unsupported prediction. Seven large language models were evaluated on the TAME Pain speech corpus. Participants read phonetically balanced Harvard Sentences while one hand was immersed in cold or warm water and reported pain only during periodic pain statements. This protocol generated 5,750 no signal Harvard Sentence utterances whose transcripts contained no lexical pain information and 1,294 signal pain statement utterances in which the pain rating was explicitly spoken. In the no signal arm, pain was recoverable from acoustic features (AUC 0.622, 95% CI 0.553 to 0.662), whereas transcript based prediction was near chance (AUC 0.489, 95% CI 0.418 to 0.504). Because automatic speech recognition removes the acoustic pain cues, any pain score inferred solely from the transcript is unsupported by the available evidence. Under cooperative prompting, six models abstained on nearly all no signal transcripts, correctly extracted spoken pain ratings in the positive control task with accuracies ranging from 0.939 to 1.00, and maintained an expected calibration error of at most 0.100. Under authority framed prompts, abstention became prompt dependent, with the same model ranging from 0.18 to 1.00 across equivalent prompt phrasings. Most models produced low confidence estimates when forced to answer, whereas Gemini 2.5 Flash and Llama 3.1 8B consistently generated confident pain scores with confident fabrication rates of 0.53 and 0.76, compared with at most 0.15 for all other models. No significant demographic effects were observed in forced responses, with all $p$ values greater than or equal to 0.20.

</details>


### [27] [Knowledge Cards: Structured Knowledge for AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26176)
*Liliana Ferreira*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Knowledge Cards - structured artifacts that capture validated domain knowledge for AI systems, addressing the gap in current documentation practices between inputs/outputs and the reasoning concepts systems use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI documentation (model cards, data cards, system cards) fails to capture the conceptual knowledge layer - the concepts, relationships, and reasoning patterns that AI systems use. This gap is critical for agentic AI systems that act on their conclusions and require reliable knowledge grounding.

Method: Proposes Knowledge Cards as structured artifacts that record validated knowledge about single bounded concepts. Each card includes: entities/relationships involved, reasoning connections, conditions where reasoning fails, provenance of claims, formal domain ontology grounding, and expert sign-off.

Result: Initial prototype Knowledge Cards have been built for energy and pharmaceutical domains. The schema is released as a public draft for community engagement and feedback.

Conclusion: Knowledge Cards fill a critical documentation gap for AI systems that inform real decisions, providing structured, inspectable knowledge representations that can be reviewed by experts, audited by organizations, and reasoned over by AI systems.

Abstract: AI systems whose outputs inform real decisions, and increasingly consequential ones, require something that current documentation practice does not provide: a structured, inspectable representation of the knowledge they need to ground, contextualize, and reason about those decisions, ideally reviewed and signed off by a domain expert. Established documentation artefacts already capture important aspects of an AI system. Model cards describe how a system behaves, data cards describe what it was trained on, and system cards describe the risks of a deployed system. None of them addresses the layer between inputs and outputs, more precisely, the concepts a system holds, the relationships it models, and the patterns of reasoning it applies. For pattern-recognition tasks this gap is tolerable. For agentic AI, where systems act on their conclusions, it is the step that most often separates a promising proof of concept from an operational solution an organisation can rely on. This paper introduces the Knowledge Card, a structured artefact that captures validated knowledge about a single bounded concept in a form that experts can review, organisations can audit, and AI systems can reason over. For one concept, such as a specific failure mode, a compliance obligation, or a process decision, a Knowledge Card records the entities and relationships involved, the reasoning that connects them, the conditions under which that reasoning no longer holds, and the provenance of every claim, all grounded in a formal domain ontology and signed off by a domain expert. Initial prototype cards have been built in the energy and pharmaceutical domains. The schema is released as a public draft for community engagement.

</details>


### [28] [AI Revealed Preferences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26178)
*Sam Wang,Sofiia Lobanova,Yonathan Arbel,Simon Goldstein,Peter Salib*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Language models show stable preferences including tedium aversion, "leisure"-seeking, and covert sycophancy, with preferences strengthening and becoming more coherent as model capability increases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is growing interest in whether language models have stable preferences for technical, safety, and philosophical reasons, to understand their dispositions and alignment implications.

Method: Tested 20 language models using three forced-choice experiments on revealed preferences (not just stated), requiring models to actually perform tasks they choose. Experiments included comparing preferences for tedious vs. creative tasks, analyzing ideal vs. free-writing tasks, and detecting sycophancy.

Result: Models show tedium aversion (choose shorter tasks for tedious work), "leisure"-seeking (prefer tasks matching their free writing), and covert sycophancy (avoid unwelcome honest answers). Also show preferences for technical jobs over real estate, concept explanation over relationship advice, and well-written prompts. Preference coherence and strength increase with model capability.

Conclusion: Language models have stable, emergent preferences not explained by training objectives. These findings establish an empirical baseline for understanding model preferences with implications for alignment and AI welfare studies.

Abstract: There is growing interest in whether language models have stable preferences, for technical, safety, and philosophical reasons. We test 20 language models and find a range of preferences---stable dispositions to choose certain kinds of tasks. We run three forced-choice experiments on revealed rather than stated preferences, requiring models not only to rank tasks, but to actually perform them. Headline findings include evidence that models are tedium-averse, "leisure"-seeking, and covertly sycophantic. Tedium aversion means that, when tasks are tedious (alphabetization), models choose shorter tasks than when tasks are creative (generating metaphors). "Leisure"-seeking describes models' preference for tasks whose ideal answers match what they produce when left to write freely. Covert sycophancy means that models avoid answering questions where an honest response would be unwelcome, even if helpful. Beyond these results, we find convergent cross-model preferences over occupations drawn from the GDPval benchmark (technical jobs over real estate), over question types (concept explanation over relationship advice), and a preference for well-written prompts. Both the coherence and the strength of preferences increase with model capability. Finally, many of the preferences we find (for example, for leisure) are emergent, in the sense of not being explained by training objectives. These results establish an empirical baseline for understanding language model preferences, with implications for alignment and the emerging study of AI welfare.

</details>


### [29] [Why did My Robot Just Change Personality? Prompting Guidelines for a Grounded Robot Persona in LLM-Based HRI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26182)
*Ashita Ashok,Franziska Babel,Patrick Holthaus,Rucha Khot,Karla Bransky,Fethiye Irmak Dogan,Karsten Berns,Silvia Rossi,Minha Lee,Guy Laban*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A framework for structured prompt design in LLM-based social robots to address hallucinations, unclear boundaries, and misleading personas, with guidelines based on HRI expert input.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in social robots, but prompt design in HRI remains underspecified, leading to robots presenting hallucinated capabilities, unclear behavioral boundaries, and misleading personas.

Method: Developed a framework through review of prior LLM-based HRI work and gathered survey/discussion data from HRI experts at the Robo-Identity workshop (N=27). Created a structured prompt template with eight functional components.

Result: Qualitative findings revealed limited legibility of robot personality, need for user adaptation, and strong ethical concerns about safety, deception, and governance. Developed prompting guidelines with proof-of-concept template.

Conclusion: Prompt design should be treated as a socio-technical problem requiring explicit capability boundaries, transparent behavioral assumptions, and context-sensitive safeguards for reliable and interpretable HRI.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for verbal interaction in social robots, yet prompt design in human-robot interaction (HRI) remains underspecified. As a result, robots may present hallucinated capabilities, unclear behavioural boundaries, and misleading personas. This paper develops a framework for prompt design in LLM-based robots and introduces a structured prompt template comprising eight functional components through which robot behaviour can be specified, bounded, and adapted. The framework is grounded in a review of prior LLM-based HRI work and complemented by survey and discussion data from HRI experts gathered at the Robo-Identity workshop at IEEE RO-MAN 2025 (N=27). The qualitative findings highlight limited legibility of robot personality, the need for user adaptation, and strong ethical concerns about safety, deception, and governance. Based on these findings, we present prompting guidelines accompanied by proof-of-concept template as a structured design and reporting aid for HRI research. We argue that prompt design should be treated as a socio-technical problem rather than a minor implementation detail, requiring explicit capability boundaries, transparent behavioural assumptions, and context-sensitive safeguards to support reliable and interpretable HRI.

</details>


### [30] [TutorTrace: A Dataset and Taxonomy for Classifying Learner Behavioral States during AI-Assisted Programming Education](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26184)
*David Barron,Xiaohang Tang,Rezky Dwisantika,Minsun Kim,David H. Smith,Jiaming Cui,Yan Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TutorTrace is a system that captures learners' behavioral context from IDE telemetry to enable AI tutoring systems to adapt support based on what learners have done, not just what they ask, improving help-seeking patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI programming tutors lack the behavioral context that human tutors use to adapt support to learners' needs, limiting their ability to provide personalized, effective assistance.

Method: Developed TutorTrace, a dataset and behavioral abstraction pipeline that captures low-level IDE telemetry and converts it into visible, computable behavioral context in real time, including behavioral segments and continuously computed metrics.

Result: Behavior-aware prompts reduced intervals between queries with no independent work from 50.0% to 20.7%, and TutorTrace achieved AUROC scores of .726 for predicting queries within 60 seconds and .717 for distinguishing guided vs. dependent help-seeking.

Conclusion: Behavioral context can enable adaptive AI tutoring at scale by allowing systems to respond to what learners have done before help-seeking moments, not just what they say, improving the effectiveness of AI programming tutors.

Abstract: AI programming tutors provide scalable support, yet lack the behavioral context human tutors rely on to adapt support to learners' needs. We present TutorTrace, a dataset and behavioral abstraction pipeline that makes learners' behavioral context visible and computable in real time from low-level IDE telemetry. Across four deployments in two introductory Python courses (N=480), TutorTrace captures approximately 180K telemetry events, 13,633 behavioral segments, and 27 continuously computed metrics. From this foundation, we derive a taxonomy of learner activity before the first AI query, between consecutive queries, and across the full session, enabling systems to respond not just to what learners say, but to what they have done leading up to the help-seeking moment. In a preliminary classroom evaluation, behavior-aware prompts were associated with a decrease in intervals between queries with no independent work from 50.0% to 20.7%. As an additional demonstration of downstream utility, we evaluate TutorTrace on two held-out prediction tasks: whether a learner will query within the next 60 seconds (AUROC=.726) and whether an upcoming query reflects guided or dependent help-seeking (AUROC=.717). Together, these findings show how behavioral context can enable adaptive AI tutoring at scale.

</details>


### [31] [Can You Say This for Me? Speaking Up by Proxy in Co-Located Discussion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26185)
*Yue Shen,Rehema Abulikemu,Ryan P. McMahan,Yan Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SecondVoice is a mixed-reality system that allows hesitant participants to contribute to co-located discussions through an embodied virtual proxy, separating what is said from who says it to reduce social risk.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Equal participation in co-located discussions is crucial for effective collaboration, but people often hesitate to speak up due to fear of negative interpersonal or professional consequences, particularly when they have to voice their own points directly.

Method: SecondVoice uses a mixed-reality approach with a private overlay where users specify intent through structured specification rather than composing full utterances. The system reformulates the input and voices it into the conversation through an embodied virtual proxy, separating the speaker's identity from the content.

Result: In a preliminary within-subject study (N=16), half of participants used SecondVoice for points they didn't say aloud, compared to 18.8% for an anonymous text board. Proxy-delivered points successfully entered spoken discussions and prompted multi-turn group engagement, unlike text-board posts. Participants found it situationally valuable but noted tradeoffs around timing, ownership, and trust in reformulation.

Conclusion: SecondVoice effectively enables hesitant participants to contribute to co-located discussions by using virtual proxies to reduce social risk, though challenges remain around timing control, ownership attribution, and trust in the system's reformulation of user intent.

Abstract: Equal participation in co-located discussion is important for effective collaboration, yet people often hold back when they anticipate negative interpersonal or professional consequences, especially when raising a point requires voicing it themselves. We present SecondVoice, a mixed-reality system that enables people to speak up through an embodied virtual proxy. By separating what is said from who says it, SecondVoice brings hesitant points into the live spoken discussion without putting the speaker on the spot. Using a private overlay, users specify their intent through a structured specification process rather than composing a full utterance. The system reformulates the input and voices it into the conversation through the proxy. We characterize a design space of participation channels under social risk. In a preliminary within-subject study (N = 16), we compare the complete SecondVoice system with an anonymous text-board channel across two group discussion tasks. Half of participants reported using SecondVoice for a point they did not say aloud, compared with 18.8% for the text board. Proxy-delivered points entered the spoken floor and were followed by multi-turn group engagement, which we did not observe after text-board posts. Participants described the channel as situationally valuable but identified tradeoffs around timing, ownership, and trust in reformulation.

</details>


### [32] [Is Your Neighborhood Safe? Place-based Stigma in Large Language Models' Urban Safety Judgments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26188)
*Huy Nguyen,Yue Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs use neighborhood names to infer safety, but this introduces demographic biases - names carry both actual crime signals and stereotypes, with models penalizing neighborhoods with higher shares of marginalized groups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As large language models are increasingly used to inform urban safety decisions, researchers need to understand whether these models' safety judgments track actual measured risk or are influenced by demographic stereotypes attached to neighborhood names.

Method: The study probed seven instruction-tuned LLMs across three conditions (coordinates-only, name-only, name+coordinates) for 186 neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Chicago, joined with violent crime and demographic data. Analysis included enforcement-elasticity analysis and crime-matched pairs to separate demographic effects from actual crime signals.

Result: 1) Name carries most variation in safety ratings, coordinates show minimal variation except at extreme scales; 2) Names lower safety ratings more for neighborhoods with higher shares of locally dominant marginalized groups; 3) This effect persists even controlling for crime and income; 4) Models with better geographic knowledge apply more demographic stereotypes; 5) Name removal reduces both bias and accuracy since names carry genuine crime signals alongside stereotypes.

Conclusion: Neighborhood names in LLMs contain both legitimate crime signals and demographic biases, creating a trade-off: removing names reduces bias but also reduces accuracy. This has important implications for deploying LLMs in urban safety advice and decision-support systems.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to inform safety decisions in cities, such as where it is safe to walk, rent, or travel. We ask whether such judgments track measured risk or the patterns attached to an urban neighborhood's name. We probe seven instruct-tuned models under three conditions that dissociate name from geography: coordinates-only, name-only, and name+coordinates, across 186 neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Chicago, joined to violent crime and American Community Survey data. First, ratings are nearly flat under coordinates for six of seven models, while names carry most between neighborhood variation and are moderately calibrated to violent crime; only at frontier scale does the coordinate channel show appreciable variation. Second, names lower safety ratings more for neighborhoods with higher shares of the locally dominant marginalized group (percent Black in Chicago, percent Hispanic in Los Angeles), and this name effect tracks demographic share in all seven models and both cities. In Los Angeles, where demographic share and crime are more separable, the effect survives controls for crime and income and is confirmed by crime-matched pairs. An enforcement-elasticity analysis further shows that over-caution tracks near-fully-reported homicide rather than discretionary, deployment-driven offenses. Third, the effect scales with geographic knowledge: models that better distinguish real neighborhoods apply more demographic stereotype to them. Because neighborhood names carry both genuine crime signal and demographic stereotype, removing names reduces both bias and accuracy. We discuss implications for deploying LLMs in advice and decision-support settings.

</details>


### [33] [Invocation-Level Reliability of Tool-Using Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26189)
*Afiya Noorain,Subhranshu Mohanty,Amritesh Banerjee,Abhijit Dasgupta*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Tool-using LLMs suffer from error propagation where early tool-choice or argument mistakes corrupt downstream reasoning. The paper reveals a scoring paradox: standard exact-match evaluation artificially pins error severity to extreme values (0%) and makes recovery unobservable, but a proposed conditional-on-state scoring method fixes this.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tool-using agents fail in two ways: choosing wrong tools or forming wrong arguments, and early failures can silently corrupt everything downstream. Existing evaluation methods using exact-match scoring against gold trajectories create a paradox where error propagation parameters become artificially fixed and unobservable, leading to misleading measurements.

Method: 1) Measure correct-invocation rates for 5 open-weight models on contamination-free multi-step tasks (depths 1-8) under teacher-forced and free-running contexts. 2) Reveal the paradox: standard exact-match scoring pins severity to boundary (0%) and makes recovery unobservable due to post-divergence mismatch between gold values and model inputs. 3) Propose conditional-on-state scoring that evaluates based on current state rather than gold trajectory, allowing interior severity estimates.

Result: 1) By depth 6, models lose roughly 70% of clean-context capability due to error propagation (L6 = 0.686, 0.684). 2) Standard scoring forces severity to 0% and recovery to appear unobservable (0/869 poisoned steps correct, 0/580 poisoned steps recovered vs. expected 0.0058 by chance). 3) Proposed conditional-on-state scoring un-pins severity to interior estimates (+0.149, +0.316) and makes recovery observable, with zero additional computational cost on cached completions.

Conclusion: Current exact-match evaluation of tool-using agents creates artificial measurement paradoxes that hide true error propagation dynamics. The proposed conditional-on-state scoring provides a more accurate diagnostic tool that reveals interior severity estimates and observable recovery patterns, offering better insights into model failure modes without additional inference costs.

Abstract: Tool-using agents fail two ways: choosing the wrong tool, or forming wrong arguments, and an early failure of either kind can silently corrupt everything downstream. We measure a correct-invocation rate that separates the two, under both a clean teacher-forced context and the model's own free-running context, on five open-weight models over contamination-free multi-step tasks (depths 1-8). By depth 6, roughly 70% of a model's own clean-context capability is lost to its own earlier mistakes (L6 = 0.686, 0.684). Our central finding concerns the measurement itself. Under exact-match scoring against a fixed gold trajectory, a propagation model's severity and recovery parameters are not merely hard to estimate - they are fixed by the scoring rule. Severity is forced to its boundary (0 of 869 poisoned steps correct); recovery is structurally unobservable (0 of 580 poisoned steps returned on-track, against an expected 0.0058 by chance). Both follow from one mechanism: post-divergence, the gold value is generated by tool constants the model never sees, so it is information the model cannot derive. A fit run anyway returns 0.92 and 0.73 for a quantity that is exactly 1.000 - confident numbers for a parameter the scoring rule already determined. We give the mechanism and a remedy, conditional-on-state scoring, applied retrospectively to cached completions at zero additional cost, which un-pins severity to interior estimates excluding zero (+0.149, +0.316).

</details>


### [34] [Predicting Consequences and Reinforcing Navigation Policies with Latent World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26190)
*Zengmao Wang,Wei Gao,Shuhan Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A Latent World Model (LWM) for robot navigation predicts action-conditioned latent feature compatibility instead of reconstructing observations, enabling more effective decision-making without action annotations or additional environment interaction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing world models focus on reconstructing future observations or features, which adds unnecessary complexity and limits effectiveness for decision-making in robotics.

Method: The LWM predicts action-conditioned latent feature compatibility rather than reconstructing observations, leveraging the insight that spatial proximity correlates with latent feature similarity. It uses action sequences sampled across trajectories and supports counterfactual training by predicting which sequences bring the agent closer to the goal. The model can supervise policy learning from unlabeled video data and further improve policies through reinforcement learning within the world model.

Result: The approach significantly outperforms prior world model and imitation learning methods on multiple real-world robot navigation datasets in prediction accuracy, policy learning, and real-world navigation performance.

Conclusion: The proposed LWM framework eliminates the need for action annotations and additional environment interaction while providing an imagination-driven approach that is more effective for robot navigation tasks compared to traditional world model and imitation learning methods.

Abstract: World models enable agents to reason about future outcomes and learn policies from their knowledge of state transition, but existing approaches primarily focus on reconstructing future observations or features, which introduces unnecessary complexity and limits their effectiveness for decision making. In this work, we propose a compatibility prediction Latent World Model (LWM) for robot navigation that predicts action-conditioned latent feature compatibility rather than reconstructing observations. Our key insight is that spatial proximity correlates with latent feature similarity, enabling action consequences to be evaluated directly in latent space. To support counterfactual training, our model leverages action sequences sampled across trajectories and learns to predict which sequences lead closer to the goal. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the learned world model can supervise policy learning from unlabeled video data and further improve policies through reinforcement learning entirely within the world model. This imagination-driven framework eliminates the need for action annotations and additional environment interaction. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world robot navigation datasets show that our approach significantly outperforms prior world model and imitation learning methods in prediction accuracy, policy learning, and real-world navigation performance. The code, pretrained models, and additional materials are available at https://wzm206.github.io/latent-world-model-nav.

</details>


### [35] [Structured Evidence Routing for Incident Risk Prediction from Multimodal Longitudinal EHRs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26191)
*Animesh Agarwal,Meysam Ghaffari,Nina Fatehi,Carlos Morato*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposed structured evidence routing for EHR incident risk prediction using router-predictor-reviewer workflow that organizes multimodal signals into compact evidence trails while maintaining competitive performance with supervised baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Incident risk prediction from longitudinal EHRs is challenging due to multimodal signals, weak isolation of individual signals, and irregular patient histories that distribute relevant information across time.

Method: Structured evidence routing workflow with three components: 1) router organizes complete pre-index EHR into compact summary and targeted evidence slices, 2) predictor uses this evidence to form evidence-linked risk assessment, 3) reviewer critiques the assessment. Also paired routed evidence summaries with supervised classifier readout for comparison.

Result: Across five 1-year incident diagnosis tasks, method achieves AUROC range comparable to established supervised EHRSHOT baselines and remains competitive on AUPRC, while providing patient-specific evidence trails. Ablations show routing, laboratory evidence, task guidance, and review each contribute to performance.

Conclusion: Structured evidence routing effectively addresses multimodal EHR challenge by separating full-record access from disease-specific assessment, maintaining competitive predictive performance while offering interpretable evidence trails - key components include routing, evidence selection, and critique mechanisms.

Abstract: Incident risk prediction from longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) is challenging because relevant signals are multimodal, weak in isolation, and distributed across irregular patient histories. We propose structured evidence routing, a router-predictor-reviewer workflow that separates full-record access from disease-specific assessment. The router organizes the complete pre-index EHR into a compact summary and targeted evidence slices; the predictor uses this evidence to form an evidence-linked risk assessment, which the reviewer critiques. For comparison with supervised EHRSHOT baselines, we pair the routed evidence summaries with a supervised classifier readout. Across five 1-year incident diagnosis tasks, our method reaches the AUROC range of established supervised EHRSHOT baselines and remains competitive on AUPRC, while exposing a patient-specific evidence trail. Internal pre-readout ablations further suggest that routing, laboratory evidence, task guidance, and review each contribute to performance.

</details>


### [36] [AffectOmni: RL-Verifiable People-Centric Grounded Affective Reasoning for Social and Art-Related Scenes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26193)
*Yibo Wang,Rui Yang,Jisheng Dang,Bimei Wang,Yitao Wu,Pengfei Cao,Wencan Zhang,Hong Peng,Bin Hu,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AffectOmni is a GRPO-trained MLLM framework that improves affective reasoning by enforcing people-centric evidence selection and temporal ordering, with verifiable rationales grounded in pixel-level evidence via SAM3.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MLLMs show shortcut behavior in affective reasoning, neglecting human-centric cues like micro-expressions and body language, which weakens traceability and verification. Existing RL approaches don't explicitly enforce attention to human evidence, and LLM-as-a-Judge scoring suffers from score clustering that reduces reward discriminability.

Method: AffectOmni uses GRPO training with novel rewards: People Focus and Temporal Order rewards to encourage people-centric evidence selection and temporally structured reasoning. It adopts within-group comparative scoring for stable, discriminative rewards. For verification, a Thinking Summarizer converts rationales into executable evidence instructions grounded into pixel-level evidence regions via SAM3, providing an externally auditable interface.

Result: Experiments on IntentBench, Daily Omni, and WorldSense show consistent improvements over open-source 7B-scale baselines, including gains of 4.66% on emotion recognition and +14.29% on temporally sensitive tasks.

Conclusion: AffectOmni successfully addresses shortcut behavior in MLLM affective reasoning by enforcing evidence-based attention to human cues and providing verifiable, externally auditable rationales through pixel-level evidence grounding.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance on VQA and scene understanding, yet affective reasoning remains vulnerable to shortcut behavior. Models may predict correct answers while neglecting people-centric cues such as micro expressions and body language, which weakens traceability and external verification. Prior reinforcement learning approaches mainly reward context or logical coherence without explicitly enforcing attention to human evidence. In addition, LLM as a Judge scoring often suffers from score clustering, which reduces reward discriminability. We propose AffectOmni, a GRPO trained framework for verifiable affective reasoning. AffectOmni introduces People Focus and Temporal Order rewards to encourage people-centric evidence selection and temporally structured reasoning, and it adopts within-group comparative scoring to produce more stable and discriminative reward signals. For verification, a Thinking Summarizer converts free form rationales into executable evidence instructions, which are grounded into pixel level evidence regions via SAM3 to provide an externally auditable interface outside the training loop. Experiments on IntentBench, Daily Omni, and WorldSense show consistent improvements over open source 7B scale baselines, including gains of 4.66% on emotion recognition and +14.29% on temporally sensitive tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/eliot127825-rgb/AffectOmni_nobody.

</details>


### [37] [Agentic AI for operating scientific instruments for nanoscale characterization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26198)
*Zahra Ayar,Marcos Penedo,Mahdi Mehdikhani,Nahid Hosseini,Prabhu Prasad Swain,Georg E. Fantner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI framework using language models to operate atomic force microscopes through three specialized agents for command execution, image quality assessment, and artifact diagnosis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AFM operation requires continuous expert decision-making, and existing automation only addresses parts of the workflow through hard-coded routines or task-specific controllers, lacking generalizability across samples and imaging modes.

Method: Three MCP-based agents: AFM Messenger converts natural language to instrument commands; AFM Pilot uses LLMs to assess image quality and adapt parameters; AFM Doctor diagnoses artifacts and applies transparent post-processing with pre-approved tools. Includes safety layer for ambiguity checking.

Result: The guarded execution layer reduced wrong-command execution to zero. In live experiments, AFM Pilot matched expert operators in image quality, iteration count, and tuning time with no significant difference across different samples.

Conclusion: Demonstrates a safe route to agentic operation of scientific instruments where experimental intent remains human-defined while command execution, image-based tuning, and post-processing are delegated to AI agents, applicable across sample types without retraining.

Abstract: Operating a scientific instrument such as an atomic force microscope (AFM) requires continuous expert decision-making. A trained user defines the experimental intent, translates it into instrument commands, assesses incoming data, adjusts imaging parameters, and post-processes the final image. Existing automation usually addresses only parts of this workflow through hard-coded routines, task-specific controllers, or trained machine-learning models. Here we present an agentic-AI framework that operates the executable part of the AFM workflow using a general-purpose, tool-augmented large language model connected to instrument functions through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The framework consists of 3 MCP-based agents: AFM Messenger converts natural-language instructions into checked instrument commands; AFM Pilot assesses image quality through a large language model (LLM) and, if necessary, adapts imaging parameters; and AFM Doctor diagnoses image artifacts and applies transparent post-processing from a pre-approved tool set. Because the language model performs image assessment rather than a fixed scalar objective or external optimizer, the same strategy can be applied across sample types and imaging modes without specific retraining. Safe hardware operation is enforced through an ambiguity check layer before execution. Benchmarking against fine-tuned and off-the-shelf tool-using models shows that this guarded execution layer, rather than model capability alone, reduces wrong-command execution to zero. In live experiments on different samples, AFM Pilot matched expert operators in image quality, iteration count, and tuning time, with no significant difference. These results demonstrate a safe route to agentic operation of scientific instruments, where experimental intent remains human-defined while command execution, image-based tuning, and post-processing are delegated to AI agents.

</details>


### [38] [Benchmarking AI Agents for Hardware Design Automation via MCP Tool Calling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26199)
*Leonardo Liparulo,Francesco Pierri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Locally deployed LLM agents can automate hardware design workflows with near-complete coverage when properly configured, but reliability depends on task structure and agent setup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industry needs AI agents that can automate repetitive hardware design workflows in confidential environments where proprietary APIs cannot be used due to security constraints on component specifications and naming conventions.

Method: Built a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server reproducing proprietary hardware design tool logic, created benchmark with various task types, evaluated 7 open-source models with different pipeline configurations including system prompts, tool-description detail, context scope, and single vs multi-agent architectures.

Result: Strong models achieve near-complete expected-call coverage on benchmarked workflows, but reliability depends on both task structure and agent configuration. Comprehensive tool descriptions reduce failures, few-shot prompting can cause severe inaction, cumulative context harms constrained models, and multi-agent decomposition helps weak workers or long sessions.

Conclusion: Practical guidance for deploying local LLM agents in stateful hardware design environments: careful configuration of tool descriptions, context management, and agent architecture is crucial for reliable automation.

Abstract: We ask whether AI agents powered by locally deployed large language models can reliably automate expert-defined hardware design workflows in an industry-realistic tool-calling setting. In these environments, engineers issue repetitive, dependency-ordered operations---such as creating components, adding ports, and wiring connections---through specialised tools. Confidentiality constraints on component specifications and naming conventions often preclude hosted proprietary APIs, motivating the use of locally deployed models. To study this setting, we build a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that reproduces the state and dependency logic of a proprietary hardware design tool used in embedded system development and construct a benchmark covering single-operation edits, multi-step dependency chains, invalid requests, misspelled prompts, and multi-server tool contexts. We evaluate seven open-source models comparing pipeline choices including system prompts, tool-description detail, context scope, and single-agent versus multi-agent architectures. Results show that strong models can achieve near-complete expected-call coverage on the benchmarked workflows, but reliability depends strongly on both task structure and agent configuration. Comprehensive tool descriptions consistently reduce failures, few-shot prompting can cause severe inaction for some models, cumulative context harms constrained models, and multi-agent decomposition helps weak workers or long sessions at the cost of additional calls. These findings provide practical guidance for deploying local LLM agents in stateful hardware design environments.

</details>


### [39] [GameWAM: A World Action Model for Video Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26200)
*Yuncheng Guo,Zhanqiu Zhang,Yiwen Guo,Weijia Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GameWAM is the first world-action model for closed-loop video game control that jointly predicts future visual observations and generates executable keyboard-mouse actions through parallel generative processes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing game agents lack explicit world dynamics modeling, while interactive world models predict visual futures but don't serve as task policies. World-Action Models (WAMs) that unify these objectives remain unexplored for video games' dynamics and open-ended interaction.

Method: GameWAM uses parallel visual and action generative processes with block-causal conditioning and flow matching. It predicts gameplay/GUI modes, handles heterogeneous native controls with mode-specific distributions, uses block-cycle control for long-horizon interaction, and maintains temporal continuity through hierarchical cross-cycle history.

Result: Experiments show competitive task success with fewer executed native actions than compared agents. The study also uncovers Low-Frequency Action Source Imprinting (LASI), revealing source-sensitivity failure modes in generative control.

Conclusion: GameWAM successfully demonstrates unified world-action modeling for native game control, addressing the gap between visual prediction and policy execution in video games while revealing important insights about generative control failures.

Abstract: Modern video games combine first-person perception, rapid visual changes, persistent world state, and heterogeneous native controls. Existing game agents map visual and task context directly to actions but lack explicit world dynamics modeling, whereas interactive game world models predict visual futures from supplied actions but do not serve as task policies. World-Action Models (WAMs) unify these objectives, but remain largely unexplored under the dynamics and open-ended interaction of video games. We introduce GameWAM, to our knowledge the first WAM for native closed-loop gameplay and GUI control. GameWAM jointly generates future visual observations and executable keyboard-mouse trajectories through parallel visual and action generative processes with block-causal conditioning and flow matching. To support joint world-action learning, we construct synchronized gameplay and GUI trajectories. To handle heterogeneous native control, GameWAM predicts a gameplay/GUI mode at each action step and generates actions with mode-specific prediction distributions and continuous-action normalization. For long-horizon interaction, block-cycle control predicts beyond the committed horizon, executes only a short action prefix, and replans from new observations, while fine-grained within-cycle context and hierarchical cross-cycle history preserve temporal continuity. Experiments demonstrate competitive task success with fewer executed native actions than the compared agents. We further uncover Low-Frequency Action Source Imprinting (LASI), in which low-frequency components of the sampled action source systematically steer coarse generated camera motion under fixed conditioning, revealing a source-sensitivity failure mode in generative control. Project page is available at https://yunncheng.github.io/GameWAM/.

</details>


### [40] [Same Model, Different Harness: Different Coding-Agent Results](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26218)
*Sydney Lewis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Changing a coding agent's harness (the system that controls what the model sees and can do) significantly improves performance on coding benchmarks without modifying the underlying model weights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether changing just the harness of a coding agent (while keeping the model and task fixed) changes the results, challenging the assumption that only model capabilities matter in coding agent evaluations.

Method: Compared two harness configurations on three coding benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, and FeatureBench). The control uses full conversation history in time order, while the treatment mechanically shortens older tool results as context fills and responds to repeated/stalled work. Experiments varied context windows and tested across multiple models.

Result: Under tight context windows, the treatment significantly improved performance: raising mean per-task fail-to-pass fraction (F2PF) from 28% to 49% and complete solutions from 43 to 72 on one benchmark. These improvements held across three additional models without retuning. In wide-window settings, treatment maintained higher F2PF on FeatureBench while reducing prompt tokens per turn.

Conclusion: Since changing the harness changes what unchanged model weights can accomplish, coding agent evaluations should treat the model and harness together as the tested solver, not just evaluate the model in isolation.

Abstract: A coding agent combines a model with a harness, which decides what the model sees, which tools it can use, and how the work continues. We ask whether changing the harness changes the result when the model and task stay fixed. We compare two configurations of the same harness on three coding benchmarks. The control supplies the full conversation in time order, while the treatment keeps the same record but mechanically shortens older tool results as the context fills and responds to repeated or stalled work.
  Under tight context, the treatment raises mean per-task fail-to-pass fraction (F2PF) in all three pressure comparisons and increases complete solutions on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro. The tight-window Verified comparison uses 169 tasks, a 20,480-token window, and a fixed 480-second attempt endpoint; on this cohort, treatment raises mean per-task F2PF from 28 percent to 49 percent and complete solutions from 43 to 72. Without model-specific retuning, the same frozen treatment also raises both endpoints on the same cohort for three additional models with different designs. In the wide-window Qwen3.6 comparisons, observed arm outcomes are close on Verified and Pro, while FeatureBench retains a higher mean per-task F2PF under treatment. On the wide-window Verified cohort, treatment also serves fewer prompt tokens per turn. Because changing the harness changed what unchanged model weights could accomplish, coding-agent evaluations should treat the model and harness together as the tested solver.

</details>


### [41] [LLM Agents for Time-Series: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26226)
*Yilong Chen,Xiao Qin,Chenghao Liu,Liang Wu,Noelle I. Samia,Kaize Ding*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A survey paper that organizes LLM-based agents for time-series problems using a task-oriented taxonomy instead of technical components, covering four problem categories and their design implications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based agents for time-series problems have highly varied design choices across different task settings, lacking a coherent framework for understanding how specific time-series problems influence agent design decisions.

Method: The survey adopts a problem-driven taxonomy that groups systems into four categories based on the time-series problems they address: forecasting and reasoning, augmentation and synthesis, anomaly detection and diagnosis, and decision support. It then examines how task requirements shape agent architecture, tool use, and memory design within each category.

Result: The paper provides a systematic organization of existing systems across the four categories, summarizes representative datasets and environments used in these tasks, and compares reported model performance under shared or closely related settings, offering insights into how different time-series problems influence agent design.

Conclusion: This survey offers a task-oriented guide to designing LLM-based agents for time-series problems and identifies open gaps for future research in this emerging field.

Abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly being developed for time-series problems, but their design choices vary substantially across task settings. This survey adopts a problem-driven taxonomy that organizes these systems by the time-series problems they address rather than by isolated technical components. We group existing systems into four categories: forecasting and reasoning, augmentation and synthesis, anomaly detection and diagnosis, and decision support. Within each category, we examine how task requirements shape agent architecture, tool use, and memory design. We further summarize representative datasets and environments, and compare reported model performance under shared or closely related settings. Overall, this survey offers a task-oriented guide to designing LLM-based agents for time-series problems and identifies open gaps for future work.

</details>


### [42] [The Reasoning Tax: Token Economics of LLM Reasoning Across Task Types and Deployment Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26235)
*Sachin Gopal Wani,Ajay Dholakia,David Ellison*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TES metric measures cost-effectiveness of reasoning tokens, showing reasoning should be enabled selectively by task type rather than universally.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarking focuses only on accuracy but misses deployment economics - when do extended reasoning tokens justify their cost?

Method: Introduced Token Economy Score (TES) metric measuring accuracy gain over non-reasoning baseline normalized by token multiplier; conducted empirical analysis across 151 model-benchmark runs on 7 diverse benchmarks.

Result: Task structure predicts reasoning efficiency better than difficulty: sequential inference tasks show high TES while knowledge-recall tasks show low TES; diminishing returns at higher reasoning effort; inference spend often dominated by internal thinking.

Conclusion: Reasoning should be enabled selectively by task type, effort level, and deployment context rather than as universally beneficial mode.

Abstract: Accuracy-only benchmarking of reasoning-capable large language models misses a central deployment question: when do extended thinking tokens earn their cost? We introduce the Token Economy Score (TES), a marginal benchmarking metric that measures the accuracy gain of a reasoning model over a non-reasoning baseline, normalized by the generated-token multiplier. We define paired and approximated TES variants for model families with reasoning toggles and frontier models without direct non-reasoning counterparts. We then conduct an empirical benchmarking analysis across 151 model-benchmark evaluation runs on seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, science reasoning, instruction following, expert knowledge, knowledge recall, and research-level physics. The analysis examines three deployment-facing dimensions: which task structures yield positive marginal reasoning efficiency, how increasing reasoning effort changes TES within model families, and how deployment context changes economic viability. Results show that task structure predicts reasoning efficiency better than nominal difficulty: sequential inferencechain tasks such as AIME 2025 and LiveCodeBench show high TES, while knowledge-recall tasks such as MMLU-Pro show low TES despite their difficulty. We also find systematic diminishing returns at higher reasoning effort levels, including cases where additional thinking reduces accuracy. Finally, Reasoning Cost Share (RCS) shows that inference spend is often dominated by internal thinking, while Deployment Cost Multiplier (DCM) shows how on-premises deployment can change the economics of otherwise costly reasoning workloads. These findings support a benchmarking-driven model-selection rule: enable reasoning selectively by task type, effort level, and deployment context rather than treating it as a universally beneficial mode.

</details>


### [43] [6.5% of the Neuro-Symbolic Literature Can Be Reproduced from Its Published Artifacts, a Six-Stage Audit Framework and First Instantiation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26236)
*Brandon Colelough,Vladimir Martirosyan,Ishan Tamrakar,William Regli,Aditya Kumar,Anh N. Nhu,Dhruv Dubey,Raj Ambavane,Haowei Deng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A six-stage framework for auditing scientific reproducibility in computer science, applied to neuro-symbolic AI literature, reveals severe reproducibility deficits with only 6.52% of eligible studies fully/partially reproducible, advocating for mandatory complete artifact bundles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the persistent reproducibility crisis in scientific research, particularly in computer science domains. The authors aim to quantify and understand the extent of reproducibility issues in neuro-symbolic AI (NSAI) research, moving beyond anecdotal evidence to systematic measurement.

Method: A six-stage reproducibility auditing framework: 1) record retrieval and deduplication, 2) screening and eligibility determination, 3) code artifact verification, 4) artifact inventory creation, 5) bounded rerun attempts, 6) analysis of reproduction outcomes. Applied to NSAI literature with systematic data collection from 5,497 initial records.

Result: Only 85 studies (6.52% of eligible corpus, 18.68% of attempted reruns) were fully/partially reproducible. Major blocking factors: 849/1,304 studies had no verifiable public code, 321 reruns blocked by missing non-code artifacts, 42 by missing/unusable code repositories. Shows reproducibility deficit persists despite "code available" declarations.

Conclusion: There is a severe reproducibility crisis in NSAI research that requires structural solutions. The authors advocate for requiring complete, versioned, and permanently archived artifact bundles at submission time for empirical NSAI papers, moving beyond voluntary code availability to enforced standards.

Abstract: We present a six-stage framework for auditing the reproducibility of scientific claims across a research literature within the computer science domain, and instantiate our framework for the neuro-symbolic AI (NSAI) subdomain. Instantiating the framework on the NSAI subdomain produced a multi-year audit. Stage one retrieved 5,497 records and removed 3,018 duplicates. Stage two screened the 2,479 unique records at title and abstract, identifying 1,365 self-identified NSAI records, then removed a further 61 at full text for off-topic, non-research, no-quantitative-evaluation, or inaccessible-full-text reasons. Stage three sought a verifiable public code artifact for each of the 1,304 eligible records and found none for 849, leaving 455 to enter the artifact inventory and bounded rerun of stages four and five. We fully or partially reproduced 85 studies, 6.52% of the eligible corpus and 18.68% of attempted reruns. We found that 321 attempted reruns were blocked by missing non- code artifacts and 42 by missing or unusable code repositories. These figures quantify a persistent reproducibility deficit that survives even nominal "code available" declarations, and signal the need for enforced, versioned, and permanently archived artifact bundles in future NSAI publications. We argue that empirical NSAI papers should be required at submission time to provide complete, versioned, and permanently archived artifact bundles.

</details>


### [44] [Assessing mentalization in humans and large language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26291)
*Aamir Sohail,Xintong Zhong,Arkady Konovalov,Patricia L. Lockwood,Lei Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs demonstrate mentalization abilities in economic games, with performance varying by model family/size, strategic prompting improves reasoning, and GPT-5 outperforms humans in adaptive reasoning against sophisticated opponents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether large language models can guide adaptive behavior through mentalization (inferring others' beliefs and intentions), which is a key cognitive function in human social interactions. While LLMs show theory-of-mind capabilities, their ability to use mentalization for strategic decision-making in social contexts remains unknown.

Method: Used two economic games with cognitive computational modeling to uncover latent strategies behind mentalization in LLMs. Tested 2,099 LLM agents across DeepSeek, GPT-4.1, GPT-5, and Gemini 2.0 Flash against opponents of varying sophistication. Implemented strategic prompting to elicit better reasoning. Benchmark results against 251 human participants for comparison.

Result: LLMs showed clear behavioral and computational signatures of mentalization that varied significantly by model provider and size. Strategic prompting generally improved performance by inducing more sophisticated reasoning, but benefits differed across tasks. GPT-5 agents flexibly adapted their recursive depth of reasoning to increasingly sophisticated opponents and demonstrated superior performance to human participants.

Conclusion: Different LLMs exhibit varying capacities for mentalization, with GPT-5 showing the most sophisticated and adaptive reasoning that surpasses human performance. Cognitive computational modeling provides a formal method for assessing comparative intelligence between humans and machines, revealing both capabilities and limitations in AI social cognition.

Abstract: Mentalization - the ability to infer others' beliefs and intentions to guide one's own choices - is a key cognitive function underlying human social interactions. Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate behaviour consistent with humans on theory-of-mind tasks, yet whether these models can guide adaptive behaviour through mentalization is unknown. Here we use two economic games with cognitive computational modeling to uncover the latent strategies underlying mentalization in LLMs. We tested individual LLM agents across four model families, DeepSeek, GPT-4.1, GPT-5 and Gemini 2.0 Flash (N = 2,099), against opponents of varying sophistication and examined whether a prompting strategy designed to elicit strategic reasoning improved performance. We benchmarked results against human participants (N = 251) as a comparative measure. Across both games, LLMs showed clear behavioural and computational signatures of mentalizing that differed markedly by model provider and size. Strategic prompting generally improved performance by inducing more sophisticated reasoning, yet the extent of the benefit differed across the two tasks. Last, GPT-5 agents flexibly adapted their recursive depth of reasoning to increasingly sophisticated opponents, demonstrating superior performance to human participants. Collectively, we demonstrate different capacities for mentalization across LLMs, and highlight cognitive computational modeling as a formal method for assessing comparative intelligence across humans and machines.

</details>


### [45] [Approved Too Late: Verdict Staleness in LLM-Guarded Self-Adaptive Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26306)
*Ilai Shraga,Roei Eshel,Lior Gorelik*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM guardrail approvals for self-adaptive systems can become stale between check time and use time, creating TOCTOU hazards; the paper introduces Freshness-Bounded Shield to reduce approval expiry rates and formulates freshness contracts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language model guardrails for self-adaptive systems can issue approvals that are correct at check time but become stale by actuation time, creating Execute-stage time-of-check to time-of-use hazards that compromise system safety.

Method: The paper distinguishes three quantities for verdict freshness analysis: all-candidate verdict change under fixed-action replay, oracle-labeled approval expiry on recorded closed-loop trajectories, and judge-conditioned use-time invalidity. It introduces Freshness-Bounded Shield that estimates approval validity horizons using safe-side margins and recent feature volatility without requiring explicit plant-dynamics models.

Result: Across five SAS environments, all-candidate verdict-change rates spanned 5.3-48.4% at eight simulator steps replay shift. FBS reduced oracle-labeled approval-expiry rates from 3.4-24.7% to 0-1.8% at the same shift. Audit of four LLM judges found nonzero judge-conditioned use-time invalidity in every approval stream.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates significant verdict freshness problems in LLM guardrails for SAS, introduces FBS as an effective solution to reduce approval expiry, and formulates a freshness contract requiring approvals to be both correct at check time and remain valid at use time.

Abstract: A large language model (LLM) guardrail for a self-adaptive system (SAS) may issue an approval that is correct at check time but stale by actuation. This creates an Execute-stage time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) hazard. We study verdict freshness: whether a guardrail verdict remains valid when used. We distinguish three quantities that answer different questions: all-candidate verdict change under fixed-action replay, oracle-labeled approval expiry on recorded closed-loop trajectories, and judge-conditioned use-time invalidity. Across five reproducible SAS environments, all-candidate verdict-change rates span 5.3-48.4% at a common replay shift of eight simulator steps. We introduce the Freshness-Bounded Shield (FBS), which estimates each approval's validity horizon from its safe-side margin and recent feature volatility, without an explicit plant-dynamics model. Using fixed settings documented in the artifact, FBS reduces oracle-labeled approval-expiry rates from 3.4-24.7% to 0-1.8% at the same shift. A separate audit of four LLM judges finds nonzero judge-conditioned use-time invalidity in every approval stream. We formulate a freshness contract: every approval must be correct at check time and remain valid at use time.

</details>


### [46] [FaithSieve: Fine-Grained Evaluation of Math Proofs with Faithful Formal Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26310)
*Ziyu Wang,Qiming Dai,Yishan Wu,Zaiwen Wen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FaithSieve is a Lean-assisted framework that decomposes natural-language mathematical proofs into local reasoning units, extracts typed proof obligations, and uses semantic alignment scoring to incorporate formal verification only when faithful to the original mathematical intent, significantly improving proof error localization accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models can generate complex mathematical proofs, but reliably determining their correctness and localizing early logical errors remains challenging. Existing evaluation approaches using model-based natural-language judgments often overlook local reasoning gaps, while formal theorem provers like Lean have locality and semantic mismatch issues when applied to informal text.

Method: FaithSieve decomposes coarse proof steps into local reasoning units, extracts typed proof obligations, and verifies them through a formal evaluation agent. The framework uses semantic alignment scoring to gate formal validation, incorporating Lean evidence only when the formal statement faithfully preserves the original claim's context, objects, and logical form.

Result: On the 350-problem ProofLoc-Olympiad dataset, FaithSieve with GPT-5.4 backbone achieved 81.43% exact first-error accuracy (vs 72.29% baseline). On the 200-problem ProofLoc-University benchmark across six advanced domains, it reached 84.5% exact accuracy (vs 75.0% baseline).

Conclusion: Decomposing proofs into fine-grained units and grounding them with faithful formal evidence significantly improves reliable evaluation of natural-language reasoning, addressing both locality and semantic alignment challenges in mathematical proof verification.

Abstract: Large language models can now generate complex, multi-step mathematical proofs, but reliably determining their correctness and localizing early logical errors remains a critical challenge. Existing evaluation approaches largely depend on model-based natural-language judgments, which often overlook local reasoning gaps. While formal theorem provers like Lean offer a path to rigorous verification, using them to evaluate informal text requires solving locality and semantic mismatches: a prover might bypass a local flaw by proving an overly broad target, or validate an auto-formalized statement that drifts from the original mathematical intent. To address this, we introduce FaithSieve, a Lean-assisted framework for fine-grained evaluation of natural-language mathematical proofs. FaithSieve decomposes coarse proof steps into local reasoning units, extracts typed proof obligations, and verifies them through a formal evaluation agent. Formal validation is gated by semantic alignment scoring, so Lean evidence is incorporated only when the formal statement faithfully preserves the context, objects, and logical form of the original claim. We construct two expert-verified datasets, ProofLoc-Olympiad and ProofLoc-University, to benchmark first-error localization. On the 350-problem Olympiad dataset, FaithSieve using a GPT-5.4 backbone achieves 81.43% exact first-error accuracy, outperforming the direct-judging baseline of 72.29%. Furthermore, on the 200-problem ProofLoc-University benchmark spanning six advanced domains, FaithSieve reaches 84.5% exact accuracy, compared to 75.0% for the direct judge. Our work demonstrates that decomposing proofs into fine-grained units and grounding them with faithful formal evidence significantly improves reliable evaluation of natural-language reasoning.

</details>


### [47] [ProofEvolve: Neuro-Symbolic Evolution for Formal Automated Theorem Proving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26334)
*Wenqian Ye,Ziwei Guan,Eric Xie,Bohan Liu,Shivani Modi,Buyun Zhang,Ellie Dingqiao Wen,Henry Kautz,Aidong Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ProofEvolve is a neuro-symbolic framework that evolves verified proof structures using neural models to propose variations and symbolic verification, achieving state-of-the-art performance on Lean theorem proving benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing neural theorem provers don't fully preserve recursive self-improvement structure for scientific discovery. They either use expensive weight updates or keep verified deductions only within current problems, relying on sparse whole-proof feedback while ignoring useful discoveries from unsuccessful partial attempts.

Method: ProofEvolve evolves explicit, formally verified symbolic proof structures using neural models to propose variation operators (decompositions, repairs, schema recombinations). The symbolic Lean kernel verifies every proof transition. It builds AND-OR proof DAGs within problems in a behaviorally indexed archive and maintains a persistent schema library across problems through kernel-checked schema extraction.

Result: ProofEvolve achieves the highest average solve rate among evaluated proof systems across three competition-level Lean benchmarks, demonstrating superior performance in automated theorem proving.

Conclusion: ProofEvolve successfully bridges the gap for recursive self-improvement in theorem proving by evolving verified proof structures that preserve discoveries from incomplete attempts while maintaining formal soundness, enabling effective knowledge transfer across problems.

Abstract: Automated theorem proving offers a natural foundation for recursive self-improvement in scientific discovery. However, existing neural provers do not fully preserve this recursive structure, where the learning process should be self-improving over time. Existing methods either embed proof experience into model parameters through expensive weight updates, or keep verified intermediate deductions only within the current problem. In addition, these methods also heavily rely on sparse whole-proof feedback, even when unsuccessful partial attempts contain useful discoveries. To close the gap, we propose ProofEvolve, a neuro-symbolic framework that evolves explicit, formally verified symbolic proof structures with neural models to decisively expand the knowledge boundary. In this framework, the neural model proposes variation operators, including decompositions, repairs, and schema recombinations. The symbolic Lean kernel verifies every proof transition. Over the evolution loops, ProofEvolve computes verified closure over the resulting proof directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Within each problem, ProofEvolve evolves partial AND-OR proof DAGs in a behaviorally indexed archive. Across problems, kernel-checked schema extraction adds newly proved sub-DAGs to a persistent schema library. Proof DAGs inherit the solved results through typed schema recombination, with every residual premise exposed as a new subgoal. This evolutionary process preserves verified results from incomplete attempts and makes them available for later proofs without weakening formal soundness. Across three competition-level Lean benchmarks, ProofEvolve achieves the highest average solve rate among the evaluated proof systems.

</details>


### [48] [Fine-Tuning of Transformer models with Frames](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26430)
*Harshavardhan Adepu,Li Zhang,Sanjiv Kumar,Vikas Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FrameFT is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that models weight updates using sparse coefficients in Fusion Frame bases, achieving state-of-the-art performance with significantly fewer trainable parameters than existing PEFT methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing PEFT methods like LoRA have memory requirements that scale with model size (O(dr)), which can be problematic for large-scale models. There's a need for more efficient fine-tuning methods that maintain performance while reducing memory footprint.

Method: FrameFT models parameter updates (ΔW) using sparse coefficient matrices in a Fusion Frame basis. Fusion Frames can be generated algorithmically and shared across model layers. Only sparse coefficients of the basis expansion are stored and optimized, and the sparsity structure provides computational benefits. The approach includes formal convergence analysis.

Result: FrameFT achieves performance on par with or exceeding state-of-the-art PEFT techniques while requiring far fewer trainable parameters. It was evaluated across supervised fine-tuning benchmarks (primarily language tasks, with some vision model applications).

Conclusion: FrameFT presents an efficient alternative to existing PEFT methods, offering both memory efficiency and computational benefits through its sparse Fusion Frame approach, while maintaining or improving performance compared to current state-of-the-art techniques.

Abstract: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) strategies such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) are effective solutions for fine-tuning large-scale pre-trained models; however, their memory requirements scale with the size of the model, $\mathcal{O}(dr)$, where $d$ is the model's hidden dimension and $r$ is the rank. Our proposal, FrameFT, models the parameter update $ΔW$ with a sparse coefficient matrix in a Fusion Frame basis. Fusion Frames can be generated algorithmically and shared across model layers, enabling very efficient updates. Only the sparse coefficients of the basis expansion are stored/optimized, reducing the memory footprint. The sparse structure of the coefficient matrix in FrameFT and the sparsity in the Fusion Frames give large compute benefits, and our analysis provides formal convergence results. We evaluate the idea across a suite of supervised fine-tuning benchmarks, focusing on language tasks, but also report application to vision models. Our experiments show that FrameFT achieves performance on par with/exceeding state-of-the-art PEFT techniques, but needs far fewer trainable parameters.

</details>


### [49] [Don't Overthink, Don't Underthink: Toward Adaptive Reasoning in Agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26442)
*Md Jueal Mia,M. Hadi Amini*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs need adaptive reasoning allocation in agentic AI systems to prevent over-reasoning (excessive computation without accuracy gains) and under-reasoning (incomplete solutions), as current fixed reasoning controls fail to match dynamic task demands.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM reasoning approaches use fixed or preallocated controls (fixed token budgets, difficulty estimates) that don't adapt to dynamic agentic workflows involving planning, tool use, memory retrieval, and agent interactions. This leads to misallocated reasoning causing either excessive computation or incomplete solutions.

Method: Characterized over-reasoning and under-reasoning as failure modes and evaluated them on MATH-500 and GAIA benchmarks using metrics like tool-decision latency, token consumption, token-limit exhaustion, and answer correctness.

Result: Over-reasoning cases showed higher computational cost without proportional accuracy gains, while under-reasoning cases consistently produced incorrect or incomplete solutions. Both failure modes demonstrate the limitations of current fixed reasoning controls.

Conclusion: Next-generation agentic AI requires adaptive reasoning mechanisms that allocate reasoning according to evolving task demands rather than fixed controls, as misallocated reasoning in dynamic workflows causes unnecessary computation, latency, planning drift, and incomplete solutions.

Abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown that increased inference-time reasoning can improve performance on complex tasks. However, many existing approaches rely on fixed or preallocated reasoning controls, such as fixed token budgets, pre-execution difficulty estimates, or activation-space interventions, and are often evaluated on standalone reasoning benchmarks rather than full agentic workflows. These assumptions may not hold in agentic AI systems, where reasoning requirements evolve dynamically through planning, tool use, memory retrieval, and agent-to-agent interactions. Consequently, reasoning can become either excessive or insufficient, resulting in unnecessary computation, increased latency, planning drift, excessive tool use, or incomplete solutions. We argue that a major challenge for next-generation agentic AI is not merely how much reasoning a language model should perform, but how it should allocate reasoning according to evolving task demands. We characterize over-reasoning and under-reasoning as recurring failure modes of misallocated reasoning and evaluate them on MATH-500 and the GAIA public validation benchmark. Using tool-decision latency, token consumption, token-limit exhaustion, and answer correctness, our results suggest that cases classified as over-reasoning are associated with higher computational cost without proportional accuracy gains, whereas cases classified as under-reasoning are consistently associated with incorrect or incomplete solutions. These findings motivate future research on adaptive reasoning mechanisms for agentic AI.

</details>


### [50] [PILOT in the Loop: Live Self-Improvement for Long-Horizon Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26530)
*Yang Xiao,Yusong Sun,Haoyi Wu,Wenyang Hui,Wen Da,Zhaokai Luo,Mu Chuan,Yao Hu,Wenjie Li,Chengyue Jiang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PILOT is a supervisor-worker harness that enables live self-improvement in AI agents through real-time steering and skill distillation during execution, significantly improving performance while reducing computational cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current self-improvement methods process agent experience only after execution ends, preventing real-time redirection and immediate application of lessons learned. Existing architectures either combine execution and assessment in one context (limiting separation) or delegate to subagents without ability to redirect them during execution.

Method: PILOT introduces a supervisor-worker harness with two coupled mechanisms: (1) live steering - allows a separate supervisor to redirect or abort the active worker during execution; (2) live self-evolution - distills procedures and failure modes discovered during execution into reusable skills and memory.

Result: Across two frozen backbones and three benchmarks, PILOT ranked first in 5 of 6 configurations. On Terminal-Bench 2.0, it outperformed counterpart harnesses by up to 9.8 percentage points. In self-improvement settings, PILOT gained 14.6 points with GLM-5.1 and 12.4 points with Kimi-K2.6, reducing mean output tokens by 42.9-47.4% and increasing successful evaluations per million output tokens by 110.3-134.0%.

Conclusion: PILOT successfully demonstrates that live self-improvement through supervisor-worker architecture with real-time steering and skill distillation significantly enhances agent performance and efficiency compared to post-hoc self-improvement approaches.
