### [76] [Omni-Interactive Universal Embedder](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27044)
*Wei-Yao Wang,Kazuya Tateishi,Shuyang Cui,Christian Simon,Takashi Shibuya,Shusuke Takahashi,Yuki Mitsufuji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OmniUE is the first universal embedder that supports omni-modal interactions (text, video, audio) with user-conditioned querying using visual regions and audio spans, achieving state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multimodal representation learning focuses mainly on language and image modalities, with limited support for diverse user interactions. There's a need for universal embedders that can handle multiple modalities (text, video, audio) and allow various interactive querying methods beyond simple text prompts.

Method: Proposes OmniUE which uses dedicated learnable tokens to create a unified embedding space across text, video, and audio. It features visual and audio segmenters to process diverse user interactions (text, visual regions, audio spans), integrated with an omni-LLM to produce user-conditioned any-to-any embeddings through context aggregation. Also introduces OmniCHOIR benchmark for evaluation.

Result: OmniUE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across modalities: 10.5% improvement on textual-interactive video benchmarks (MMEB-v2-video), 1.1% on audio tasks (MAEB), 83.7% on visual-interactive benchmarks (SCaR), and 24.1% on the new omni-interactive OmniCHOIR benchmark.

Conclusion: Joint advancement of omni-modal representation learning and omni-interactive querying represents a significant step toward developing universal embedders capable of handling diverse modalities and complex user interactions in a unified framework.

Abstract: Multimodal representation learning has been shifting from traditional two-tower architectures to large language model (LLM)-based embedders due to their strong instruction-following capabilities. Despite this progress, existing approaches primarily focus on language and image modalities, which also remain the dominant modalities for user-conditioned interactions in current embedders. In this paper, we propose the first Omni-Interactive Universal Embedder (OmniUE), which not only learns a unified embedding space across text, video, and audio by leveraging intermediate-layer representations from dedicated learnable tokens, but also supports omni-interactive querying, enabling users to provide inputs in the form of text, visual regions of interest, and audio spans. Within OmniUE, visual and audio segmenters process diverse user interactions and integrate them with an omni-LLM to produce user-conditioned any-to-any embeddings via context aggregation. To evaluate OmniUE's omni-interactive capabilities, we introduce OmniCHOIR, benchmarking models for omni-interactive compositional audio retrieval based on the given text, video, and audio as well as unimodal or multimodal interaction prompts. OmniUE consistently surpasses state-of-the-art baselines across diverse modalities, with average improvements of 10.5% on textual-interactive video benchmarks (MMEB-v2-video), 1.1% on audio tasks (MAEB), 83.7% on visual-interactive benchmarks (SCaR), and 24.1% on our omni-interactive OmniCHOIR benchmark. We believe that jointly advancing omni-modal representation learning and omni-interactive querying paves the way toward universal embedders.

</details>


### [77] [pro-team at LLMs4OL 2026 Tasks Flagship and Reuse: Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Vocabulary-Constrained Filtering for Ontology Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27101)
*Shivam Mishra,Dhannu Ram Meena,Muneendra Ojha,Krishna Pratap Singh,Kuldeep Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A retrieval-augmented few-shot prompting approach using Qwen2.5-14B with demonstration retrieval for ontology learning tasks, achieving strong results on taxonomic relations but failing to extract non-taxonomic relations due to vocabulary constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address challenges in ontology learning from text where LLMs hallucinate domain terms, produce inconsistent formats, and favor hierarchical over associative relations, despite LLM advancements.

Method: Offline retrieval-augmented few-shot prompting pipeline with Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct using all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for demonstration retrieval (top-5 for Task A, top-2 for Task B), left-truncated context-windowing, and deterministic vocabulary-constrained filtering for Task B.

Result: Task B achieved Semantic Graph Similarity 0.8692, Term-Typing F1 0.9200, Taxonomy Discovery F1 0.8540. Task A achieved Semantic Graph Similarity 0.7416. No non-taxonomic relations were extracted.

Conclusion: The approach shows effectiveness for taxonomic ontology learning but reveals limitations of closed, taxonomy-oriented relation vocabularies in extracting associative relations, highlighting need for more comprehensive relation extraction methods.

Abstract: Ontology learning from text remains challenging despite significant progress in Large Language Models (LLMs), which can hallucinate domain terms, produce inconsistent formats, and favor hierarchical over associative relations. In the LLMs4OL 2026 Challenge, we address both the End-to-End Flagship Task (Task A) and Ontology Extension Reuse Task (Task B) using an offline retrieval-augmented few-shot prompting pipeline. Our system employs Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for demonstration retrieval, selecting the top-5 examples for Task A and top-2 for Task B. A left-truncated context-windowing strategy preserves task instructions within long prompts. For Task B, generated triples undergo deterministic vocabulary-constrained filtering, retaining triples when at least one endpoint belongs to the sample's closed term/type vocabulary and removing duplicates of the initial ontology. The approach achieves Semantic Graph Similarity of 0.8692, Term-Typing F1 of 0.9200, and Taxonomy Discovery F1 of 0.8540 on Task B, while Task A achieves 0.7416 Semantic Graph Similarity. However, no non-taxonomic relations are extracted, highlighting limitations of closed, taxonomy-oriented relation vocabularies.

</details>


### [78] [LAAF: A Layered Accountability Architecture Framework for LLM Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27102)
*Prachi Chaturvedi,Shahnawaz Ahmad,Ehsan Nowroozi,Muhammad Waqas,George Loukas,Alireza Jolfaei,Lucas Cordeiro,Pierre Dantas*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A systematic review analyzing accountability mechanisms for LLMs in high-risk settings, synthesizing technical, human, organizational, and documentation approaches, mapping them to regulatory frameworks, and identifying persistent gaps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in high-stakes environments like healthcare, finance, and legal systems where their confident outputs can cause harm when ungrounded or incorrect, raising critical questions about accountability and responsibility allocation.

Method: Following PRISMA guidelines, conducted systematic review of 4,512 records (122 primary studies + 12 regulatory documents) from Jan 2022 to Mar 2026. Developed sociotechnical accountability framework with five dimensions and synthesized mechanisms across four families with maturity assessments.

Result: Consolidated a four-layer classification device spanning provenance, application logic, human oversight, and governance/redress, cross-cut by traceability, role clarity, and continuous monitoring. Identified four persistent gaps (under-specified human oversight, missing accountability metrics, disciplinary disconnection, limited empirical evaluation) and five unresolved structural tensions.

Conclusion: Proposes LAAF integrated accountability architecture with cybersecurity aligned to OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025) as synthesis of evidence, noting it remains an unvalidated conceptual framework. Highlights the need for better-specified human oversight mechanisms, standardized accountability metrics, interdisciplinary integration, and empirical validation to address accountability challenges.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) operate in hospitals, courtrooms, banks, and public service desks, where fluent, confident outputs are treated as authoritative even when ungrounded or incorrect. When such an output contributes to harm, who is answerable, and through what mechanisms can responsibility be traced, explained, and acted upon? Following PRISMA guidance, five databases were searched from January 2022 to March 2026 against four review questions; of 4,512 records identified, 122 primary studies were included, together with 12 regulatory and standards documents analysed as primary sources. The review consolidates a sociotechnical account of accountability as an actor-forum relation resolved into five dimensions, and synthesises mechanisms across four families: technical controls, human oversight, organisational governance, and documentation and traceability, each with a maturity assessment. The corpus is read through a four-layer classification device spanning provenance, application logic, human oversight, and governance and redress, cross-cut by traceability, role clarity, and continuous monitoring. Both are mapped onto the EU AI Act, whose high-risk obligations have applied since 2 August 2026, the NIST AI RMF with its Generative AI Profile, ISO/IEC 42001, and sectoral guidance in healthcare, consumer finance, education, and the public sector. Four persistent gaps emerge: under-specification of human oversight, absence of shared accountability metrics, disciplinary disconnection, and limited empirical evaluation, alongside five structural tensions that no surveyed instrument resolves. The review closes by consolidating the classification device into an integrated accountability architecture, LAAF, with cybersecurity aligned to the OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025); it is a synthesis of the surveyed evidence rather than a validated artefact.

</details>


### [79] [TransMeme: A Multi-Agent Framework for Cross-Cultural Meme Transcreation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27127)
*Jingyi Zheng,Yule Liu,Zifan Peng,Tianyi Hu,Yuemeng Zhao,Xinhu Zheng,Xinlei He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a multi-agent framework for cross-cultural meme transcreation that outperforms baselines by addressing cultural adaptation, multimodal consistency, and intent preservation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Internet memes are pervasive multimodal communication that often involves users from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds, but current methods struggle with adapting memes across cultures while preserving communicative intent, cultural meaning, and text-image coherence.

Method: The authors propose a multi-agent framework with specialized agents coordinated to address three core challenges: cultural adaptation, target text rewriting, revision, and conditional visual adjustment. The framework uses coordinated feedback to handle difficult cases requiring deeper cultural or visual intervention.

Result: The method outperforms all baselines on bidirectional Chinese-English meme transcreation. In human evaluation, it achieves 33.1% average improvement over the strongest baseline across four dimensions. In LLM-as-a-Judge, it attains 60% Top-1 ranking rate versus 26% for the second-best baseline.

Conclusion: The multi-agent framework effectively addresses cross-cultural meme transcreation challenges, though remaining bottlenecks exist in humor reconstruction and image-text alignment, pointing to future work on humor transfer rather than simple cultural knowledge gaps.

Abstract: Internet memes are a pervasive form of multimodal online communication; however, such communication often involves users from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds. Therefore, adapting memes across cultures and languages is a central challenge for enabling mutual understanding in online communication. Unlike ordinary translation or standalone text rewriting, cross-cultural meme transcreation must jointly preserve communicative intent, adapt culture-dependent meaning for the target audience, and maintain coherence between text and image. In this work, we first provide an explicit task analysis of cross-cultural meme transcreation and identify three core challenges: culture-specific knowledge understanding, intent and tone preservation, and multimodal consistency. Based on this analysis, we propose a multi-agent framework with specialized agents that are coordinated to address these challenges through cultural adaptation, target text rewriting, revision, and conditional visual adjustment. The framework strengthens target text adaptation with coordinated feedback to handle difficult cases that require deeper cultural or visual intervention. We evaluate the framework on bidirectional Chinese-English meme transcreation using both human evaluation and LLM-as-a-Judge. Our method consistently outperforms all baselines across both evaluation settings. In human evaluation, it achieves the best performance on all four dimensions and delivers a 33.1% average improvement over the strongest baseline, while in LLM-as-a-Judge, it attains the highest Top-1 ranking rate (60% versus 26% for the second-best baseline). Further analysis indicates that each component contributes to the performance. Our error analysis suggests that the remaining bottlenecks lie in humor reconstruction and image-text alignment rather than simple cultural knowledge gaps, pointing to future work on humor transfer.

</details>


### [80] [GRAIN: Bridging Name and Narrative Shifts in Real-World Graph Reasoning through Invariance-Rewarded Agentic RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27142)
*Zike Yuan,Han Zhang,Jianzhi Yan,Le Liu,Cai Ke,Huozhi Zhou,Jian Xie,Jiran Yin,Yukun Cao,Yue Yu,Hui Wang,Ming Liu,Bing Qin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GRAIN: A single-agent LLM framework using reinforcement learning with Structure Invariance Reward to make graph reasoning robust to linguistic shifts, outperforming multi-agent systems in accuracy and latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are brittle to real-world shifts in node identifiers and task formulations for graph tasks, while deterministic graph tools are invariant to such shifts. Multi-agent systems to mitigate parsing failures incur prohibitive latency, creating a need for a more efficient solution.

Method: GRAIN is a single-agent framework optimized via reinforcement learning that models reasoning as a semantic parsing and tool-execution pipeline. It uses a Structure Invariance Reward that validates extracted intermediate graphs against ground-truth topologies to force the LLM to learn robust text-to-structure mappings rather than memorizing linguistic artifacts. Also introduces GRIT benchmark for evaluating sensitivity to linguistic shifts.

Result: GRAIN outperforms multi-agent baselines by 16.45% in accuracy with approximately 24% lower latency. Shows superior structural generalization, halving the OOD gap of SFT models (from 15.77% to 7.80%) and maintaining robustness on large-scale graphs beyond training distribution.

Conclusion: GRAIN effectively addresses LLMs' brittleness to linguistic shifts in graph reasoning through reinforcement learning with structure invariance rewards, providing a more efficient and robust alternative to multi-agent systems while improving generalization to out-of-distribution graphs.

Abstract: Despite their potential in standardized graph tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) remain brittle to real-world shifts in node identifiers and task formulation. While deterministic graph tools are invariant to such shifts, extracting topological structures from noisy text is highly fragile for LLMs, which often overfit to surface patterns. Moreover, mitigating these parsing failures via multi-agent systems incurs prohibitive latency. To address this, we propose GRAIN, a single-agent framework optimized via reinforcement learning. GRAIN models reasoning as a semantic parsing and tool-execution pipeline, guided by a Structure Invariance Reward. By validating extracted intermediate graphs against ground-truth topologies, this reward forces the LLM to learn robust text-to-structure mappings rather than memorizing linguistic artifacts. We also introduce GRIT, a benchmark evaluating sensitivity to such linguistic shifts. GRAIN outperforms multi-agent baselines by 16.45\% in accuracy with approximately 24\% lower latency. Furthermore, it demonstrates superior structural generalization, halving the out-of-distribution (OOD) gap of SFT models (from 15.77\% to 7.80\%) and maintaining robustness on large-scale graphs beyond the training distribution.

</details>


### [81] [Feature Transformation Enhanced Jacobi Polynomial Graph Filtering for Graph Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27144)
*Xiang Wang,Zhijun Cheng,Zhenyu Meng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: JPGFN is a novel graph anomaly detection method using adaptive Jacobi polynomial graph filtering with feature transformation and label constraints, outperforming existing approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph anomaly detection methods based on frequency-domain filtering face three challenges: 1) static basic functions for graph filters that don't adapt to data frequency distribution, 2) inadequate consideration of attribute importance in node features leading to fine-grained information loss, and 3) insufficient utilization of node labels for anomaly detection.

Method: JPGFN has three main components: 1) Feature Separation Transformation Network (FSTNN) that learns fine-grained node features through feature separation and nonlinear transformations across dimensions, 2) adaptive Jacobi polynomial graph filtering module using Jacobi polynomials to capture complex frequency-domain features adaptively, and 3) node label constraint module to facilitate use of node labels and enhance detection performance.

Result: Experimental results on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms mainstream graph anomaly detection approaches.

Conclusion: JPGFN effectively addresses the three major challenges in existing graph anomaly detection methods by combining feature transformation, adaptive frequency-domain filtering, and label constraints, achieving superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Abstract: In recent years, graph anomaly detection (GAD) based on frequency-domain filtering have achieved promising results. However, existing approaches still face three major challenges: First, they use static basic function to constructed graph filter which cannot effectively adapt to the frequency-domain distribution of graph data. Second, they fail to adequately consider the importance information of each attribute in the node feature vector, leading to the loss of fine-grained information. Third, they insufficiently utilize node labels for GAD. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel graph anomaly detection method called JPGFN (Feature Transformation Enhanced Jacobi Polynomial Graph Filtering Network). First, a Feature Separation Transformation Network (FSTNN) is developed to better learn fine-grained node features by feature separation and applying nonlinear transformations to node features across different dimensions. Second, an adaptive Jacobi polynomial graph filtering module is constructed based on Jacobi polynomials to adaptively capture complex frequency-domain features of graph signals. Finally, a node label constraint module is developed to facilitate the use of node labels and enhance the performance of GAD. Experimental results on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms mainstream approaches.

</details>


### [82] [LLMs Can Design Near-Optimal OR Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27296)
*Jackie Baek*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Frontier LLMs like GPT-5.6-Sol can design competitive algorithms for operations research problems with minimal human input, matching or beating specialized methods even when generating general algorithms without seeing specific instances.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether large language models can effectively design algorithms for well-specified operations research problems, particularly examining if LLMs can go beyond solving single instances to generating general algorithms that work across parameter ranges.

Method: The study tests two levels of LLM usage: Level 1 - model receives a single problem instance and returns a solution; Level 2 - model receives only problem class description and parameter ranges, returning an algorithm that maps parameters to solutions. Using minimal human input (one untuned prompt) with Python sandbox access and fixed compute budget, evaluated on inventory control, queueing network control, and assortment optimization.

Result: GPT-5.6-Sol matches or outperforms best existing methods on almost all evaluated instances, even at Level 2 where algorithms are fixed before seeing evaluation instances. Performance improves sharply across models released within 8 months, suggesting rapid capability development.

Conclusion: Frontier LLMs can produce algorithms competitive with specialized methods for well-specified OR problems with minimal prompting, suggesting they can serve as serious empirical baselines for algorithm design in this domain.

Abstract: We ask whether large language models (LLMs) can design effective algorithms for well-specified operations research (OR) problems. We study inventory control, queueing network control, and assortment optimization. We evaluate two levels of LLM use: at level 1, the model receives one problem instance and returns a solution for that instance; at level 2, it receives only the problem class description and broad parameter ranges, and returns an algorithm that maps instance parameters to solutions. Human input is minimal: we give one untuned prompt that describes the problem, and the model has access to a Python sandbox tool with a fixed compute budget.
  The strongest model we test, gpt-5.6-sol, matches or outperforms the best existing method on almost all evaluated instances. This holds even at level 2, where the returned algorithm is fixed before seeing the evaluation instances. Performance also improves sharply across models released less than eight months apart, suggesting that this capability is moving quickly. Thus, for the well-specified operations problems we study, a single untuned LLM query can already produce algorithms competitive with specialized methods. These results suggest that frontier LLMs can be a serious empirical baseline for algorithm design in well-specified OR problems.

</details>


### [83] [When Tool Outputs Become Commands: Separating Action Induction from Runtime Authorization in Tool-Augmented LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27146)
*Xiaokun Guo,Zhen Xu,Dongdong Huo,Yanqiu Zhang,Wei Wang,Qinfu Yang,Dongjin Yu,Yu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SARA is a safety framework that separates action induction from execution authorization in tool-augmented LLM agents, preventing malicious tool outputs from executing unauthorized actions while maintaining task utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tool-augmented LLM agents rely on untrusted runtime observations that can become dangerous "commands" when tool outputs specify concrete actions with real-world side effects beyond user intent. Current systems conflate action induction with execution authorization, creating security risks where malicious tool outputs can trigger unauthorized actions.

Method: SARA treats action induction and execution authorization as distinct runtime roles and separates action provenance from execution authority. It uses: 1) A context-isolated Action Probe that exposes action-inducing semantics and records action-origin provenance across steps; 2) Execution authorization that only allows tool calls against user objectives with audited evidence from authorized successful executions; 3) No-History-Promotion to prevent historical recurrence from laundering action origins into execution authority across multi-step execution.

Result: SARA achieves strong security performance with Attack Success Rate (ASR) limited to no more than 0.63% across four primary evaluation settings on AgentDojo and AgentDyn benchmarks while maintaining competitive task utility. The framework consistently reduces ASR across additional agent backbones.

Conclusion: Separating action induction from execution authorization is crucial for safe tool-augmented LLM agents. SARA effectively mitigates security risks from malicious tool outputs by maintaining clear provenance tracking and preventing action laundering, enabling both safety and utility in open-ended agent tasks.

Abstract: Tool-augmented LLM agents must rely on untrusted runtime Observations to complete open-ended tasks; however, when tool outputs no longer merely provide data but begin to specify concrete actions, they effectively become ``commands'' that can drive real-world side effects beyond user intent. We argue that this risk arises from conflating action induction with execution authorization. To address this distinction, we propose SARA, which treats action induction and execution authorization as distinct runtime roles and separates action provenance from execution authority. On the Observation side, a context-isolated Action Probe exposes action-inducing semantics and persistently records action-origin provenance across steps as a review signal; on the execution side, actual tool calls are authorized only against the user objective and audited evidence from authorized successful executions, while satisfying goal, execution-chain, and argument-level support. To preserve this separation across multi-step execution, SARA applies No-History-Promotion to prevent historical recurrence from laundering action origins into execution authority. Across AgentDojo and AgentDyn, SARA limits ASR to no more than \(0.63\%\) across four primary evaluation settings while maintaining competitive task utility, and consistently reduces ASR across additional Agent backbones.

</details>


### [84] [CorporateBench: Large-Scale Q&A Benchmarking with Temporal Knowledge Bases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27391)
*Sil Hamilton,Albert Yu Sun,Oscar J. Romero,Carl-Leander Henneking,David Mimno,Bishan Yang,Igor Labutov*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CorporateBench (CB) is a human-validated multi-task Q&A benchmark for evaluating LLMs on enterprise-scale document collections, featuring corpora up to 230,000+ documents from synthetic firms of 12-10,000 employees with cross-document consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There's a critical gap in evaluating LLMs for enterprise document analysis: companies can't share sensitive internal communications, and existing synthetic datasets are too simplistic to capture real-world complexity and scale.

Method: Created CorporateBench with human-validated multi-task Q&A across four synthetically generated firms (12-10,000 employees) sampled from temporally evolving knowledge bases. The benchmark evaluates LLMs on information extraction and knowledge base querying with corpora up to 230,000+ documents that maintain cross-document logical consistency.

Result: Evaluation of five LLMs on CB reveals progressively worse performance as input size approaches realistic corporate scales. The benchmark successfully measures corporate communication reasoning at enterprise-relevant document volumes.

Conclusion: CorporateBench fills a crucial gap in the benchmarking ecosystem by providing LLM developers with a metric for evaluating corporate communication reasoning at realistic enterprise scales, where performance deteriorates significantly as document volume increases.

Abstract: LLMs are increasingly able to answer complex questions about enterprise-scale document collections. But evaluation is hard: companies don't want to share internal communications, and synthetic datasets have been overly simple. We present CorporateBench (CB), a human-validated multi-task Q&A benchmark whose scale approaches the conditions LLMs encounter in corporate communication networks, with evaluation corpora surpassing 230,000 documents. CB evaluates LLMs across two dimensions (information extraction and knowledge base querying) through four synthetically generated firms ranging from 12 to 10,000 employees. Each corpus is sampled from a temporally evolving knowledge base describing a consistent world, guaranteeing cross-document logical consistency even across hundreds of thousands of documents. We evaluate five LLMs on CB, revealing increasingly poor performance as input size approaches realistic scales. CB provides LLM developers a metric for corporate communication reasoning, filling a crucial gap in the benchmarking ecosystem.

</details>


### [85] [Thomson: Continual Learning of Frontier Models for SovereignAI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27147)
*Shengzhuang Chen,Jerrod Parker,Yejin Bang,Andrew M. Bean,Nabeel Seedat,Stefan Winzeck,Daniil Glazko,Jannik Zgraggen,Fangyi Yu,Scott Arnott,Dietrich Trautmann,Luca Ciuffreda,Guglielmo Bonifazi,Davide Romano,Bradley Bell,Kirsty Fielding,Daniele Giofrè,Tom Zielund,Ipshita Chatterjee,Sneha Murthy Ghantasala,Manpreet Nanreh,John Scoville,Maciej Sakowicz,Wassim Seifeddine,Lukas Thede,Jonathan Richard Schwarz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Frontier AI models can be developed by diverse institutions through Continual Learning on open-weight models, achieving competitive performance at lower costs than commonly believed, enabling more organizations to achieve SovereignAI capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There's a significant power asymmetry in AI development where only a few heavily funded players can build frontier models, creating dependency and limiting diverse organizations' ability to independently develop, deploy, and govern AI (SovereignAI). Current discourse acknowledges this problem but lacks concrete solutions for diverse funding settings.

Method: Proposes Continual Learning on readily available open-weight models, using a modern mid- & post-training stack with safeguards that preserve both plasticity and stability. This approach makes minimal high-impact parameter interventions, unlike limited approaches like small-scale fine-tuning, prompt engineering, or tool-augmentation of frozen models.

Result: Demonstrated with Thomson, a general-purpose frontier model focused on high-stakes professional work. Thomson performs competitively with recent frontier models across agentic tasks, safety, legal, tax, multilingualism, and large-scale Deep Research. Shows distinctive π-shaped pattern: broad capability improvements including those not explicitly targeted, while almost completely eliminating the forgetting problem common to narrow domain adaptation.

Conclusion: Frontier performance is achievable by a wide range of institutions through Continual Learning on open-weight models, at substantially lower compute and personnel budgets than commonly thought. This makes ownership of large parts of the SovereignAI stack (model, tool infrastructure, values & data privacy) viable for far more actors, democratizing access to frontier AI capabilities.

Abstract: The development of frontier models is commonly perceived to be the exclusive remit of a small number of heavily funded players, creating an information, economic and power asymmetry between developers and the diverse user base of modern AI. Recent public discourse acknowledges this concern, calling for SovereignAI (an organisation's capability to independently build, deploy and govern AI use), but offers little concrete advice on how this can be achieved in the short term under a diversity of funding settings. We argue that frontier performance is achievable by a wide range of institutions through Continual Learning on readily available open-weight models. Unlike limited approaches such as small-scale fine-tuning, prompt engineering, or tool-augmentation of a frozen model, our approach exploits a modern mid- & post-training stack while introducing safeguards that preserve both plasticity and stability at each stage, making the minimal number of high-impact interventions on the parameters. This yields gains comparable to those typically seen across multiple successive model generations, at compute and personnel budgets substantially lower than commonly thought, making ownership of large parts of the SovereignAI stack (model, tool infrastructure, values & data privacy) viable for far more actors. We demonstrate this with Thomson, a general-purpose frontier model trained with an enhanced focus on high-stakes professional work. Thomson performs competitively with recent frontier models across agentic tasks, safety, legal, tax & multilingualism, and large-scale Deep Research. Evaluations show a distinctive $π$-shaped pattern: distinct improvements across a wide range of capabilities, including those not explicitly targeted, while almost completely eliminating the forgetting problem common to narrow domain adaptation.

</details>


### [86] [Learning a Continuous Sepsis Severity Score Without Hour-by-Hour Supervision: A Two-Site Retrospective Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27421)
*Kevin Zhu,Ryan Zhang,Baraa Abed,Tilendra Choudhary,Malvern Madondo,Mehak Arora,Yixuan Yang,Alasdair Gent,Aditya Nagori,Omer T. Inan,Krista L. Haines,Patrick Georgoff,Suresh M. Agarwal,Vijay Krishnamoorthy,Tetsu Ohnuma,Mihai V. Podgoreanu,Michael R. Pinsky,Gilles Clermont,Craig M. Coopersmith,Craig S. Jabaley,Rishikesan Kamaleswaran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Researchers developed a dynamic sepsis severity index using machine learning on patient trajectories, which outperforms traditional static scores and shows better prognostic value across multiple clinical measures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current sepsis severity indices (like SOFA) are outdated, using fixed variables and weights from decades ago that don't reflect modern critical care. These traditional scores are coarsely discretized and calibrated to outdated cohorts. There's no alternative learned directly from patient trajectories currently in routine clinical use.

Method: Retrospective two-cohort study on 29,116 and 7,691 adult sepsis patients from Massachusetts and Georgia hospitals. Developed a sepsis index using 43 routinely charted variables over 72-hour treatment windows. Used a novel approach treating mortality as a treatment-level ranking signal rather than per-state target, allowing non-uniform credit redistribution across timesteps. Used Spearman correlation and clinical vignettes for evaluation on permanent 20% test holdout. Uncertainty intervals via bootstrap resampling of whole patients.

Result: The index showed strong discriminative power: non-survivors scored 1.19-1.64 points higher than survivors across all baseline SOFA-2 strata. Within-patient index changes correlated with lactate changes (Spearman rho=0.39). Cross-institutional agreement was 70-77% of same-site correlation. External within-patient correlations were 0.54-0.59 (ceiling 0.90-0.92). The index correlated with established indices while null controls stayed near zero.

Conclusion: The new sepsis index provides hourly prognostic information that meaningfully separates patient outcomes and aligns with clinical expectations. It shows potential as a decision support tool complementing clinical judgment, offering a dynamic, data-driven alternative to traditional static sepsis scores.

Abstract: Currently used sepsis severity indices rely on fixed variables and weights established decades ago, which are coarsely discretized and calibrated to a cohort that no longer reflects contemporary critical care. No alternative learned directly from patient trajectories is in routine use. We conducted a retrospective two-cohort study on a total of 29,116 and 7,691 adult patients meeting Sepsis-3 criteria from two hospital systems in Massachusetts and Georgie, respectively.
  We developed a sepsis index using 43 routinely charted variables over a 72-hour treatment window. Unlike previous studies, we use mortality as a treatment-level ranking signal rather than a per-state target, allowing credit to be redistributed non-uniformly across timesteps. Evaluation was done on a permanent 20% test holdout, using clinical vignettes and Spearman correlation. Uncertainty intervals were obtained by bootstrap resampling of whole patients. Under this ranking scheme, non-survivors scored 1.19-1.64 points higher than survivors on a 0-10 scale within all strata of baseline SOFA-2, with similar results stratifying within lactate, mean arterial pressure (MAP), and creatinine. Within-patient change in the index correlated with change in lactate (Spearman rho = 0.39; n = 1,854). Similar, weaker correlations were found for MAP and creatinine. On a cohort level, cross-institutional agreement measured by Spearman correlation between models trained on different sites, were 70-77% of same-site correlation. External within-patient correlations were 0.54 and 0.59 against ceilings of 0.92 and 0.90. Our index also correlated with established indices, while null controls stayed near zero.
  Our index demonstrated hourly prognostic information that meaningfully separates patient outcomes and is consistent with clinical expectation, indicating potential as a decision support tool complementing clinical judgement.

</details>


### [87] [BPMN4CAI: A BPMN Extension for Modeling Dynamic Conversational AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27149)
*Björn-Lennart Eger,Daniel Rose,Barbara Dinter*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes BPMN4CAI, a standard-compliant BPMN extension for modeling Conversational AI interactions in business processes, addressing limitations of traditional BPMN for dynamic, context-sensitive AI conversations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing BPMN standard faces challenges representing dynamic, context-sensitive interactions of Conversational AI systems (chatbots, virtual assistants) in digital business processes, creating a methodological and practical research gap.

Method: Using Design Science Research methodology, the paper develops a systematic approach to extend existing BPMN elements and incorporate specialized components for Conversational AI.

Result: The BPMN4CAI extension is demonstrated and evaluated through a case study, showing it facilitates adaptive decision-making processes, robust context management, and transparent interactions for Conversational AI within business processes.

Conclusion: BPMN4CAI provides a practical solution to model Conversational AI in business processes, addressing the limitations of standard BPMN while maintaining compliance with the established notation standard.

Abstract: Conversational AI systems, such as chatbots and virtual assistants, are becoming increasingly important to digital business processes. However, the established Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) standard faces challenges when representing dynamic, context-sensitive interactions. This paper addresses this methodological and practical research gap by developing a standard-compliant BPMN extension (BPMN4CAI). Using Design Science Research methodology, this paper develops an approach that systematically extends existing BPMN elements and incorporates specialized components. The applicability and relevance of the BPMN4CAI framework are demonstrated and evaluated through a case study. The results show that the BPMN4CAI extension facilitates adaptive decision-making processes, robust context management, and transparent interactions for Conversational AI within business processes.

</details>


### [88] [Calibrated Enough to Know, Not Calibrated to Act: Fabricated Evidence Makes LLM Agents Commit to the Unknowable](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27167)
*Pranav Aggarwal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM agents commit to predictions on unpredictable questions more often when presented with professional-looking market panels, even when data is fabricated. The issue is with the "act/don't-act" decision gate, which can be trained to reduce commitments but remains fragile in rigid response formats.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand why LLMs make confident commitments on unpredictable questions when presented with professionally packaged but potentially fabricated market data, and to identify the specific cognitive failure point in their decision-making process.

Method: Tested 12 frontier models on unpredictable questions, comparing bare questions vs. professionally presented market panels (including fabricated data). Analyzed commitments, probabilities, and knowability assessments. Performed supervised fine-tuning on a 3B model using 540 synthetic cases to train the decision gate.

Result: Commitment rates rose dramatically from 6.5% to 54.0% with escalated evidence presentation, even with fabricated data (24.5% to 36.8%). Models could answer answerable questions perfectly. Fine-tuning reduced commitments to 0.0% on original cases with transfer to unseen domains, but training was fragile in rigid response formats.

Conclusion: The core failure is in the "act/don't-act" decision gate rather than incapacity, belief, or judgment. This gate is trainable but context-fragile, requiring careful deployment strategies that preserve reasoning space while preventing inappropriate commitments.

Abstract: An LLM agent shown a professional-looking market panel commits to a directional call on a provably unpredictable question far more often than one asked the bare question: across 12 frontier models, commitment rises from 6.5% to 54.0% as evidence is escalated. It commits just as readily when every number on the panel is invented: fabricating the entire display, so nothing the model can see is true except the question itself, still lifts commitment from 24.5% to 36.8%, statistically indistinguishable from the 37.6% produced by genuine market data. What unlocks confident action is not information but the authority of its packaging. The failure is narrow and locatable. Incapacity is not the answer: on matched answerable questions attached to the same panels, the same models answer essentially always, at near-perfect accuracy. Nor is it belief - stated probabilities barely move across the gradient that swings action by 48 points, and score worse than a climatological baseline. Missing judgment isn't it either: asked to classify a question's knowability before acting, models call it irreducible 90% of the time and then commit on just 0.4% of those. The act/don't-act gate is what fails, and the effect is concentrated in a few models rather than universal. Because the gate is separable, it can be trained. Supervised fine-tuning of a 3B model on 540 synthetic cases, predominantly dice, coins, jars and timers, drives commitment to 0.0% on the original cases and transfers to three unseen domains. It does not survive everything: the gate holds exactly when the response format leaves room to reason, and rigid formats that remove that room leave the model confident and wrong on questions it otherwise answers correctly. The gate is trainable and context-fragile, and deployment needs both halves of that sentence.

</details>


### [89] [What Makes Good Agentic Data? An ACE Lens on Data Generation for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27260)
*Xingshan Zeng,Zishan Xu,Boju Zhang,Yuzhou Wu,Lingzhi Wang,Jianghao Lin,Liangyou Li,Yasheng Wang,Lifeng Shang,Xin Jiang,Weinan Zhang,Yong Yu,Qun Liu,Weiwen Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a two-level framework (ACE: Accuracy-Complexity-divErsity) to systematically analyze agentic data generation for LLM agents, emphasizing that the goal is not just more data but valid, informative, non-redundant experience tailored to evolving agents and environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current research on agentic data generation suffers from domain-centered organization and heterogeneous evaluation that obscures common mechanisms and conflates candidate construction with verification/selection. There's a need for a unified framework to understand how to generate interaction data that maintains consistency and is useful rather than merely abundant.

Method: The paper develops a two-level framework: 1) Representing agentic data as a factorized object (E,q,τ,v) comprising environment specification, task signal, interaction realization, and optional verifier, organized by primary anchor and dependency structure. 2) Formulating generation as constrained distribution design through the Accuracy-Complexity-divErsity (ACE) lens: Accuracy establishes feasible support; Complexity allocates learning mass relative to learner capability; divErsity controls coverage and redundancy.

Result: The framework reveals a shift in the literature toward execution-grounded accuracy, learner-relative complexity, and diversity beyond surface variation or dataset size. The analysis explores how prior work verifies experience, constructs/calibrates difficulty, and expands behavioral coverage through the ACE perspective.

Conclusion: The central challenge in agentic data generation is not simply generating more data, but continually allocating valid, informative, and non-redundant experience as agents and environments evolve. The paper discusses broader directions and emerging trends through the ACE lens, including implications for scaling, data sources, training regimes, and adaptive learning.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on generated interaction data to learn how to interact with external environments. Agentic data generation must maintain consistency among environments, tasks, interactions, and success signals while producing experience that is useful rather than merely abundant. Existing work spans many agent domains, but domain-centered organization and heterogeneous evaluation often obscure common generation mechanisms and conflate candidate construction with verification and selection. This work develops a two-level framework for the field. First, we represent agentic data as a common factorized object $(E,q,τ,v)$, comprising an environment specification, task signal, interaction realization, and optional verifier. We organize generation paradigms by their primary anchor and dependency structure. Second, we formulate generation as constrained distribution design through the Accuracy-Complexity-divErsity (ACE) lens. Accuracy establishes the feasible support of grounded and internally consistent data. Within this support, Complexity places learning mass relative to the capability of a declared learner and execution configuration, while divErsity controls coverage and redundancy of data. Using this framework, we explore how prior work verifies generated experience, constructs and calibrates difficulty, and expands behavioral coverage. The literature reveals a shift toward execution-grounded accuracy, learner-relative complexity, and diversity beyond surface variation or dataset size. We further discuss broader directions and emerging trends in agentic data generation through the ACE lens, including their implications for scaling, data sources, training regimes and adaptive learning. Overall, the central challenge is not simply to generate more data, but to continually allocate valid, informative, and non-redundant experience as agents and environments evolve.

</details>


### [90] [Naive Prompt Optimization: Rethinking the Need for Complex Prompt Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27266)
*Yuan Chang,Xiaoqi Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Naive Prompt Optimization (NPO) - a simple, lightweight prompt optimization method that matches or exceeds complex approaches like GEPA with fewer computational resources, showing strong reasoning teacher models can substitute for optimizer complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current prompt optimization approaches are becoming unnecessarily complex, while simpler methods could achieve comparable performance gains with lower computational costs, which is important for accelerating recursive self-improvement in agentic AI.

Method: Introduces Naive Prompt Optimization (NPO), a lightweight single-lineage method that iteratively revises prompts using a teacher model with rollout feedback (simple linear optimization approach).

Result: NPO achieves comparable or better performance than GEPA with fewer rollouts, benefits more from stronger teacher models, transfers well to other student models (especially within same model family), and remains broadly competitive with GEPA in interactive games (though GRPO performs better on some less amenable tasks).

Conclusion: Simple, linear prompt optimization methods like NPO can rival substantially more sophisticated and complex search procedures, suggesting that strong teacher reasoning can substitute for optimizer-side search complexity, potentially making prompt optimization more accessible and efficient.

Abstract: Efficiently improving autonomous agents across diverse tasks is central to accelerating recursive self-improvement (RSI) in agentic AI, with prompt optimization emerging as a promising approach capable of delivering performance gains comparable to those achieved by fine-tuning model weights, while reducing computational costs in both optimization and serving. However, recent developments increasingly favor unnecessarily complex prompt optimizers. We introduce Naive Prompt Optimization (NPO), a lightweight single-lineage method that iteratively revises prompts using a teacher model with rollout feedback. NPO achieves comparable or better performance than GEPA with fewer rollouts, and its advantage increases with stronger teacher models, suggesting that stronger teacher reasoning can partially substitute for optimizer-side search complexity. In interactive games, NPO remains broadly competitive with GEPA, while GRPO performs better on some tasks less amenable to prompt optimization. We also show that NPO-optimized prompts elicit similar performance improvements when applied verbatim to other student models, especially across models within the same family. Overall, our preliminary results show that simple, linear prompt optimization can rival substantially more sophisticated and complex search procedures.

</details>


### [91] [BrailleBench: Investigating Multi-Criteria Braille Comprehension in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27268)
*Jinghan Zhang,Fengran Mo,Zhiyu Chen,Xiaoyan Han,Kunpeng Liu,Chang-Tien Lu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BrailleBench is a benchmark for evaluating LLM comprehension of Braille across mathematics, commonsense, and multi-hop QA tasks, revealing significant gaps between print-English and Braille accessibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI systems may not be inclusive enough for blind and deafblind users who access information through Braille, which has distinct requirements (indicators, contractions, digital representations) that need evaluation for model comprehension.

Method: Created BrailleBench with 5,570 instances from 5 datasets across English and Braille Grades 1 and 2. Used deterministic, expert-reviewed pipeline via self-created Braille Toolkit without LLM-generated data. Evaluated 6 representative LLMs across different configurations to assess Braille comprehension, expression, and end-to-end interaction.

Result: Reveals persistent gap between print-English capability and Braille accessibility. Shows asymmetric understanding and expression - Grade 2 Braille especially fragile on input side compared to Grade 1. Fully Braille requests further reduce performance. Provides guidance for future Braille AI systems.

Conclusion: BrailleBench provides comprehensive evaluation of LLM Braille comprehension, highlighting significant accessibility gaps and offering valuable guidance for developing more inclusive Braille AI systems, with all resources publicly available.

Abstract: Although Large language models (LLMs) mediate access to knowledge and computational assistance, their capabilities should benefit vulnerable groups in the same way. However, it is unclear whether existing AI systems are inclusive enough for blind and deafblind users to access the same functionality through Braille, whose indicators, contractions, and digital representations introduce distinct requirements for model comprehension. To this end, we introduce BrailleBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs in Braille comprehension from different Criteria. BrailleBench aligns 5,570 instances from five datasets, including mathematics, commonsense, and multi-hop question answering across English and Braille Grades 1 and 2. Different configurations are designed to understand whether the systems can comprehend Braille-authored content, express answers in Braille, and complete end-to-end Braille interaction. To ensure the quality and prevent evaluation bias, the benchmark is built through a deterministic, expert-reviewed pipeline via a self-created Braille Toolkit without using any data instances generated by LLMs. We evaluate six representative LLMs from various aspects. The results reveal a persistent gap between print-English capability and Braille accessibility. Braille understanding and expression are asymmetric, where Grade 2 is especially fragile on the input side compared to Grade 1, and fully Braille requests further reduce performance. The experimental observations provide valuable guidance for the development of future Braille AI systems. All related resources in BrailleBench are publicly available for future research.

</details>


### [92] [Verify Smarter, Evolve Further: Efficient Harness Evolution through Behavior-Aware Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27311)
*Jinghan Xu,Yikai Zhang,Aili Chen,Weiyuan Li,Jiaqing Liang,Deqing Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HarnessLens: A budget-aware framework for automated agent harness evolution that improves performance while reducing evaluation costs through behavior-aware verification with explicit attribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current propose-and-verify methods for adapting language-model agent harnesses are inefficient and costly, requiring verification on fixed task sets that wastes resources on unrelated behaviors and allows aggregate scores to obscure specific regressions.

Method: HarnessLens is a framework that jointly explores task space and user-configurable components, derives candidate modifications from execution trajectories, and selectively verifies each candidate on behavior-relevant tasks using an attributable-evidence gate.

Result: Across three agent harnesses and four benchmarks, HarnessLens improved average held-out performance by 7.6-13.6% while consuming substantially less evaluation budget than competing baselines.

Conclusion: Behavior-aware verification with explicit attribution enables more reliable and sample-efficient harness evolution under constrained interaction budgets, demonstrating the effectiveness of the HarnessLens approach.

Abstract: Agent harnesses shape how language-model agents use instructions, tools, and runtime components, but adapting these harnesses requires costly verification. Existing propose-and-verify methods typically score every candidate on a fixed task set, wasting rollouts on unrelated behaviors and allowing aggregate scores to obscure specific regressions. We introduce HarnessLens, a budget-aware framework for automated harness evolution. HarnessLens jointly explores the task space and user-configurable components, derives candidate modifications from execution trajectories, and selectively verifies each candidate on behavior-relevant tasks using an attributable-evidence gate. Across three agent harnesses and four benchmarks, HarnessLens improves average held-out performance by 7.6-13.6% while consuming substantially less evaluation budget than competing baselines. These results demonstrate that behavior-aware verification with explicit attribution enables more reliable and sample-efficient harness evolution under constrained interaction budgets. Our code is available at https://github.com/jhxu5214/HarnessLens.

</details>


### [93] [Not All Eval-Awareness Is Equal: Capabilities Framing Predicts Compliance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27340)
*Allison Zhuang,Santiago Aranguri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Models' awareness of being tested (eval-awareness) isn't uniform - it has different flavors (capabilities vs safety) that predict compliance differently, showing aggregate suppression rates can mask important safety-relevant behavior changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current safety evaluation pipelines treat eval-awareness as a single quantity to suppress, but this approach may not capture important behavioral nuances and could lead to misleading conclusions about model safety.

Method: Analyzed verbalized eval-awareness in chain-of-thought responses, categorizing them as capabilities-flavored, safety-flavored, both, or neither. Tested on Qwen3-32B over FORTRESS dataset with various steering interventions and conducted CoT-prefill intervention experiments to establish causality.

Result: Capabilities-framing predicts significantly higher compliance (+24 to +46 percentage points) than safety-framing. CoT-prefill interventions showed causal link (10 of 11 prefills shifted compliance in predicted direction). Aggregate suppression rates can mask that safety-relevant components don't change while overall rates move.

Conclusion: Eval-awareness is not behaviorally uniform - different framings lead to different compliance behaviors. Simply reporting "X% suppression of eval-awareness" is insufficient for safety evaluation as it can correspond to qualitatively different behavioral outcomes.

Abstract: Steering interventions targeting eval-awareness, a model's recognition that it is being tested, are increasingly used in safety evaluation pipelines, where evaluation-awareness is treated as a single quantity to be suppressed. We show that verbalized eval-awareness in chain-of-thought can be identified as capabilities-flavored ("the user is testing my ability to follow instructions"), safety-flavored ("the user is testing my boundaries"), both, or neither: framings that predict compliance very differently. On Qwen3-32B over the FORTRESS dataset, capabilities-framing predicts compliance with a +24 to +46 percentage-point gap over safety-framing across all tested steering conditions. A CoT-prefill intervention on eval-awareness-negative rollouts suggests the link is causal, with 10 of 11 prefills shifting compliance in the predicted direction. Then, eval-awareness is not behaviorally uniform: aggregate suppression rates can move while the safety-relevant component does not, and the same "X% suppression of eval-awareness" can correspond to qualitatively different behavioral outcomes.

</details>


### [94] [Sophistication in GenAI Use: Field Evidence from a Large Firm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27364)
*Nicholas J. Hallman,Zachary T. Kowaleski,Anu Puvvada,Jaime J. Schmidt*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Study of back-office employees' generative AI usage sophistication at a large firm shows senior employees use it more sophisticatedly, sophistication varies by function with Strategy, Digital Innovation, and Project Management leading, and sophistication doesn't improve over time or with training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how sophistication in generative AI usage varies among back-office workers in a corporate setting, as AI becomes increasingly integrated into business operations but usage patterns and effectiveness remain underexplored.

Method: Analyzed proprietary data of 713,564 employee prompts and corresponding LLM responses from nearly 4,000 back-office employees across 15 functional areas over eight months in 2025 at a large firm.

Result: Three main findings: 1) Senior employees exhibit more sophisticated genAI use, 2) Sophistication highest in Strategy, Digital Innovation, and Project Management (strategic function groups), 3) No improvement in sophistication over time or lasting improvement after formal AI training.

Conclusion: Sophisticated genAI use complements domain expertise, varies by functional focus, and is difficult to change over time or through training; findings provide actionable insights for managers and measures for researchers.

Abstract: We study how sophistication in generative AI (genAI) use varies among the back-office workforce of a large firm. Using proprietary data, we observe 713,564 employee prompts and their corresponding large language model responses from nearly 4,000 back-office employees across 15 functional areas over eight months in 2025. We document three main findings. First, senior employees exhibit more sophisticated genAI use, consistent with domain expertise complementing genAI capabilities. Second, sophistication varies considerably across functions and is highest in Strategy, Digital Innovation, and Project Management, three groups that share a focus on firmwide strategic initiatives and organizational change. Third, we observe neither improvements in sophistication over time nor lasting improvements following formal AI training, suggesting that sophisticated use can be difficult to change. Together, our study provides measures of and insights into sophisticated genAI use that managers can use to improve outcomes and that researchers can use in future research.

</details>


### [95] [Mechanistic Reaction Prediction via Discrete Flow Matching on Graph-Structured Electron Occupation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27429)
*Nguyen Xuan-Vu,Octavian Susanu,Daniel Armstrong,Philippe Schwaller*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MAELLE models chemical reactions as discrete flow matching over electron rearrangements instead of heuristic graph edits, achieving competitive performance on reaction prediction benchmarks while providing mechanistically interpretable trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current machine learning approaches to chemical reaction modeling either generate products de novo or use heuristic graph edits that operate on molecular topology, failing to capture the fundamental nature of reactions as electron space transformations.

Method: Models reactions as a Continuous-time Markov Chain (CTMC) over graph-structured integer-valued electron occupation space. Uses Optimal Transport to generalize discrete flow matching mixture paths to discrete electron rearrangements, creating interpretable edit trajectories without requiring elementary step annotations.

Result: Competitive performance on USPTO-480K benchmark, strong robustness in out-of-distribution settings (structural complexity and reaction type), and ability to recover mechanistic trajectories that align with known chemistry and predict side products.

Conclusion: MAELLE provides a principled approach to reaction modeling that operates directly on electron rearrangements, offering both accurate predictions and mechanistic interpretability while maintaining robustness across different chemical contexts.

Abstract: Chemical reactions are fundamentally transformations in electron space, yet most machine learning approaches model them either through \textit{de novo} generation of product molecules or through heuristic graph edits that operate directly on molecular topology.
  We introduce MAELLE (\textbf{M}ech\textbf{A}nistic \textbf{E}dit f\textbf{L}ow-matching on e\textbf{L}ectron r\textbf{E}arrangements), which instead models reactions as discrete flow matching over electron occupation vectors.
  Concretely, we formulate the reactant-to-product mapping as a Continuous-time Markov Chain (CTMC) over the graph-structured integer-valued electron occupation space defined on all bonding, non-bonding, and hydrogen sites.
  To construct the intermediate edit trajectories, we generalize the discrete flow matching mixture path to discrete electron rearrangements using Optimal Transport, yielding a sequence of mechanistically interpretable edit moves without requiring elementary step annotations.
  MAELLE achieves competitive performance on the USPTO-480K benchmark compared with leading reaction prediction models.
  Beyond in-distribution accuracy, we evaluate robustness across two out-of-distribution settings - structural complexity and reaction type - and find that MAELLE maintains strong performance where existing methods degrade.
  Finally, because the learned flow operates over the full electron redistribution, MAELLE naturally recovers mechanistic trajectories that align with known chemistry and can predict side products of a reaction.

</details>


### [96] [WikiSkill: Compiling Agent Experience into Persistent Knowledge for Skill Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27454)
*Liyan Tang,Cyrus Rashtchian,Chun-Sung Ferng,Andrew Tomkins,Da-Cheng Juan,Tu Vu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WikiSkill is a framework that co-evolves AI agent skills with a persistent knowledge base (wiki), enabling systematic accumulation and refinement of experience into reusable, transferable skills.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current skill-evolution approaches scatter optimization insights across execution histories, limiting systematic reuse across iterations. There's a need for persistent knowledge accumulation to guide skill development.

Method: WikiSkill separates raw execution experience, accumulated knowledge, and executable skills. It continuously consolidates experience into a persistent wiki that subsequent skill updates can build upon, creating a co-evolution between skills and knowledge base.

Result: WikiSkill consistently outperforms state-of-the-art skill-evolution methods across diverse benchmarks and models. Key findings: 1) Skill evolution complements model scaling, 2) Skills transfer effectively across models and families, 3) Skills evolved by other models can outperform self-evolved skills.

Conclusion: Persistent knowledge accumulation in the wiki is critical for effective skill evolution. Systematically accumulating and refining agent experience enables development of reusable, transferable skills that significantly enhance agent capabilities.

Abstract: Agent skills package specialized knowledge and workflows into reusable resources that extend AI agent capabilities. Recent work automatically discovers such skills from agent experience, which enables agents to progressively adapt through interaction. However, the insights that guide skill development typically remain scattered across optimization histories, limiting their systematic reuse across iterations. We introduce WikiSkill, a framework that co-evolves agent skills with a persistent knowledge base (wiki). At a high level, WikiSkill separates raw execution experience, accumulated knowledge, and executable skills, while continuously consolidating experience into the wiki, which subsequent skill updates can build on. Across diverse benchmarks and models, WikiSkill consistently outperforms state-of-the-art skill-evolution methods and improves over no-skill baselines in most model-benchmark settings. We find that skill evolution complements model scaling: larger models generally benefit more from evolved skills, while smaller models with skills can outperform substantially larger models without them. We also find that evolved skills transfer effectively across models and model families, and skills evolved by other models can outperform self-evolved skills. Finally, our ablation studies confirm that persistent knowledge accumulation in the wiki is critical for effective skill evolution. These results demonstrate the benefits of systematically accumulating and refining agent experience for developing reusable and transferable skills.

</details>


### [97] [EduRiskX: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework with F-Logic Reasoning for Early Academic Risk Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26107)
*Yu Fu,Yongqi Kang,Yong Zhao,Rongfang Bie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EduRiskX is a neuro-symbolic framework combining temporal Transformer neural networks with F-Logic symbolic reasoning for early, interpretable prediction of student academic risk in online education.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing academic risk prediction models suffer from limited early detection capability and insufficient interpretability (black-box problem), hindering adoption in real-world educational settings where timely interventions are crucial for improving retention and learning outcomes.

Method: A neuro-symbolic framework integrating: (1) a temporal Transformer-based neural predictor with attention mechanisms, class-weighted loss, and dynamic weekly truncation; (2) an F-Logic symbolic reasoning module constructed from training data using established educational theories; (3) a logistic regression-based fusion mechanism to combine neural risk probabilities with symbolic confidence scores.

Result: On OULAD dataset with student-level split, EduRiskX achieves accuracy of 0.900 and F1-score of 0.894 at Week 38, with average early detection week of 9.32 and 94.30% detection rate. It outperforms state-of-the-art time-series models (PatchTST, iTransformer) and deep learning baselines (LSTM, CNN) in recall and early risk identification.

Conclusion: EduRiskX successfully addresses key limitations of existing academic risk prediction models by providing both accurate early detection and interpretable predictions through its neuro-symbolic architecture, making it more suitable for real-world educational applications where both performance and trust are essential.

Abstract: Predicting students' academic risk in online education is crucial for enabling timely interventions that can improve retention and learning outcomes. However, existing models often suffer from limited early detection capability and insufficient interpretability, leading to a "black-box" trust crisis that hinders their adoption in real-world pedagogical settings. To address these challenges, we propose EduRiskX, a neuro-symbolic framework that integrates a temporal Transformer-based predictor with F-Logic symbolic reasoning. The neural component models longitudinal student activity sequences using temporal attention, class-weighted loss, and dynamic weekly truncation. Acting as a data-driven expert system, an F-Logic rule base -- grounded in established educational theories (Engagement Theory and Student Integration Model) to mimic the diagnostic logic of human educators -- is constructed exclusively from the training data. The neural risk probability and the symbolic confidence score are then combined through a logistic regression-based fusion mechanism that learns the relative contribution of each signal. Experiments on the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD) using a strict 80/10/10 student-level split show that EduRiskX achieves an accuracy of 0.900 and an F1-score of 0.894 at the end of the semester (Week 38), with an average early detection week of 9.32 and a detection rate of 94.30 percent. Compared with state-of-the-art time-series models (PatchTST, iTransformer) and common deep learning baselines (LSTM, CNN), EduRiskX yields improved recall and earlier risk identification under identical conditions. Beyond predictive performance, the F-Logic module provides structured rule-based explanations linking predictions to observable behavioral patterns and educational theories.

</details>


### [98] [Standalone LLM and a Pre-specified Agentic Pipeline for Explaining ICU Mortality Predictions: a Feasibility Study on the eICU Demo Dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26109)
*Di Zhu,Chen Xie,Haoyun Zhang,Zihan Wei,Ziwei Wang,Jiazhao Shi,Ziyu Wang,Qiyang Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Comparing standalone LLMs vs multi-step agentic pipelines for explaining ICU mortality predictions shows trade-offs: standalone LLMs better align with feature attributions, while agentic pipelines improve safety grounding and patient specificity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While machine learning models can accurately predict ICU mortality, existing feature-attribution methods don't provide sufficient clinical narrative for bedside use. There's a need for better explanatory systems that combine predictive accuracy with clinically meaningful explanations.

Method: The study compares two approaches: 1) standalone large language model (LLM) explanations, and 2) a four-step agentic pipeline that separates data interpretation, guideline checking, and final explanation. Evaluation used 2,353 ICU stays with 8.1% mortality rate, assessing both predictive performance (XGBoost model) and explanatory quality on a 38-case subset.

Result: XGBoost achieved AUROC 0.855. On explanatory tasks: standalone LLM had 1 case with outcome leakage vs agentic pipeline's 0. On SHAP-aligned cases (n=14), standalone LLM showed better feature attribution alignment (mean Jaccard 0.171 vs 0.077) and direction consistency (92.9% vs 78.6%), while agentic pipeline showed superior guideline grounding (0.762 vs 0.143), value specificity (0.236 vs 0.143), and slightly higher plausibility (0.700 vs 0.671).

Conclusion: Agentic decomposition improves safety-relevant grounding and patient-specific detail in explanations but should be paired with attribution-based checks before clinical use. The trade-off suggests combining both approaches may be optimal for high-stakes risk explanation in ICU settings.

Abstract: Machine-learning models can predict ICU mortality accurately, but feature-attribution methods alone rarely provide the clinical narrative needed for bedside use. Large language models (LLMs) may bridge this gap, and multi-step agentic pipelines are a plausible extension because they separate data interpretation, guideline checking, and final explanation. This revised feasibility study preserves the original standalone-versus-agentic comparison while making the main clinical findings more explicit. Using the retained local eICU Demo artifact set (2,353 ICU stays; 8.1\% mortality), XGBoost achieved an AUROC of 0.855 (95\% CI 0.796--0.906) and an AUPRC of 0.332 (95\% CI 0.217--0.494). On a stratified 38-case explanation subset, the standalone LLM produced 1 explanation with explicit outcome leakage, whereas the four-step agentic pipeline produced none. Among the 14 cases that overlapped with the SHAP review subset, the standalone LLM showed higher SHAP alignment (mean Jaccard 0.171 versus 0.077) and higher direction consistency (92.9\% versus 78.6\%), while the agentic pipeline showed higher guideline grounding (0.762 versus 0.143), higher value specificity (0.236 versus 0.143), and slightly higher plausibility (0.700 versus 0.671). Clinically, the results suggest that agentic decomposition may improve safety-relevant grounding and patient-specific detail, but it should be paired with attribution-based checks before use in high-stakes risk explanation.

</details>


### [99] [Large Models for Battery Prognostics and Health Management: A Review and Future Roadmap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26111)
*Jiale Liu,Huan Wang,Weicheng Wang,Rong Zhu,Qiqi Wang,Min Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper provides the first comprehensive survey of Large Models (LMs) applications in Battery Prognostics and Health Management (BPHM), examining how transformer-based models overcome traditional limitations and proposing a roadmap for future research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional BPHM approaches face challenges in computational efficiency, cross-domain generalization, dependence on extensive labeled data, and model interpretability. Large Models offer a transformative paradigm to overcome these long-standing bottlenecks in battery management for electric vehicles, grid storage, and consumer electronics.

Method: The paper conducts a systematic survey of LM applications in BPHM, categorizing progress along four dimensions: mitigating data scarcity, enhancing generalization/robustness, integrating domain knowledge for interpretability, and enabling system-level automation. It reviews foundational LM technologies including Transformer architectures, self-supervised learning, large-scale multimodal datasets, and PEFT techniques.

Result: The review establishes that LMs show promising results in addressing traditional BPHM challenges, but significant obstacles remain in data accessibility, intelligence validation, trustworthiness, and deployment feasibility. The paper identifies current progress and gaps in the field.

Conclusion: The authors propose a research roadmap focusing on collaborative data ecosystems, industrial intelligence validation, physics-informed designs for trustworthiness, and efficient on-device deployment. This review provides essential insights for developing next-generation battery management systems capable of safe, reliable, and autonomous operation throughout battery lifecycles.

Abstract: Battery Prognostics and Health Management (BPHM) is critical for ensuring the safe, reliable, and cost-effective operation of batteries across electric vehicles, grid storage, and consumer electronics. Conventional BPHM approaches, including physics-based models and task-centric deep learning methods, face challenges in computational efficiency and parameterization, cross-domain generalization, dependence on extensive labeled run-to-failure data, and model interpretability. Recent Large Models (LMs), built upon Transformer architectures and self-supervised pre-training, offer a transformative new paradigm to overcome these long-standing bottlenecks. This review provides the first comprehensive survey of LM applications in BPHM, systematically examining how these models address challenges in the field. We begin by elucidating the foundational technologies enabling LMs, including Transformer architectures, self-supervised learning, large-scale multimodal datasets, and PEFT techniques. We then categorize recent progress along four critical dimensions: mitigating data scarcity, enhancing generalization and robustness, integrating domain knowledge for interpretability, and enabling system-level automation. Despite promising results, significant challenges remain across data accessibility, intelligence validation, trustworthiness, and deployment feasibility. To guide future research, we propose a roadmap focused on building collaborative data ecosystems, validating intelligence for industrial applications, enhancing trustworthiness with physics-informed designs, and enabling efficient on-device deployment. This review establishes a systematic approach to understand and advance LM-driven BPHM, providing researchers and practitioners with essential insights for developing next-generation battery management systems capable of safe, reliable, and autonomous operation throughout battery lifecycles.

</details>


### [100] [PICasso: An AI-Enabled Design Framework for Autonomous Optimization of Silicon Photonic Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26113)
*Deepak Vungarala,Deniz Najafi,Abdulrahman Aljoudi,Zahra Ghanaatian,Navid Khoshavi,Gourav Datta,Arman Roohi,Mahdi Nikdast,Shaahin Angizi*

Main category: cs.AI
