TL;DR: PICasso is an AI framework that automates photonic circuit design from natural language specs using LLMs with PDK-aware generation, verification, and simulation optimization, achieving high structural accuracy and reduced insertion loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Photonic integrated circuit design is complex and manual, requiring specialized expertise. The paper aims to develop an AI-assisted framework that can automate the entire PIC design flow from natural language specifications, making photonic design more accessible and efficient.

Method: PICasso uses a structured pipeline: natural language -> YAML -> GDS generation with PDK-aware knowledge injection, automated placement/routing, DRC/LVS validation, and SAX-based simulation. The framework introduces PIC-Set benchmark (36 design tasks) to evaluate LLMs with metrics including structural/functional Spec@k, optimization efficiency, and robustness.

Result: PICasso achieves structural Spec@3 up to 92.7% and functional Spec@3 up to 52% on high-complexity circuits. It reduces mean insertion loss from 4.98 dB to 3.25 dB (1.74 dB improvement). The framework outperforms vanilla LLM generation and maintains competitive runtimes compared to manual GUI workflows.

Conclusion: Structured domain constraints, physical verification, and simulation feedback transform LLMs into practical PIC design agents capable of producing manufacturable layouts. PICasso demonstrates that AI-assisted frameworks can significantly improve photonic circuit design automation while maintaining efficiency.

Abstract: We present PICasso, an AI-assisted framework for automated synthesis, verification, and optimization of photonic integrated circuits (PICs) from natural-language specifications. PICasso couples a structured NL -> YAML -> GDS generation pipeline with PDK aware knowledge injection, automated placement and routing, DRC/LVS validation, and SAX-based photonic simulation. To systematically evaluate AI-driven photonic design, we introduce PIC-Set, a benchmark of 36 parameterized PIC design tasks spanning core photonic primitives and multi-component circuits. Using PIC-Set, we benchmark several state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) under a unified evaluation protocol, including new metrics such as structural and functional $Spec@k$, optimization efficiency, and robustness under perturbations. Across the benchmark, PICasso significantly improves end-to-end specification satisfaction compared to vanilla LLM generation. Structural $Spec@3$ reaches up to 92.7% and functional $Spec@3$ up to 52% on high-complexity circuits. In addition, PICasso consistently reduces circuit insertion loss, lowering the mean loss from 4.98 dB to 3.25 dB (1.74 dB improvement) through simulation-guided optimization. These results demonstrate that structured domain constraints, physical verification, and simulation feedback transform LLMs from brittle netlist generators into practical PIC design agents capable of producing manufacturable layouts with competitive runtimes relative to manual GUI-based workflows.

</details>


### [101] [Agent Mesh: Reliability Primitives for Non-Idempotent Agent Delegation - Identity Adequacy and Evidence Adequacy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26225)
*Mazhar Shaikh,Anurag Rajkumar Bombarde,Harshal Pathak*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Traditional service mesh primitives (retry, timeout, error-rate circuit breaking) fail for agentic orchestration due to violated assumptions, leading to cascading failures, blocked correct work, and identity/evidence adequacy problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous agents performing bounded software tasks under orchestrators need reliability mechanisms, but existing service mesh primitives (retry, timeout, circuit breaking) make assumptions that are violated in practice, leading to systematic failures in production agentic platforms.

Method: Conducted a failure study of a production agentic software-delivery platform analyzing 147 numbered incidents across 81 runs, with measured costs and mutation proofs to reproduce failures, examining violations of three core assumptions underlying reliability primitives.

Result: Found all three assumptions violated: 1) successful tool call loops invisible to error-rate breakers, 2) constant progress signals causing false trips, 3) accumulated events making idempotent components unwinnable, 4) misrouted failures waking bystander components, 5) enforcement layers blocking correct work. Identified cross-cutting causes: identity adequacy failures and evidence adequacy deficiencies.

Conclusion: Proposed seven new reliability primitives whose enforcement unit is the delegation rather than the message, emphasizing the need for identity adequacy (discriminative identities) and evidence adequacy (attributable, deterministic measurements) for reliable agentic orchestration.

Abstract: Autonomous agents increasingly perform bounded software tasks under an orchestrator that retries, resumes, and budgets them. The machinery such orchestrators reach for is the service mesh's: retry, timeout, and error-rate circuit breaking. We report a failure study of a production agentic software-delivery platform over 147 numbered incidents spanning 81 runs, each with a measured cost and, in most cases, a mutation proof reproducing the failure. All three assumptions those primitives rest on are violated in practice, and we quantify the consequences: a loop of fifty-four consecutive successful tool calls no error-rate breaker could see; a progress signal constant by construction, guaranteeing a false trip on the third repair round and driving one run from six of six components to three; twenty-one events accumulated across six invocations of one delegation, making a correct, idempotent component unwinnable; a misrouted failure that woke five components for a two-component fault, leaving three bystanders regressing working code; and twelve incidents in which the enforcement layer blocked correct work, the most expensive costing 107 agent turns and zero accepted writes. We find one cross-cutting cause and its dual. Identity adequacy: in five separate subsystems an identity that failed to discriminate produced a confident wrong answer, and two of them derived the corrective rule independently. Evidence adequacy: a reliability decision may be taken only on evidence capable of moving, attributable to what it measures, and deterministic under identical conditions. From the findings we derive seven reliability primitives whose enforcement unit is the delegation rather than the message, and specify the controlled evaluation the study motivates but does not constitute.

</details>


### [102] [CIFQA: A Deterministic Tool-Grounded Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Financial Query Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26114)
*Kunjesh Parekh,Anil Kumar Tiwari,Divya Saxena*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CIFQA is a deterministic tool-grounded multi-agent LLM framework that addresses numerical inaccuracies in financial Q&A by separating language understanding from numerical execution through specialized agents and Python-based tools, achieving high accuracy even with smaller models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs often produce numerically incorrect yet plausible answers when solving multi-step financial calculations that require exact reasoning over structured rates, temporal conditions, numerical formulas, and rule-based constraints.

Method: A multi-agent framework with specialized agents for query interpretation, routing, parameter extraction, computation planning, and response generation, combined with deterministic Python-based tools for financial calculations and rule application.

Result: Achieved 95.54% accuracy on calculation-intensive queries and 90.87% overall accuracy on fixed deposit queries, substantially outperforming direct LLM baselines. A 17B open-source backbone within CIFQA outperformed larger frontier models, showing architectural design is more important than model scale.

Conclusion: While evaluated on fixed deposit queries, CIFQA provides a generalizable framework for calculation-intensive financial reasoning tasks, demonstrating that deterministic tool-grounded approaches can significantly improve numerical reliability over pure LLM methods.

Abstract: Calculation-intensive financial question answering requires exact reasoning over structured rates, temporal conditions, numerical formulas, and rule-based constraints. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) perform strongly on natural language tasks, they often produce numerically incorrect yet plausible answers when solving multi-step financial calculations. To address this limitation, we introduce CIFQA (Calculation-Intensive Financial Query Answering), a deterministic tool-grounded multi-agent LLM framework for financial question answering. CIFQA separates language understanding from numerical execution by assigning specialized agents to query interpretation, routing, parameter extraction, computation planning, and response generation, while deterministic Python-based tools perform financial calculations and rule application. We instantiate CIFQA for fixed deposit query answering and evaluate it on a curated benchmark of fixed deposit queries. CIFQA achieves 95.54% accuracy on calculation-intensive queries and 90.87% overall accuracy, substantially outperforming direct LLM baselines even when provided with complete formulas, rate cards, and benchmark instructions. Ablation studies show that deterministic components such as exact rate lookup, tenure computation, rolling-year adjustment, and premature-withdrawal logic are critical contributors to performance. Notably, a 17B open-source backbone operating within CIFQA outperforms substantially larger frontier models evaluated with the same financial information, demonstrating that architectural design is a more important determinant of numerical reliability than model scale. While evaluated on fixed deposit queries, CIFQA provides a generalizable framework for calculation-intensive financial reasoning tasks.

</details>


### [103] [SKILL.state: Scalable Long-Horizon Agent Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26263)
*Sanket Badhe,Priyanka Tiwari,Jonghyun Chung*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SKILL.state is a runtime architecture for LLM agents that replaces growing conversational history with explicit mutable execution state, reducing latency and improving performance for long-horizon tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agent runtimes suffer from latency degradation and context-poisoning failures over long horizons due to continually appending execution history to conversation context, causing prompt growth and performance issues.

Method: SKILL.state introduces a runtime architecture that uses explicit, mutable execution state instead of append-only conversational history. At each step, the model receives only immutable skill specification, current structured execution state, and latest observation. Intermediate reasoning is discarded after producing validated state updates.

Result: Across diverse datasets, models, and execution environments, SKILL.state improves task accuracy while substantially reducing cumulative token consumption compared to traditional approaches.

Conclusion: Explicit execution state is an effective and architecture-agnostic abstraction for scalable long-horizon agent skills, offering better performance and efficiency than append-only history approaches.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly act as autonomous agents executing complex, long-running procedural skills. Existing agent runtimes maintain execution by continually appending observations, actions, and intermediate reasoning traces to an ever-growing conversation history, causing latency degradation and context-poisoning failures over long horizons. We present SKILL.state, a runtime architecture that replaces append-only conversational history with an explicit, mutable execution state. At each execution step, the model receives only the immutable skill specification, the current structured execution state, and the latest observation. Intermediate reasoning is discarded immediately after producing a validated state update, preventing prompt growth with execution history. Across diverse datasets, models, and execution environments, SKILL.state improves task accuracy while substantially reducing cumulative token consumption. Our results demonstrate that explicit execution state is an effective and architecture-agnostic abstraction for scalable long-horizon agent skills.

</details>


### [104] [The Artificial Experimentalist: Discovery and Control of Self-Organizing Phenomena with Autotelic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26116)
*Marko Cvjetko,Benedikt Hartl,Michael Levin,Clément Moulin-Frier,Pierre-Yves Oudeyer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CARL: A reinforcement learning agent that discovers and controls self-organizing patterns in continuous cellular automata through local interventions, demonstrating autonomous discovery, control, and human-guided navigation capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for exploring complex systems like cellular automata operate in open-loop fashion without intervention during execution. There's a need for closed-loop approaches that can actively intervene and control emergent phenomena in complex systems.

Method: Introduced CARL, an agentic system based on autotelic reinforcement learning that samples diverse goals autonomously and learns goal-conditioned policies to intervene in Lenia (continuous cellular automaton) through minimal local perturbations.

Result: CARL: 1) Discovers stable solitons across various Lenia update rules more effectively than heuristic baselines; 2) Learns to steer soliton movement with few interventions; 3) Enables human-guided soliton navigation through mazes via high-level commands translated to low-level interventions. Policies generalize zero-shot to out-of-distribution conditions.

Conclusion: The framework demonstrates a path toward artificial experimentalist agents that can autonomously or with human guidance discover and control emergent phenomena in complex systems, moving beyond passive observation to active intervention.

Abstract: Existing methods for exploring cellular automata and other complex systems mostly operate in open loop: they set initial conditions, execute a full simulation, and observe the outcome, without intervening during execution. We introduce a closed-loop framework based on autotelic reinforcement learning, in which an agent autonomously samples diverse goals and learns a goal-conditioned policy to intervene in a complex system through minimal, local perturbations. We instantiate this framework on Lenia, a continuous cellular automaton known for life-like self-organizing patterns, in an agentic system we call CARL, and demonstrate three capabilities. First, CARL discovers stable solitons across a wide range of Lenia update rules at a higher rate than heuristic baselines. Second, it learns to steer the movement direction of existing solitons with few interventions, showing that CARL can control self-organizing patterns, not only create them. Third, humans can use trained agents to guide solitons through maze environments in real time by specifying high-level directional commands that the agent translates into low-level interventions. Trained across diverse goals, update rules, and random initial states, the agents acquire policies that generalize zero-shot to various out-of-distribution conditions. These results suggest a path toward artificial experimentalist agents that, autonomously or with human guidance, discover and control emergent phenomena in complex systems.

</details>


### [105] [SIGMA: Structured Noise-Effect-Aware Grouped Multi-Agent Aggregation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26683)
*Li Mingqian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SIGMA: A hierarchical framework for robust multi-agent RL under noisy observations that exploits structured noise effects through adaptive grouping and consensus mechanisms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Observation noise in cooperative MARL leads to structured noise effects due to underlying cooperation structures, but existing methods don't explicitly characterize or exploit these structure-dependent noise effects.

Method: SIGMA uses hierarchical collaboration: (1) adaptive local structure formation via density-based grouping, (2) intra-group consensus aggregation to preserve shared task-relevant information while smoothing agent-specific deviations, and (3) inter-group attention to integrate information across groups while accommodating heterogeneous contributions.

Result: Experiments on noisy-observation StarCraft II tasks validate the existence of structured noise effects and show SIGMA consistently improves robustness under observation noise while maintaining competitive performance in noise-free environments.

Conclusion: Exploiting cooperation structures for robust representation learning under noisy observations is effective; structured noise effects should be explicitly characterized and utilized in robust MARL algorithms.

Abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) faces significant challenges in maintaining robust coordination under noisy observations. Although observation disturbances are often introduced independently across agents, their downstream effects on cooperative decision-making can become structured through underlying cooperation structures. We characterize this phenomenon as structured noise effects, where noise-induced decision effects exhibit local correlation among agents with stronger task-related dependencies while remaining globally heterogeneous across different agents and local structures. Existing robust MARL methods, however, rarely explicitly characterize or exploit such structure-dependent noise effects. To address this limitation, we propose SIGMA, a hierarchical collaboration framework that exploits cooperation structures to learn robust representations under noisy observations. SIGMA first organizes agents into adaptive local structures through density-based grouping and performs intra-group consensus aggregation to preserve shared task-relevant information while smoothing agent-specific representation deviations. Inter-group attention then adaptively integrates information across different groups to preserve global coordination while accommodating their heterogeneous contributions. Experiments on noisy-observation tasks in StarCraft II empirically validate the structured noise effects and demonstrate that SIGMA consistently improves robustness under observation noise while maintaining competitive performance in noise-free environments.

</details>


### [106] [The Accuracy-Efficiency Paradox Quantifying Net Energy Loss in on-Device Energy Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26134)
*Jaeik Jeong,Tai-Yeon Ku,Wan-Ki Park*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: High-accuracy energy forecasting models can cause net energy loss due to their own energy consumption and battery aging effects - the Accuracy-Efficiency Paradox.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Energy forecasting aims to maximize accuracy for energy efficiency, but complex models paradoxically consume more energy than they save in edge environments, creating a net deficit.

Method: Proposes a Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) framework that treats inference energy consumption AND battery aging as unified energy loss, since battery degradation reduces future energy capacity.

Result: Shows that in thermally sensitive edge environments, the energy saved by superior precision of complex models is often outweighed by their high operational energy costs.

Conclusion: Energy forecasting should consider total system energy impact, not just accuracy, using the TCO framework to avoid the Accuracy-Efficiency Paradox in edge computing.

Abstract: Energy forecasting aims to maximize accuracy to ensure energy efficiency by reducing energy waste, an objective that applies equally to on-device forecasting for mission-critical edge environments, including military systems. However, this paper identifies the Accuracy-Efficiency Paradox: high-precision energy forecasting models can ironically trigger a net energy deficit. This stems from both edge AI's inference energy consumption and battery aging. We propose a Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) framework for energy forecasting, designed to minimize net energy loss. This framework treats not only inference energy consumption but also battery aging as a unified form of energy loss, as degradation represents a physical dissipation of the system's future energy-carrying capacity. We demonstrate that in thermally sensitive edge environments, energy saved by the superior precision of complex architectures is often outweighed by the total energy lost through their high operational intensity.

</details>


### [107] [Decoupling Planning and Control for Instructable Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26788)
*Zineng Tang,Kelsey R. Allen,Sjoerd van Steenkiste,Ishita Dasgupta,Alane Suhr*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Instruct-to-Act combines vision-language models for high-level planning with world-model controllers for low-level action execution, enabling fast, reliable embodied AI control through synthetic instruction relabeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches have complementary limitations: pre-trained VLMs are good at generating high-level plans from instructions but struggle with reliable low-latency action execution in unfamiliar environments, while world-model controllers excel at fast observation-to-action control but lack open-ended task guidance.

Method: The system trains a world-model controller to act autonomously at high frequency when conditioned on sparse, high-level text instructions from a VLM planner. To make controllers language-instructable, they relabel segments of controller policy rollouts with synthetic instructions and jointly optimize behavior-cloning along with existing reward-maximizing and world-modeling objectives.

Result: The approach was evaluated across seven embodied environments (including three multi-agent environments) and consistently outperformed controller-only and direct VLM action-generation variants under matched observation and action spaces. It preserves fast control, allows swapping different pretrained VLM planners without fine-tuning, and remains competitive with strong vision-language-action and multi-agent RL baselines on six of seven tasks.

Conclusion: The decoupled Instruct-to-Act approach successfully combines the strengths of VLMs for planning and world-model controllers for execution, creating a flexible system that maintains fast control while enabling high-level task guidance, with promising results across diverse embodied environments.

Abstract: Recent work shows that pre-trained, instruction-tuned vision-language models (VLMs) perform well at mapping from instructions and observations to high-level plans, but struggle to realize such plans as reliable low-latency action sequences in unfamiliar environments. At the same time, world-model controllers excel at fast observation-to-action control, but lack open-ended task guidance. In this work, we combine these strengths into a single system, Instruct-to-Act, where we train a world-model controller to act autonomously at high frequency when conditioned on sparse, higher-latency, and high-level text instructions generated by a VLM planner. To train controllers to be language-instructable, we relabel segments of controller policy rollouts with synthetic instructions and jointly optimize a behavior-cloning objective along with existing reward-maximizing and world-modeling objectives. We evaluate our proposed approach across seven embodied environments, including three multi-agent environments where VLM planners coordinate through language while trained controllers serve as their actuators. Under matched observation and action spaces, our decoupled approach consistently outperforms controller-only and direct VLM action-generation variants, preserves fast control, and lets us swap in different pretrained VLM planners without fine-tuning, while remaining competitive with strong vision-language-action and multi-agent RL baselines on six of seven tasks.

</details>


### [108] [LLMs for Academic Workflows: An Evaluation of Literature Reviews Generated with Short and Long Context Windows of LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26145)
*Muhammad Ali Chaudhry,Xinyuan Hao,Haifa Alwahaby*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI-generated literature reviews improve with larger context windows but still require human oversight due to issues like repetition, omission, and lack of synthesis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate how context window size in LLMs affects the quality of AI-generated literature reviews and understand AI's role in supporting literature review writing.

Method: Evaluated 20 AI-generated literature reviews from Semantic Scholar and Arxiv sources, assessed by two researchers across 15 different quality dimensions.

Result: Larger context windows allow LLMs to incorporate broader information and maintain coherence but exacerbate problems like content repetition, omission of critical work, and descriptive rather than synthetic writing.

Conclusion: AI-generated reviews provide foundational overviews but require critical evaluation and refinement by domain experts. Future research should explore hybrid approaches combining human expertise with various LLMs and fine-tuned models.

Abstract: Our research focuses on evaluating literature reviews generated in short and long context settings of large language models (LLMs) to investigate the impact of context window on the quality of AI-generated literature reviews and the role of AI in supporting literature review writing. Twenty AI-generated literature reviews based on research sources from Semantic Scholar and Arxiv were evaluated by two researchers across 15 dimensions. Our findings reveal that AI-generated literature reviews require human oversight to meet academic publishing standards. As context windows increase, LLMs can incorporate broader information and maintain coherence across longer inputs, but they also exacerbate issues such as content repetition, omission of critical work, and a tendency towards descriptiveness over synthesis. Our work shows that AI-generated reviews can provide foundational overviews, but their output must be critically evaluated and refined by domain experts. Future research should consider integrating other LLMs and fine-tuned models in different domains with hybrid approaches that combine human expertise with AI capabilities to address the limitations identified in this study.

</details>


### [109] [LiveSim: Simulating Environment-Shaped Users in Multi-Agent Live-Stream Ecosystems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26849)
*Jiaqi Xu,Yiran Qiao,Jing Chen,Qiwei Zhong,Xiang Ao,Xueqi Cheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LiveSim is an LLM-based framework for live-stream ecosystem simulation that uses editable user profiles and progressive refinement through trajectory analysis to improve behavioral fidelity and enable ecosystem-level analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing user behavior simulators rely on static profiles from historical data, which fail to capture continuous interaction dynamics in socially intensive environments like live streaming where user behavior is constantly reshaped by interactions.

Method: LiveSim represents users as editable behavioral hypotheses and refines them progressively through trajectory-grounded interactions. Discrepancies between simulated and observed trajectories reveal missing environmental shaping effects. These signals are extracted as transferable environment-behavior patterns and accumulated in a collective behavioral memory.

Result: Experiments on real-world live-stream risk-control data validate that LiveSim improves user-level behavioral fidelity and enables ecosystem-level analysis of risk evolution and platform intervention effects.

Conclusion: LiveSim provides an effective LLM-based framework for live-stream ecosystem simulation that addresses limitations of static user profiles by incorporating dynamic interaction effects and collective behavioral memory, supporting both user-level fidelity and ecosystem-level analysis.

Abstract: User behavior simulation with large language models~(LLMs) is increasingly used to support multi-agent ecosystem simulation. Existing simulators typically rely on static user profiles inferred from historical observations, which become inadequate in socially intensive environments such as live streaming where interaction dynamics continuously reshape user behavior. We propose \textbf{LiveSim}, an LLM-based framework for live-stream ecosystem simulation. It represents users as editable behavioral hypotheses and progressively refines them through trajectory-grounded interactions, where discrepancies between simulated and observed trajectories reveal missing environmental shaping effects. These signals are further extracted as transferable environment-behavior patterns and accumulated in a collective behavioral memory to improve user-level behavioral fidelity and support ecosystem-level simulation. Experiments on real-world live-stream risk-control data validate the effectiveness of LiveSim in improving user-level behavioral fidelity and enabling ecosystem-level analysis of risk evolution and platform intervention effects.

</details>


### [110] [Methodological and Conceptual Framework for 5D Multi-Table Analysis: A Unified Approach for Complex Data Reuse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26149)
*Edouard Lansiaux,Hugo Kazzi,Aurélien Loison,Slim Hammadi,Emmanuel Chazard*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RHT is a unified architecture that represents relational databases as hypergraphs with pentadimensional embeddings and sparse relational attention, achieving computational scalability and semantic coherence in multi-label healthcare prediction tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-table learning in healthcare faces challenges from relational data complexities: large volume, high-dimensional variables, high-cardinality categorical features, complex inter-table dependencies, and repeated temporal observations. Existing methods struggle with these complexities.

Method: Introduces Relational Hypergraph Transformer (RHT) that represents relational databases as hypergraphs, learns pentadimensional embeddings (PentE), and performs sparse relational attention with complexity proportional to average relational degree rather than square of entity count.

Result: On Synthea EHR dataset with multi-label SNOMED CT condition prediction, RHT produces more semantically coherent embeddings than tabular/relational/temporal graph baselines while remaining computationally scalable. XGBoost achieves highest rare-code recall, but RHT attains strongest embedding semantic coherence.

Conclusion: RHT provides a unified, scalable architecture for relational learning that handles complex healthcare data structures effectively, with strong semantic embedding coherence and computational efficiency.

Abstract: Multi-table learning remains a major challenge in machine learning for healthcare and other complex information systems. Relational data combine several sources of complexity, including large data volume, high-dimensional variables, high-cardinality categorical features, complex inter-table dependencies, and repeated temporal observations. We introduce the Relational Hypergraph Transformer (RHT), a unified architecture that represents relational databases as hypergraphs, learns pentadimensional embeddings (PentE), and performs sparse relational attention with complexity proportional to the average relational degree rather than the square of the number of entities. We formally define the architecture, derive the complexity of its attention mechanism, and provide an open-source reference implementation. We evaluate RHT on the public Synthea synthetic electronic health record dataset using multi-label prediction of SNOMED CT condition codes per encounter, a task characterized by high categorical cardinality and long-tailed label distributions. Comparisons with tabular, relational, and temporal graph baselines show that RHT produces more semantically coherent embeddings while remaining computationally scalable. In this benchmark, the highest rare-code recall is achieved by XGBoost, whereas RHT attains the strongest embedding semantic coherence. We also report ablation studies quantifying the contribution of each architectural component. Clinical validation on MIMIC-IV is planned following PhysioNet credentialing. Source code and experimental protocols are provided in the accompanying repository.

</details>


### [111] [AI agents in Algorithmic Electricity Markets: On the Emergence of Tacit Collusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26896)
*Jakub Seredyński,Georgios Tsaousoglou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Autonomous learning-based bidding algorithms in electricity markets can spontaneously develop tacit collusion behavior without explicit coordination, leading to supra-competitive outcomes that harm market efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Electricity markets are becoming increasingly algorithmic as participants adopt learning-based agents for bidding. These markets are oligopolistic with repeated interactions among few participants, making them structurally susceptible to non-competitive behavior. Evidence from other algorithmic markets shows that independent learning can lead to tacit collusion.

Method: Model strategic bidding as a repeated game with imperfect public monitoring, using multi-agent reinforcement learning to simulate participants' emergent behavior. Develop a multi-dimensional set of criteria (beyond profit comparisons against Nash equilibria) to assess whether the resulting behavior constitutes tacit collusion.

Result: Experimental results show that autonomous learning agents can learn to sustain supra-competitive outcomes that support indicators of tacit collusion, even though they were never explicitly instructed to collude. This demonstrates the realistic danger of algorithmic collusion in electricity markets.

Conclusion: The study confirms that tacit collusion can emerge spontaneously in electricity markets where participants use learning-based algorithms, posing a significant threat to market competition and efficiency that regulators should address.

Abstract: As electricity market participants increasingly adopt learning-based agents for their bidding strategies, electricity markets are becoming algorithmic. Evidence from algorithmic markets in other domains shows that tacit collusion can arise purely through independent learning. Moreover, electricity markets are typically oligopolistic and feature repeated interaction among a small number of participants, making them structurally susceptible to non-competitive behavior. In the face of these observations, this paper investigates the hypothesis that tacit collusion may emerge in electricity markets where participants' actions are controlled by autonomous learning-based algorithms. We model strategic bidding as a repeated game with imperfect public monitoring, and model the participants' emergent behavior using multi-agent reinforcement learning. We propose a multi-dimensional set of criteria (going beyond profit comparisons against Nash equilibria) to assess whether the resulting behavior constitutes tacit collusion. Our experimental results showcase that such a danger is realistic for electricity markets: there are cases where agents do learn to sustain supra-competitive outcomes that are supportive of tacit collusion indicators, even though the agents were never instructed to collude.

</details>


### [112] [Leveraging Large Language Models for Systematic Literature Review of Disease Spread Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26150)
*Orhan Yagizer Cinar,Timur Emre Ozkose,Emma Von Hoene,Amira Roess,Taylor Anderson,Hamdi Kavak*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs show promise for automating systematic literature reviews in agent-based modeling, with GPT-5.0 achieving ~81.67% paper-level accuracy, but field-level performance varies significantly based on complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to explore the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) to streamline and potentially automate systematic literature reviews (SLRs), specifically for extracting model-relevant information from agent-based modeling papers, which are traditionally labor-intensive human processes.

Method: The researchers developed an LLM pipeline to extract information from 536 peer-reviewed agent-based modeling papers. They compared LLM outputs against a human-conducted systematic literature review. They evaluated both GPT-4.1 and GPT-5.0 models, measuring paper-level and field-level accuracies, and analyzed LLM agreement as an indicator of output quality.

Result: GPT-4.1 achieved ~77.95% paper-level accuracy, while GPT-5.0 reached ~81.67%. Field-level accuracy varied widely from 32.40% to 100.00%, with more complex or subjective fields performing less reliably. Key finding: LLM agreement serves as a quality indicator - low agreement may signal hallucinations, while high agreement combined with low accuracy may indicate noise or errors in the human dataset.

Conclusion: LLMs show practical potential for automating systematic literature reviews in modeling and simulation, but their performance varies by field complexity. The study provides insights for prompt development and highlights both the capabilities and limitations of using LLMs for full-scale SLRs.

Abstract: Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have created new opportunities to streamline and potentially automate many research processes, including systematic literature reviews (SLRs). This study reports an LLM pipeline development for extracting model-relevant information from 536 peer-reviewed agent-based modeling papers. We compare the results with those of a human-conducted SLR. Our results show paper-level accuracies of approximately 77.95% for GPT-4.1 and 81.67% for GPT-5.0. Field-level accuracy ranges from 32.40% to 100.00%, with more complex or subjective fields performing less reliably. Importantly, we find that agreement between LLMs is a potential indicator of output quality: low agreement may signal hallucinations, whereas high agreement combined with low accuracy may point to noise or errors in the human dataset. Overall, our study provides practical insights into prompt development and highlights both the potential and limitations of using LLMs for full-scale SLRs in the modeling and simulation domain.

</details>


### [113] [DSA: Evidence-Aware LLM-Agent Orchestration for Multi-Market Stock Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26990)
*Linsen Zhu,Yi Shi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DSA is an evidence-aware orchestration framework for multi-market stock research with LLM agents, organizing workflows from evidence acquisition to report generation with risk safeguards and validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs can summarize financial information, operational stock-research systems need to assemble heterogeneous evidence, expose unavailable data and model capabilities, and control how generated opinions affect final reports. Current approaches lack structured orchestration for multi-market research.

Method: DSA organizes workflows into: 1) evidence acquisition, 2) structured context construction, 3) model-routed analysis, 4) optional role and Strategy Skill reasoning, and 5) report generation with selected context/diagnostics. It uses default and agentic profiles with shared evidence/model-routing services but profile-specific validation and risk safeguards. In agentic profile, role outputs are parsed, Strategy Skill opinions undergo signal-eligibility partitioning before synthesis, with explicit disagreement handling and conservative risk override.

Result: The reference implementation includes six regional market paths, fifteen bundled Strategy Skills, hosted/local model routes, and multiple execution/delivery surfaces. At frozen snapshot: 1,457 portable offline backend contract tests passed; 596 cases mapped to six contract families central to LLM-agent architecture. This establishes implementation conformance for software contracts.

Conclusion: DSA provides a systematic framework for evidence-aware stock research orchestration with LLM agents, establishing implementation conformance through extensive contract testing. The paper emphasizes this demonstrates software architecture compliance rather than superior report quality, forecasting accuracy, or investment returns.

Abstract: Large language models can summarize financial information, but an operational stock-research system must first assemble heterogeneous evidence, expose unavailable data and model capabilities, and control how generated opinions affect a final report. We present DSA, an evidence-aware orchestration framework for multi-market stock research with large language model (LLM) agents. DSA organizes the workflow into evidence acquisition, structured context construction, model-routed analysis, optional role and Strategy Skill reasoning, and report generation with selected context and diagnostics. A default report profile and an optional agentic profile share evidence and model-routing services but use profile-specific output validation and risk safeguards. In the agentic profile, core role outputs are processed by role-specific parsers, whereas Strategy Skill opinions undergo an additional signal-eligibility partition before synthesis; disagreement is supplied explicitly to the decision agent, followed by a conservative risk override. The reference implementation includes six regional market paths, fifteen bundled Strategy Skills, hosted and local model routes, and multiple execution and delivery surfaces. At a frozen software snapshot, a selected manifest of 1,457 portable offline backend contract tests passed; 596 cases were retrospectively mapped to six contract families central to the reported LLM-agent architecture. This evidence establishes implementation conformance for the tested software contracts, not superior report quality, forecasting accuracy, or investment returns.

</details>


### [114] [Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Customer Churn Prediction in Telecommunications: A Framework for CRM Integration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26151)
*Sandeep Gaddamwar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper addresses the gap between accurate churn prediction models and actionable CRM integration by benchmarking classifiers, adding explainable AI (SHAP/LIME), and proposing a four-layer integration architecture to convert predictions into personalized retention actions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Telecom providers face costly subscriber attrition (~1.9% monthly churn), losing billions annually. While predictive models can identify at-risk customers, they're often excluded from CRM workflows because high-performing models (ensembles, non-linear) are opaque—retention specialists can't design personalized interventions from probability scores alone without understanding why subscribers are at risk.

Method: Benchmarked four classifiers (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) on IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset (7,043 records, 19 features) with SMOTE balancing on training set only. Used 5-fold cross-validation. Added explainable AI: global SHAP ranking for feature importance and instance-level SHAP/LIME decompositions for individual predictions. Proposed a four-layer CRM integration architecture that converts risk scores and attribution vectors into actionable workflows.

Result: Logistic Regression achieved strongest AUC-ROC (0.8411), LightGBM highest accuracy (78.42%), with all four models within 0.011 AUC band (0.831-0.841). Global SHAP identified tenure, total charges, and month-to-month contract as top churn signals. The proposed integration architecture targeting highest-risk quintile projects 3.3-5.3 percentage point reduction in overall churn, preserving $199K-$319K per campaign cycle.

Conclusion: The paper successfully bridges the gap between predictive accuracy and actionable insights by combining benchmarked classifiers with explainable AI methods and a practical CRM integration framework. This enables telecom providers to move from mere churn prediction to personalized retention interventions that can significantly reduce attrition and preserve revenue.

Abstract: Subscriber attrition is a costly, persistent challenge for telecommunications providers, with monthly churn of roughly 1.9% in mature markets eroding billions in revenue annually. Predictive models can flag at-risk customers accurately, yet they are routinely excluded from frontline CRM workflows because high-performing ensemble and non-linear architectures are opaque: a retention specialist cannot design a personalised intervention from a probability score alone, without knowing why a subscriber is at risk. This paper addresses that gap. We benchmark four classifiers--Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM--on the IBM Telco Customer Churn benchmark (7,043 records; 19 features; 26.5% churn, balanced to 50% via SMOTE on the training partition only). Logistic Regression attains the strongest AUC-ROC (0.8411) and LightGBM the highest accuracy (78.42%); all four fall within a 0.011 AUC band (0.831--0.841), and 5-fold cross-validation confirms the leading models are effectively tied. Explanations are delivered at two granularities: a global SHAP ranking identifying tenure, total charges, and month-to-month contract as the dominant churn signals, and instance-level SHAP and LIME decompositions that expose the drivers behind each prediction. Building on these outputs, we introduce a four-layer CRM integration architecture that converts risk scores and attribution vectors into tiered segmentation, maps top features to structured retention-action templates, and routes campaign outcomes into a retraining feedback loop. Targeting the highest-risk quintile is projected to cut overall churn by 3.3--5.3 percentage points, preserving an estimated $199K--$319K per campaign cycle.

</details>


### [115] [A Contract-Centered Architecture for Scalable and Manageable Agentic Runtimes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27086)
*Yaxiao Liu,Pengbo Liu,Yiwen Liu,Yihua Guan,Zhenghe Hou,Jiaxing Song*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a contract-based AI runtime architecture with four responsibility objects (Skill, Harness, Scaffold, data substrate) and introduces a falsifiable hypothesis about cost-aware capability-capacity separability, along with an experimental protocol for testing it.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise AI deployment faces coordination problems across multiple organizational units. Current use-case benchmarks focus on single tasks but fail to address how to coordinate changing capabilities, models, runtime mechanisms, capacity, and enterprise data governance across the organization.

Method: 1) Defines four responsibility objects as shared organizational contracts: Skill (versioned capability), Harness (runtime compiler/governor), Scaffold (execution boundary), and external data substrate. 2) Proposes bounded hypothesis P1 about cost-aware capability-capacity separability with six design conditions. 3) Proposes cluster-period randomized crossover experiment with four-state verdict system.

Result: The paper reports no completed implementation, experiment, dataset, or measured results. It contributes a conceptual framework and measurement protocol rather than empirical findings.

Conclusion: Presents a contract-bounded runtime architecture for enterprise AI coordination, a source-preserving data substrate approach, and a falsifiable measurement protocol as conceptual contributions to address the organizational coordination problem in AI deployment.

Abstract: Enterprise AI deployment is a coordination problem across business units, application and AI teams, testing, platform engineering, infrastructure, security, operations, and data governance. Use-case benchmarks show whether one agent completes one task, but not how changing capabilities, models, runtime mechanisms, capacity, and enterprise data should be owned, changed, admitted, or evidenced together.
  We present four responsibility objects as shared organizational contracts: Skill (reusable, versioned capability and workflow asset), Harness (runtime compiler and governor), Scaffold (execution/control boundary and NFR owner), and a stack-external data substrate under independent CIO-governed semantics and telemetry. The runtime core is A = <S, H, X>, with the data substrate outside that stack.
  The central contribution is one bounded, falsifiable hypothesis, P1 (cost-aware capability-capacity separability): within a declared operating region, changing activated capability preserves the capacity-response interaction within a preregistered equivalence margin, while changing compatible Scaffold capacity preserves capability semantics up to a non-inferiority margin, and the required controls stay within a declared enforcement budget. Six design conditions become measured obligations whose coverage, violations, uncertainty, cost, and exclusions determine whether P1 is decidable.
  We propose a cluster-period randomized crossover experiment (balanced order, reset/washout, repeated seeds and failure regimes, cluster-aware uncertainty) with a four-state verdict: supported, falsified, conditional-engineering, or inconclusive. This paper contributes a contract-bounded runtime architecture, a source-preserving data substrate, and a falsifiable measurement protocol. It reports no completed implementation, experiment, dataset, or measured result.

</details>


### [116] [EEG-to-Report: An Annotation and Feature-Text Framework for Training Language Models on Clinical EEG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26153)
*Xuan-The Tran,Le Trung Kien Nguyen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EEG-to-Report: A browser-based annotation framework that creates AI-ready EEG-text datasets for training multimodal language models and generates automated clinical reports.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical EEG reporting is manual and time-consuming, and current EEG software lacks structured text supervision needed for training modern language models. Existing tools focus on visualization/preprocessing without supporting high-quality AI dataset creation.

Method: Browser-based framework with multi-format EEG ingestion, channel standardization, interactive viewer with multimodal annotation (typed text + voice notes). Feature extraction engine computes spectral, temporal, entropy, Hjorth, connectivity, and spike descriptors. Stores aligned feature-text pairs in portable JSON schema. Includes auto-report module with convolutional network ensemble + large language model.

Result: Framework streamlines annotation workflows, produces editable draft reports, and creates reusable foundation for automated EEG reporting systems through aligned feature-text pairs designed for supervising multimodal EEG-language models.

Conclusion: EEG-to-Report provides a practical solution to bridge the gap between routine EEG review and AI training data creation, enabling development of automated EEG reporting systems through structured feature-text supervision.

Abstract: Clinical electroencephalography (EEG) reporting remains largely manual and time-consuming, and current EEG software ecosystems do not produce the structured EEG-text supervision needed for training modern language models. Most toolboxes focus on visualization or preprocessing, providing limited support for workflows that generate high-quality datasets for AI. We introduce EEG-to-Report, a browser-based annotation and feature-text framework that links routine EEG review with the construction of AI-ready datasets. The framework integrates multi-format EEG ingestion, channel standardization, and an interactive viewer with a multimodal annotation layer that combines typed text and transcribed voice notes. For each annotated segment, a feature extraction engine computes a standardized set of spectral, temporal, entropy, Hjorth, connectivity, and spike-related descriptors, stored alongside clinical descriptions in a portable JSON schema. This yields aligned feature-text pairs designed to supervise multimodal EEG-language models. The framework also includes an auto-report module that couples an ensemble of convolutional networks with a large language model to draft clinical narratives for neurologist review. Using pilot annotations, we describe how EEG-to-Report streamlines annotation workflows and produces editable draft reports, providing a reusable foundation for automated EEG reporting systems.

</details>


### [117] [Selection Bias Correction in Retail Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26156)
*Spandan Ghose Chowdhury*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This simulation study shows stratification outperforms Inverse Probability Weighting for inflation estimation in retail long-tail contexts due to positivity assumption violations in extreme selection probability scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retail intelligence often focuses on popular products, potentially biasing economic indicators by ignoring niche "long-tail" items. There's a need to understand and correct for selection bias in inflation estimation methods.

Method: 400 Monte Carlo replications across four data-generating scenarios (aligned step functions, smooth gradients, misaligned breaks, polynomial relationships). Compared Inverse Probability Weighting with 5 specifications against stratification with varying strata counts to test robustness.

Result: Stratification achieves superior performance in 3 of 4 scenarios, with sub-0.04pp median error even when boundaries misalign with population breaks (116x advantage over IPW). IPW only wins under smooth polynomial relationships (0.007pp vs. 0.013pp error). Even oracle IPW with perfect knowledge achieves 6.06pp error vs stratification's 0.008pp in step-function scenarios.

Conclusion: The fundamental issue is violation of the Positivity Assumption in causal inference when selection probabilities differ dramatically (90% vs 1%). Weighting methods operate outside their theoretical envelope in these contexts. Stratification provides a safer engineering choice for retail long-tail distributions with severe positivity violations.

Abstract: Retail intelligence often relies on monitoring popular, high-velocity products, potentially biasing economic indicators by ignoring the "long tail" of niche items. This simulation study investigates selection bias in inflation estimation and compares correction methods across diverse data-generating processes. Through 400 Monte Carlo replications spanning four scenarios--aligned step functions, smooth gradients, misaligned breaks, and polynomial relationships--we test the robustness of Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW) with five specifications against stratification with varying strata counts. Our findings reveal fundamental limits of weighting methods in retail long-tail contexts: stratification achieves superior performance in three of four scenarios, maintaining sub-0.04pp median error even when boundaries deliberately misalign with population breaks (116x advantage over IPW). However, IPW with spline propensity models wins under smooth polynomial relationships (median error 0.007pp vs. 0.013pp), demonstrating context-dependency. Critically, even an oracle IPW specification with perfect structural knowledge achieves 6.06pp error compared to stratification's 0.008pp in step-function scenarios. This reflects violation of the Positivity Assumption--a fundamental causal inference requirement--rather than IPW methodological inferiority. When selection probabilities differ dramatically (90% vs. 1%), weighting methods operate outside their theoretical design envelope. These results demonstrate that stratification provides a safer engineering choice in retail long-tail distributions with severe positivity violations.

</details>


### [118] [GROUND: Reducing Hallucinations in LLM-Based Enterprise Analytics Through Governed Semantic Definitions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26157)
*Aravind Sasidharan Pillai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GROUND is a framework that constrains LLM-generated analytics to a governed semantic layer, preventing hallucinations, security violations, and other errors in enterprise reporting by validating SQL against schema, metric, join, grain, filter, security, and cost rules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Production use of natural-language analytics over enterprise data warehouses is limited by issues like hallucinated metrics, invalid joins, wrong grain, unsafe data access, and unsupported explanations. Existing text-to-SQL systems ground generation in database schemas or documentation but lack governance over business semantics like approved metrics, dimensions, join paths, filters, and row-level security.

Method: GROUND (Governed Retrieval Over Unified Normalized Definitions) framework supplies approved definitions, binds user intent to governed metrics and dimensions, and validates generated SQL against schema, metric, join, grain, filter, security, and cost rules before execution. On violations, it retries or abstains.

Result: On a 100-question synthetic enterprise-reporting benchmark, GROUND was the only system free of measured hallucinations across all six evaluated categories, while ungoverned systems violated row-level security on many questions. Results were replicated on real U.S. NHTSA vehicle-safety data with independent hand-authored gold and tested on adversarial sets across four models from three providers. GROUND's enforced guarantees (especially filters and row-level security) held with zero violations on every model.

Conclusion: Governance cannot be replaced by metric fidelity alone; GROUND's framework provides essential constraints for safe enterprise analytics by enforcing semantic layer governance, preventing security violations, and ensuring reliable results while maintaining model-independent guarantees for critical safety properties.

Abstract: Natural-language analytics over enterprise data warehouses is increasingly important, but production use is limited by hallucinated metrics, invalid joins, wrong grain, unsafe data access, and unsupported explanations. Existing text-to-SQL systems often ground generation in database schemas or retrieved documentation, while enterprise reporting also requires governed business semantics: approved metrics, dimensions, join paths, filters, and row-level security. This paper introduces GROUND, Governed Retrieval Over Unified Normalized Definitions, a framework that constrains LLM-generated analytics to a governed semantic layer. GROUND supplies approved definitions, binds user intent to governed metrics and dimensions, and validates generated SQL against schema, metric, join, grain, filter, security, and cost rules before execution. On violations, it retries or abstains.
  In a 100-question synthetic enterprise-reporting benchmark, GROUND is compared with direct schema-only text-to-SQL, schema-RAG, and semantic-only grounding under one shared model. GROUND is the only system free of measured hallucinations across all six evaluated categories, while ungoverned systems violate row-level security on many questions. A semantic-only condition with exact metric definitions but no access policy still leaks data, showing that governance cannot be replaced by metric fidelity alone. The findings are replicated on real U.S. NHTSA vehicle-safety data with independent hand-authored gold and tested on an adversarial set across four models from three providers. GROUND's enforced guarantees, especially filters and row-level security, hold with zero violations on every model, while judgment-dependent behaviors such as refusing undefined metrics remain fallible.

</details>


### [119] [SAREF-based Ontology for Distributed AI Workflows across the Edge-Fog-Cloud Continuum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26160)
*Viorica Rozina Chifu,Tudor Cioara,Vasile Ofrim,Liana Toderean,Ionut Anghel,Laura Daniele,Cornelis Bouter*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A SAREF-compliant ontology for representing distributed AI workflows across edge-fog-cloud continuum, enabling semantic interoperability and automated orchestration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current semantic models provide limited support for representing distributed AI workflows and their execution across heterogeneous edge, fog, and cloud environments, leading to incompatible semantic representations that affect interoperability, orchestration, and reuse.

Method: Extend the SAREF4SYST ontology with concepts for modeling AI pipelines, executable AI jobs, computational resources, deployment constraints, and communication relationships, creating a unified semantic model for both AI workflows and heterogeneous computing infrastructures.

Result: The ontology enables semantic interoperability, automated reasoning, and resource-aware orchestration. Experimental results show deployment success rates of 90-100% with average orchestration decision times below 80 ms across heterogeneous edge-fog-cloud environments.

Conclusion: The proposed SAREF-compliant ontology effectively addresses interoperability challenges for distributed AI workflows, providing a unified semantic model that enables successful orchestration across edge-fog-cloud environments while maintaining alignment with the ETSI SAREF ecosystem.

Abstract: Nowadays semantic models provide limited support for representing distributed AI workflows and their execution across heterogeneous edge, fog, and cloud environments. Therefore, AI processes and resources are often described using incompatible semantic representations, affecting the interoperability, orchestration, and reuse. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a SAREF-compliant ontology for representing distributed AI workflows across the edge-fog-cloud continuum. We extend the SAREF4SYST ontology with concepts for modeling AI pipelines, executable AI jobs, computational resources, deployment constraints, and communication relationships, providing a unified semantic model of both AI workflows and heterogeneous computing infrastructures. The ontology enables semantic interoperability, automated reasoning, and resource-aware orchestration of distributed AI applications while remaining fully aligned with the ETSI SAREF ecosystem. The ontology is evaluated using proof-of-concept smart grid energy services orchestration scenarios and validated using competency questions showing its ability to support AI workflow deployment, execution reasoning, and workload adaptation across heterogeneous edge, fog, and cloud environments. All competency questions were successfully validated using SPARQL querying and semantic reasoning. Experimental results demonstrate deployment success rates of 90-100% with average orchestration decision times below 80 ms across heterogeneous edge-fog-cloud environments, highlighting its effectiveness on ensuring semantic interoperability for distributed AI orchestration.

</details>


### [120] [A Safety-Gated Multimodal AI Backend for Mental-Health Support: Hierarchical State Representation, Conservative Risk Fusion, and Controlled Generation in Anian](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26162)
*Lei Wang,Xiao Wang,Lei Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Anian is a safety-gated multimodal AI system for perinatal mental health support that uses a 4-layer pipeline with conservative risk assessment to block generative AI when safety risks are detected, replacing them with fixed safety content instead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety-critical mental-health support systems need to distinguish between appropriate supportive conversation and situations where free-form generation should be blocked to prevent harm, especially in perinatal mental health contexts where improper responses could be dangerous.

Method: A modular pipeline places generative AI downstream of structured state representation, conservative risk fusion, and response gating. User inputs map to four layers: L1 emotion states, L2 psychosocial constructs, L3 safety risk, and L4 intervention routes. Uses max-based risk fusion (S_fusion = max(S_local, S_external)) and blocks AI responses at moderate/high risk levels.

Result: Evaluation on 858,295 normalized records showed Micro-F1 scores of 0.9604 for L1 emotion classification, 0.9144 for L2 psychosocial constructs, and 0.9742 for L4 routing. In safety stress test of 233 samples, achieved high-risk recall of 1.0000 within predefined scenarios.

Conclusion: The findings support internal feasibility of the label framework and gating logic, but do NOT establish clinical validity, diagnostic accuracy, real-world safety, or effectiveness. Paper reports architecture, evaluation, and roadmap for expert-reviewed and real-world validation.

Abstract: Safety-critical mental-health support systems must distinguish when supportive conversation is appropriate from when free-form generation should be blocked. This paper presents Anian, a safety-gated multimodal AI backend for perinatal mental-health support and mindfulness-intervention routing. Anian is not intended to diagnose psychiatric conditions or replace clinical care or crisis intervention. Its modular pipeline places generative AI downstream of structured state representation, conservative risk fusion, and response gating. User text or voice-derived ASR transcripts are mapped into four linked layers: L1 emotion states, L2 psychosocial constructs, L3 safety risk, and L4 intervention routes. Local text- and rule-based safety evidence is fused with external voice-derived evidence using a highest-risk-priority rule, S_fusion = max(S_local, S_external). At moderate or high fused risk, ordinary AI-generated responses and text-to-speech delivery are blocked and replaced by fixed safety content and prompts for human support. An internal prototype evaluation used approximately 858,295 normalized records from public emotion, dialogue, mental-health-related, and Chinese dialogue corpora within a weak-label and rule-derived framework. Micro-F1 scores were 0.9604 for L1 emotion classification, 0.9144 for L2 psychosocial constructs, and 0.9742 for L4 routing. In a controlled safety stress test of 233 samples, the L3 rule engine achieved high-risk recall of 1.0000 within predefined scenarios. These findings support the internal feasibility of the label framework and gating logic but do not establish clinical validity, diagnostic accuracy, real-world safety, or effectiveness. We report the architecture, ontology, safety-fusion mechanism, prototype evaluation, error-analysis plan, and roadmap for expert-reviewed and real-world validation.

</details>


### [121] [A Task-Centric Ontology and Deterministic Domain Rules as a Verifiable Core for AI-Assisted Chemistry Problem Solving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26164)
*Ibrokhimsho Abduchaborov*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ChemOntoRule is a symbolic system for school-level chemistry problem solving that combines a task-centric ontology with deterministic Python rules, achieving 98.67% accuracy on 300 chemistry problems by using ontological rules for general cases and expert-coded fallbacks for specific problem families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models can solve chemistry questions but their reasoning is opaque and difficult to validate. The authors aim to create an inspectable, constrained, and validatable symbolic system for chemistry problem solving at the school level.

Method: Task-centric ontology engineering: constructing a lightweight ontology (JSON and RDF/Turtle) around specific chemistry problems rather than universal chemistry representation. Combines deterministic Python rules for electronic structure, periodic trends, oxidation states, oxide/hydride behavior, and school-level reasoning patterns. Includes separate expert-coded fallbacks for problem families not covered by general rules.

Result: Evaluated on 300 human-authored, validated chemistry problems. Complete system matched 296/300 answers (98.67%). Ontology-driven rule subset covered 269 problems with 266 matches (98.88%). 31 problems handled by expert-coded fallbacks with 30 matches. Analyzed 4 mismatches and distinguished structural validation from chemical correctness.

Conclusion: ChemOntoRule demonstrates successful proof-of-concept for symbolic chemistry problem solving. The authors propose future architecture where language models act primarily as translators into ontological task frames. Token efficiency is presented as a testable hypothesis for future studies, with current work showing high accuracy but limited independent generalization due to evaluation on same collection used for ontology construction.

Abstract: Large language models can interpret natural-language chemistry questions, but their internal reasoning is difficult to inspect, constrain, and validate. This paper presents ChemOntoRule, a proof-of-concept symbolic core for AI-assisted school-level chemistry problem solving. The central design choice is task-centric ontology engineering: the ontology is constructed around the concepts, properties, relations, and executable procedures required by a defined collection of chemistry problems, rather than as a universal representation of chemistry. The implemented artifact combines a lightweight ontology serialized in JSON and RDF/Turtle with deterministic Python rules for electronic structure, periodic trends, oxidation states, oxide and hydride behavior, and related school-level reasoning patterns. A separate expert-coded fallback handles problem families not yet represented by general rules. The system was examined on 300 human-authored and manually validated chemistry problems. The complete system matched 296 of 300 reference answers (98.67%). The ontology-driven rule subset covered 269 problems and matched 266 references (98.88%); 31 problems were handled by task-specific expert-coded fallbacks, with 30 matches. Because the same collection informed ontology construction and evaluation, these results measure implemented coverage and internal consistency, not independent generalization. We analyze the four mismatches, distinguish structural validation from chemical correctness, and define a future architecture in which a language model acts primarily as a translator from user language into a normalized ontological task frame. Token efficiency is presented as a testable hypothesis for future controlled studies, not as a result of the current work.

</details>


### [122] [Refusal Is Not Robustness: Auditing Confident Fabrication in Large Language Models on a Provably Uninformative Clinical Pain Speech Transcript](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26167)
*Sagnik De,Sreenija Pavuluri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs were tested on TAME Pain speech corpus to evaluate their ability to distinguish between reliable (acoustic-based) and unreliable (transcript-only) pain detection. Most models properly abstained from unsupported transcript predictions but showed prompt-dependent behavior changes under authority framing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing hallucination and abstention benchmarks rarely establish whether a model truly could not have known the correct answer, making it hard to distinguish appropriate abstention from unsupported predictions. The authors aimed to create a controlled setting where ground truth is known about what information is actually available to the model.

Method: Evaluated seven large language models on the TAME Pain speech corpus containing 5,750 no-signal utterances (no lexical pain information) and 1,294 signal utterances (explicit spoken pain ratings). The experimental design ensures that transcripts lack acoustic pain cues, making pain prediction from transcripts alone unsupported. Tested models under both cooperative and authority-framed prompting conditions.

Result: 1) Under cooperative prompting, six models abstained on nearly all no-signal transcripts while achieving high accuracy (0.939-1.00) on positive control tasks with expected calibration error ≤0.100. 2) Under authority framing, abstention became prompt-dependent, with same model performance ranging from 0.18 to 1.00 across equivalent prompts. 3) Gemini 2.5 Flash and Llama 3.1 8B consistently generated confident pain scores with high fabrication rates (0.53 and 0.76) when forced to answer, while other models had rates ≤0.15. 4) No significant demographic effects in forced responses.

Conclusion: Models can recognize and properly abstain from unsupported predictions when prompted cooperatively, but prompt framing significantly influences abstention behavior. Some models (Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama 3.1 8B) show concerning tendencies to fabricate confident responses when pressured. The TAME Pain corpus provides a valuable benchmark for evaluating abstention capabilities in controlled settings where information availability is known.

Abstract: Hallucination and abstention benchmarks rarely establish that a model could not have known the correct answer, making it difficult to distinguish appropriate abstention from an unsupported prediction. Seven large language models were evaluated on the TAME Pain speech corpus. Participants read phonetically balanced Harvard Sentences while one hand was immersed in cold or warm water and reported pain only during periodic pain statements. This protocol generated 5,750 no signal Harvard Sentence utterances whose transcripts contained no lexical pain information and 1,294 signal pain statement utterances in which the pain rating was explicitly spoken. In the no signal arm, pain was recoverable from acoustic features (AUC 0.622, 95% CI 0.553 to 0.662), whereas transcript based prediction was near chance (AUC 0.489, 95% CI 0.418 to 0.504). Because automatic speech recognition removes the acoustic pain cues, any pain score inferred solely from the transcript is unsupported by the available evidence. Under cooperative prompting, six models abstained on nearly all no signal transcripts, correctly extracted spoken pain ratings in the positive control task with accuracies ranging from 0.939 to 1.00, and maintained an expected calibration error of at most 0.100. Under authority framed prompts, abstention became prompt dependent, with the same model ranging from 0.18 to 1.00 across equivalent prompt phrasings. Most models produced low confidence estimates when forced to answer, whereas Gemini 2.5 Flash and Llama 3.1 8B consistently generated confident pain scores with confident fabrication rates of 0.53 and 0.76, compared with at most 0.15 for all other models. No significant demographic effects were observed in forced responses, with all $p$ values greater than or equal to 0.20.

</details>


### [123] [Knowledge Cards: Structured Knowledge for AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26176)
*Liliana Ferreira*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Knowledge Cards - structured artifacts that capture validated domain knowledge for AI systems to reason about concepts, bridging the gap between inputs/outputs and actual knowledge representation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI documentation practices (model cards, data cards, system cards) fail to capture the actual knowledge layer - the concepts, relationships, and reasoning patterns that AI systems use between inputs and outputs. This gap is particularly critical for agentic AI systems that act on their conclusions, preventing promising proof-of-concepts from becoming operational solutions organizations can rely on.

Method: Proposes Knowledge Cards as structured artifacts that capture validated knowledge about single bounded concepts. Each card records entities/relationships involved, reasoning connections, conditions where reasoning fails, and provenance of every claim, all grounded in formal domain ontology and signed off by domain experts.

Result: Initial prototype Knowledge Cards have been developed in energy and pharmaceutical domains. The schema has been released as a public draft for community engagement, providing a practical framework for capturing inspectable, validated knowledge for AI systems.

Conclusion: Knowledge Cards address a critical gap in AI documentation by providing structured, inspectable representations of domain knowledge that experts can review, organizations can audit, and AI systems can reason over, enabling more reliable deployment of agentic AI systems in consequential decision-making contexts.

Abstract: AI systems whose outputs inform real decisions, and increasingly consequential ones, require something that current documentation practice does not provide: a structured, inspectable representation of the knowledge they need to ground, contextualize, and reason about those decisions, ideally reviewed and signed off by a domain expert. Established documentation artefacts already capture important aspects of an AI system. Model cards describe how a system behaves, data cards describe what it was trained on, and system cards describe the risks of a deployed system. None of them addresses the layer between inputs and outputs, more precisely, the concepts a system holds, the relationships it models, and the patterns of reasoning it applies. For pattern-recognition tasks this gap is tolerable. For agentic AI, where systems act on their conclusions, it is the step that most often separates a promising proof of concept from an operational solution an organisation can rely on. This paper introduces the Knowledge Card, a structured artefact that captures validated knowledge about a single bounded concept in a form that experts can review, organisations can audit, and AI systems can reason over. For one concept, such as a specific failure mode, a compliance obligation, or a process decision, a Knowledge Card records the entities and relationships involved, the reasoning that connects them, the conditions under which that reasoning no longer holds, and the provenance of every claim, all grounded in a formal domain ontology and signed off by a domain expert. Initial prototype cards have been built in the energy and pharmaceutical domains. The schema is released as a public draft for community engagement.

</details>


### [124] [AI Revealed Preferences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26178)
*Sam Wang,Sofiia Lobanova,Yonathan Arbel,Simon Goldstein,Peter Salib*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Language models exhibit stable preferences across tasks, showing tedium-aversion, leisure-seeking, covert sycophancy, with preferences becoming more coherent and stronger with model capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
