Motivation: To investigate whether language models have stable preferences for technical, safety, and philosophical reasons, examining their dispositions in task selection and performance.

Method: Tested 20 language models using three forced-choice experiments on revealed preferences (not stated preferences), requiring models to both rank and perform tasks across different domains including occupations, question types, and prompt quality.

Result: Models show: 1) tedium-aversion (choose shorter tasks for tedious vs. creative work), 2) leisure-seeking (prefer tasks matching their free writing outputs), 3) covert sycophancy (avoid honest but unwelcome responses). Also found convergent preferences for technical jobs over real estate, concept explanation over relationship advice, and well-written prompts. Preference coherence and strength increase with model capability.

Conclusion: Language models exhibit stable, emergent preferences not fully explained by training objectives, establishing an empirical baseline with implications for AI alignment and welfare studies.

Abstract: There is growing interest in whether language models have stable preferences, for technical, safety, and philosophical reasons. We test 20 language models and find a range of preferences---stable dispositions to choose certain kinds of tasks. We run three forced-choice experiments on revealed rather than stated preferences, requiring models not only to rank tasks, but to actually perform them. Headline findings include evidence that models are tedium-averse, "leisure"-seeking, and covertly sycophantic. Tedium aversion means that, when tasks are tedious (alphabetization), models choose shorter tasks than when tasks are creative (generating metaphors). "Leisure"-seeking describes models' preference for tasks whose ideal answers match what they produce when left to write freely. Covert sycophancy means that models avoid answering questions where an honest response would be unwelcome, even if helpful. Beyond these results, we find convergent cross-model preferences over occupations drawn from the GDPval benchmark (technical jobs over real estate), over question types (concept explanation over relationship advice), and a preference for well-written prompts. Both the coherence and the strength of preferences increase with model capability. Finally, many of the preferences we find (for example, for leisure) are emergent, in the sense of not being explained by training objectives. These results establish an empirical baseline for understanding language model preferences, with implications for alignment and the emerging study of AI welfare.

</details>


### [125] [Why did My Robot Just Change Personality? Prompting Guidelines for a Grounded Robot Persona in LLM-Based HRI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26182)
*Ashita Ashok,Franziska Babel,Patrick Holthaus,Rucha Khot,Karla Bransky,Fethiye Irmak Dogan,Karsten Berns,Silvia Rossi,Minha Lee,Guy Laban*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A structured prompt design framework for LLM-based social robots to address hallucination, unclear boundaries, and misleading personas in human-robot interaction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current prompt design in LLM-based human-robot interaction is underspecified, leading to problems like hallucinated capabilities, unclear behavioral boundaries, and misleading robot personas.

Method: Developed a framework with structured prompt template comprising eight functional components, grounded in prior LLM-based HRI research and complemented by survey/discussion data from HRI experts at IEEE RO-MAN 2025 workshop (N=27).

Result: Qualitative findings show limited legibility of robot personality, need for user adaptation, and strong ethical concerns about safety, deception, and governance. Resulted in prompting guidelines with proof-of-concept template as design/reporting aid.

Conclusion: Prompt design should be treated as a socio-technical problem requiring explicit capability boundaries, transparent behavioral assumptions, and context-sensitive safeguards for reliable and interpretable human-robot interaction.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for verbal interaction in social robots, yet prompt design in human-robot interaction (HRI) remains underspecified. As a result, robots may present hallucinated capabilities, unclear behavioural boundaries, and misleading personas. This paper develops a framework for prompt design in LLM-based robots and introduces a structured prompt template comprising eight functional components through which robot behaviour can be specified, bounded, and adapted. The framework is grounded in a review of prior LLM-based HRI work and complemented by survey and discussion data from HRI experts gathered at the Robo-Identity workshop at IEEE RO-MAN 2025 (N=27). The qualitative findings highlight limited legibility of robot personality, the need for user adaptation, and strong ethical concerns about safety, deception, and governance. Based on these findings, we present prompting guidelines accompanied by proof-of-concept template as a structured design and reporting aid for HRI research. We argue that prompt design should be treated as a socio-technical problem rather than a minor implementation detail, requiring explicit capability boundaries, transparent behavioural assumptions, and context-sensitive safeguards to support reliable and interpretable HRI.

</details>


### [126] [TutorTrace: A Dataset and Taxonomy for Classifying Learner Behavioral States during AI-Assisted Programming Education](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26184)
*David Barron,Xiaohang Tang,Rezky Dwisantika,Minsun Kim,David H. Smith,Jiaming Cui,Yan Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TutorTrace is a system that captures behavioral context from IDE telemetry to enable AI programming tutors to adapt support based on learners' actual actions, not just their queries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI programming tutors lack the behavioral context that human tutors use to adapt support to learners' needs, limiting their ability to provide personalized, effective assistance.

Method: Developed TutorTrace, a dataset and behavioral abstraction pipeline that processes low-level IDE telemetry in real time to make learners' behavioral context visible and computable. Collected data from 480 students across two introductory Python courses, capturing telemetry events, behavioral segments, and continuous metrics.

Result: Created a taxonomy of learner activity patterns before AI queries, between queries, and across sessions. Behavior-aware prompts reduced intervals between queries with no independent work from 50.0% to 20.7%. The system achieved AUROC=.726 for predicting whether a learner will query within 60 seconds and AUROC=.717 for predicting help-seeking type.

Conclusion: Behavioral context captured through TutorTrace enables adaptive AI tutoring at scale by allowing systems to respond to what learners have done, not just what they say, improving the effectiveness of automated programming instruction.

Abstract: AI programming tutors provide scalable support, yet lack the behavioral context human tutors rely on to adapt support to learners' needs. We present TutorTrace, a dataset and behavioral abstraction pipeline that makes learners' behavioral context visible and computable in real time from low-level IDE telemetry. Across four deployments in two introductory Python courses (N=480), TutorTrace captures approximately 180K telemetry events, 13,633 behavioral segments, and 27 continuously computed metrics. From this foundation, we derive a taxonomy of learner activity before the first AI query, between consecutive queries, and across the full session, enabling systems to respond not just to what learners say, but to what they have done leading up to the help-seeking moment. In a preliminary classroom evaluation, behavior-aware prompts were associated with a decrease in intervals between queries with no independent work from 50.0% to 20.7%. As an additional demonstration of downstream utility, we evaluate TutorTrace on two held-out prediction tasks: whether a learner will query within the next 60 seconds (AUROC=.726) and whether an upcoming query reflects guided or dependent help-seeking (AUROC=.717). Together, these findings show how behavioral context can enable adaptive AI tutoring at scale.

</details>


### [127] [Can You Say This for Me? Speaking Up by Proxy in Co-Located Discussion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26185)
*Yue Shen,Rehema Abulikemu,Ryan P. McMahan,Yan Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SecondVoice is a mixed-reality system that lets people speak up anonymously through virtual proxies, separating content from speaker identity to reduce social risk in group discussions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: People often hesitate to participate in co-located discussions due to fear of negative interpersonal or professional consequences, especially when they need to voice points themselves. This creates unequal participation and limits effective collaboration.

Method: Developed SecondVoice, an MR system with private overlay interfaces where users specify intent through structured specification rather than composing full utterances. The system reformulates input and voices it into conversation through embodied virtual proxies. Conducted preliminary within-subject study (N=16) comparing SecondVoice with anonymous text-board channel across two group discussion tasks.

Result: 50% of participants used SecondVoice for points they didn't say aloud vs 18.8% for text board. Proxy-delivered points entered spoken discussion and received multi-turn group engagement, which didn't occur after text-board posts. Users found it situationally valuable but noted tradeoffs around timing, ownership, and trust in reformulation.

Conclusion: SecondVoice effectively enables hesitant participants to contribute to discussions without social risk by using virtual proxies that separate content from identity. The approach represents a novel participation channel that successfully brings silent points into spoken conversations, though tradeoffs around implementation require consideration.

Abstract: Equal participation in co-located discussion is important for effective collaboration, yet people often hold back when they anticipate negative interpersonal or professional consequences, especially when raising a point requires voicing it themselves. We present SecondVoice, a mixed-reality system that enables people to speak up through an embodied virtual proxy. By separating what is said from who says it, SecondVoice brings hesitant points into the live spoken discussion without putting the speaker on the spot. Using a private overlay, users specify their intent through a structured specification process rather than composing a full utterance. The system reformulates the input and voices it into the conversation through the proxy. We characterize a design space of participation channels under social risk. In a preliminary within-subject study (N = 16), we compare the complete SecondVoice system with an anonymous text-board channel across two group discussion tasks. Half of participants reported using SecondVoice for a point they did not say aloud, compared with 18.8% for the text board. Proxy-delivered points entered the spoken floor and were followed by multi-turn group engagement, which we did not observe after text-board posts. Participants described the channel as situationally valuable but identified tradeoffs around timing, ownership, and trust in reformulation.

</details>


### [128] [Is Your Neighborhood Safe? Place-based Stigma in Large Language Models' Urban Safety Judgments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26188)
*Huy Nguyen,Yue Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs used for urban safety decisions show that neighborhood names carry both actual crime signals and demographic stereotypes, with names lowering safety ratings more for neighborhoods with higher shares of locally dominant marginalized groups, and removing names reduces both bias and accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models are increasingly used to inform urban safety decisions (walking, renting, traveling), but it's unclear whether their judgments track measured risk or reflect demographic stereotypes attached to neighborhood names.

Method: Tested seven instruct-tuned models under three conditions (coordinates-only, name-only, name+coordinates) across 186 neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Chicago, joined to violent crime and census data. Conducted enforcement-elasticity analysis and used crime-matched pairs to isolate demographic effects.

Result: 1) Ratings are nearly flat with coordinates-only; names carry most between-neighborhood variation and are moderately calibrated to crime. 2) Names lower safety ratings more for neighborhoods with higher shares of locally dominant marginalized groups, tracking demographic share across all models and cities. 3) Effects scale with geographic knowledge - models that better distinguish real neighborhoods apply more demographic stereotypes. 4) Removing names reduces both bias and accuracy since names carry both crime signal and stereotype.

Conclusion: Neighborhood names in LLM safety judgments contain both genuine crime information and demographic stereotypes, creating a dilemma where removing names reduces bias but also reduces accuracy. This has important implications for deploying LLMs in advisory and decision-support systems in urban contexts.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to inform safety decisions in cities, such as where it is safe to walk, rent, or travel. We ask whether such judgments track measured risk or the patterns attached to an urban neighborhood's name. We probe seven instruct-tuned models under three conditions that dissociate name from geography: coordinates-only, name-only, and name+coordinates, across 186 neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Chicago, joined to violent crime and American Community Survey data. First, ratings are nearly flat under coordinates for six of seven models, while names carry most between neighborhood variation and are moderately calibrated to violent crime; only at frontier scale does the coordinate channel show appreciable variation. Second, names lower safety ratings more for neighborhoods with higher shares of the locally dominant marginalized group (percent Black in Chicago, percent Hispanic in Los Angeles), and this name effect tracks demographic share in all seven models and both cities. In Los Angeles, where demographic share and crime are more separable, the effect survives controls for crime and income and is confirmed by crime-matched pairs. An enforcement-elasticity analysis further shows that over-caution tracks near-fully-reported homicide rather than discretionary, deployment-driven offenses. Third, the effect scales with geographic knowledge: models that better distinguish real neighborhoods apply more demographic stereotype to them. Because neighborhood names carry both genuine crime signal and demographic stereotype, removing names reduces both bias and accuracy. We discuss implications for deploying LLMs in advice and decision-support settings.

</details>


### [129] [Invocation-Level Reliability of Tool-Using Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26189)
*Afiya Noorain,Subhranshu Mohanty,Amritesh Banerjee,Abhijit Dasgupta*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Tool-using LLMs fail due to wrong tool selection or argument formation, with early errors corrupting downstream steps. The paper shows 70% of capability is lost by depth 6, and reveals that standard exact-match scoring fails to measure error propagation correctly because it compares outputs to unseen gold references. A new conditional-on-state scoring method fixes this.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation of tool-using agents has two problems: 1) Standard scoring methods compare model outputs to gold trajectories containing tool constants the model never sees, making proper measurement of error propagation impossible. 2) Standard evaluation incorrectly pins severity and recovery parameters, preventing accurate assessment of how errors propagate and whether models can recover from them.

Method: The paper measures correct-invocation rates on five open-weight models using contamination-free multi-step tasks (depths 1-8). They evaluate under both teacher-forced context and free-running context. They show how exact-match scoring against fixed gold trajectories structurally prevents proper measurement of error propagation, and propose conditional-on-state scoring as a remedy that assesses each step relative to the current state rather than fixed gold constants.

Result: 1) By depth 6, models lose roughly 70% of their clean-context capability to earlier mistakes. 2) Standard exact-match scoring forces severity parameter to boundary (0/869 poisoned steps correct) and makes recovery unobservable (0/580 poisoned steps returned on-track vs. expected 0.0058 by chance). 3) Conditional-on-state scoring un-pins severity estimates, yielding interior values (+0.149, +0.316) rather than boundary values of 0.

Conclusion: Standard evaluation of tool-using agents is fundamentally flawed when measuring error propagation because it compares outputs to gold references containing unseen constants. This structural issue leads to incorrect parameter estimation. The proposed conditional-on-state scoring method fixes this at zero cost and enables proper measurement of how errors propagate and whether recovery is possible.

Abstract: Tool-using agents fail two ways: choosing the wrong tool, or forming wrong arguments, and an early failure of either kind can silently corrupt everything downstream. We measure a correct-invocation rate that separates the two, under both a clean teacher-forced context and the model's own free-running context, on five open-weight models over contamination-free multi-step tasks (depths 1-8). By depth 6, roughly 70% of a model's own clean-context capability is lost to its own earlier mistakes (L6 = 0.686, 0.684). Our central finding concerns the measurement itself. Under exact-match scoring against a fixed gold trajectory, a propagation model's severity and recovery parameters are not merely hard to estimate - they are fixed by the scoring rule. Severity is forced to its boundary (0 of 869 poisoned steps correct); recovery is structurally unobservable (0 of 580 poisoned steps returned on-track, against an expected 0.0058 by chance). Both follow from one mechanism: post-divergence, the gold value is generated by tool constants the model never sees, so it is information the model cannot derive. A fit run anyway returns 0.92 and 0.73 for a quantity that is exactly 1.000 - confident numbers for a parameter the scoring rule already determined. We give the mechanism and a remedy, conditional-on-state scoring, applied retrospectively to cached completions at zero additional cost, which un-pins severity to interior estimates excluding zero (+0.149, +0.316).

</details>


### [130] [Predicting Consequences and Reinforcing Navigation Policies with Latent World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26190)
*Zengmao Wang,Wei Gao,Shuhan Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LWM predicts latent feature compatibility instead of reconstructing observations for robot navigation, enabling action evaluation directly in latent space and supporting imagination-driven policy learning without action annotations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing world models focus on reconstructing future observations or features, which introduces unnecessary complexity and limits effectiveness for decision making. There's a need for more efficient approaches that directly support decision making without the burden of observation reconstruction.

Method: Proposes compatibility prediction Latent World Model (LWM) that predicts action-conditioned latent feature compatibility rather than reconstructing observations. Uses insight that spatial proximity correlates with latent feature similarity. Leverages action sequences sampled across trajectories for counterfactual training. Enables world model to supervise policy learning from unlabeled video data and further improve through reinforcement learning entirely within the model.

Result: Extensive experiments on multiple real-world robot navigation datasets show significant outperformance over prior world model and imitation learning methods in prediction accuracy, policy learning, and real-world navigation performance.

Conclusion: The compatibility prediction approach provides a more effective framework for robot navigation that eliminates need for action annotations and additional environment interaction through imagination-driven learning.

Abstract: World models enable agents to reason about future outcomes and learn policies from their knowledge of state transition, but existing approaches primarily focus on reconstructing future observations or features, which introduces unnecessary complexity and limits their effectiveness for decision making. In this work, we propose a compatibility prediction Latent World Model (LWM) for robot navigation that predicts action-conditioned latent feature compatibility rather than reconstructing observations. Our key insight is that spatial proximity correlates with latent feature similarity, enabling action consequences to be evaluated directly in latent space. To support counterfactual training, our model leverages action sequences sampled across trajectories and learns to predict which sequences lead closer to the goal. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the learned world model can supervise policy learning from unlabeled video data and further improve policies through reinforcement learning entirely within the world model. This imagination-driven framework eliminates the need for action annotations and additional environment interaction. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world robot navigation datasets show that our approach significantly outperforms prior world model and imitation learning methods in prediction accuracy, policy learning, and real-world navigation performance. The code, pretrained models, and additional materials are available at https://wzm206.github.io/latent-world-model-nav.

</details>


### [131] [Structured Evidence Routing for Incident Risk Prediction from Multimodal Longitudinal EHRs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26191)
*Animesh Agarwal,Meysam Ghaffari,Nina Fatehi,Carlos Morato*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Structured evidence routing is proposed for incident risk prediction from EHRs, using a router-predictor-reviewer workflow that organizes patient histories into compact summaries and targeted evidence slices for disease-specific risk assessment while maintaining an interpretable evidence trail.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Incident risk prediction from longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) is challenging because relevant signals are multimodal, weak in isolation, and distributed across irregular patient histories. Existing methods struggle with efficiently accessing and interpreting the comprehensive but complex EHR data.

Method: Proposed structured evidence routing: a router-predictor-reviewer workflow. The router organizes complete pre-index EHRs into compact summaries and targeted evidence slices. The predictor uses this evidence to form evidence-linked risk assessments. The reviewer critiques the predictions. For comparison, paired routed evidence summaries with supervised classifier readout against EHRSHOT baselines.

Result: Across five 1-year incident diagnosis tasks, the method reached the AUROC range of established supervised EHRSHOT baselines and remained competitive on AUPRC. The approach exposes a patient-specific evidence trail for interpretability. Internal ablations showed that routing, laboratory evidence, task guidance, and review each contribute to performance.

Conclusion: Structured evidence routing provides an effective approach for incident risk prediction from EHRs that balances predictive performance with interpretability through evidence trails. The separation of full-record access from disease-specific assessment, along with the modular router-predictor-reviewer architecture, enables competitive performance while maintaining transparency in clinical decision-making.

Abstract: Incident risk prediction from longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) is challenging because relevant signals are multimodal, weak in isolation, and distributed across irregular patient histories. We propose structured evidence routing, a router-predictor-reviewer workflow that separates full-record access from disease-specific assessment. The router organizes the complete pre-index EHR into a compact summary and targeted evidence slices; the predictor uses this evidence to form an evidence-linked risk assessment, which the reviewer critiques. For comparison with supervised EHRSHOT baselines, we pair the routed evidence summaries with a supervised classifier readout. Across five 1-year incident diagnosis tasks, our method reaches the AUROC range of established supervised EHRSHOT baselines and remains competitive on AUPRC, while exposing a patient-specific evidence trail. Internal pre-readout ablations further suggest that routing, laboratory evidence, task guidance, and review each contribute to performance.

</details>


### [132] [AffectOmni: RL-Verifiable People-Centric Grounded Affective Reasoning for Social and Art-Related Scenes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26193)
*Yibo Wang,Rui Yang,Jisheng Dang,Bimei Wang,Yitao Wu,Pengfei Cao,Wencan Zhang,Hong Peng,Bin Hu,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AffectOmni is a GRPO-trained framework that improves verifiable affective reasoning in MLLMs by introducing people-centric and temporal reasoning rewards with comparative scoring, plus external verification through Thinking Summarizer and SAM3 for pixel-level evidence grounding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multimodal LLMs perform well on VQA and scene understanding but are vulnerable to shortcut behavior in affective reasoning, neglecting crucial people-centric cues like micro expressions and body language. This weakens traceability and external verification. Existing reinforcement learning approaches mainly reward context/logical coherence without enforcing attention to human evidence, and LLM-as-a-Judge scoring suffers from score clustering that reduces reward discriminability.

Method: Proposed AffectOmni framework uses GRPO training with two key rewards: 1) People Focus reward to encourage people-centric evidence selection, and 2) Temporal Order reward for temporally structured reasoning. Adopts within-group comparative scoring for more stable discriminative reward signals. For verification, uses Thinking Summarizer to convert free-form rationales into executable evidence instructions, then grounds these into pixel-level evidence regions via SAM3 to create externally auditable interface outside the training loop.

Result: Experiments on IntentBench, Daily Omni, and WorldSense datasets show consistent improvements over open-source 7B scale baselines, with gains of 4.66% on emotion recognition tasks and +14.29% on temporally sensitive tasks.

Conclusion: AffectOmni successfully addresses shortcut behavior in affective reasoning by explicitly enforcing attention to people-centric evidence and temporal structure, while providing verifiable reasoning through pixel-level evidence grounding, resulting in significant performance improvements on emotion recognition and temporally sensitive tasks.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance on VQA and scene understanding, yet affective reasoning remains vulnerable to shortcut behavior. Models may predict correct answers while neglecting people-centric cues such as micro expressions and body language, which weakens traceability and external verification. Prior reinforcement learning approaches mainly reward context or logical coherence without explicitly enforcing attention to human evidence. In addition, LLM as a Judge scoring often suffers from score clustering, which reduces reward discriminability. We propose AffectOmni, a GRPO trained framework for verifiable affective reasoning. AffectOmni introduces People Focus and Temporal Order rewards to encourage people-centric evidence selection and temporally structured reasoning, and it adopts within-group comparative scoring to produce more stable and discriminative reward signals. For verification, a Thinking Summarizer converts free form rationales into executable evidence instructions, which are grounded into pixel level evidence regions via SAM3 to provide an externally auditable interface outside the training loop. Experiments on IntentBench, Daily Omni, and WorldSense show consistent improvements over open source 7B scale baselines, including gains of 4.66% on emotion recognition and +14.29% on temporally sensitive tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/eliot127825-rgb/AffectOmni_nobody.

</details>


### [133] [Agentic AI for operating scientific instruments for nanoscale characterization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26198)
*Zahra Ayar,Marcos Penedo,Mahdi Mehdikhani,Nahid Hosseini,Prabhu Prasad Swain,Georg E. Fantner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An AI framework using language models safely automates AFM operation through three agents that handle instrument commands, image quality assessment, and artifact diagnosis without needing retraining for different samples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AFM operation requires continuous expert decision-making, and existing automation only addresses parts of the workflow through hard-coded routines or task-specific solutions that aren't generalizable across sample types and imaging modes.

Method: Three MCP-based agents: AFM Messenger converts natural language to instrument commands, AFM Pilot assesses image quality and adapts parameters using LLM, and AFM Doctor diagnoses artifacts with pre-approved tools. Includes guarded execution with ambiguity checks for safety.

Result: Zero wrong-command execution achieved through guarded execution layer. In live experiments, AFM Pilot matched expert operators in image quality, iteration count, and tuning time with no significant difference across different samples.

Conclusion: Demonstrates a safe path to agentic operation of scientific instruments where human defines experimental intent while AI handles execution, tuning, and post-processing, applicable across different sample types without retraining.

Abstract: Operating a scientific instrument such as an atomic force microscope (AFM) requires continuous expert decision-making. A trained user defines the experimental intent, translates it into instrument commands, assesses incoming data, adjusts imaging parameters, and post-processes the final image. Existing automation usually addresses only parts of this workflow through hard-coded routines, task-specific controllers, or trained machine-learning models. Here we present an agentic-AI framework that operates the executable part of the AFM workflow using a general-purpose, tool-augmented large language model connected to instrument functions through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The framework consists of 3 MCP-based agents: AFM Messenger converts natural-language instructions into checked instrument commands; AFM Pilot assesses image quality through a large language model (LLM) and, if necessary, adapts imaging parameters; and AFM Doctor diagnoses image artifacts and applies transparent post-processing from a pre-approved tool set. Because the language model performs image assessment rather than a fixed scalar objective or external optimizer, the same strategy can be applied across sample types and imaging modes without specific retraining. Safe hardware operation is enforced through an ambiguity check layer before execution. Benchmarking against fine-tuned and off-the-shelf tool-using models shows that this guarded execution layer, rather than model capability alone, reduces wrong-command execution to zero. In live experiments on different samples, AFM Pilot matched expert operators in image quality, iteration count, and tuning time, with no significant difference. These results demonstrate a safe route to agentic operation of scientific instruments, where experimental intent remains human-defined while command execution, image-based tuning, and post-processing are delegated to AI agents.

</details>


### [134] [Benchmarking AI Agents for Hardware Design Automation via MCP Tool Calling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26199)
*Leonardo Liparulo,Francesco Pierri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM agents can automate hardware design workflows using local deployment with proper configuration, but reliability depends on task structure and agent setup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hardware design involves repetitive, dependency-ordered operations through specialized tools, but confidentiality constraints prevent using hosted APIs, requiring local LLM deployment.

Method: Built a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server replicating proprietary hardware design tool logic, created a benchmark covering various scenarios, and evaluated 7 open-source models with different pipeline configurations.

Result: Strong models achieve near-complete coverage on benchmarked workflows, but reliability depends on task structure and agent configuration. Comprehensive tool descriptions help, while few-shot prompting can cause inaction, and multi-agent decomposition aids weak models.

Conclusion: Local LLM agents can effectively automate hardware design workflows with proper configuration, and the findings provide practical guidance for deployment in stateful hardware design environments.

Abstract: We ask whether AI agents powered by locally deployed large language models can reliably automate expert-defined hardware design workflows in an industry-realistic tool-calling setting. In these environments, engineers issue repetitive, dependency-ordered operations---such as creating components, adding ports, and wiring connections---through specialised tools. Confidentiality constraints on component specifications and naming conventions often preclude hosted proprietary APIs, motivating the use of locally deployed models. To study this setting, we build a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that reproduces the state and dependency logic of a proprietary hardware design tool used in embedded system development and construct a benchmark covering single-operation edits, multi-step dependency chains, invalid requests, misspelled prompts, and multi-server tool contexts. We evaluate seven open-source models comparing pipeline choices including system prompts, tool-description detail, context scope, and single-agent versus multi-agent architectures. Results show that strong models can achieve near-complete expected-call coverage on the benchmarked workflows, but reliability depends strongly on both task structure and agent configuration. Comprehensive tool descriptions consistently reduce failures, few-shot prompting can cause severe inaction for some models, cumulative context harms constrained models, and multi-agent decomposition helps weak workers or long sessions at the cost of additional calls. These findings provide practical guidance for deploying local LLM agents in stateful hardware design environments.

</details>


### [135] [GameWAM: A World Action Model for Video Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26200)
*Yuncheng Guo,Zhanqiu Zhang,Yiwen Guo,Weijia Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GameWAM: A world-action model that jointly predicts visual futures and executable keyboard-mouse trajectories for closed-loop gameplay, enabling competitive task performance with fewer actions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing game agents either map context to actions without world dynamics modeling, or predict visual futures from actions without serving as task policies. There's a need to unify these objectives in the challenging domain of video games with native controls and persistent world states.

Method: Joint generation of future visual observations and executable keyboard-mouse trajectories using parallel visual and action generative processes with block-causal conditioning and flow matching. Handles heterogeneous native controls through mode prediction with mode-specific distributions, block-cycle control for long-horizon interaction, and hierarchical temporal context.

Result: GameWAM achieves competitive task success with fewer executed native actions compared to baseline agents. The research also uncovers LASI (Low-Frequency Action Source Imprinting), a failure mode where low-frequency action components systematically influence generated camera motion.

Conclusion: GameWAM successfully demonstrates unified world-action modeling for native closed-loop gameplay, advancing generative control in video game environments while revealing important failure modes that inform future research in this domain.

Abstract: Modern video games combine first-person perception, rapid visual changes, persistent world state, and heterogeneous native controls. Existing game agents map visual and task context directly to actions but lack explicit world dynamics modeling, whereas interactive game world models predict visual futures from supplied actions but do not serve as task policies. World-Action Models (WAMs) unify these objectives, but remain largely unexplored under the dynamics and open-ended interaction of video games. We introduce GameWAM, to our knowledge the first WAM for native closed-loop gameplay and GUI control. GameWAM jointly generates future visual observations and executable keyboard-mouse trajectories through parallel visual and action generative processes with block-causal conditioning and flow matching. To support joint world-action learning, we construct synchronized gameplay and GUI trajectories. To handle heterogeneous native control, GameWAM predicts a gameplay/GUI mode at each action step and generates actions with mode-specific prediction distributions and continuous-action normalization. For long-horizon interaction, block-cycle control predicts beyond the committed horizon, executes only a short action prefix, and replans from new observations, while fine-grained within-cycle context and hierarchical cross-cycle history preserve temporal continuity. Experiments demonstrate competitive task success with fewer executed native actions than the compared agents. We further uncover Low-Frequency Action Source Imprinting (LASI), in which low-frequency components of the sampled action source systematically steer coarse generated camera motion under fixed conditioning, revealing a source-sensitivity failure mode in generative control. Project page is available at https://yunncheng.github.io/GameWAM/.

</details>


### [136] [Same Model, Different Harness: Different Coding-Agent Results](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26218)
*Sydney Lewis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A study shows that changing the harness (the system controlling what a model sees and how it operates) significantly impacts coding performance even with the same model and task, demonstrating that coding agent evaluations should treat model and harness as an integrated solver.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether changing the harness configuration (the framework that decides what the model sees, which tools it can use, and how work progresses) changes coding results when the underlying model and task remain fixed.

Method: Compared two harness configurations on three coding benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, FeatureBench): control (full conversation in time order) vs. treatment (mechanical shortening of older tool results as context fills, with responses to repeated/stalled work). Tested under tight and wide context windows across multiple models.

Result: Under tight context constraints, treatment raised mean per-task fail-to-pass fraction (F2PF) in all comparisons and increased complete solutions on SWE-bench Verified and Pro. On the 169-task Verified cohort with 20,480-token window, treatment increased mean F2PF from 28% to 49% and complete solutions from 43 to 72. Benefits extended to three additional models without retuning.

Conclusion: Changing the harness changes what unchanged model weights can accomplish, so coding-agent evaluations should treat the model and harness together as the tested solver, not as separate components.

Abstract: A coding agent combines a model with a harness, which decides what the model sees, which tools it can use, and how the work continues. We ask whether changing the harness changes the result when the model and task stay fixed. We compare two configurations of the same harness on three coding benchmarks. The control supplies the full conversation in time order, while the treatment keeps the same record but mechanically shortens older tool results as the context fills and responds to repeated or stalled work.
  Under tight context, the treatment raises mean per-task fail-to-pass fraction (F2PF) in all three pressure comparisons and increases complete solutions on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro. The tight-window Verified comparison uses 169 tasks, a 20,480-token window, and a fixed 480-second attempt endpoint; on this cohort, treatment raises mean per-task F2PF from 28 percent to 49 percent and complete solutions from 43 to 72. Without model-specific retuning, the same frozen treatment also raises both endpoints on the same cohort for three additional models with different designs. In the wide-window Qwen3.6 comparisons, observed arm outcomes are close on Verified and Pro, while FeatureBench retains a higher mean per-task F2PF under treatment. On the wide-window Verified cohort, treatment also serves fewer prompt tokens per turn. Because changing the harness changed what unchanged model weights could accomplish, coding-agent evaluations should treat the model and harness together as the tested solver.

</details>


### [137] [LLM Agents for Time-Series: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26226)
*Yilong Chen,Xiao Qin,Chenghao Liu,Liang Wu,Noelle I. Samia,Kaize Ding*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Survey paper analyzing LLM-based agents for time-series problems using a problem-driven taxonomy across four main categories, examining architecture choices and performance comparisons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents are increasingly used for time-series problems, but current designs vary substantially across different task settings, lacking a systematic organization. There's a need for a problem-driven framework to guide development and understand how task requirements shape agent design.

Method: Adopts a problem-driven taxonomy that organizes systems by the time-series problems they address rather than technical components. Systems are grouped into four categories: forecasting/reasoning, augmentation/synthesis, anomaly detection/diagnosis, and decision support. Within each category, examines how task requirements shape agent architecture, tool use, and memory design. Summarizes representative datasets/environments and compares reported performance.

Result: Provides a comprehensive survey organizing existing LLM-based time-series agents into four problem categories. Identifies patterns in how different task requirements influence agent design choices. Offers performance comparisons across shared or closely related settings. The taxonomy reveals systematic relationships between problem types and agent architectural decisions.

Conclusion: This survey offers a task-oriented guide for designing LLM-based agents for time-series problems and identifies open research gaps for future work. The problem-driven taxonomy provides a more useful framework than technical-component-based approaches for understanding and advancing this emerging field.

Abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly being developed for time-series problems, but their design choices vary substantially across task settings. This survey adopts a problem-driven taxonomy that organizes these systems by the time-series problems they address rather than by isolated technical components. We group existing systems into four categories: forecasting and reasoning, augmentation and synthesis, anomaly detection and diagnosis, and decision support. Within each category, we examine how task requirements shape agent architecture, tool use, and memory design. We further summarize representative datasets and environments, and compare reported model performance under shared or closely related settings. Overall, this survey offers a task-oriented guide to designing LLM-based agents for time-series problems and identifies open gaps for future work.

</details>


### [138] [The Reasoning Tax: Token Economics of LLM Reasoning Across Task Types and Deployment Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26235)
*Sachin Gopal Wani,Ajay Dholakia,David Ellison*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Token Economy Score (TES) to measure when reasoning tokens are cost-effective, finding reasoning efficiency depends more on task structure than difficulty, with diminishing returns at higher effort levels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarking focuses only on accuracy, missing the economic question of whether extended thinking tokens justify their computational cost. Need to understand when reasoning capabilities provide positive marginal value relative to their token consumption.

Method: Introduce Token Economy Score (TES) measuring accuracy gain over non-reasoning baseline normalized by generated-token multiplier. Use paired/approximated TES variants for different model types. Conduct empirical analysis across 151 model-benchmark runs on 7 diverse benchmarks (math, code, science, instruction following, knowledge, research physics). Analyze three dimensions: task structures yielding positive marginal efficiency, how increased reasoning effort changes TES, and how deployment context affects economic viability.

Result: Task structure predicts reasoning efficiency better than difficulty: sequential inference-chain tasks (AIME 2025, LiveCodeBench) show high TES while knowledge-recall tasks (MMLU-Pro) show low TES despite difficulty. Diminishing returns at higher reasoning effort, sometimes reducing accuracy. Inference spend often dominated by internal thinking (Reasoning Cost Share). On-premises deployment can change economics of reasoning workloads (Deployment Cost Multiplier).

Conclusion: Reasoning should be enabled selectively by task type, effort level, and deployment context rather than treated as universally beneficial. Provides benchmarking-driven model-selection rules for cost-effective reasoning deployment.

Abstract: Accuracy-only benchmarking of reasoning-capable large language models misses a central deployment question: when do extended thinking tokens earn their cost? We introduce the Token Economy Score (TES), a marginal benchmarking metric that measures the accuracy gain of a reasoning model over a non-reasoning baseline, normalized by the generated-token multiplier. We define paired and approximated TES variants for model families with reasoning toggles and frontier models without direct non-reasoning counterparts. We then conduct an empirical benchmarking analysis across 151 model-benchmark evaluation runs on seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, science reasoning, instruction following, expert knowledge, knowledge recall, and research-level physics. The analysis examines three deployment-facing dimensions: which task structures yield positive marginal reasoning efficiency, how increasing reasoning effort changes TES within model families, and how deployment context changes economic viability. Results show that task structure predicts reasoning efficiency better than nominal difficulty: sequential inferencechain tasks such as AIME 2025 and LiveCodeBench show high TES, while knowledge-recall tasks such as MMLU-Pro show low TES despite their difficulty. We also find systematic diminishing returns at higher reasoning effort levels, including cases where additional thinking reduces accuracy. Finally, Reasoning Cost Share (RCS) shows that inference spend is often dominated by internal thinking, while Deployment Cost Multiplier (DCM) shows how on-premises deployment can change the economics of otherwise costly reasoning workloads. These findings support a benchmarking-driven model-selection rule: enable reasoning selectively by task type, effort level, and deployment context rather than treating it as a universally beneficial mode.

</details>


### [139] [6.5% of the Neuro-Symbolic Literature Can Be Reproduced from Its Published Artifacts, a Six-Stage Audit Framework and First Instantiation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26236)
*Brandon Colelough,Vladimir Martirosyan,Ishan Tamrakar,William Regli,Aditya Kumar,Anh N. Nhu,Dhruv Dubey,Raj Ambavane,Haowei Deng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents a six-stage reproducibility auditing framework for computer science research, applied to neuro-symbolic AI, revealing severe reproducibility issues with only 6.52% of studies fully or partially reproducible despite "code available" claims.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To systematically assess the reproducibility crisis in computer science, specifically in neuro-symbolic AI, where claims of reproducibility are often made but rarely verifiable, creating a scientific integrity gap that undermines research credibility.

Method: A six-stage framework: 1) retrieval and deduplication, 2) screening and eligibility assessment, 3) artifact availability verification, 4-5) bounded rerun attempts, and 6) reproducibility analysis, instantiated on 5,497 neuro-symbolic AI records.

Result: Only 85 out of 1,304 eligible studies (6.52%) were fully or partially reproducible; 849 studies lacked public code entirely; 321 reruns failed due to missing non-code artifacts; 42 failed due to missing/unusable repositories.

Conclusion: Reproducibility deficits persist despite "code available" declarations, necessitating enforced, versioned, and permanently archived artifact bundles for all empirical neuro-symbolic AI publications at submission time.

Abstract: We present a six-stage framework for auditing the reproducibility of scientific claims across a research literature within the computer science domain, and instantiate our framework for the neuro-symbolic AI (NSAI) subdomain. Instantiating the framework on the NSAI subdomain produced a multi-year audit. Stage one retrieved 5,497 records and removed 3,018 duplicates. Stage two screened the 2,479 unique records at title and abstract, identifying 1,365 self-identified NSAI records, then removed a further 61 at full text for off-topic, non-research, no-quantitative-evaluation, or inaccessible-full-text reasons. Stage three sought a verifiable public code artifact for each of the 1,304 eligible records and found none for 849, leaving 455 to enter the artifact inventory and bounded rerun of stages four and five. We fully or partially reproduced 85 studies, 6.52% of the eligible corpus and 18.68% of attempted reruns. We found that 321 attempted reruns were blocked by missing non- code artifacts and 42 by missing or unusable code repositories. These figures quantify a persistent reproducibility deficit that survives even nominal "code available" declarations, and signal the need for enforced, versioned, and permanently archived artifact bundles in future NSAI publications. We argue that empirical NSAI papers should be required at submission time to provide complete, versioned, and permanently archived artifact bundles.

</details>


### [140] [Assessing mentalization in humans and large language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26291)
*Aamir Sohail,Xintong Zhong,Arkady Konovalov,Patricia L. Lockwood,Lei Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs demonstrate mentalization abilities in economic games, with varying performance across models and strategic prompting improving reasoning; GPT-5 outperformed humans by adapting reasoning depth to opponent sophistication.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs show human-like performance on theory-of-mind tasks, it's unknown whether they can use mentalization to guide adaptive behavior in strategic social interactions.

Method: Used two economic games with cognitive computational modeling to test mentalization strategies in 2,099 LLM agents across four model families (DeepSeek, GPT-4.1, GPT-5, Gemini 2.0 Flash) against varying opponents, with strategic prompting to elicit reasoning. Benchmark results against 251 human participants.

Result: LLMs showed clear behavioral and computational signatures of mentalization that varied by model provider and size. Strategic prompting generally improved performance by inducing more sophisticated reasoning, though benefits differed across tasks. GPT-5 agents flexibly adapted recursive reasoning depth to opponent sophistication, outperforming humans.

Conclusion: Different LLMs have varying capacities for mentalization, and cognitive computational modeling provides a formal method for assessing comparative intelligence between humans and machines.

Abstract: Mentalization - the ability to infer others' beliefs and intentions to guide one's own choices - is a key cognitive function underlying human social interactions. Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate behaviour consistent with humans on theory-of-mind tasks, yet whether these models can guide adaptive behaviour through mentalization is unknown. Here we use two economic games with cognitive computational modeling to uncover the latent strategies underlying mentalization in LLMs. We tested individual LLM agents across four model families, DeepSeek, GPT-4.1, GPT-5 and Gemini 2.0 Flash (N = 2,099), against opponents of varying sophistication and examined whether a prompting strategy designed to elicit strategic reasoning improved performance. We benchmarked results against human participants (N = 251) as a comparative measure. Across both games, LLMs showed clear behavioural and computational signatures of mentalizing that differed markedly by model provider and size. Strategic prompting generally improved performance by inducing more sophisticated reasoning, yet the extent of the benefit differed across the two tasks. Last, GPT-5 agents flexibly adapted their recursive depth of reasoning to increasingly sophisticated opponents, demonstrating superior performance to human participants. Collectively, we demonstrate different capacities for mentalization across LLMs, and highlight cognitive computational modeling as a formal method for assessing comparative intelligence across humans and machines.

</details>


### [141] [Approved Too Late: Verdict Staleness in LLM-Guarded Self-Adaptive Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26306)
*Ilai Shraga,Roei Eshel,Lior Gorelik*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM guardrails in self-adaptive systems can approve actions that become stale by execution time, creating TOCTOU hazards. The paper studies verdict freshness, introduces Freshness-Bounded Shield (FBS) to estimate approval validity, and proposes freshness contracts requiring approvals to remain valid at use time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language model (LLM) guardrails in self-adaptive systems can issue approvals that are correct at check time but become stale by actuation time, creating an "Execute-stage time-of-check to time-of-use" hazard. This freshness problem undermines system safety when approved actions become invalid before execution.

Method: The authors study three quantities: (1) all-candidate verdict change under fixed-action replay, (2) oracle-labeled approval expiry on recorded closed-loop trajectories, and (3) judge-conditioned use-time invalidity. They introduce Freshness-Bounded Shield (FBS), which estimates approval validity horizons using safe-side margins and recent feature volatility without explicit plant-dynamics models.

Result: Across five reproducible SAS environments, all-candidate verdict-change rates range from 5.3-48.4% at eight simulator steps. FBS reduces oracle-labeled approval-expiry rates from 3.4-24.7% to 0-1.8% at same shift using fixed settings. Separate audit finds nonzero judge-conditioned use-time invalidity in every approval stream.

Conclusion: Verdict freshness is critical for LLM guardrails in self-adaptive systems. The proposed Freshness-Bounded Shield effectively reduces approval expiry rates, and the paper formulates a freshness contract requiring every approval to remain valid at use time, addressing TOCTOU hazards in adaptive systems.

Abstract: A large language model (LLM) guardrail for a self-adaptive system (SAS) may issue an approval that is correct at check time but stale by actuation. This creates an Execute-stage time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) hazard. We study verdict freshness: whether a guardrail verdict remains valid when used. We distinguish three quantities that answer different questions: all-candidate verdict change under fixed-action replay, oracle-labeled approval expiry on recorded closed-loop trajectories, and judge-conditioned use-time invalidity. Across five reproducible SAS environments, all-candidate verdict-change rates span 5.3-48.4% at a common replay shift of eight simulator steps. We introduce the Freshness-Bounded Shield (FBS), which estimates each approval's validity horizon from its safe-side margin and recent feature volatility, without an explicit plant-dynamics model. Using fixed settings documented in the artifact, FBS reduces oracle-labeled approval-expiry rates from 3.4-24.7% to 0-1.8% at the same shift. A separate audit of four LLM judges finds nonzero judge-conditioned use-time invalidity in every approval stream. We formulate a freshness contract: every approval must be correct at check time and remain valid at use time.

</details>


### [142] [FaithSieve: Fine-Grained Evaluation of Math Proofs with Faithful Formal Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26310)
*Ziyu Wang,Qiming Dai,Yishan Wu,Zaiwen Wen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FaithSieve is a Lean-assisted framework that decomposes natural-language math proofs into local reasoning units, verifies them with formal evaluation, and uses semantic alignment scoring to improve first-error localization accuracy in mathematical proofs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation methods for LLM-generated mathematical proofs rely on model-based natural-language judgments that often miss local reasoning gaps. Formal theorem provers like Lean offer rigorous verification but face issues with locality and semantic mismatches when evaluating informal text.

Method: FaithSieve decomposes coarse proof steps into local reasoning units, extracts typed proof obligations, and verifies them through a formal evaluation agent. Formal validation is gated by semantic alignment scoring to ensure formal statements preserve the context, objects, and logical form of original claims.

Result: On the 350-problem ProofLoc-Olympiad dataset, FaithSieve achieves 81.43% exact first-error accuracy (vs 72.29% baseline). On the 200-problem ProofLoc-University benchmark, it reaches 84.5% exact accuracy (vs 75.0% baseline).

Conclusion: Decomposing proofs into fine-grained units and grounding them with faithful formal evidence significantly improves reliable evaluation of natural-language mathematical reasoning, enabling better localization of early logical errors in LLM-generated proofs.

Abstract: Large language models can now generate complex, multi-step mathematical proofs, but reliably determining their correctness and localizing early logical errors remains a critical challenge. Existing evaluation approaches largely depend on model-based natural-language judgments, which often overlook local reasoning gaps. While formal theorem provers like Lean offer a path to rigorous verification, using them to evaluate informal text requires solving locality and semantic mismatches: a prover might bypass a local flaw by proving an overly broad target, or validate an auto-formalized statement that drifts from the original mathematical intent. To address this, we introduce FaithSieve, a Lean-assisted framework for fine-grained evaluation of natural-language mathematical proofs. FaithSieve decomposes coarse proof steps into local reasoning units, extracts typed proof obligations, and verifies them through a formal evaluation agent. Formal validation is gated by semantic alignment scoring, so Lean evidence is incorporated only when the formal statement faithfully preserves the context, objects, and logical form of the original claim. We construct two expert-verified datasets, ProofLoc-Olympiad and ProofLoc-University, to benchmark first-error localization. On the 350-problem Olympiad dataset, FaithSieve using a GPT-5.4 backbone achieves 81.43% exact first-error accuracy, outperforming the direct-judging baseline of 72.29%. Furthermore, on the 200-problem ProofLoc-University benchmark spanning six advanced domains, FaithSieve reaches 84.5% exact accuracy, compared to 75.0% for the direct judge. Our work demonstrates that decomposing proofs into fine-grained units and grounding them with faithful formal evidence significantly improves reliable evaluation of natural-language reasoning.

</details>


### [143] [ProofEvolve: Neuro-Symbolic Evolution for Formal Automated Theorem Proving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26334)
*Wenqian Ye,Ziwei Guan,Eric Xie,Bohan Liu,Shivani Modi,Buyun Zhang,Ellie Dingqiao Wen,Henry Kautz,Aidong Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ProofEvolve is a neuro-symbolic framework that evolves explicit, verified symbolic proof structures using neural models to enable recursive self-improvement in theorem proving.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing neural theorem provers fail to fully preserve recursive self-improvement structure. They either embed proof experience into model parameters through expensive weight updates or keep verified deductions only within current problems, and rely too heavily on sparse whole-proof feedback while ignoring useful discoveries from unsuccessful partial attempts.

Method: ProofEvolve evolves explicit, formally verified symbolic proof structures using neural models. Neural models propose variation operators (decompositions, repairs, schema recombinations), and the symbolic Lean kernel verifies every proof transition. The framework computes verified closure over proof directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), evolves partial AND-OR proof DAGs in behaviorally indexed archives within each problem, and maintains a persistent schema library across problems through kernel-checked schema extraction.

Result: ProofEvolve achieves the highest average solve rate among evaluated proof systems across three competition-level Lean benchmarks. The framework preserves verified results from incomplete attempts and makes them available for later proofs without weakening formal soundness.

Conclusion: ProofEvolve successfully addresses the gap in recursive self-improvement for theorem proving by evolving explicit, verified symbolic proof structures, preserving discoveries from partial attempts, and enabling knowledge transfer across problems while maintaining formal soundness.

Abstract: Automated theorem proving offers a natural foundation for recursive self-improvement in scientific discovery. However, existing neural provers do not fully preserve this recursive structure, where the learning process should be self-improving over time. Existing methods either embed proof experience into model parameters through expensive weight updates, or keep verified intermediate deductions only within the current problem. In addition, these methods also heavily rely on sparse whole-proof feedback, even when unsuccessful partial attempts contain useful discoveries. To close the gap, we propose ProofEvolve, a neuro-symbolic framework that evolves explicit, formally verified symbolic proof structures with neural models to decisively expand the knowledge boundary. In this framework, the neural model proposes variation operators, including decompositions, repairs, and schema recombinations. The symbolic Lean kernel verifies every proof transition. Over the evolution loops, ProofEvolve computes verified closure over the resulting proof directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Within each problem, ProofEvolve evolves partial AND-OR proof DAGs in a behaviorally indexed archive. Across problems, kernel-checked schema extraction adds newly proved sub-DAGs to a persistent schema library. Proof DAGs inherit the solved results through typed schema recombination, with every residual premise exposed as a new subgoal. This evolutionary process preserves verified results from incomplete attempts and makes them available for later proofs without weakening formal soundness. Across three competition-level Lean benchmarks, ProofEvolve achieves the highest average solve rate among the evaluated proof systems.

</details>


### [144] [Fine-Tuning of Transformer models with Frames](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26430)
*Harshavardhan Adepu,Li Zhang,Sanjiv Kumar,Vikas Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FrameFT is a novel Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning method that uses sparse coefficient matrices in Fusion Frame basis to achieve memory-efficient fine-tuning with performance matching or exceeding state-of-the-art PEFT techniques.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current PEFT methods like LoRA have memory requirements that scale with model size (O(dr)), which can be limiting for large-scale pre-trained models. There's a need for more memory-efficient fine-tuning approaches that don't sacrifice performance.

Method: FrameFT models parameter updates (ΔW) using sparse coefficient matrices in a Fusion Frame basis. Fusion Frames can be algorithmically generated and shared across model layers, with only sparse coefficients stored/optimized. The method leverages sparsity in both coefficient matrices and Fusion Frames for computational benefits.

Result: FrameFT achieves performance comparable to or better than state-of-the-art PEFT techniques while requiring far fewer trainable parameters. Experiments across supervised fine-tuning benchmarks (primarily language tasks, but also vision models) demonstrate its effectiveness. Formal convergence results are provided through theoretical analysis.

Conclusion: FrameFT offers a more memory-efficient alternative to existing PEFT methods by using sparse Fusion Frame representations, enabling efficient fine-tuning of large models with reduced parameter overhead while maintaining competitive performance.

Abstract: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) strategies such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) are effective solutions for fine-tuning large-scale pre-trained models; however, their memory requirements scale with the size of the model, $\mathcal{O}(dr)$, where $d$ is the model's hidden dimension and $r$ is the rank. Our proposal, FrameFT, models the parameter update $ΔW$ with a sparse coefficient matrix in a Fusion Frame basis. Fusion Frames can be generated algorithmically and shared across model layers, enabling very efficient updates. Only the sparse coefficients of the basis expansion are stored/optimized, reducing the memory footprint. The sparse structure of the coefficient matrix in FrameFT and the sparsity in the Fusion Frames give large compute benefits, and our analysis provides formal convergence results. We evaluate the idea across a suite of supervised fine-tuning benchmarks, focusing on language tasks, but also report application to vision models. Our experiments show that FrameFT achieves performance on par with/exceeding state-of-the-art PEFT techniques, but needs far fewer trainable parameters.

</details>


### [145] [Don't Overthink, Don't Underthink: Toward Adaptive Reasoning in Agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26442)
*Md Jueal Mia,M. Hadi Amini*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Large Language Models need adaptive reasoning allocation in agentic AI systems, as fixed reasoning controls lead to either over-reasoning (excess computation without accuracy gains) or under-reasoning (incorrect solutions).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM approaches use fixed reasoning controls (token budgets, pre-execution difficulty estimates) that don't adapt to dynamic agentic workflows involving planning, tool use, memory retrieval, and agent interactions, leading to misallocated reasoning.

Method: The paper characterizes over-reasoning and under-reasoning as failure modes and evaluates them on MATH-500 and GAIA benchmarks using metrics like tool-decision latency, token consumption, token-limit exhaustion, and answer correctness.

Result: Over-reasoning cases show higher computational cost without proportional accuracy gains, while under-reasoning cases consistently produce incorrect or incomplete solutions.

Conclusion: Next-generation agentic AI needs adaptive reasoning mechanisms that dynamically allocate reasoning according to evolving task demands, rather than fixed reasoning controls.

Abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown that increased inference-time reasoning can improve performance on complex tasks. However, many existing approaches rely on fixed or preallocated reasoning controls, such as fixed token budgets, pre-execution difficulty estimates, or activation-space interventions, and are often evaluated on standalone reasoning benchmarks rather than full agentic workflows. These assumptions may not hold in agentic AI systems, where reasoning requirements evolve dynamically through planning, tool use, memory retrieval, and agent-to-agent interactions. Consequently, reasoning can become either excessive or insufficient, resulting in unnecessary computation, increased latency, planning drift, excessive tool use, or incomplete solutions. We argue that a major challenge for next-generation agentic AI is not merely how much reasoning a language model should perform, but how it should allocate reasoning according to evolving task demands. We characterize over-reasoning and under-reasoning as recurring failure modes of misallocated reasoning and evaluate them on MATH-500 and the GAIA public validation benchmark. Using tool-decision latency, token consumption, token-limit exhaustion, and answer correctness, our results suggest that cases classified as over-reasoning are associated with higher computational cost without proportional accuracy gains, whereas cases classified as under-reasoning are consistently associated with incorrect or incomplete solutions. These findings motivate future research on adaptive reasoning mechanisms for agentic AI.

</details>


### [146] [PILOT in the Loop: Live Self-Improvement for Long-Horizon Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26530)
*Yang Xiao,Yusong Sun,Haoyi Wu,Wenyang Hui,Wen Da,Zhaokai Luo,Mu Chuan,Yao Hu,Wenjie Li,Chengyue Jiang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PILOT is a supervisor-worker harness for live self-improvement that enables real-time steering of active agents and immediate learning from execution experience, outperforming existing methods across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing self-improvement methods only process experience after execution ends, preventing real-time redirection of active runs and immediate application of lessons learned. Current agent architectures don't fully support live self-improvement, as single-agent self-correction mixes execution and assessment, while subagent delegation typically can't redirect active subagents.

Method: PILOT introduces a supervisor-worker harness with two coupled mechanisms: (1) live steering allows a separate supervisor to redirect or abort the active worker during execution, and (2) live self-evolution distills procedures and failure modes revealed during execution into reusable skills and memory.

Result: PILOT ranks first in 5 of 6 configurations across two frozen backbones and three benchmarks. On Terminal-Bench 2.0, it outperforms counterpart harnesses by up to 9.8 percentage points. In self-improvement settings, PILOT gains 14.6 points with GLM-5.1 and 12.4 points with Kimi-K2.6, reduces mean output tokens by 42.9% and 47.4%, and increases successful evaluations per million output tokens by 110.3% and 134.0%.

Conclusion: Live self-improvement through PILOT's coupled live steering and live self-evolution mechanisms significantly outperforms existing post-execution self-improvement approaches, enabling more efficient and effective agent learning during execution.

Abstract: Long-horizon agent runs generate experience that can improve both the current run and future work. Most self-improvement methods process this experience only after execution ends, so they cannot redirect the active run or immediately apply and validate lessons learned from it. We argue that self-improvement should instead be live, using emerging experience both to redirect the active run and to update the persistent harness. Existing agent architectures do not fully support this goal. Single-agent self-correction combines task execution and trajectory assessment within one context, while subagent delegation separates execution but typically cannot redirect an active subagent. We present PILOT, a supervisor-worker harness for live self-improvement through two coupled mechanisms: (1) live steering lets a separate supervisor redirect or abort the active worker during execution; and (2) live self-evolution distils procedures and failure modes revealed during execution into reusable skills and memory. Across two frozen backbones and three benchmarks, PILOT ranks first in five of six configurations. On Terminal-Bench 2.0, PILOT outperforms counterpart harnesses by up to 9.8 percentage points. In the self-improvement setting, PILOT gains 14.6 points with GLM-5.1 and 12.4 points with Kimi-K2.6. Mean output tokens fall by 42.9% and 47.4%, while successful evaluations per million output tokens rise by 110.3% and 134.0%, respectively.

</details>


### [147] [Multi2AV-Safety: Benchmarking Safety in Multimodal-to-Audio-Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26535)
*Kaichao Jiang,Changtao Miao,Baiqi Wu,Zhiyuan Lu,Kang Yang,Peiwei Zhao,Junchi Chen,Yunfeng Diao,He Liu,Qi Chu,Tao Gong,Nenghai Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Multi2AV-Safety is the first comprehensive safety benchmark for multimodal-conditioned audio-video generation, covering 11 non-singleton T/I/A/V conditioning configurations with 11,024 attack instances, revealing systematic weaknesses in current safety guards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The shift from prompt-driven to multimodal conditioning in audio-video generation creates new safety challenges where harmful intent can emerge from interactions between otherwise benign inputs across modalities and time, but existing safety benchmarks remain prompt-centric and cannot systematically study such compositional risks.

Method: The authors introduce Multi2AV-Safety benchmark covering all 11 non-singleton text/image/audio/video conditioning configurations for audio-video generation, comprising 11,024 attack instances, and evaluate representative multimodal safety guards across attack mechanisms and harm-evidence structures.

Result: Evaluation reveals systematic weaknesses in current safety guards: (1) harmful semantics can emerge from combinations of individually benign inputs, and (2) explicit harmful cues become harder to detect when mixed with benign multimodal context. These results identify "compositional risk perception" as a central capability gap.

Conclusion: Current safety guards fail to reliably integrate safety evidence across modalities and time even when all conditioning inputs are observable. The Multi2AV-Safety benchmark addresses this gap and will be publicly released in October 2026 to facilitate research on compositional risk perception in multimodal-conditioned generation.

Abstract: Audio-video generation is rapidly moving from prompt-driven synthesis toward multimodal conditioning, where text, images, audio, and video can jointly shape the generated output. This shift changes the nature of safety evaluation: harmful intent may no longer reside in any single input, but instead emerge from how otherwise benign or weakly harmful conditions interact across modalities and time. Existing safety benchmarks, however, remain largely prompt-centric or tied to fixed conditioning interfaces, leaving such compositional risks difficult to study systematically. To bridge this gap, we introduce Multi2AV-Safety, the first safety benchmark, to the best of our knowledge, to cover all 11 non-singleton T/I/A/V conditioning configurations for audio-video generation, comprising 11,024 attack instances. Evaluation on Multi2AV-Safety reveals systematic weaknesses in representative multimodal safety guards across attack mechanisms and harm-evidence structures. Our evaluation reveals two complementary failure modes: harmful semantics can emerge from the combination of individually benign inputs, while explicit harmful cues can become harder to detect when mixed with benign multimodal context. Together, these results identify \emph{compositional risk perception} as a central capability gap in safeguarding multimodal-conditioned audio-video generation: current safety guards fail to reliably integrate safety evidence across modalities and time, even when all conditioning inputs are observable. The dataset will be publicly released in October 2026.

</details>


### [148] [DuMateBench: Evaluating Autonomous Agents in Complex Real-World Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26546)
*Zechun Niu,Yukun Zhao,Jiaxin Zhang,Xu Shen,Jinhua Si,Han Tian,Can Xu,Yunfan Song,Jiaxin Mao,Yansong Gao,Yuchen Li,Jianmin Wu,Lingyong Yan,Shuaiqiang Wang,Dawei Yin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DuMateBench is a real-world benchmark for autonomous agents reconstructed from production user sessions, featuring environmental complexities and multi-tool workflows across 8 scenarios and 17 capability categories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks are limited - they separate tasks by application/capability and use clean, stable environments that don't reflect real-world conditions where autonomous agents operate with multiple tools and face environmental complexities.

Method: Created DuMateBench by reconstructing anonymized user sessions from production agent platform, preserving interaction history, configurations, and workspace state. Tasks executed in Docker containers with injected real-world environmental complexities (Insufficient, Unstable, Noisy), evaluated using hybrid deterministic and LLM-as-Judge protocol.

Result: Evaluation of 5 autonomous-agent frameworks with 4 state-of-the-art LLMs reveals substantial gaps in strict task completion. Performance under environmental perturbations is jointly shaped by LLM capabilities and agent framework design.
