Conclusion: Real-world autonomous agent evaluation requires benchmarks with realistic environmental complexities and multi-tool coordination. Both LLM capabilities and agent framework architecture significantly impact performance in practical deployment scenarios.

Abstract: Autonomous agents are increasingly adopted to complete complex, multi-tool workflows in real-world settings. However, existing benchmarks typically separate tasks by application or capability and evaluate agents in environments that are cleaner and more stable than those encountered in practice. We introduce DuMateBench, a real-session benchmark reconstructed from anonymized and privacy-screened user sessions collected from a large-scale production agent platform. Each task preserves the relevant pre-solution interaction history, persistent configurations, and workspace state, and is then validated through human verification. The resulting benchmark comprises 200 tasks spanning 8 broad scenarios and 17 fine-grained capability categories, with most tasks requiring multiple capability coordination. We execute these tasks in isolated Docker containers injected with three forms of real-world environmental complexity: Insufficient, Unstable, and Noisy, and assess performance using a hybrid deterministic and LLM-as-Judge evaluation protocol. Experiments across five representative autonomous-agent frameworks paired with four state-of-the-art LLMs reveal substantial gaps in strict task completion. Complementary robustness, efficiency, and diagnostic analyses further show that performance under environmental perturbations is jointly shaped by the capabilities of the LLM and the surrounding agent framework. The code and data are publicly available at https://dumatebench.com/.

</details>


### [149] [AgentJudgeBench: A Multi-Difficulty Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Judges on Agentic Tool-Calling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26623)
*Abhigya Verma,Amit Kumar Saha,Seganrasan Subramanian,Sai Harshitha Aluru*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM judges for agentic tool-calling systems have reliability limitations, especially on structured workflows without ground truth, with performance converging to 77-82% ceiling regardless of model scale, though structured rubrics can help.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM judges are widely used to evaluate agentic tool-calling systems, but their reliability on structured, dependency-driven workflows (represented as DAGs) remains largely unexamined, creating a gap in understanding how well these judges perform on complex, structured evaluation tasks.

Method: Created AgentJudgeBench, the first benchmark for LLM judge reliability on agentic tool-calling over workflow DAGs. The benchmark includes 3,808 instances across six DAG topologies and three difficulty tiers. Evaluated with five generator models (3B-70B open-weight models and GPT-5.4) and six judges (20B to frontier scale) under paired conditions: with and without ground truth. Also tested mitigation strategies including chain-of-thought reasoning, judge temperature adjustments, and structured evaluation rubrics.

Result: Judge alignment degrades with task difficulty, 1.5x faster without ground truth. On hard queries without ground truth, all six judges converge to narrow 77-82% band regardless of scale. Ground-truth exposure sometimes reduces alignment (GPT-5.4: -1.5pp, Gemini-2.5-Pro: -3.9pp). Chain-of-thought and temperature adjustments have negligible effects, while structured rubrics improve alignment by up to 6.5pp but don't generalize well. With ground truth, QwQ-32B best matches programmatic reference; without it, frontier judges lead only marginally. Human validation identifies GPT-OSS-120B as most human-aligned judge.

Conclusion: Current LLM judges have fundamental limitations for evaluating agentic tool-calling systems, with performance ceilings driven by task difficulty rather than model scale. The research provides practical guidelines: structured rubrics help but don't generalize well, ground truth isn't always beneficial, and model capacity alone cannot overcome structural limitations. These findings are crucial for reliable evaluation in agentic systems.

Abstract: LLM judges are widely used to evaluate agentic tool-calling systems, yet their reliability on structured, dependency-driven workflows remains largely unexamined. We present AgentJudgeBench, the first benchmark to systematically study LLM-as-a-judge reliability for agentic tool-calling over workflow DAGs, as distinct from the broader LLM-as-a-judge task of open-ended text or preference evaluation. The benchmark comprises 3,808 instances spanning six DAG topologies and three difficulty tiers, evaluated with five generators (3B-70B open-weight models and GPT-5.4) and six judges (20B to frontier scale) under paired with- and without-ground-truth conditions. Judge alignment degrades monotonically with task difficulty, 1.5x faster without ground truth, and on hard queries without ground truth all six judges converge to a narrow 77-82% band regardless of scale, revealing a structural ceiling driven primarily by task difficulty, though its height is partly prompt-dependent for weaker generators, that model capacity alone cannot overcome. Ground-truth exposure is not uniformly beneficial: it reduces alignment for GPT-5.4 (1.5 pp) and Gemini-2.5-Pro (3.9 pp), consistent with over-anchoring. Among mitigation strategies, chain-of-thought reasoning and judge temperature both have negligible effect, while structured evaluation rubrics improve alignment by up to 6.5 pp but do not generalize uniformly across judge-generator pairs. With ground truth, QwQ-32B best matches the programmatic reference, while a human validation study identifies GPT-OSS-120B as the most human-aligned judge; without it, frontier judges lead only marginally within the shared ceiling. These results expose fundamental limitations of current LLM judges and yield practical guidelines for reliable evaluation in agentic systems.

</details>


### [150] [Relational Over-Regularization: Graph-Based AI-Generated Text Detection via Sentence Transition Deviation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26694)
*Hyeonchu Park,Bugeun Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes CSFG, a graph-based framework that detects AI-generated text by analyzing structural signals at the sentence-pair level, specifically identifying that LLMs produce inflated inter-sentence transition variance compared to human writing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI-generated text detection methods overfit to specific generators and fail under distribution shift because they rely on token-level statistical signals or independent stylometric features. The authors identify a need for more robust detection that can generalize to unseen LLMs.

Method: The paper introduces Cross-Source Stylometric Fingerprint Graph (CSFG), a graph-based framework that encodes four types of signals as learnable GNN edge features: positional, sequential, semantic, and transition deviation. The method formalizes Relational Over-Regularization (ROR) - the observation that LLMs produce inter-sentence transition variance that deviates from human writing through inflated variance driven by recurring similarity bursts at paragraph boundaries and templated transitions.

Result: CSFG achieves 97.14% accuracy under binary detection, outperforming the strongest graph-based baseline by 11.14 percentage points, with a false-positive rate of 1.57%. The method shows robust generalization to unseen LLMs in the inflated-variance regime, though detection degrades for generators whose transition variance falls at or below the human baseline. The ROR signal is validated across four benchmarks with statistical significance (p < 0.001).

Conclusion: The central contribution is the relational problem formulation (ROR) that identifies structural signals at the sentence-pair level, rather than a novel GNN architecture. CSFG operationalizes this insight through a graph-based framework that effectively detects AI-generated text by capturing LLMs' tendency toward "over-regularized" inter-sentence transitions.

Abstract: Detecting AI-generated text (AIGT) remains challenging because existing approaches rely on token-level statistical signals or independent stylometric features, causing them to overfit to specific generators and fail under distribution shift. We identify a structural signal at the sentence-pair level: LLMs produce inter-sentence transition variance that deviates from human writing through inflated variance driven by recurring similarity bursts at paragraph boundaries and templated transitions. We formalize this as Relational Over-Regularization (ROR) and validate it across four benchmarks (p < 0.001). The central contribution is this relational problem formulation, not a novel GNN architecture; CSFG is one concrete instantiation for operationalizing ROR. To exploit this signal, we propose the Cross-Source Stylometric Fingerprint Graph (CSFG), a graph-based framework that encodes positional, sequential, semantic, and transition deviation signals as learnable GNN edge features. The per-edge signed deviation δ_ij operationalizes ROR without hand-crafted thresholds and acts as a false-positive calibrator. CSFG achieves 97.14% accuracy under binary detection, outperforming the strongest graph-based baseline by 11.14 pp, with a false-positive rate of 1.57% and robust generalization to unseen LLMs in the inflated-variance regime; detection degrades for generators whose transition variance falls at or below the human baseline.

</details>


### [151] [Five Primitives for Governing Autonomous AI Agents at Runtime](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26696)
*Jiten Oswal,John Cadeddu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Enterprise AI agents require runtime governance due to their ephemeral nature, unpredictable model-driven actions, and spontaneous discovery, necessitating five primitives: discovery, identity, governance, attestation, and supply chain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current enterprise control models designed for human users and long-lived services fail for autonomous AI agents because: 1) agents are ephemeral with rapid appearance/disappearance, 2) their actions are model-selected rather than pre-programmed (making their behavior unpredictable), and 3) agents are discovered rather than provisioned (anyone can create one via API). This creates governance gaps that require runtime solutions.

Method: The paper proposes five governance primitives: discovery (finding agents), identity (verifying who/what acts), governance (policy enforcement), attestation (action verification), and supply chain (dependencies). They implement an architecture where: 1) agent actions are mediated against policy before execution, 2) actions are authorized against per-tenant vocabularies, and 3) actions are recorded in hash-linked signed ledgers for third-party verification without vendor involvement.

Result: Implementation costs include: enforcement point on request's critical path, identity requiring a sidecar per workload, and fail-closed mediation converting availability incidents into denial. Four primitives are built and running in private pilots, with the fifth built as separate tooling not yet integrated into request path.

Conclusion: Governing enterprise AI agents is fundamentally a runtime problem, not a model-alignment or build-time issue. The proposed five-primitive framework provides necessary governance structure, though implementation reveals trade-offs in performance, architecture, and availability that must be addressed.

Abstract: Enterprise deployments of autonomous AI agents inherit a control model built for human users and long-lived services, and the fit fails in three specific ways: agent principals are ephemeral, appearing and vanishing faster than provisioning; their actions are selected by a model rather than programmed, so the set of things they may attempt is not known in advance; and the population is discovered rather than provisioned, because anyone who can call an API can create one. We argue that governing such agents is a runtime problem -- not a model-alignment problem and not a build-time problem -- and we derive five primitives from the questions that must be answered before an action takes effect and after it has: discovery, identity, governance, attestation, and supply chain. For each we state what fails if it is absent and why the others cannot structurally supply it. We describe an implementation in which an agent's action is mediated against policy before it takes effect, authorised against a per-tenant action vocabulary, and recorded in a hash-linked signed ledger a third party can verify with the vendor out of the loop. We report what the architecture costs: the enforcement point sits on the request's critical path, identity requires a sidecar per workload, and fail-closed mediation converts availability incidents into denial. We are explicit about implementation status: four primitives are built and running in private pilots, and the fifth is built as separate tooling and not yet integrated into the request path. We keep it in the set deliberately: a five-part decomposition that exactly matches what its authors happened to build is not a taxonomy but a description of a codebase.

</details>


### [152] [Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini in the Real-World](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26701)
*Samuel Schmidgall,Xiaokai Zhu,Marian Shaw,Lin Yang,Valentin Liévin,Jingyun Yang,Yuchen Zhuang,Tim Strother,Alex Bijamov,Min Woo Sun,Anil Palepu,Justin Chen,David Steiner,Jacqueline Shreibati,Wei-Hung Weng,Yilin Zhao,Xingjian Hu,Nicholas Zahn,Sadhya Garg,Julia Kirby,Yuxiang Gan,Jiaoli Li,Divy Thakkar,Shekoofeh Azizi,David Racz,Juraj Gottweis,Vivek Natarajan,Chenglin Wu,Tal Danino,Keran Rong,Haozhe Wang,Benoit Schillings,Yong Cheng,Quoc V. Le,Tao Tu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Co-Scientist, a Gemini-based multi-agent AI system, accelerates end-to-end scientific research through hypothesis generation, experimentation, and manuscript generation across materials science, biology, and computer science with validated real-world results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To extend and validate Co-Scientist's capabilities beyond in silico hypothesis generation to become an execution-grounded research partner that can advance closed-loop scientific workflows across multiple disciplines.

Method: Gemini-based multi-agent system interfaced with experimental hardware (chemical vapor deposition reactor for materials science) and used lab-in-the-loop execution with Gemini 3 Deep Think for rapid recipe optimization. Applied across three domains: materials science, biology, and computer science with validation through real experiments.

Result: Successfully designed safe precursor route for MXenes producing lamellar 2D material similar to Ti3C2Tx MXene; grew monolayer MoS2, MoSe2, and WS2 semiconductors with single-attempt growth; predicted emergent swarming phenotypes of engineered E. coli matching wet-lab measurements; autonomously discovered inference-time scaling architecture outperforming six frontier models on HealthBench; double-blind study showed reduced hallucination and plagiarism in generated papers.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate significant progress toward closed-loop multi-agent scientific AI systems capable of accelerating real-world scientific discovery across multiple disciplines while improving research safety and reliability.

Abstract: We present an extension and comprehensive real-world validation of Co-Scientist, a Gemini-based multi-agent system designed to accelerate end-to-end scientific research across hypothesis generation, experimentation, and manuscript generation. Moving beyond in silico hypothesis generation, this specialized configuration transitions Co-Scientist into an execution-grounded research partner advancing closed-loop scientific workflows across materials science, biology, and computer science. In materials science, Co-Scientist interfaced with a semi-automated chemical vapor deposition reactor to design a safe precursor route for MXenes; experimental execution produced a lamellar 2D material sharing key structural similarities with the Ti3C2Tx MXene lattice, although further experiments are needed to confirm the atomic structure. Leveraging Gemini 3 Deep Think for rapid, lab-in-the-loop execution, it also tailored growth recipes to laboratory constraints in minutes, enabling single-attempt growth of monolayer MoS2, MoSe2, and WS2 semiconductors. In biology, Co-Scientist predicted emergent swarming phenotypes of engineered E. coli across inducer (IPTG) gradients from sparse imaging data, quantitatively matching unpublished wet-lab morphological measurements. In computer science, Co-Scientist autonomously discovered an inference-time scaling architecture that outperformed six frontier models on HealthBench (Hard and Professional) while reducing potential clinical harm under blinded physician evaluation. Finally, a double-blind study of end-to-end generated papers with 30 domain experts across 450 reviews demonstrates that Co-Scientist's reliability modules reduce hallucination and plagiarism while improving research safety. Together, these results demonstrate progress toward closed-loop multi-agent scientific AI systems capable of accelerating real-world scientific discovery.

</details>


### [153] [Style as a Confound: False Positives in AI Detection of Non-Native Academic Writing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26710)
*Hyeonchu Park,Gahye Jeong,Bugeun Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI text detectors show inconsistent performance and high false-positive rates, with professional editing style emerging as a key confounding variable rather than actual AI authorship.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is uncertainty about whether AI text detectors actually identify AI authorship or simply respond to polished academic English features, with previous studies showing high false-positive rates for non-native English writing but confounded by various factors.

Method: Analyzed 135,389 document pairs from a professional English editing service (2018-2025), comparing non-native manuscripts with their native-edited versions to assess how editing affects detector responses while controlling for content and authorship across 13 AI text detectors.

Result: False-positive rates for human-written texts varied widely (0.0% to 100.0%), with inconsistent detector responses to the same edits (some increased AI scores, others decreased them), and score changes correlated with the extent of editing.

Conclusion: Professional editing style is a key confounding variable in AI detector outputs rather than a reliable indicator of text origin, raising serious concerns about fairness and reliability in academic settings where these detectors are increasingly used.

Abstract: AI text detectors are increasingly employed in academic settings, but it remains unclear whether their outputs reflect AI authorship itself or broader linguistic features associated with polished academic English. Previous studies have reported high false-positive rates (FPRs) for non-native English writing, but population-level comparisons confound authorship with differences in topic, domain, and writing style. Professional editing provides a useful setting for examining this issue because it changes the linguistic form of manuscripts while preserving authorship and content. We examined 135,389 document pairs from a professional English editing service (2018-2025), comprising non-native manuscripts and their native-edited versions, to assess how editing affects detector responses controlling for content and authorship. For the 13 AI text detectors, FPRs for human-written texts varied widely, from 0.0% to 100.0%. Responses varied across detectors: the same edits increased AI scores in some detectors but decreased them in others. Notably, score changes correlated with the extent of editing. The findings identify professional editing style as a key confounding variable in AI detector outputs, rather than establishing a full separation of text origin from linguistic style, raising concerns about fairness and reliability in academic settings.

</details>


### [154] [Knowing When Not to Reuse: Conditional Experience Transfer in Autonomous LLM Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26730)
*Tingyun Li,Wenfeng Feng,Weiqing Li,Abudukelimu Wuerkaixi,Guohua Liu,Yuewei Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BCIT (Boundary-Calibrated Intervention Transfer) is a method for conditional experience transfer in autonomous LLM post-training that selectively authorizes reuse of past update evidence based on current model state and context, preventing harmful updates and improving final model quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous systems for LLM adaptation rely on past update evidence to propose new updates, but this evidence becomes problematic when the parent model changes. Past successes may not transfer to new contexts, leading to wasted compute and potential degradation of training trajectories. The core problem is determining which past update evidence remains actionable after subsequent training.

Method: BCIT (Boundary-Calibrated Intervention Transfer) binds observed update effects to their source context, checks applicability conditions, vetoes candidates with named hard conflicts, and obtains current-state evidence through bounded training trials when needed. It only authorizes experience reuse before weight-changing training and extends memory only with observed events.

Result: On a 4B model adapted across finance reasoning, text-to-SQL, and function calling, BCIT authorizes fewer harmful updates and achieves higher equal-budget final-model quality than alternatives. Candidate updates showed heterogeneous target and retention effects across different contexts, confirming the need for conditional authorization.

Conclusion: Experience authorization should be treated as a distinct problem in autonomous post-training systems. BCIT provides a principled approach for conditional experience transfer that prevents harmful updates while maintaining efficiency, supporting better adaptation trajectories for evolving LLMs.

Abstract: Large language models offer broad capabilities, but adapting them to evolving domains, tools, and requirements often entails repeated post-training. Autonomous systems automate parts of this process by proposing updates, training candidates, and using evaluation feedback to select subsequent proposals. As evidence accumulates, a central problem emerges: which past update evidence remains actionable after subsequent training has changed the parent model? An update's effect depends on its parent, data, and training stage. Treating past success as context-free permission can waste compute. If the resulting child is promoted, it can also degrade the subsequent training trajectory. We formulate this problem as conditional experience transfer and introduce Boundary-Calibrated Intervention Transfer (BCIT), a method that authorizes experience reuse before weight-changing training. BCIT binds an observed effect to its source context, checks applicability conditions, vetoes candidates with named hard conflicts, and obtains current-state evidence through a bounded training trial when needed. Fully trained candidates still face a shared adoption rule, and only observed events extend memory. On one 4B model adapted across finance reasoning, text-to-SQL, and function calling, candidate updates exhibit heterogeneous target and retention effects across the evaluated contexts. Under matched candidates, evidence, and compute, BCIT authorizes fewer harmful updates and attains higher equal-budget final-model quality than the evaluated alternatives. These results support treating experience authorization as a distinct problem in autonomous post-training.

</details>


### [155] [Graph-Guided Selective Unlearning for Language Models: Controlling Support Routes Beyond Forget Seeds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26743)
*Waqas Khan,Tabinda Sarwar,Jingyue Cong,Xun Yi,Estrid He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GRAPHSU introduces a graph-guided controller for selective unlearning that expands deletion scope beyond explicitly identified "forget" examples to include high-risk paraphrases and neighboring training examples, reducing knowledge leakage by up to 49.5 percentage points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise fine-tuned language models need selective knowledge removal for privacy, contractual, or compliance reasons, but existing methods only delete explicitly identified examples, leaving target knowledge recoverable through paraphrases, aliases, or neighboring examples.

Method: GRAPHSU constructs a weighted support-route graph to expand deletion scope beyond forget seeds, propagates deletion pressure through the graph, and applies graded forgetting strengths to high-risk neighbors based on their connectivity and similarity.

Result: On TOFU and PISTOL benchmarks with GPT-2 Medium and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, GRAPHSU achieves lowest utility-feasible soft leakage across all deletion settings, reducing leakage by up to 49.5 percentage points over seed-only baseline.

Conclusion: Effective enterprise unlearning requires controlling support routes (paraphrases and neighboring examples), not just forget seeds, and GRAPHSU demonstrates this through graph-guided deletion scope expansion.

Abstract: Enterprises fine-tune language models on proprietary data that may later require removal due to privacy, contractual, or compliance obligations. Selective unlearning removes requested knowledge while preserving model utility, offering a practical alternative to full retraining, but existing methods treat the explicitly identified forget examples as the complete deletion scope. This is insufficient when target knowledge remains recoverable through paraphrases, aliases, or neighboring training examples. We propose GRAPHSU, a graph-guided controller that expands the deletion scope beyond forget seeds by constructing a weighted support-route graph, propagating deletion pressure through it, and applying graded forgetting strengths to high-risk neighbors. On the Task of Fictitious Unlearning (TOFU), a synthetic author-profile question-answering benchmark, and PISTOL, a structural-unlearning benchmark built around interconnected factual samples, with GPT-2 Medium and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, GRAPHSU achieves the lowest utility-feasible soft leakage across all deletion settings, reducing leakage by up to 49.5 percentage points over a matched seed-only baseline, demonstrating that effective enterprise unlearning requires controlling support routes, not just forget seeds.

</details>


### [156] [AgentFold: Closed-Loop Agentic Search for Protein Folding Model Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26747)
*Mingquan Liu,Jiangyu Chen,Hanqun Cao,Xujun Zhang,Pengsen Ma,Xiangru Tang,Shuting Jin,Zhuo Yang,Tianfan Fu,Fang Wu,Xiangxiang Zeng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgentFold is a multi-agent framework that autonomously improves protein folding models through executable code modifications and computationally expensive validation, demonstrating 7.5% performance improvement over baseline methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific LLM agents show promise in literature reasoning and tool use, but it's unclear if they can autonomously improve large, tightly-coupled scientific ML systems through code changes and expensive validation. The paper investigates this in protein folding, which requires coordinated architectural modifications, multi-objective evaluation, and domain-aware interpretation.

Method: AgentFold formulates folding-model development as closed-loop search over executable code variants. Starting from ESMFold, it uses multi-agent framework to: propose hypotheses, implement/debug code-level modifications, evaluate model variants, analyze experimental outcomes, store interventions in structured memory. An MCTS-style policy allocates computational resources across high-scoring search branches.

Result: On a 2,000+ LOC engineering-scale codebase, AgentFold explored ~80 model variants using ~5,000 GPU-hours and 170M LLM tokens. Under matched computational budget, it improved best lDDT by 7.5% over independent Codex proposals and outperformed random-search control. Intervention traces revealed empirical design patterns: stable gains from early, soft, learnable priors and gated refinement, while direct geometric perturbations and geometry-conditioned feedback often destabilized training.

Conclusion: AgentFold demonstrates that scientific LLM agents can autonomously improve large ML systems through executable code changes and expensive validation. The framework successfully navigates complex scientific engineering challenges, revealing valuable empirical design patterns while achieving measurable performance improvements in protein folding.

Abstract: Scientific LLM agents have shown promise in literature reasoning, tool use, and experiment planning, but it remains unclear whether they can autonomously improve large, tightly coupled scientific machine-learning systems through executable code changes and computationally expensive validation. We study this question in protein folding, where progress requires coordinated architectural modifications, multi-objective evaluation, and domain-aware interpretation. We present AgentFold, a multi-agent framework that formulates folding-model development as a closed-loop search over executable code variants. Starting from ESMFold, AgentFold proposes hypotheses, implements and debugs code-level modifications, evaluates model variants, analyzes experimental outcomes, and stores both successful and failed interventions in structured memory. An MCTS-style policy allocates computational resources across high-scoring search branches. On an engineering-scale protein-folding codebase comprising more than 2,000 lines of code, AgentFold explores approximately 80 model variants using approximately 5,000 GPU-hours and 170 million LLM tokens. Under a matched computational budget, AgentFold improves the best lDDT by 7.5% over independent Codex proposals and outperforms a random-search control. Beyond model improvement, the resulting intervention traces reveal recurring empirical design patterns: stable gains tend to arise from early, soft, learnable priors and gated refinement, whereas direct geometric perturbations and geometry-conditioned feedback often destabilize training. The code and experimental resources are publicly available at https://github.com/lmqfly/AgentFold.

</details>


### [157] [Discovering Relationships in Data Lakes Using Large Language Models: An Industrial Case](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26750)
*Ahlame Diouan,Eric Ferey,Sabine Loudcher,Jérôme Darmont*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ColRel is a two-stage method that creates column embeddings from metadata and data to discover column relationships in data lakes, especially for ERP datasets with coded schema labels, using business dictionaries for better interpretation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data lakes lack sufficient metadata for column relationship discovery, particularly in ERP-derived datasets where schema labels are often coded or abbreviated, making relationship discovery difficult.

Method: Two-stage approach: 1) Build column embeddings from available metadata and data at ingestion time, 2) Use business dictionaries to interpret coded column names and generate short natural-language descriptions to enhance relationship discovery.

Result: Experiments on public benchmarks and an industrial ERP dataset demonstrate that ColRel is particularly effective in semantically related, weak-signal settings where traditional methods struggle.

Conclusion: ColRel provides an effective solution for column relationship discovery in data lakes, especially for challenging ERP datasets with coded schemata, by leveraging both metadata and data with business dictionary support.

Abstract: Data lakes rely on metadata to remain usable, yet this meta data is often limited or weakly informative for column relationship discovery, especially in ERP-derived datasets with coded or abbreviated schema labels. We propose ColRel, a two-stage method that builds column embeddings from metadata and data available at ingestion time. In difficult cases, such as coded schemata, business dictionaries help better interpret column names and support the generation of short natural-language descriptions used in the second stage. Experiments on public benchmarks and an industrial ERP dataset show that ColRel is particularly effective in semantically related, weak-signal settings.

</details>


### [158] [DEEPCHART: How Far are LLMs from Faithful Data-Science Chart Generation?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26757)
*Jiahui tang,Kuicai Dong,Dexun Li,Hongchao Gu,Haocheng Yu,Wei Han,Chen Zhang,Yong Liu,Hao Wang,Enhong Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DEEPCHART is a benchmark for evaluating LLM-based chart generation, focusing on detecting data-level hallucinations in realistic scenarios by assessing extraction, reasoning, and visualization capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern LLMs can produce visually plausible charts but often suffer from data-level hallucinations that are hard to detect in long, noisy, and multimodal contexts commonly found in real-world data science workflows.

Method: They introduce DEEPCHART, an expert-annotated benchmark of 1,482 chart-generation instances from real-world scientific papers, financial filings, and ecosystem reports. It formulates chart generation as an Extract-Reason-Visualize pipeline and evaluates each stage separately.

Result: Experiments with state-of-the-art models reveal that visually plausible charts often conceal data-level hallucinations, with extraction and reasoning errors being common in realistic long and multimodal settings.

Conclusion: Larger context windows alone are insufficient for faithful chart generation; reliable evidence extraction and quantitative reasoning are crucial before rendering. The benchmark helps measure and address this gap.

Abstract: Faithful chart generation in real-world data-science workflows requires grounding visualizations in scattered evidence, computing chart-ready quantities, and rendering them accurately. Modern LLMs can produce visually plausible, instruction-compliant charts, yet data-level hallucinations remain difficult to detect in long, noisy, and multimodal contexts. To measure this gap, we introduce DEEPCHART, an expert-annotated benchmark of 1,482 task-conditioned chart-generation instances drawn from real-world scientific papers, financial filings, and ecosystem reports. DEEPCHART formulates chart generation as an Extract--Reason--Visualize pipeline and evaluates source-data extraction, derived-data reasoning, and chart rendering stage by stage. Experiments with state-of-the-art models show that visually plausible charts often conceal data-level hallucinations, with extraction and reasoning errors common in realistic long and multimodal settings. These findings suggest that larger context windows alone are insufficient; faithful chart generation also requires reliable evidence extraction and quantitative reasoning before rendering. Our benchmark and associated resources are available at https://github.com/tangdouer1005/DeepChart.

</details>


### [159] [Categorizer Automata for Discounted-Sum Payoffs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26763)
*Nathalie Bertrand,Pranav Ghorpade,Senthil Rajasekaran,Sasha Rubin,Moshe Vardi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces categorizer automata for discretizing continuous discounted-sum rewards into bins, generalizing comparator automata. Shows linear state-space construction and applies to MDP synthesis with discontinuous utility functions, providing exact or ε-optimal pseudo-polynomial algorithms with PSPACE-hardness results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need to categorize continuous data into discrete bins is fundamental in AI. Current comparator automata (special case with 2 bins) are useful for quantitative synthesis but don't scale well to multiple bins - cross-product construction leads to exponential state spaces. Also, there's a need to handle discontinuous utility functions in MDPs that traditional approaches can't handle efficiently.

Method: Introduces categorizer automata as deterministic automata that read infinite reward sequences and categorize their discounted sums into finitely many bins. Main technical contribution: construction of categorizer automata with linear state space (vs. exponential from cross-product). Applied to MDP synthesis with discontinuous utility functions (piecewise-constant and piecewise-Lipschitz).

Result: 1) Linear-state-space categorizer automata construction. 2) For piecewise-constant utilities: exact algorithm in pseudo-polynomial time. 3) For piecewise-Lipschitz utilities (including bounded-slope functions with finite jumps): ε-optimal policy algorithm in pseudo-polynomial time. 4) PSPACE-hardness proof even for piecewise-constant utilities.

Conclusion: Categorizer automata provide an efficient framework for discretizing continuous discounted sums into multiple bins, enabling practical synthesis algorithms for MDPs with discontinuous utility functions while maintaining computational tractability, though the fundamental problem remains PSPACE-hard.

Abstract: Categorizing continuous data into discrete bins is a fundamental operation in artificial intelligence. We introduce the categorizer automaton, a deterministic automaton that reads an infinite sequence of rewards and identifies which of finitely many bins contains its discounted sum. Categorizer automata generalize comparator automata, the special case of two bins, which have already proven useful in quantitative synthesis. Our main technical contribution is the construction of a categorizer automaton whose state space is linear in the number of bins, rather than exponential as obtained by a cross-product of comparator automata. We then apply categorizer automata to Markov decision processes, where they allow one to synthesize policies that maximize the expected utility of a discounted-sum payoff for utility functions that may be discontinuous. For piecewise-constant utility functions, the resulting algorithm is exact and runs in pseudo-polynomial time. For piecewise-Lipschitz utility functions, a class that includes any utility with bounded slope between finitely many jumps, it again runs in pseudo-polynomial time and yields an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy. We also show that the synthesis problem considered is PSPACE-hard already for piecewise-constant utilities.

</details>


### [160] [AI Control Scientist: LLM-driven Agentic System for Automated Control Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26780)
*Haiteng Wang,Weihao Li,Jing Zhang,Lei Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AICS is an LLM-driven agent that automatically generates optimized controllers from language requirements using a three-agent system, outperforming existing automated baselines in design success and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional control system design relies heavily on expert knowledge and manual parameter tuning, leading to limited efficiency and scalability in critical industrial applications like chemical process temperature regulation and aero-engine control.

Method: A three-agent system: 1) Task Modeling Agent interprets user requirements to engineering constraints; 2) Controller Design Agent generates candidate controller structures and executable code; 3) Parameter Tuning Agent refines controller parameters under closed-loop performance criteria.

Result: The agentic system automatically generates multiple representative control systems and outperforms existing automated baselines in both design success rate and optimization efficiency.

Conclusion: This work has the potential to transform control system design from human-driven to agent-driven, paving the way for automated design of model predictive control and other advanced control systems.

Abstract: Control system design is critical for modern industry, such as chemical process temperature regulation and aero-engine control. However,traditional control design workflows rely heavily on expert knowledge and extensive manual parameter tuning, resulting in limited efficiency and scalability. To this end, this paper proposes AI Control Scientist (AICS), the first large language model (LLM)-driven agent capable of automatically generating optimized controller from language design requirements. Specifically, a Task Modeling Agent interprets user requirements to engineering constraints; a Controller Design Agent generate candidate controller structures and executable code; and a Parameter Tuning Agent refine controller parameters under closed-loop performance criteria. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed agentic system can automatically generate multiple representative control systems, outperforms existing automated baselines in both design success rate and optimization efficiency. This work has the potential to transform control system design from human-driven to agent-driven, paving the way for model predictive control and other advanced control systems design.

</details>


### [161] [SymbolLKG: Towards Verifiable Logical Reasoning via Logical Knowledge Graph and Symbolic Solvers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26836)
*Haizhao Fan,Yuchi Xiong,Jize Wang,Xinping Guan,Xinyi Le*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A neuro-symbolic architecture that integrates a Logical Knowledge Graph with dynamic solver routing to improve LLM reasoning accuracy and verifiability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs struggle with strict multi-step reasoning, suffering from hallucinations and inconsistency. Existing solutions like Chain-of-Thought lack verification mechanisms, and standard RAG misses complex structural dependencies in logical tasks.

Method: Proposes a neuro-symbolic architecture with: 1) ontology-based Logical Knowledge Graph treating logical rules/constraints as first-class topological nodes, 2) Logic Router for dynamic task dispatch to optimal symbolic engines, 3) topology-aware hybrid retrieval mechanism.

Result: Experimental results on logical reasoning benchmarks show the framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art prompting and RAG baselines, delivering higher accuracy and verifiable reasoning paths.

Conclusion: The neuro-symbolic integration of Logical Knowledge Graph with dynamic solver routing bridges the gap in LLM reasoning capabilities, providing a more reliable and verifiable approach to complex logical tasks.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in natural language understanding, yet they struggle with strict multi-step reasoning, frequently suffering from hallucinations and inconsistency. Existing solutions like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) lack rigorous verification mechanisms, while standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) often misses the complex, structural dependencies inherent in logical tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose a Neuro-Symbolic architecture that integrates a Logical Knowledge Graph (LKG) with dynamic solver routing. Specifically, we introduce an ontology-based LKG that treats logical rules and constraints as first-class topological nodes, enabling explicit modeling of dependencies extracted from text. We further design a Logic Router to dynamically dispatch tasks to the optimal symbolic engine, which is supported by a topology-aware hybrid retrieval mechanism. Experimental results on logical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art prompting and RAG baselines, delivering higher accuracy and verifiable reasoning paths.

</details>


### [162] [BekchiAI: Measuring, Observing, and Controlling LLM Agents in One Click](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26867)
*Mesut Toruk*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BekchiAI introduces both a benchmark for measuring agentic skills in LLM agents and an observability platform, addressing the limitations of accuracy-only evaluations for complex agent behaviors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current leaderboards only measure accuracy, failing to properly evaluate critical agentic skills like tool sequencing, planning under dependencies, judging untrusted inputs, and grounding generated arguments in complex multi-step agent operations.

Method: Created BekchiAI-Benchmark with 13 tool-using ReAct agents across 7 task categories (2,057 deterministic test tasks), using verifier-checkable gold answers computed via canonical SQL, DAG schedule computation, and closed-form lambda evaluation. Also developed BekchiAI-Platform for agent observability and control.

Result: Benchmark enables behavioral metrics beyond accuracy (tool-call adherence, URL hallucination, source-match, token cost) with initial comparison of four models (Qwen3.7-Max, gemma-4-31B-it, gemma4:26b, gpt-oss-120b). The platform provides full telemetry and remote control capabilities.

Conclusion: BekchiAI provides comprehensive measurement of agentic skills through deterministic verification methods and practical observability tools, addressing the gap in evaluating complex agent behaviors beyond simple accuracy metrics.

Abstract: Large language model agents reason, call tools, and act autonomously over many steps, but their agentic skills-correctly sequencing tools, planning under dependencies, judging untrusted inputs, and grounding generated arguments-are hard to measure with accuracy-only leaderboards. We present BekchiAI, which addresses both sides: a benchmark for measuring agentic skill and a platform for observing and controlling live agents. The BekchiAI-Benchmark, a suite of 13 tool-using ReAct agents across 7 task categories (arithmetic, structured/SQL, security detection, URL grounding, planning, orchestration, and tool-policy), totalling 2,057 deterministic, committed test tasks. Every task is verifier-checkable gold answers are computed by running canonical SQL against a real database, computing the exact schedule of a directed acyclic graph (DAG), or evaluating closed-form lambdas including adversarial security samples paired with deliberately imperfect signature scanners so a score reflects the model's own judgment, not the copying of an oracle. We define a small set of behavioral metrics beyond accuracy-tool-call adherence, URL hallucination and source-match, and per-model token cost and report a four-model comparison (Qwen3.7-Max, gemma-4-31B-it, gemma4:26b, gpt-oss-120b) whose story is in the per-family spread, not the aggregate. The benchmark runs are executed using the provided evaluation scripts. BekchiAI-Platform is a complementary web-based observability and control layer for deployed agents, providing full token and latency telemetry as well as remote run termination. The benchmark, evaluation tools, and platform are publicly released.

</details>


### [163] [C-Unseen: Weak Signal Detection in Dynamic Temporal Knowledge Graphs via LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26870)
*Yassir Lairgi,Ludovic Moncla,Khalid Benabdeslem,Rémy Cazabet,Pierre Cléau*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: C-Unseen is a self-interpretable framework for detecting weak signals in Dynamic Temporal Knowledge Graphs using rare, semantically coherent subgraphs that proliferate across time steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing weak signal detection methods based on keyword frequency, topic modeling, or untyped graph topology fail to capture the semantic and relational structure through which weak signals manifest, necessitating a better approach.

Method: The framework has two modules: 1) Rare Subgraphs Extractor where an LLM identifies subgraphs in tension with dominant snapshot narrative via chain-of-thought reasoning, and 2) Weak Signal Alerter that tracks persistence of these rare subgraphs across consecutive TKG snapshots.

Result: Experimental results demonstrate that C-Unseen outperforms keyword-, topic-, and graph-based baselines for weak signal detection.

Conclusion: C-Unseen provides an effective, self-interpretable framework for detecting weak signals in Dynamic Temporal Knowledge Graphs by leveraging semantic coherence and temporal persistence of rare subgraphs.

Abstract: Weak signals are early, low-visibility indicators that precede significant changes before those changes become established. Existing detection methods, based on keyword frequency, topic modeling, or untyped graph topology, fail to capture the semantic and relational structure through which such signals manifest. In this paper, we propose C-Unseen, a self-interpretable framework for weak signal detection in Dynamic Temporal Knowledge Graphs (DTKGs). We define a weak signal as a rare, semantically coherent subgraph that proliferates across consecutive TKG snapshots. The framework operates through two modules: a Rare Subgraphs Extractor, in which an LLM identifies subgraphs whose content is in tension with the dominant snapshot narrative via chain-of-thought reasoning, and a Weak Signal Alerter, in which the persistence of these rare subgraphs is tracked across time steps to isolate true weak signals. Experimental results demonstrate that C-Unseen outperforms keyword-, topic-, and graph-based baselines.

</details>


### [164] [Evaluating human and LLM screening workflows in a conceptually complex scoping review: Recall--workload trade-offs and run-to-run consistency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26885)
*Nikol Figalová,Lynn Huestegge,Anne Böckler-Raettig*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM screening performance depends on workflow design, not just model identity, with human-supervised workflows performing better than autonomous exclusion for high-recision tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for screening in evidence synthesis, but false negatives can remove relevant studies. There's a need to compare human and LLM screening workflows in conceptually complex reviews to understand their performance differences.

Method: Preregistered study embedded in a scoping review comparing human and LLM title-and-abstract screening. After conservative title-only screen, 1,131 records were screened by one review lead, four trained assistants, and seven complete LLM runs using different models (GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.1) and processing configurations, including nominally identical repeat run.

Result: No workflow recovered all verified eligible records. Human workflows and two GPT-5.4 file-batch runs retained 42.2-45.0% of records with 82.3-82.9% recall. Gemini 3.1 achieved highest recall (83.9%) but retained 56.7% of records. Processing configuration affected performance, with file-batch configurations outperforming all-at-once. Identical runs differed on 94 records including 29 verified eligible records.

Conclusion: LLM screening performance depends on implemented workflow, not model identity alone. For high-recall tasks, LLMs are better suited to validated, auditable, human-supervised workflows than autonomous exclusion.

Abstract: Background. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for screening in evidence synthesis, where false negatives can remove relevant studies before full-text assessment. We compared human and LLM title-and-abstract screening workflows in a preregistered study embedded in a conceptually complex scoping review.
  Methods. After a conservative title-only screen, 1,131 records were screened by one review lead, four trained assistants screening non-overlapping subsets, and seven complete LLM runs using different models and processing configurations, including a nominally identical repeat run. We compared retained workload, operational recall against 316 verified eligible records, agreement, run-to-run consistency, and procedural burden. Because eligibility was verified only for records advanced and assessed in the parent review, recall estimates were operational.
  Results. No workflow recovered all verified eligible records. The human workflows and two GPT-5.4 file-batch runs retained 42.2-45.0% of records while achieving 82.3-82.9% recall. Gemini 3.1 file batches achieved the highest recall (83.9%) but retained 56.7% of records. All-at-once configurations recovered fewer eligible records than corresponding file-batch configurations. Two nominally identical GPT-5.4 file-batch runs agreed on 91.7% of records but differed on 94 records, including 29 verified eligible records retained by only one run.
  Discussion. LLM screening performance depended on the implemented workflow, not model identity alone. Processing configuration, workload, record-level variation, and human-LLM decision integration are therefore substantive properties of deployed systems. For high-recall tasks, LLMs are better suited to validated, auditable, human-supervised workflows than autonomous exclusion.

</details>


### [165] [Learning-Augmented Online Allocation under Unreliable Advice: Robustness, Exposure Fairness, and Distribution Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26889)
*Fredy Pokou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a learning-augmented online allocation algorithm with fairness corrections that combines predictions with conservative fallback, achieving robustness against unreliable advice while reducing exposure disparities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learning-augmented algorithms rely on predictions, but unreliable advice can harm both efficiency and fairness in online decision-making. The paper addresses this problem in online allocation with finite candidate sets, irreversible decisions, and exposure constraints where both robustness and fairness are crucial.

Method: The proposed method combines advice with a conservative fallback mechanism and fairness correction. It creates a robust and fair decision rule that integrates predictions while maintaining safety through a fallback option and explicitly addresses exposure disparities through fairness corrections.

Result: Under bounded-error assumptions, the algorithm achieves consistency (performing well when predictions are accurate) and robustness (performing well even with poor predictions) with loss proportional to prediction error. Experiments demonstrate algorithm stability under adversarial advice and significant reductions in exposure disparity compared to baseline approaches.

Conclusion: The paper successfully develops a learning-augmented online allocation framework that balances the benefits of predictions with robustness against unreliable advice, while explicitly addressing fairness concerns. The proposed approach provides theoretical guarantees and empirical evidence of improved fairness and stability in decision-making systems.

Abstract: Learning-augmented algorithms improve online decisions using predictions, but unreliable advice may harm efficiency and fairness. We study an online allocation problem with finite candidate sets, irreversible decisions, and exposure constraints. We propose a robust and fair rule combining advice with a conservative fallback and fairness correction. Under bounded-error assumptions, we prove consistency and robustness with loss proportional to prediction error. Experiments show stability under adversarial advice and significant reductions in exposure disparity.

</details>


### [166] [Counterfactual Bias Testing for Application Tracking System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26899)
*Sai Yashwant,Shruti Bansal,Anurag Dubey,Samaroha Chatterjee,Satyam Kumar,Shreyash Gupta,Gantala Thulsiram*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A scalable, automated fairness auditing methodology for candidate-job matching systems using LLM agents to synthesize resumes, inject demographic treatments, and compute a comprehensive 9-metric fairness suite with automated reporting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Candidate-job matching systems are increasingly regulated as high-risk AI, but traditional correspondence-audit studies are expensive and don't scale with fast pipeline retraining cycles, requiring automated, scalable auditing solutions.

Method: 1) Use LLM agents to create identity-neutral base resumes and inject controlled demographic treatments across five protected characteristics; 2) Qualitatively flag inferred protected characteristics using EU AI Act-aligned prompts; 3) Rank candidates against job descriptions using fine-tuned sentence embeddings; 4) Compute comprehensive 9-metric fairness suite with statistical validation and automated reporting.

Result: On test corpus (5 jobs, 100 candidates, 10 demographic treatments): most metrics within tolerance, but rank-stability (MARC) and nDCG@K metrics revealed borderline issues, including one in the neutral baseline, demonstrating need for multi-metric auditing beyond just score or retention metrics.

Conclusion: LLM-agent-generated audits provide practical, low-cost complement to human-curated audits, and multi-metric, multi-family auditing is essential to detect fairness issues that single-metric approaches would miss.

Abstract: Automated candidate-job matching systems are increasingly classified as high-risk AI under emerging regulation, yet auditing them for demographic bias is expensive: classical correspondence-audit studies require hand-crafted resumes and manual submission, which does not scale to fast pipeline retraining cycles. This paper presents a general, reusable methodology that (1) uses task-specialized LLM agents to synthesize identity-neutral base resumes and inject controlled demographic treatments across five protected-characteristic axes (sex/gender, age, residence, language, disability), producing a K x (1+N) correspondence-audit matrix; (2) qualitatively flags inferred protected characteristics per an EU AI Act-aligned prompt; (3) ranks candidates against a job description via a fine-tuned sentence-embedding model and cosine similarity; and (4) computes a nine-metric fairness suite spanning counterfactual (score delta, mean absolute rank change, flip rate), group-fairness (top-K retention, four-fifths/impact ratio), and merit-aware (Recall@K, nDCG@K, equal opportunity, equalized odds) families, each with bootstrap confidence intervals, significance tests, and Benjamini-Hochberg correction, culminating in an automated PASS/INVESTIGATE/FAIL report with a composite risk score. On an example corpus of 5 job orders, 100 base candidates, and 10 demographic treatments (90 metric x variant evaluations): score shifts, top-K retention, and merit-aware rate gaps stay within tolerance for every treatment, but a rank-stability metric (MARC) and nDCG@K each surface borderline findings - including one on the neutral baseline itself - that a score- or retention-only view would miss. The results argue for multi-metric, multi-family auditing over any single aggregate score, and for LLM-agent-generated audits as a practical, low-cost complement to human-curated audits for any candidate-job matching pipeline.

</details>


### [167] [A Table Is Worth 64 Tokens: Pixel-level Compression for Multi-Table Document Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26949)
*Iñigo Alonso,Mirella Lapata*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A two-step method that uses pixel compression to first identify relevant tables in documents, then reasons over them at native resolution, saving 41% tokens while improving accuracy by 7 points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Answering questions over real-world documents requires processing long inputs with tables, and optical context compression (representing context as images) could reduce token costs, but its effect on table understanding remains unclear.

Method: A training-free, two-step method where the model first identifies which tables are needed to answer a question from pixel-compressed context, then reasons over those identified tables at native resolution.

Result: On long documents, the method saves 41% of total tokens and gains 7 accuracy points over single-step QA with native resolution tables. It also uses 15% fewer tokens than the most efficient single-step compressed configuration with no accuracy loss.

Conclusion: Pixel-level compression is effective for identifying relevant tables in long documents, and a two-step approach leveraging this asymmetry (compressed for identification, native for reasoning) provides optimal balance of efficiency and accuracy.

Abstract: Answering questions over real-world documents requires processing long inputs that interleave text with tables. Optical context compression, which represents context as images, promises to reduce token cost, but its effect on table understanding remains unclear. We study pixel-level table compression for question answering over documents with multiple tables, evaluating five VLMs across two benchmarks and five visual-token budgets. Representing tables as images at native resolution matches text in both performance and efficiency, but downscaling them makes models compensate the loss in readability with longer, less effective reasoning traces that cancel the expected savings. Highly downscaled tables, however, preserve enough signal to identify whether they are relevant to a question. We exploit this asymmetry with a training-free, two-step method: the model first identifies the tables needed to answer a question from a pixel-compressed context, and then reasons over those at native resolution. On long documents, our method saves 41% of total tokens and gains 7 accuracy points over single-step QA with native resolution tables. It also uses 15% fewer tokens than the most efficient single-step compressed configuration, with no accuracy loss.

</details>


### [168] [From Atomic to Agentic: Towards Interpretable Evaluation of LLMs' Agentic Mathematical Capabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26950)
*Jiayi Kuang,Yinghui Li,Yunze Song,Keyu Chen,Zhifeng Shen,Yangning Li,Yidong Wang,Di Yin,Ruizhi Qiao,Xing Sun,Kai Jin,Ying Shen,Liang Lin,Philip S. Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a process-level benchmark for evaluating LLM agentic mathematical reasoning, moving beyond outcome-oriented evaluation to assess structured problem-solving capabilities through planning, action, and feedback tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing math benchmarks evaluate only final answers, providing limited diagnostic value for identifying process-level failures or rigorous logic. This outcome-oriented evaluation fails to guide the transformation of LLMs into robust mathematical agents, as it cannot reveal the underlying reasoning processes and atomic capabilities.

Method: The authors develop a process-level benchmark framework that aligns agentic mathematical behaviors with a structured taxonomy of reusable mathematical atomic capabilities. They create planning, action, and feedback tasks across textual and multimodal contexts, supported by an automated pipeline that synthesizes high-quality trajectories and produces fine-grained annotations through controlled LLM rewriting.

Result: Experiments show that models with similar end-to-end accuracy can exhibit markedly different agentic capability profiles. This reveals that process-level evaluation provides crucial insights into LLMs' true potential that cannot be captured by outcome-oriented assessment alone.

Conclusion: Process-level evaluation is essential for interpreting LLMs' true capabilities and guiding the development of next-generation mathematical agents. The proposed benchmark framework enables deeper understanding of agentic mathematical reasoning and supports more targeted improvement of LLM-based mathematical problem-solving systems.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are evolving from performing end-to-end mathematical reasoning to integrating agentic intelligence. However, most existing math benchmarks evaluate only final answers. This outcome-oriented evaluation provides limited diagnostic value for identifying process-level failures or rigorous logic, failing to guide the transformation of LLMs into robust agents. To bridge this gap, we present a process-level benchmark designed to evaluate the inherent agentic mathematical reasoning abilities of LLMs. Our framework aligns problem-solving agentic behaviors with a structured taxonomy of reusable mathematical atomic capabilities. We design a comprehensive suite of planning, action, and feedback tasks across both textual and multimodal contexts, supported by an automated pipeline that synthesizes high-quality trajectories and produces fine-grained annotations via controlled LLM rewriting. Experiments reveal that models with similar end-to-end accuracy can exhibit markedly different agentic capability profiles. This demonstrates that process-level evaluation is crucial for interpreting the true potential of LLMs and guiding the development of next-generation mathematical agents.

</details>


### [169] [GraphMemix: Query-Aware Evidence Forests for Long-Term Multimodal Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26983)
*Geng Li,Yuhao Wang,Dong Li,Jianye Hao,Yuxin Peng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GraphMemix is a combinatorial-optimization graph memory framework that organizes long-term multimodal memory as query-aware evidence forests, improving accuracy while reducing lifecycle costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for long-term multimodal memory organization suffer from expensive question-agnostic offline summaries or naive embedding similarity matching, leading to incomplete and redundant context retrieval.

Method: The framework models memory organization as query-aware evidence-forest construction with three components: (1) candidate graph construction expanding multi-view seed memories via schema/semantic relations, (2) evidence utility and activation costs to suppress redundancy/conflicts, and (3) forest optimization selecting memory context under budget constraints.

Result: Experimental results across four long-term multimodal memory benchmarks show significant improvements with different foundation models and establish a new Pareto frontier between accuracy and lifecycle cost.

Conclusion: GraphMemix effectively organizes memory into query-relevant subgraphs, avoiding substantial lifecycle costs while recovering low-similarity complementary evidence, addressing key limitations of existing multimodal memory approaches.

Abstract: Organizing long-term memory for multimodal agents remains challenging because existing methods either suffer from expensive question-agnostic offline summaries or naive embedding similarity matching that introduces incomplete and redundant context. To address these issues, we propose GraphMemix, a combinatorial-optimization graph memory framework that models memory organization as query-aware evidence-forest construction. Specifically, our method consists of three key components:(1) candidate graph construction, which expands multi-view seed memories through schema and semantic relations to acquire query-aware original context; (2) evidence utility and activation costs, which decouples direct memory support from anchor-conditioned relation verification to suppress redundant or conflicting information; and (3) forest optimization, which jointly selects a forest-format memory context under a maximum evidence budget and its reliable relational structure. By organizing memory into a query-relevant subgraph, the method avoids substantial lifecycle cost and recovers low-similarity complementary evidence. Experimental results across four long-term multimodal memory benchmarks demonstrate significant improvements with different foundation models and establish a new Pareto frontier between accuracy and lifecycle cost.

</details>


### [170] [ASIL: Replacing Screenshot-and-Click with Structured State and Semantic Actions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26991)
*Rui Xie,Lu Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ASIL is an agent-native interface that replaces screenshot-and-click interactions with structured JSON observations and code-executable actions, achieving high success rates with fewer actions compared to GUI-based approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current screenshot-and-click interfaces for software-operating agents are inefficient: screenshots provide incomplete state information, GUI actions are brittle and semantically weak, and they're poorly matched for long-horizon planning tasks.

Method: ASIL exposes software through structured JSON observations and code-executable semantic actions, implemented through the deepest feasible access path for each application. It was instantiated across 15 applications and benchmarked on 300 single-application and 80 multi-application tasks.

Result: ASIL achieves above 80% success with closed models while executing fewer than 5 actions per task. In comparison, screenshot-and-click approaches yield only 6.6-26.6% success. ASIL exceeds LibreOffice's UNO API by 28-38 points but matches draw.io's MCP contract. Small-scale supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning significantly improve model performance.

Conclusion: Structured agent-software interfaces like ASIL significantly outperform traditional GUI-based interactions for software-operating agents, offering more efficient, reliable, and semantically-rich interactions that are better suited for training and long-horizon planning.

Abstract: Powerful code agents can execute scripts, call tools, and manage files, yet many important applications remain accessible primarily through graphical user interfaces. We argue that screenshot-and-click is an inefficient interface for software-operating agents: screenshots are state-incomplete, and GUI actions are brittle, semantically weak, and poorly matched to long-horizon planning. We introduce ASIL (Agent-Software Interaction Layer), an agent-native interface that exposes software through structured JSON observations and code-executable semantic actions, realized through the deepest feasible access path for each application. We instantiate ASIL across 15 applications and a benchmark of 300 single-application and 80 multi-application tasks. ASIL reaches above 80 with closed models while executing fewer than five actions per task. Under a repaired runtime and a 50-step screenshot budget, the same tasks yield 6.6 and 26.6 strict success under screenshot-and-click control, rising to 15.0 and 53.3 on an easier OSWorld-comparable band. Against application-native interfaces on matched tasks, ASIL exceeds LibreOffice's UNO API by 28-38 strict points but only matches draw.io's MCP content contract. The structured modality also suits training: small-scale SFT raises Qwen3.5-2B from 58.0 to 72.1 and Qwen3.5-9B from 66.6 to 80.4, and resource-limited on-policy RL further raises them to 74.4 and 82.2.

</details>


### [171] [A Multi-Modal AI Framework for Real-Time Queue Prediction, Management and Optimisation in Intelligent Border Control Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27010)
*Varvara Mama,Eleni Veroni,Nikolaos Kapsalis,Christos D. Nikolopoulos,Anargyros T. Baklezos*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes an AI-driven border control management system that uses LSTM networks for queue prediction and MPC/scheduling optimization for resource management, reducing queue prediction error by 35% and waiting time by 30% compared to traditional methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional border control queue management systems rely on static data, which limits their performance in dynamic traffic conditions and uncertain scenarios. There's a need for more adaptive, real-time systems that can handle variable border traffic.

Method: Develops a multi-modal AI framework that integrates heterogeneous data sources into a unified representation. Uses LSTM networks for real-time queue forecasting, and combines Model Predictive Control (MPC) with scheduling optimization to generate actionable control policies for border officers.

Result: Evaluation with synthetic realistic traffic data shows: 35% reduction in queue prediction error, 30% reduction in average waiting time, and nearly 20% increase in average throughput compared to ARIMA and rule-based methods.

Conclusion: The proposed AI-optimization framework effectively enables proactive and adaptive border traffic management, demonstrating superior performance over traditional methods and highlighting the value of combining AI architectures with optimization techniques for border control operations.

Abstract: In the present work an efficient border control management procedure is proposed. Compared to operational queue management systems, whose operations are based on mostly static data, the proposed work takes into account dynamic traffic conditions, thus enabling optimal performance, even in cases of uncertainty. To this end, we are proposing a multi-modal Artificial Intelligence (AI) framework, tailored to th needs of border control systems, which enables real-time queue prediction, management, and resource optimization. The novel proposed approach integrates heterogeneous data sources and presents them through a unified representation by employing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for queue forecasting. Furthermore, it leverages Model Predictive Control (MPC) and scheduling optimization to derive actionable control policies, which in turn can be presented to border control officers. The proposed work has been evaluated using synthetic data simulating realistic traffic. The evaluation results demonstrate that the proposed method reduces queue prediction error by up to 35% and average waiting time by 30%. Accordingly, the average throughput increases by nearly 20%, compared to ARIMA and rule-based methods. The abovementioned results show the effectiveness and efficiency of combining AI architectures with optimization techniques for proactive and adaptive border traffic management.

</details>


### [172] [Omni-Interactive Universal Embedder](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27044)
*Wei-Yao Wang,Kazuya Tateishi,Shuyang Cui,Christian Simon,Takashi Shibuya,Shusuke Takahashi,Yuki Mitsufuji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OmniUE is the first omni-interactive universal embedder that supports text, video, and audio modalities with user interaction via text, visual regions, and audio spans, significantly outperforming existing baselines across diverse benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multimodal representation learning has focused primarily on language and image modalities, with limited support for user-conditioned interactions. There's a need for embedders that can handle diverse modalities (text, video, audio) and support various interaction types (text, visual regions, audio spans) to enable more comprehensive and flexible multimodal understanding.

Method: OmniUE uses dedicated learnable tokens to create a unified embedding space across text, video, and audio. It employs visual and audio segmenters to process diverse user interactions and integrates them with an omni-LLM to produce user-conditioned any-to-any embeddings through context aggregation. The system supports omni-interactive querying where users can provide inputs in various forms.

Result: OmniUE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse modalities: 10.5% improvement on textual-interactive video benchmarks (MMEB-v2-video), 1.1% on audio tasks (MAEB), 83.7% on visual-interactive benchmarks (SCaR), and 24.1% on the newly introduced omni-interactive OmniCHOIR benchmark.

Conclusion: OmniUE represents significant progress toward universal embedders by jointly advancing omni-modal representation learning and omni-interactive querying. The introduction of OmniCHOIR benchmark facilitates evaluation of omni-interactive capabilities, and the substantial performance gains demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach for handling diverse modalities and interaction types.

Abstract: Multimodal representation learning has been shifting from traditional two-tower architectures to large language model (LLM)-based embedders due to their strong instruction-following capabilities. Despite this progress, existing approaches primarily focus on language and image modalities, which also remain the dominant modalities for user-conditioned interactions in current embedders. In this paper, we propose the first Omni-Interactive Universal Embedder (OmniUE), which not only learns a unified embedding space across text, video, and audio by leveraging intermediate-layer representations from dedicated learnable tokens, but also supports omni-interactive querying, enabling users to provide inputs in the form of text, visual regions of interest, and audio spans. Within OmniUE, visual and audio segmenters process diverse user interactions and integrate them with an omni-LLM to produce user-conditioned any-to-any embeddings via context aggregation. To evaluate OmniUE's omni-interactive capabilities, we introduce OmniCHOIR, benchmarking models for omni-interactive compositional audio retrieval based on the given text, video, and audio as well as unimodal or multimodal interaction prompts. OmniUE consistently surpasses state-of-the-art baselines across diverse modalities, with average improvements of 10.5% on textual-interactive video benchmarks (MMEB-v2-video), 1.1% on audio tasks (MAEB), 83.7% on visual-interactive benchmarks (SCaR), and 24.1% on our omni-interactive OmniCHOIR benchmark. We believe that jointly advancing omni-modal representation learning and omni-interactive querying paves the way toward universal embedders.

</details>


### [173] [pro-team at LLMs4OL 2026 Tasks Flagship and Reuse: Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Vocabulary-Constrained Filtering for Ontology Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27101)
*Shivam Mishra,Dhannu Ram Meena,Muneendra Ojha,Krishna Pratap Singh,Kuldeep Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A retrieval-augmented few-shot prompting approach using Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct for ontology learning tasks, achieving competitive scores but failing to extract non-taxonomic relations due to vocabulary constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ontology learning from text remains challenging despite LLM advances, as LLMs can hallucinate domain terms, produce inconsistent formats, and favor hierarchical over associative relations, necessitating more reliable approaches.

Method: An offline retrieval-augmented few-shot prompting pipeline using Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for demonstration retrieval (top-5 examples for Task A, top-2 for Task B), left-truncated context-windowing to preserve instructions, and deterministic vocabulary-constrained filtering for Task B.

Result: Task B: Semantic Graph Similarity 0.8692, Term-Typing F1 0.9200, Taxonomy Discovery F1 0.8540. Task A: Semantic Graph Similarity 0.7416. However, no non-taxonomic relations were extracted, highlighting limitations of closed, taxonomy-oriented relation vocabularies.
