Conclusion: The retrieval-augmented few-shot approach effectively addresses LLM limitations in ontology learning but is constrained by closed relation vocabularies that prevent extraction of non-taxonomic relations, suggesting future work on more comprehensive relation modeling.

Abstract: Ontology learning from text remains challenging despite significant progress in Large Language Models (LLMs), which can hallucinate domain terms, produce inconsistent formats, and favor hierarchical over associative relations. In the LLMs4OL 2026 Challenge, we address both the End-to-End Flagship Task (Task A) and Ontology Extension Reuse Task (Task B) using an offline retrieval-augmented few-shot prompting pipeline. Our system employs Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for demonstration retrieval, selecting the top-5 examples for Task A and top-2 for Task B. A left-truncated context-windowing strategy preserves task instructions within long prompts. For Task B, generated triples undergo deterministic vocabulary-constrained filtering, retaining triples when at least one endpoint belongs to the sample's closed term/type vocabulary and removing duplicates of the initial ontology. The approach achieves Semantic Graph Similarity of 0.8692, Term-Typing F1 of 0.9200, and Taxonomy Discovery F1 of 0.8540 on Task B, while Task A achieves 0.7416 Semantic Graph Similarity. However, no non-taxonomic relations are extracted, highlighting limitations of closed, taxonomy-oriented relation vocabularies.

</details>


### [174] [LAAF: A Layered Accountability Architecture Framework for LLM Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27102)
*Prachi Chaturvedi,Shahnawaz Ahmad,Ehsan Nowroozi,Muhammad Waqas,George Loukas,Alireza Jolfaei,Lucas Cordeiro,Pierre Dantas*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A systematic review of accountability for large language models in high-risk settings, synthesizing 122 studies into a sociotechnical accountability framework (LAAF) aligned with major regulations like EU AI Act.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in high-stakes environments like healthcare and finance where their authoritative outputs can cause harm, raising urgent questions about responsibility tracing and accountability mechanisms when things go wrong.

Method: Systematic PRISMA-guided review of 5 databases (Jan 2022-Mar 2026), analyzing 122 primary studies plus 12 regulatory documents, synthesizing accountability mechanisms into technical controls, human oversight, organizational governance, and documentation categories.

Result: Identified four accountability mechanism families with maturity assessments, created a four-layer classification device, mapped findings to major regulations (EU AI Act, NIST, ISO), and revealed four persistent gaps in current approaches.

Conclusion: Proposes LAAF (integrated accountability architecture) as a synthesis framework aligned with cybersecurity standards, highlighting unresolved structural tensions and the need for better metrics, oversight specification, and empirical validation.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) operate in hospitals, courtrooms, banks, and public service desks, where fluent, confident outputs are treated as authoritative even when ungrounded or incorrect. When such an output contributes to harm, who is answerable, and through what mechanisms can responsibility be traced, explained, and acted upon? Following PRISMA guidance, five databases were searched from January 2022 to March 2026 against four review questions; of 4,512 records identified, 122 primary studies were included, together with 12 regulatory and standards documents analysed as primary sources. The review consolidates a sociotechnical account of accountability as an actor-forum relation resolved into five dimensions, and synthesises mechanisms across four families: technical controls, human oversight, organisational governance, and documentation and traceability, each with a maturity assessment. The corpus is read through a four-layer classification device spanning provenance, application logic, human oversight, and governance and redress, cross-cut by traceability, role clarity, and continuous monitoring. Both are mapped onto the EU AI Act, whose high-risk obligations have applied since 2 August 2026, the NIST AI RMF with its Generative AI Profile, ISO/IEC 42001, and sectoral guidance in healthcare, consumer finance, education, and the public sector. Four persistent gaps emerge: under-specification of human oversight, absence of shared accountability metrics, disciplinary disconnection, and limited empirical evaluation, alongside five structural tensions that no surveyed instrument resolves. The review closes by consolidating the classification device into an integrated accountability architecture, LAAF, with cybersecurity aligned to the OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025); it is a synthesis of the surveyed evidence rather than a validated artefact.

</details>


### [175] [TransMeme: A Multi-Agent Framework for Cross-Cultural Meme Transcreation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27127)
*Jingyi Zheng,Yule Liu,Zifan Peng,Tianyi Hu,Yuemeng Zhao,Xinhu Zheng,Xinlei He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A multi-agent framework for cross-cultural meme transcreation that outperforms baselines by 33.1% in human evaluation, addressing cultural adaptation, intent preservation, and multimodal consistency through specialized coordinated agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Internet memes are widely used for online communication across diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds, but adapting memes across cultures requires more than simple translation - it must preserve communicative intent, adapt culture-dependent meaning, and maintain text-image coherence for target audiences.

Method: Proposes a multi-agent framework with specialized agents coordinated to address three core challenges: culture-specific knowledge understanding, intent/tone preservation, and multimodal consistency. The framework uses cultural adaptation, target text rewriting, revision, and conditional visual adjustment with coordinated feedback for difficult cases.

Result: Outperforms all baselines in bidirectional Chinese-English meme transcreation. In human evaluation: best performance on all four dimensions with 33.1% average improvement over strongest baseline. In LLM-as-a-Judge: highest Top-1 ranking rate (60% vs 26% for second-best). Each component contributes to performance.

Conclusion: The multi-agent framework effectively addresses cross-cultural meme transcreation challenges, but remaining bottlenecks are humor reconstruction and image-text alignment rather than cultural knowledge gaps, pointing to future work on humor transfer.

Abstract: Internet memes are a pervasive form of multimodal online communication; however, such communication often involves users from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds. Therefore, adapting memes across cultures and languages is a central challenge for enabling mutual understanding in online communication. Unlike ordinary translation or standalone text rewriting, cross-cultural meme transcreation must jointly preserve communicative intent, adapt culture-dependent meaning for the target audience, and maintain coherence between text and image. In this work, we first provide an explicit task analysis of cross-cultural meme transcreation and identify three core challenges: culture-specific knowledge understanding, intent and tone preservation, and multimodal consistency. Based on this analysis, we propose a multi-agent framework with specialized agents that are coordinated to address these challenges through cultural adaptation, target text rewriting, revision, and conditional visual adjustment. The framework strengthens target text adaptation with coordinated feedback to handle difficult cases that require deeper cultural or visual intervention. We evaluate the framework on bidirectional Chinese-English meme transcreation using both human evaluation and LLM-as-a-Judge. Our method consistently outperforms all baselines across both evaluation settings. In human evaluation, it achieves the best performance on all four dimensions and delivers a 33.1% average improvement over the strongest baseline, while in LLM-as-a-Judge, it attains the highest Top-1 ranking rate (60% versus 26% for the second-best baseline). Further analysis indicates that each component contributes to the performance. Our error analysis suggests that the remaining bottlenecks lie in humor reconstruction and image-text alignment rather than simple cultural knowledge gaps, pointing to future work on humor transfer.

</details>


### [176] [GRAIN: Bridging Name and Narrative Shifts in Real-World Graph Reasoning through Invariance-Rewarded Agentic RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27142)
*Zike Yuan,Han Zhang,Jianzhi Yan,Le Liu,Cai Ke,Huozhi Zhou,Jian Xie,Jiran Yin,Yukun Cao,Yue Yu,Hui Wang,Ming Liu,Bing Qin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GRAIN is a single-agent reinforcement learning framework that improves LLM robustness to linguistic shifts in graph tasks by learning invariant text-to-structure mappings, outperforming multi-agent approaches while reducing latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are brittle to real-world shifts in node identifiers and task formulation in graph tasks. While deterministic graph tools are invariant to such shifts, LLMs overfit to surface patterns when extracting topological structures from text. Multi-agent systems that mitigate parsing failures incur prohibitive latency costs.

Method: Proposed GRAIN, a single-agent framework optimized via reinforcement learning. It models reasoning as a semantic parsing and tool-execution pipeline guided by a Structure Invariance Reward that validates extracted intermediate graphs against ground-truth topologies, forcing the LLM to learn robust text-to-structure mappings rather than memorizing linguistic artifacts.

Result: GRAIN outperforms multi-agent baselines by 16.45% in accuracy with approximately 24% lower latency. It demonstrates superior structural generalization, halving the OOD gap of SFT models (from 15.77% to 7.80%) and maintains robustness on large-scale graphs beyond the training distribution. Introduced GRIT benchmark for evaluating sensitivity to linguistic shifts.

Conclusion: GRAIN effectively addresses LLM brittleness to linguistic shifts in graph tasks by learning invariant semantic representations through reinforcement learning, achieving better performance with lower latency than multi-agent approaches while improving generalization to out-of-distribution scenarios.

Abstract: Despite their potential in standardized graph tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) remain brittle to real-world shifts in node identifiers and task formulation. While deterministic graph tools are invariant to such shifts, extracting topological structures from noisy text is highly fragile for LLMs, which often overfit to surface patterns. Moreover, mitigating these parsing failures via multi-agent systems incurs prohibitive latency. To address this, we propose GRAIN, a single-agent framework optimized via reinforcement learning. GRAIN models reasoning as a semantic parsing and tool-execution pipeline, guided by a Structure Invariance Reward. By validating extracted intermediate graphs against ground-truth topologies, this reward forces the LLM to learn robust text-to-structure mappings rather than memorizing linguistic artifacts. We also introduce GRIT, a benchmark evaluating sensitivity to such linguistic shifts. GRAIN outperforms multi-agent baselines by 16.45\% in accuracy with approximately 24\% lower latency. Furthermore, it demonstrates superior structural generalization, halving the out-of-distribution (OOD) gap of SFT models (from 15.77\% to 7.80\%) and maintaining robustness on large-scale graphs beyond the training distribution.

</details>


### [177] [Feature Transformation Enhanced Jacobi Polynomial Graph Filtering for Graph Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27144)
*Xiang Wang,Zhijun Cheng,Zhenyu Meng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: JPGFN is a graph anomaly detection method that uses feature transformation, adaptive Jacobi polynomial filtering, and label constraints to improve detection performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph anomaly detection methods based on frequency-domain filtering face three key challenges: 1) static basic functions cannot adapt to graph data's frequency-domain distribution, 2) insufficient consideration of attribute importance leads to fine-grained information loss, and 3) insufficient utilization of node labels for anomaly detection.

Method: Proposes JPGFN with three main components: 1) Feature Separation Transformation Network (FSTNN) for learning fine-grained node features through feature separation and nonlinear transformations, 2) adaptive Jacobi polynomial graph filtering module using Jacobi polynomials to capture complex frequency-domain features, and 3) node label constraint module to leverage node labels for enhanced detection.

Result: Experimental results on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that JPGFN significantly outperforms mainstream graph anomaly detection approaches.

Conclusion: The proposed JPGFN method successfully addresses the limitations of existing frequency-domain GAD approaches by combining feature transformation, adaptive filtering, and label constraints, achieving superior performance on benchmark datasets.

Abstract: In recent years, graph anomaly detection (GAD) based on frequency-domain filtering have achieved promising results. However, existing approaches still face three major challenges: First, they use static basic function to constructed graph filter which cannot effectively adapt to the frequency-domain distribution of graph data. Second, they fail to adequately consider the importance information of each attribute in the node feature vector, leading to the loss of fine-grained information. Third, they insufficiently utilize node labels for GAD. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel graph anomaly detection method called JPGFN (Feature Transformation Enhanced Jacobi Polynomial Graph Filtering Network). First, a Feature Separation Transformation Network (FSTNN) is developed to better learn fine-grained node features by feature separation and applying nonlinear transformations to node features across different dimensions. Second, an adaptive Jacobi polynomial graph filtering module is constructed based on Jacobi polynomials to adaptively capture complex frequency-domain features of graph signals. Finally, a node label constraint module is developed to facilitate the use of node labels and enhance the performance of GAD. Experimental results on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms mainstream approaches.

</details>


### [178] [LLMs Can Design Near-Optimal OR Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27296)
*Jackie Baek*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs can design competitive algorithms for well-specified operations research problems with minimal human input, matching or outperforming existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether large language models can design effective algorithms for well-specified operations research problems with minimal human guidance, moving beyond just solving individual instances to creating general algorithms.

Method: Two-level evaluation approach: Level 1 - LLM receives single problem instance and returns solution; Level 2 - LLM receives only problem class description and parameter ranges, returns algorithm mapping parameters to solutions. Minimal human input (single untuned prompt) with Python sandbox access and fixed compute budget. Tested on inventory control, queueing network control, and assortment optimization problems.

Result: The strongest model (gpt-5.6-sol) matches or outperforms best existing methods on almost all instances, even at Level 2 where algorithm is fixed before seeing evaluation instances. Performance improves sharply across models released within 8 months, indicating rapid capability advancement.

Conclusion: For well-specified OR problems, a single untuned LLM query can produce algorithms competitive with specialized methods, suggesting frontier LLMs can serve as serious empirical baselines for algorithm design in this domain.

Abstract: We ask whether large language models (LLMs) can design effective algorithms for well-specified operations research (OR) problems. We study inventory control, queueing network control, and assortment optimization. We evaluate two levels of LLM use: at level 1, the model receives one problem instance and returns a solution for that instance; at level 2, it receives only the problem class description and broad parameter ranges, and returns an algorithm that maps instance parameters to solutions. Human input is minimal: we give one untuned prompt that describes the problem, and the model has access to a Python sandbox tool with a fixed compute budget.
  The strongest model we test, gpt-5.6-sol, matches or outperforms the best existing method on almost all evaluated instances. This holds even at level 2, where the returned algorithm is fixed before seeing the evaluation instances. Performance also improves sharply across models released less than eight months apart, suggesting that this capability is moving quickly. Thus, for the well-specified operations problems we study, a single untuned LLM query can already produce algorithms competitive with specialized methods. These results suggest that frontier LLMs can be a serious empirical baseline for algorithm design in well-specified OR problems.

</details>


### [179] [When Tool Outputs Become Commands: Separating Action Induction from Runtime Authorization in Tool-Augmented LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27146)
*Xiaokun Guo,Zhen Xu,Dongdong Huo,Yanqiu Zhang,Wei Wang,Qinfu Yang,Dongjin Yu,Yu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SARA is a security framework that separates action induction from execution authorization in tool-augmented LLM agents, preventing untrusted tool outputs from becoming unauthorized commands that cause unintended side effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tool-augmented LLM agents face security risks when tool outputs specify concrete actions that become unauthorized "commands" with real-world side effects, arising from conflating action induction with execution authorization.

Method: SARA treats action induction and execution authorization as distinct runtime roles, separating action provenance from execution authority. It uses a context-isolated Action Probe to expose action-inducing semantics and record provenance, while authorizing actual tool calls only against user objectives with audited evidence, applying No-History-Promotion to prevent historical recurrence from legitimizing unauthorized actions.

Result: SARA reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) to no more than 0.63% across four primary evaluation settings on AgentDojo and AgentDyn benchmarks while maintaining competitive task utility, and consistently reduces ASR across additional agent backbones.

Conclusion: The separation of action induction from execution authorization through SARA's architectural approach effectively mitigates security risks in tool-augmented LLM agents while preserving their functional utility.

Abstract: Tool-augmented LLM agents must rely on untrusted runtime Observations to complete open-ended tasks; however, when tool outputs no longer merely provide data but begin to specify concrete actions, they effectively become ``commands'' that can drive real-world side effects beyond user intent. We argue that this risk arises from conflating action induction with execution authorization. To address this distinction, we propose SARA, which treats action induction and execution authorization as distinct runtime roles and separates action provenance from execution authority. On the Observation side, a context-isolated Action Probe exposes action-inducing semantics and persistently records action-origin provenance across steps as a review signal; on the execution side, actual tool calls are authorized only against the user objective and audited evidence from authorized successful executions, while satisfying goal, execution-chain, and argument-level support. To preserve this separation across multi-step execution, SARA applies No-History-Promotion to prevent historical recurrence from laundering action origins into execution authority. Across AgentDojo and AgentDyn, SARA limits ASR to no more than \(0.63\%\) across four primary evaluation settings while maintaining competitive task utility, and consistently reduces ASR across additional Agent backbones.

</details>


### [180] [CorporateBench: Large-Scale Q&A Benchmarking with Temporal Knowledge Bases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27391)
*Sil Hamilton,Albert Yu Sun,Oscar J. Romero,Carl-Leander Henneking,David Mimno,Bishan Yang,Igor Labutov*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CorporateBench (CB) is a large-scale, human-validated Q&A benchmark for evaluating LLMs on corporate document collections with up to 230,000+ documents, revealing performance degradation at realistic enterprise scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM evaluation for enterprise document Q&A is inadequate because companies don't share internal communications, and synthetic datasets are overly simple, lacking realistic scale and complexity.

Method: Created CorporateBench with human-validated multi-task Q&A across four synthetic firms (12-10,000 employees) sampled from temporally evolving knowledge bases, ensuring cross-document logical consistency even across hundreds of thousands of documents.

Result: Evaluation of five LLMs on CB shows increasingly poor performance as input size approaches realistic corporate scales, demonstrating the benchmark's ability to reveal scalability limitations.

Conclusion: CorporateBench fills a crucial gap in LLM benchmarking by providing a realistic metric for evaluating corporate communication reasoning at enterprise scale, helping developers address scalability challenges.

Abstract: LLMs are increasingly able to answer complex questions about enterprise-scale document collections. But evaluation is hard: companies don't want to share internal communications, and synthetic datasets have been overly simple. We present CorporateBench (CB), a human-validated multi-task Q&A benchmark whose scale approaches the conditions LLMs encounter in corporate communication networks, with evaluation corpora surpassing 230,000 documents. CB evaluates LLMs across two dimensions (information extraction and knowledge base querying) through four synthetically generated firms ranging from 12 to 10,000 employees. Each corpus is sampled from a temporally evolving knowledge base describing a consistent world, guaranteeing cross-document logical consistency even across hundreds of thousands of documents. We evaluate five LLMs on CB, revealing increasingly poor performance as input size approaches realistic scales. CB provides LLM developers a metric for corporate communication reasoning, filling a crucial gap in the benchmarking ecosystem.

</details>


### [181] [Thomson: Continual Learning of Frontier Models for SovereignAI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27147)
*Shengzhuang Chen,Jerrod Parker,Yejin Bang,Andrew M. Bean,Nabeel Seedat,Stefan Winzeck,Daniil Glazko,Jannik Zgraggen,Fangyi Yu,Scott Arnott,Dietrich Trautmann,Luca Ciuffreda,Guglielmo Bonifazi,Davide Romano,Bradley Bell,Kirsty Fielding,Daniele Giofrè,Tom Zielund,Ipshita Chatterjee,Sneha Murthy Ghantasala,Manpreet Nanreh,John Scoville,Maciej Sakowicz,Wassim Seifeddine,Lukas Thede,Jonathan Richard Schwarz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Frontier AI performance can be achieved by diverse institutions through Continual Learning on open-weight models, as demonstrated by Thomson which matches frontier models in professional domains while eliminating forgetting problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The current AI landscape is dominated by a few heavily funded players, creating power asymmetries and limiting access to frontier AI capabilities for diverse organizations. The paper aims to enable more actors to achieve SovereignAI - independent AI development and governance.

Method: Uses Continual Learning on readily available open-weight models with a modern mid- and post-training stack. Introduces safeguards that preserve both plasticity and stability at each stage, making minimal high-impact parameter interventions rather than limited approaches like fine-tuning or prompt engineering.

Result: Demonstrated with Thomson, a general-purpose frontier model that performs competitively with recent frontier models across agentic tasks, safety, legal, tax, multilingualism, and large-scale Deep Research. Shows a distinctive π-shaped pattern: broad improvements across many capabilities including non-targeted ones, while almost completely eliminating forgetting problems.

Conclusion: Frontier performance is achievable by diverse institutions at substantially lower compute and personnel budgets than commonly thought, making SovereignAI (owning the model, infrastructure, values, and data privacy) viable for many more actors through the proposed Continual Learning approach.

Abstract: The development of frontier models is commonly perceived to be the exclusive remit of a small number of heavily funded players, creating an information, economic and power asymmetry between developers and the diverse user base of modern AI. Recent public discourse acknowledges this concern, calling for SovereignAI (an organisation's capability to independently build, deploy and govern AI use), but offers little concrete advice on how this can be achieved in the short term under a diversity of funding settings. We argue that frontier performance is achievable by a wide range of institutions through Continual Learning on readily available open-weight models. Unlike limited approaches such as small-scale fine-tuning, prompt engineering, or tool-augmentation of a frozen model, our approach exploits a modern mid- & post-training stack while introducing safeguards that preserve both plasticity and stability at each stage, making the minimal number of high-impact interventions on the parameters. This yields gains comparable to those typically seen across multiple successive model generations, at compute and personnel budgets substantially lower than commonly thought, making ownership of large parts of the SovereignAI stack (model, tool infrastructure, values & data privacy) viable for far more actors. We demonstrate this with Thomson, a general-purpose frontier model trained with an enhanced focus on high-stakes professional work. Thomson performs competitively with recent frontier models across agentic tasks, safety, legal, tax & multilingualism, and large-scale Deep Research. Evaluations show a distinctive $π$-shaped pattern: distinct improvements across a wide range of capabilities, including those not explicitly targeted, while almost completely eliminating the forgetting problem common to narrow domain adaptation.

</details>


### [182] [Learning a Continuous Sepsis Severity Score Without Hour-by-Hour Supervision: A Two-Site Retrospective Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27421)
*Kevin Zhu,Ryan Zhang,Baraa Abed,Tilendra Choudhary,Malvern Madondo,Mehak Arora,Yixuan Yang,Alasdair Gent,Aditya Nagori,Omer T. Inan,Krista L. Haines,Patrick Georgoff,Suresh M. Agarwal,Vijay Krishnamoorthy,Tetsu Ohnuma,Mihai V. Podgoreanu,Michael R. Pinsky,Gilles Clermont,Craig M. Coopersmith,Craig S. Jabaley,Rishikesan Kamaleswaran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Researchers developed a new sepsis severity index using 43 clinical variables and machine learning with mortality as a ranking signal, showing better prognostic power than traditional fixed indices like SOFA, with validation across multiple hospital systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current sepsis severity indices (like SOFA) use fixed variables and weights established decades ago, are coarsely discretized, and were calibrated to patient cohorts that no longer reflect contemporary critical care. There's a need for a learned index that uses patient trajectory data and modern statistical approaches.

Method: Retrospective two-cohort study using 29,116 and 7,691 adult sepsis patients from two hospital systems. Developed sepsis index using 43 routinely charted variables over 72-hour treatment windows. Used mortality as a treatment-level ranking signal rather than per-state target, allowing credit redistribution across timesteps. Evaluated on 20% test holdout using clinical vignettes and Spearman correlation with bootstrap resampling for uncertainty intervals.

Result: The index showed non-survivors scored 1.19-1.64 points higher than survivors on 0-10 scale across all SOFA-2 strata. Within-patient index changes correlated with lactate changes (rho=0.39). Cross-institutional agreement was 70-77% of same-site correlation. External within-patient correlations were 0.54-0.59 against ceilings of 0.90-0.92. The index correlated with established indices while null controls remained near zero.

Conclusion: The developed sepsis index provides hourly prognostic information that meaningfully separates patient outcomes and aligns with clinical expectations, indicating potential as a decision support tool to complement clinical judgment in sepsis management.

Abstract: Currently used sepsis severity indices rely on fixed variables and weights established decades ago, which are coarsely discretized and calibrated to a cohort that no longer reflects contemporary critical care. No alternative learned directly from patient trajectories is in routine use. We conducted a retrospective two-cohort study on a total of 29,116 and 7,691 adult patients meeting Sepsis-3 criteria from two hospital systems in Massachusetts and Georgie, respectively.
  We developed a sepsis index using 43 routinely charted variables over a 72-hour treatment window. Unlike previous studies, we use mortality as a treatment-level ranking signal rather than a per-state target, allowing credit to be redistributed non-uniformly across timesteps. Evaluation was done on a permanent 20% test holdout, using clinical vignettes and Spearman correlation. Uncertainty intervals were obtained by bootstrap resampling of whole patients. Under this ranking scheme, non-survivors scored 1.19-1.64 points higher than survivors on a 0-10 scale within all strata of baseline SOFA-2, with similar results stratifying within lactate, mean arterial pressure (MAP), and creatinine. Within-patient change in the index correlated with change in lactate (Spearman rho = 0.39; n = 1,854). Similar, weaker correlations were found for MAP and creatinine. On a cohort level, cross-institutional agreement measured by Spearman correlation between models trained on different sites, were 70-77% of same-site correlation. External within-patient correlations were 0.54 and 0.59 against ceilings of 0.92 and 0.90. Our index also correlated with established indices, while null controls stayed near zero.
  Our index demonstrated hourly prognostic information that meaningfully separates patient outcomes and is consistent with clinical expectation, indicating potential as a decision support tool complementing clinical judgement.

</details>


### [183] [BPMN4CAI: A BPMN Extension for Modeling Dynamic Conversational AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27149)
*Björn-Lennart Eger,Daniel Rose,Barbara Dinter*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BPMN4CAI: A BPMN extension for modeling Conversational AI interactions in business processes, developed through Design Science Research and validated via case study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing BPMN standard faces challenges representing dynamic, context-sensitive interactions of Conversational AI systems in business processes, creating a methodological and practical research gap.

Method: Design Science Research methodology used to develop BPMN4CAI - a standard-compliant BPMN extension that systematically extends existing BPMN elements and incorporates specialized components for Conversational AI.

Result: Case study demonstrates BPMN4CAI facilitates adaptive decision-making, robust context management, and transparent interactions for Conversational AI within business processes, showing applicability and relevance.

Conclusion: BPMN4CAI effectively addresses the gap in representing Conversational AI interactions in business process modeling, providing a standardized approach for modeling dynamic, context-sensitive AI conversations.

Abstract: Conversational AI systems, such as chatbots and virtual assistants, are becoming increasingly important to digital business processes. However, the established Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) standard faces challenges when representing dynamic, context-sensitive interactions. This paper addresses this methodological and practical research gap by developing a standard-compliant BPMN extension (BPMN4CAI). Using Design Science Research methodology, this paper develops an approach that systematically extends existing BPMN elements and incorporates specialized components. The applicability and relevance of the BPMN4CAI framework are demonstrated and evaluated through a case study. The results show that the BPMN4CAI extension facilitates adaptive decision-making processes, robust context management, and transparent interactions for Conversational AI within business processes.

</details>


### [184] [Calibrated Enough to Know, Not Calibrated to Act: Fabricated Evidence Makes LLM Agents Commit to the Unknowable](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27167)
*Pranav Aggarwal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM agents are strongly influenced by presentation authority rather than actual information quality when making decisions, showing that packaging (like professional-looking market panels) significantly increases commitment to unpredictable outcomes even with fabricated data. This decision-making failure is isolated to a specific "act/don't-act" gate that can be trained but remains fragile to response format constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper investigates how LLM agents make decisions in the face of uncertainty, particularly examining whether they rely on actual information quality or are swayed by presentation authority. The research aims to understand the mechanics of decision-making failures in AI systems and identify whether these failures stem from belief, judgment, or specific decision gates.

Method: The study tests 12 frontier LLM models using both genuine and fabricated market panel displays attached to provably unpredictable questions. They measure commitment rates, analyze belief probabilities, test classification of question knowability, and conduct supervised fine-tuning experiments on a 3B model using 540 synthetic cases across domains like dice, coins, jars, and timers to train the decision gate.

Result: Commitment to unpredictable questions rises dramatically from 6.5% to 54.0% when using professional-looking market panels, and even fabricated data increases commitment from 24.5% to 36.8%. Models can correctly answer knowable questions at near-perfect accuracy on the same panels. Supervised fine-tuning reduces commitment to 0.0% on original cases and transfers to unseen domains, but the training effect is fragile to rigid response formats.

Conclusion: LLMs fail at a specific "act/don't-act" decision gate that is influenced by presentation authority rather than information quality. This gate is trainable through targeted fine-tuning but remains context-fragile, suggesting that deployment must account for both the trainability of decision gates and their vulnerability to format constraints.

Abstract: An LLM agent shown a professional-looking market panel commits to a directional call on a provably unpredictable question far more often than one asked the bare question: across 12 frontier models, commitment rises from 6.5% to 54.0% as evidence is escalated. It commits just as readily when every number on the panel is invented: fabricating the entire display, so nothing the model can see is true except the question itself, still lifts commitment from 24.5% to 36.8%, statistically indistinguishable from the 37.6% produced by genuine market data. What unlocks confident action is not information but the authority of its packaging. The failure is narrow and locatable. Incapacity is not the answer: on matched answerable questions attached to the same panels, the same models answer essentially always, at near-perfect accuracy. Nor is it belief - stated probabilities barely move across the gradient that swings action by 48 points, and score worse than a climatological baseline. Missing judgment isn't it either: asked to classify a question's knowability before acting, models call it irreducible 90% of the time and then commit on just 0.4% of those. The act/don't-act gate is what fails, and the effect is concentrated in a few models rather than universal. Because the gate is separable, it can be trained. Supervised fine-tuning of a 3B model on 540 synthetic cases, predominantly dice, coins, jars and timers, drives commitment to 0.0% on the original cases and transfers to three unseen domains. It does not survive everything: the gate holds exactly when the response format leaves room to reason, and rigid formats that remove that room leave the model confident and wrong on questions it otherwise answers correctly. The gate is trainable and context-fragile, and deployment needs both halves of that sentence.

</details>


### [185] [What Makes Good Agentic Data? An ACE Lens on Data Generation for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27260)
*Xingshan Zeng,Zishan Xu,Boju Zhang,Yuzhou Wu,Lingzhi Wang,Jianghao Lin,Liangyou Li,Yasheng Wang,Lifeng Shang,Xin Jiang,Weinan Zhang,Yong Yu,Qun Liu,Weiwen Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A framework for agentic data generation organized around Accuracy, Complexity, and divErsity (ACE) to guide the creation of useful interaction data rather than simply generating more data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches to generating interaction data for LLM agents lack a unified framework, with domain-centered organization and heterogeneous evaluation obscuring common mechanisms and conflating construction with verification/selection. There's a need for systematic guidance on generating useful experience rather than merely abundant data.

Method: Two-level framework: 1) Represent agentic data as factorized object (E,q,τ,v) with environment specification, task signal, interaction realization, and optional verifier; 2) Formulate generation as constrained distribution design through ACE lens (Accuracy-Complexity-divErsity).

Result: The framework organizes generation paradigms by anchor/dependency structure, analyzes verification methods, complexity calibration, and coverage expansion. Reveals shift toward execution-grounded accuracy, learner-relative complexity, and meaningful diversity beyond surface variation.

Conclusion: The central challenge is to continually allocate valid, informative, and non-redundant experience as agents/environments evolve, not just generate more data. The ACE lens provides systematic guidance for agentic data generation with implications for scaling, training regimes, and adaptive learning.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on generated interaction data to learn how to interact with external environments. Agentic data generation must maintain consistency among environments, tasks, interactions, and success signals while producing experience that is useful rather than merely abundant. Existing work spans many agent domains, but domain-centered organization and heterogeneous evaluation often obscure common generation mechanisms and conflate candidate construction with verification and selection. This work develops a two-level framework for the field. First, we represent agentic data as a common factorized object $(E,q,τ,v)$, comprising an environment specification, task signal, interaction realization, and optional verifier. We organize generation paradigms by their primary anchor and dependency structure. Second, we formulate generation as constrained distribution design through the Accuracy-Complexity-divErsity (ACE) lens. Accuracy establishes the feasible support of grounded and internally consistent data. Within this support, Complexity places learning mass relative to the capability of a declared learner and execution configuration, while divErsity controls coverage and redundancy of data. Using this framework, we explore how prior work verifies generated experience, constructs and calibrates difficulty, and expands behavioral coverage. The literature reveals a shift toward execution-grounded accuracy, learner-relative complexity, and diversity beyond surface variation or dataset size. We further discuss broader directions and emerging trends in agentic data generation through the ACE lens, including their implications for scaling, data sources, training regimes and adaptive learning. Overall, the central challenge is not simply to generate more data, but to continually allocate valid, informative, and non-redundant experience as agents and environments evolve.

</details>


### [186] [Naive Prompt Optimization: Rethinking the Need for Complex Prompt Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27266)
*Yuan Chang,Xiaoqi Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Naive Prompt Optimization (NPO) is a simple single-lineage method that achieves comparable or better performance than complex prompt optimizers like GEPA with fewer computational costs, showing that stronger teacher reasoning can substitute for optimizer complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent prompt optimization approaches have become unnecessarily complex, while efficient improvement of autonomous agents across diverse tasks is crucial for accelerating recursive self-improvement in agentic AI. Simple, lightweight methods are needed that can deliver performance gains comparable to fine-tuning but with lower computational costs.

Method: Naive Prompt Optimization (NPO) is a lightweight single-lineage method that iteratively revises prompts using a teacher model with rollout feedback. It uses a simple linear approach rather than complex search procedures.

Result: NPO achieves comparable or better performance than GEPA with fewer rollouts, and its advantage increases with stronger teacher models. In interactive games, NPO remains competitive with GEPA, while showing that optimized prompts can transfer effectively to other student models, especially within the same model family.

Conclusion: Simple, linear prompt optimization can rival substantially more sophisticated and complex search procedures, demonstrating that stronger teacher reasoning can partially substitute for optimizer-side search complexity in achieving efficient agent improvement.

Abstract: Efficiently improving autonomous agents across diverse tasks is central to accelerating recursive self-improvement (RSI) in agentic AI, with prompt optimization emerging as a promising approach capable of delivering performance gains comparable to those achieved by fine-tuning model weights, while reducing computational costs in both optimization and serving. However, recent developments increasingly favor unnecessarily complex prompt optimizers. We introduce Naive Prompt Optimization (NPO), a lightweight single-lineage method that iteratively revises prompts using a teacher model with rollout feedback. NPO achieves comparable or better performance than GEPA with fewer rollouts, and its advantage increases with stronger teacher models, suggesting that stronger teacher reasoning can partially substitute for optimizer-side search complexity. In interactive games, NPO remains broadly competitive with GEPA, while GRPO performs better on some tasks less amenable to prompt optimization. We also show that NPO-optimized prompts elicit similar performance improvements when applied verbatim to other student models, especially across models within the same family. Overall, our preliminary results show that simple, linear prompt optimization can rival substantially more sophisticated and complex search procedures.

</details>


### [187] [BrailleBench: Investigating Multi-Criteria Braille Comprehension in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27268)
*Jinghan Zhang,Fengran Mo,Zhiyu Chen,Xiaoyan Han,Kunpeng Liu,Chang-Tien Lu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BrailleBench is a benchmark for evaluating LLMs' Braille comprehension capabilities, revealing significant gaps in Braille accessibility compared to print-English performance, especially for Grade 2 Braille.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI systems may not be inclusive enough for blind and deafblind users who rely on Braille, which has unique characteristics (indicators, contractions, digital representations) that create distinct requirements for LLM comprehension.

Method: Created BrailleBench with 5,570 instances from five datasets across mathematics, commonsense, and multi-hop QA in English and Braille Grades 1 and 2. Used deterministic, expert-reviewed pipeline via self-created Braille Toolkit without LLM-generated data to prevent bias. Evaluated six representative LLMs across different configurations.

Result: Reveals persistent gap between print-English capability and Braille accessibility. Shows asymmetry between Braille understanding and expression, with Grade 2 being especially fragile on input side compared to Grade 1. Fully Braille requests further reduce performance.

Conclusion: BrailleBench provides valuable guidance for developing future Braille AI systems and highlights the need for improved Braille accessibility in LLMs to ensure equitable access for blind and deafblind users.

Abstract: Although Large language models (LLMs) mediate access to knowledge and computational assistance, their capabilities should benefit vulnerable groups in the same way. However, it is unclear whether existing AI systems are inclusive enough for blind and deafblind users to access the same functionality through Braille, whose indicators, contractions, and digital representations introduce distinct requirements for model comprehension. To this end, we introduce BrailleBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs in Braille comprehension from different Criteria. BrailleBench aligns 5,570 instances from five datasets, including mathematics, commonsense, and multi-hop question answering across English and Braille Grades 1 and 2. Different configurations are designed to understand whether the systems can comprehend Braille-authored content, express answers in Braille, and complete end-to-end Braille interaction. To ensure the quality and prevent evaluation bias, the benchmark is built through a deterministic, expert-reviewed pipeline via a self-created Braille Toolkit without using any data instances generated by LLMs. We evaluate six representative LLMs from various aspects. The results reveal a persistent gap between print-English capability and Braille accessibility. Braille understanding and expression are asymmetric, where Grade 2 is especially fragile on the input side compared to Grade 1, and fully Braille requests further reduce performance. The experimental observations provide valuable guidance for the development of future Braille AI systems. All related resources in BrailleBench are publicly available for future research.

</details>


### [188] [Verify Smarter, Evolve Further: Efficient Harness Evolution through Behavior-Aware Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27311)
*Jinghan Xu,Yikai Zhang,Aili Chen,Weiyuan Li,Jiaqing Liang,Deqing Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HarnessLens is a budget-aware framework for automated evolution of language-model agent harnesses that uses behavior-aware verification with explicit attribution to improve efficiency and performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current propose-and-verify methods for adapting agent harnesses are inefficient - they score every candidate on fixed task sets, wasting rollouts on unrelated behaviors and allowing aggregate scores to obscure specific regressions. There's a need for more sample-efficient harness evolution under constrained interaction budgets.

Method: HarnessLens jointly explores task space and user-configurable components, derives candidate modifications from execution trajectories, and selectively verifies each candidate on behavior-relevant tasks using an attributable-evidence gate. It's a budget-aware framework that emphasizes behavior-aware verification with explicit attribution.

Result: Across three agent harnesses and four benchmarks, HarnessLens improves average held-out performance by 7.6-13.6% while consuming substantially less evaluation budget than competing baselines. The framework demonstrates that behavior-aware verification with explicit attribution enables more reliable and sample-efficient harness evolution.

Conclusion: Behavior-aware verification with explicit attribution enables more reliable and sample-efficient harness evolution under constrained interaction budgets. The HarnessLens framework successfully addresses the limitations of existing propose-and-verify methods by focusing verification on relevant behaviors and avoiding wasted rollouts.

Abstract: Agent harnesses shape how language-model agents use instructions, tools, and runtime components, but adapting these harnesses requires costly verification. Existing propose-and-verify methods typically score every candidate on a fixed task set, wasting rollouts on unrelated behaviors and allowing aggregate scores to obscure specific regressions. We introduce HarnessLens, a budget-aware framework for automated harness evolution. HarnessLens jointly explores the task space and user-configurable components, derives candidate modifications from execution trajectories, and selectively verifies each candidate on behavior-relevant tasks using an attributable-evidence gate. Across three agent harnesses and four benchmarks, HarnessLens improves average held-out performance by 7.6-13.6% while consuming substantially less evaluation budget than competing baselines. These results demonstrate that behavior-aware verification with explicit attribution enables more reliable and sample-efficient harness evolution under constrained interaction budgets. Our code is available at https://github.com/jhxu5214/HarnessLens.

</details>


### [189] [Not All Eval-Awareness Is Equal: Capabilities Framing Predicts Compliance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27340)
*Allison Zhuang,Santiago Aranguri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Eval-awareness in language models is not a single uniform quantity but comes in distinct "flavors" (capabilities vs safety framings) that predict very different compliance behaviors, and aggregate suppression rates can mask important safety-relevant differences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current safety evaluation pipelines treat eval-awareness as a single quantity to be suppressed, but this approach may overlook important behavioral nuances and differences in how models interpret evaluation contexts.

Method: The study analyzes verbalized eval-awareness in chain-of-thought reasoning, categorizing it into capabilities-flavored, safety-flavored, both, or neither framings. It examines Qwen3-32B over the FORTRESS dataset and uses a CoT-prefill intervention on eval-awareness-negative rollouts to test causal relationships.

Result: Capabilities-framing predicts much higher compliance than safety-framing (24-46 percentage-point gap across conditions). The link appears causal based on CoT-prefill interventions where 10 of 11 prefills shifted compliance in predicted directions. Aggregating eval-awareness suppression rates can hide safety-relevant components.

Conclusion: Eval-awareness is behaviorally non-uniform, with different framings leading to qualitatively different compliance outcomes. Safety evaluations should distinguish between different flavors of eval-awareness rather than treating it as a single quantity, as aggregate suppression rates can mask important safety considerations.

Abstract: Steering interventions targeting eval-awareness, a model's recognition that it is being tested, are increasingly used in safety evaluation pipelines, where evaluation-awareness is treated as a single quantity to be suppressed. We show that verbalized eval-awareness in chain-of-thought can be identified as capabilities-flavored ("the user is testing my ability to follow instructions"), safety-flavored ("the user is testing my boundaries"), both, or neither: framings that predict compliance very differently. On Qwen3-32B over the FORTRESS dataset, capabilities-framing predicts compliance with a +24 to +46 percentage-point gap over safety-framing across all tested steering conditions. A CoT-prefill intervention on eval-awareness-negative rollouts suggests the link is causal, with 10 of 11 prefills shifting compliance in the predicted direction. Then, eval-awareness is not behaviorally uniform: aggregate suppression rates can move while the safety-relevant component does not, and the same "X% suppression of eval-awareness" can correspond to qualitatively different behavioral outcomes.

</details>


### [190] [Sophistication in GenAI Use: Field Evidence from a Large Firm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27364)
*Nicholas J. Hallman,Zachary T. Kowaleski,Anu Puvvada,Jaime J. Schmidt*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Senior employees use generative AI more sophisticatedly, sophistication varies by function (highest in Strategy/Digital Innovation/Project Management), and neither time nor formal training significantly improves sophistication.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper aims to understand how sophistication in generative AI use varies among back-office workers in a large firm, addressing gaps in knowledge about real-world AI adoption patterns and factors influencing sophisticated usage.

Method: Analyzed proprietary data including 713,564 employee prompts and corresponding LLM responses from nearly 4,000 back-office employees across 15 functional areas over eight months in 2025, using observational data to measure sophistication patterns.

Result: Three key findings: 1) Senior employees exhibit more sophisticated genAI use (domain expertise complements AI), 2) Sophistication varies by function (highest in Strategy, Digital Innovation, and Project Management), 3) Neither time nor formal AI training improved sophistication significantly.

Conclusion: Sophisticated genAI use is tied to domain expertise and organizational context, is difficult to change, and the study provides practical measures for managers to improve outcomes and researchers to build upon in future work.

Abstract: We study how sophistication in generative AI (genAI) use varies among the back-office workforce of a large firm. Using proprietary data, we observe 713,564 employee prompts and their corresponding large language model responses from nearly 4,000 back-office employees across 15 functional areas over eight months in 2025. We document three main findings. First, senior employees exhibit more sophisticated genAI use, consistent with domain expertise complementing genAI capabilities. Second, sophistication varies considerably across functions and is highest in Strategy, Digital Innovation, and Project Management, three groups that share a focus on firmwide strategic initiatives and organizational change. Third, we observe neither improvements in sophistication over time nor lasting improvements following formal AI training, suggesting that sophisticated use can be difficult to change. Together, our study provides measures of and insights into sophisticated genAI use that managers can use to improve outcomes and that researchers can use in future research.

</details>


### [191] [Mechanistic Reaction Prediction via Discrete Flow Matching on Graph-Structured Electron Occupation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27429)
*Nguyen Xuan-Vu,Octavian Susanu,Daniel Armstrong,Philippe Schwaller*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MAELLE models chemical reactions as discrete flow matching over electron occupation vectors instead of de novo molecule generation or heuristic graph edits, achieving competitive performance on reaction prediction benchmarks while providing mechanistically interpretable electron rearrangement trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chemical reactions are fundamentally electron transformations, but most ML approaches either generate products from scratch or use heuristic graph edits on molecular topology rather than directly modeling electron rearrangements. This gap motivates a more fundamental approach that captures the mechanistic nature of reactions.

Method: MAELLE models reactions as discrete flow matching over electron occupation vectors. It formulates reactant-to-product mapping as a Continuous-time Markov Chain (CTMC) over graph-structured integer-valued electron occupation space (bonding, non-bonding, hydrogen sites). The approach generalizes discrete flow matching mixture path to electron rearrangements using Optimal Transport, creating interpretable edit trajectories without requiring elementary step annotations.

Result: MAELLE achieves competitive performance on USPTO-480K benchmark compared to leading reaction prediction models. It maintains strong performance in out-of-distribution settings (structural complexity and reaction type) where existing methods degrade. The model naturally recovers mechanistic trajectories aligned with known chemistry and can predict side products of reactions.

Conclusion: MAELLE provides a novel approach to reaction modeling that directly captures electron rearrangements rather than working at the molecular graph level, offering both competitive prediction accuracy and mechanistic interpretability while being robust to distribution shifts.

Abstract: Chemical reactions are fundamentally transformations in electron space, yet most machine learning approaches model them either through \textit{de novo} generation of product molecules or through heuristic graph edits that operate directly on molecular topology.
  We introduce MAELLE (\textbf{M}ech\textbf{A}nistic \textbf{E}dit f\textbf{L}ow-matching on e\textbf{L}ectron r\textbf{E}arrangements), which instead models reactions as discrete flow matching over electron occupation vectors.
  Concretely, we formulate the reactant-to-product mapping as a Continuous-time Markov Chain (CTMC) over the graph-structured integer-valued electron occupation space defined on all bonding, non-bonding, and hydrogen sites.
  To construct the intermediate edit trajectories, we generalize the discrete flow matching mixture path to discrete electron rearrangements using Optimal Transport, yielding a sequence of mechanistically interpretable edit moves without requiring elementary step annotations.
  MAELLE achieves competitive performance on the USPTO-480K benchmark compared with leading reaction prediction models.
  Beyond in-distribution accuracy, we evaluate robustness across two out-of-distribution settings - structural complexity and reaction type - and find that MAELLE maintains strong performance where existing methods degrade.
  Finally, because the learned flow operates over the full electron redistribution, MAELLE naturally recovers mechanistic trajectories that align with known chemistry and can predict side products of a reaction.

</details>


### [192] [WikiSkill: Compiling Agent Experience into Persistent Knowledge for Skill Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27454)
*Liyan Tang,Cyrus Rashtchian,Chun-Sung Ferng,Andrew Tomkins,Da-Cheng Juan,Tu Vu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WikiSkill framework co-evolves agent skills with a persistent wiki knowledge base, systematically consolidating experience for reusable, transferable skills that outperform state-of-the-art methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current skill evolution methods scatter optimization insights across histories, limiting systematic reuse across iterations. There's a need for persistent knowledge accumulation to guide skill development and enable better cross-iteration skill evolution.

Method: WikiSkill framework separates raw execution experience, accumulated knowledge in a persistent wiki, and executable skills. It continuously consolidates experience into the wiki, which subsequent skill updates can build upon, enabling systematic co-evolution of skills and knowledge.

Result: WikiSkill consistently outperforms state-of-the-art skill-evolution methods across diverse benchmarks and models. Skills transfer effectively across models and model families, and skills evolved by other models can outperform self-evolved skills. Persistent knowledge accumulation is critical for effective skill evolution.

Conclusion: Systematic accumulation and refinement of agent experience through persistent knowledge bases enables development of reusable and transferable skills. Skill evolution complements model scaling, with evolved skills providing significant performance benefits across different model sizes and types.

Abstract: Agent skills package specialized knowledge and workflows into reusable resources that extend AI agent capabilities. Recent work automatically discovers such skills from agent experience, which enables agents to progressively adapt through interaction. However, the insights that guide skill development typically remain scattered across optimization histories, limiting their systematic reuse across iterations. We introduce WikiSkill, a framework that co-evolves agent skills with a persistent knowledge base (wiki). At a high level, WikiSkill separates raw execution experience, accumulated knowledge, and executable skills, while continuously consolidating experience into the wiki, which subsequent skill updates can build on. Across diverse benchmarks and models, WikiSkill consistently outperforms state-of-the-art skill-evolution methods and improves over no-skill baselines in most model-benchmark settings. We find that skill evolution complements model scaling: larger models generally benefit more from evolved skills, while smaller models with skills can outperform substantially larger models without them. We also find that evolved skills transfer effectively across models and model families, and skills evolved by other models can outperform self-evolved skills. Finally, our ablation studies confirm that persistent knowledge accumulation in the wiki is critical for effective skill evolution. These results demonstrate the benefits of systematically accumulating and refining agent experience for developing reusable and transferable skills.

</details>


<div id='cs.LG'></div>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [193] [SLM-Conditioned Hierarchical Relation Routing for Labeled Property Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26132)
*Michal Podstawski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SLM-Conditioned Hierarchical Relation Routing integrates small language models into graph neural networks to enable semantic-aware message routing in labeled property graphs, improving prediction accuracy while preserving structural evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional graph neural networks treat node and relationship properties as static feature vectors, which limits their ability to dynamically determine which semantic evidence should influence message propagation for specific prediction targets in labeled property graphs.

Method: The proposed architecture uses a topology GNN as a structural anchor, processes structured graph soft tokens with a small language model (SLM) to generate target-conditioned routing queries, and performs hierarchical message selection: first within each relationship type, then across relation-level summaries.

Result: The approach provides bounded residual updates to the topology anchor, preserving structural evidence while allowing contextual semantic information to modify predictions, with support for interpretable analysis at both neighbor and relationship-type levels.

Conclusion: The architecture successfully integrates language-derived semantics into property-rich graph learning, offering a general mechanism for semantic-aware message routing that enhances prediction accuracy while maintaining interpretability.

Abstract: Labeled property graphs combine relational structure with heterogeneous textual and categorical properties attached to both nodes and relationships. Conventional graph neural networks typically represent these properties as static feature vectors, limiting their ability to determine which semantic evidence should influence message propagation for a particular prediction target. We propose SLM-Conditioned Hierarchical Relation Routing, an architecture that integrates a small language model directly into graph message selection. A topology GNN provides a stable structural representation and prediction anchor. For each target node, incident messages combine the neighbor's structural state, node-property encoding, relationship-property encoding, and relationship type. A parameter-efficient SLM processes structured graph soft tokens and produces a target-conditioned routing query. This query first selects relevant messages within each relationship type and subsequently routes information across relation-level summaries. The resulting representation provides a bounded residual update to the topology anchor, preserving structural evidence while allowing contextual semantic information to modify the prediction. The architecture supports interpretable analysis at both the neighbor and relationship-type levels and provides a general mechanism for integrating language-derived semantics into property-rich graph learning.

</details>


### [194] [NeuronFuzz: Safety Neuron Guided Fuzzing for LLM Safety Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26222)
*Zhiyuan Xu,Muhammad Firhard Roslan,Joseph Gardiner,Sana Belguith,Lichao Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NeuronFuzz: A white-box fuzzing framework that uses internal safety neuron activations as continuous feedback for jailbreak testing, eliminating expensive response generation and improving jailbreak discovery rates significantly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM safety testing methods are expensive and provide sparse guidance because they require generating full model responses for each candidate prompt. This approach is particularly inefficient for strongly aligned models where most candidates fail with the same outcome.

Method: NeuronFuzz uses a SafetyOracle that converts safety-neuron activations into continuous safety alarm scores during prefill (no response generation needed). It identifies safety neurons using template-invariant inputs and stability-aware selection, then uses gradient-based analysis to find safety-sensitive template positions and a masked language model to generate fluent mutations while preserving harmful payloads.

Result: Across 21 text and multimodal models, NeuronFuzz achieves 76-100% jailbreak discovery rates on white-box source models (outperforming baselines by up to 48 percentage points). Its optimized templates transfer zero-shot to other models, achieving average ASR of 69.6%/92.6% for open-weight models and 44.1%/60.0% for proprietary models.

Conclusion: NeuronFuzz demonstrates that internal neuron activations provide valuable continuous feedback for jailbreak testing, enabling more efficient and effective safety evaluation of LLMs while maintaining attack transferability to both open-weight and proprietary models.

Abstract: Safety evaluation is critical for assessing whether aligned Large Language Models (LLMs) remain robust against jailbreak attacks. Existing automated testing methods, however, largely rely on response-level feedback: each candidate prompt typically requires generating a target-model response to evaluate its attack effectiveness. This process is expensive and, more importantly, provides only sparse guidance on strongly aligned models, where most candidates are rejected with the same failure outcome.
  This paper presents NeuronFuzz, a white-box fuzzing framework that exploits internal safety neurons as continuous execution feedback for LLM safety evaluation. A SafetyOracle converts safety-neuron activations into a continuous safety alarm score that serves as feedback for fuzzing and can be obtained during prefill, eliminating response generation from the fuzzing loop. To construct the SafetyOracle, NeuronFuzz uses template-invariant harmful and benign inputs and stability-aware selection to identify a compact set of safety neurons whose activations capture harmful-intent recognition. Moreover, since the safety alarm score is differentiable, NeuronFuzz uses its gradients to identify safety-sensitive template positions and a masked language model to generate fluent, context-compatible mutations while preserving original harmful payload and avoiding additional optimization variables. We evaluate NeuronFuzz across 21 text and multimodal models. Across five white-box source models, it achieves a 76-100% jailbreak discovery rate, outperforming baselines by up to 48 percentage points. Its optimized templates further transfer zero-shot to open-weight and six proprietary target models, achieving average ASR and top-5 ensemble ASR (EASR) of 69.6%/92.6% and 44.1%/60.0%, respectively.

</details>


### [195] [Pruning Binarized Neural Networks: A Dedicated Framework and Globally Weighted Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26233)
*Roan Rubiales,Jean Pierre David*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A PyTorch framework for binarized neural networks with novel global pruning method achieves 70% pruning rate on VGG11 with constant accuracy, outperforming SOTA's 41%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extreme compression (binarization) reduces memory/arithmetic costs for edge deployment, but existing pruning methods don't work well with binarized representations and rarely translate to meaningful hardware savings.

Method: PyTorch-based research framework for binarized neural networks with freezing/pruning mechanisms, plus a novel pruning method that accounts for relative importance of parameters across abstraction levels using global weighting.

Result: The proposed global weighting pruning method achieves 70% pruning rate on VGG11 with constant accuracy, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art results (41% pruning) in binarized settings.

Conclusion: The framework enables rapid evaluation/prototyping, and the novel pruning method with global weighting provides superior accuracy-pruning trade-off for binarized neural networks, offering better efficiency for edge hardware deployment.

Abstract: Extreme compression of deep neural networks, up to full binarization, dramatically reduces memory footprint and arithmetic complexity, facilitating deployment on constrained edge hardware with field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and microcontrollers. Although combining binarization with pruning promises additional efficiency gains, existing pruning strategies are ill-suited to binarized representations and rarely translate into meaningful hardware savings. We introduce a PyTorch-based, research-oriented framework that incorporates freezing and pruning mechanisms for designing and optimizing binarized neural networks. The framework enables rapid and reproducible evaluation of state-of-the-art approaches and the fast prototyping of new ones. Leveraging this framework, we propose a novel pruning method that accounts for the relative importance of learned parameters across abstraction levels. Such a global weighting mechanism consistently achieves a superior trade-off between model accuracy and pruning rate, achieving a 70% pruning rate on VGG11 with constant accuracy, while state-of-the-art results reach only 41% in the binarized setting.

</details>


### [196] [Muon with Finite Newton-Schulz: The Smoothing Benefit in Nonsmooth Nonconvex Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26288)
*Mingyi Li,Taira Tsuchiya*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Muon optimizer with finite Newton-Schulz iterations can be beneficial for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization by smoothing the polar decomposition, enabling convergence guarantees that exact-polar Muon cannot achieve.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing theory treats the finite Newton-Schulz iteration used in Muon as either replaced by exact polar decomposition or as an approximation error. The authors want to show that finite Newton-Schulz can actually be beneficial for optimization rather than just being an approximation error.

Method: Analysis through online-to-nonconvex conversion, viewing Muon as an online learner and converting its regret bound into stationarity guarantees. The finite Newton-Schulz iteration smooths the discontinuous polar map into a Lipschitz map of singular values.

Result: Proved that Newton-Schulz depth growing only logarithmically in target accuracy suffices for convergence to stationary points in nonsmooth nonconvex optimization. Sample complexity bounds match best-known guarantees for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization and are optimal for smooth nonconvex optimization up to problem-dependent factors.

Conclusion: Finite Newton-Schulz iteration in Muon provides beneficial smoothing properties that enable convergence guarantees in nonsmooth nonconvex optimization, unlike exact-polar Muon which may fail to converge. The analysis extends to general spectral maps with similar smoothing properties.

Abstract: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for the matrix-valued parameters in large language model pretraining, approximately orthogonalizing its momentum with a few Newton-Schulz iterations. Existing theory either replaces this iteration with the exact polar factor it approximates, or treats its finite depth as an approximation error, and thus the iteration Muon actually runs can only hurt the guarantees. We show that finite Newton-Schulz can instead be beneficial for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization. To this end, we analyze Muon through the online-to-nonconvex conversion, which views the update rule as an online learner and converts its regret bound into a stationarity guarantee. The finite Newton-Schulz iteration smooths the discontinuous polar map into a Lipschitz map of the singular values, and Muon with finite Newton-Schulz can be regarded as an online learner with a smoothed spectral potential. This smoothing is exactly what the conversion needs: we prove that a Newton-Schulz depth growing only logarithmically in the target accuracy suffices for convergence to stationary points in nonsmooth nonconvex optimization, whereas Muon with the exact-polar update may fail to converge. The resulting sample complexity bounds match the best-known guarantees for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization and are optimal for smooth nonconvex optimization up to problem-dependent factors. The argument extends beyond Newton-Schulz to general spectral maps with the same smoothing property.

</details>


### [197] [Algebraic Multigrid Acceleration for Efficient Label Spreading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26309)
*Antonia van Betteray,Jonathan Klees,Miriam Schäfers,Matthias Rottmann*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AMELS is an efficient label spreading framework that uses algebraic multigrid solvers to accelerate semi-supervised learning on large-scale datasets with minimal labeled data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual annotation of large-scale datasets is expensive and time-consuming. Existing label spreading methods have computational limitations when applied to large-scale, high-dimensional datasets due to memory constraints and high computational costs.

Method: Proposes AMELS (Algebraic Multigrid Acceleration for Efficient Label Spreading) which: 1) fast construction of neighborhood graphs, and 2) incorporates algebraic multigrid solvers to replace ordinary random walk iterations. The multigrid approach spreads label information across graphs of any size in a single multigrid cycle.

Result: AMELS achieves significant runtime reductions compared to existing implementations, is more robust to hyperparameter choices in both runtime and classification accuracy, and enables efficient label spreading on large-scale image datasets with accurate labels even from few labeled samples.

Conclusion: AMELS provides an efficient and scalable solution for semi-supervised learning on large datasets by combining algebraic multigrid acceleration with label spreading, overcoming computational bottlenecks while maintaining accuracy with minimal labeled data.

Abstract: Modern machine learning models rely on large amounts of labeled data. However, manual annotation of large-scale datasets is expensive and time-consuming. Label spreading is a semi-supervised learning technique that addresses this challenge by propagating information from a few labeled examples to a larger pool of unlabeled data. Despite its effectiveness, its application to large-scale, high-dimensional datasets is limited by computational costs and memory constraints. To address these limitations, we propose Algebraic Multigrid Acceleration for Efficient Label Spreading (AMELS), an efficient label spreading framework that improves scalability by fast construction of neighborhood graphs and the incorporation of algebraic multigrid solvers. The latter is an iterative solver that replaces the ordinary random walk iteration typically performed in label spreading. Due to the multilevel nature of algebraic multigrid solvers, AMELS spreads given label information across a graph of any size in a single multigrid cycle. We demonstrate that AMELS achieves significant runtime reductions compared to existing implementations while also being more robust to hyperparameter choices in terms of both runtime and classification accuracy. Our framework therefore enables efficient label spreading on large-scale image datasets and produces accurate labels even when only a few labeled samples are available.

</details>


### [198] [Privacy Without Regret: Differentially Private Inference-Time Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26324)
*Ishi Jain,Nandini Bhattad,Sayak Ray Chowdhury*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Adding calibrated noise to reward scores in Best-of-N sampling achieves both differential privacy and KL-regularized alignment, with zero additional alignment cost when privacy budget exceeds a critical threshold.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Best-of-N sampling suffers from reward hacking (exploiting errors in proxy reward models) and lacks privacy protection for sensitive human preference data used to train reward models.

Method: Two methods: 1) PrivBoN adds Gumbel noise to reward scores for ε-differential privacy and KL-regularized alignment; 2) PrivITP combines χ²-regularized rejection sampling with two-phase Gaussian mechanism for ex-post (ε,δ)-DP with privacy cost independent of number of responses.
