Abstract: Model merging promises to construct a single multi-task model from independently fine-tuned task models without accessing the original task data. This makes it attractive when task data cannot be centralized, but released task models may still leak private fine-tuning data. Differential privacy (DP) provides a principled mechanism for limiting such leakage, yet its effect on model merging remains poorly understood. In this paper, we study the geometry of differentially private model merging and identify two geometric obstacles that make private task models difficult to merge: \emph{local sharpness}, which makes task losses sensitive to the parameter displacement induced by merging, and \emph{reference drift}, which measures the displacement of private task models from the shared pretrained initialization and amplifies cross-task interference. Based on these observations, we propose \textbf{DP-Merging}, a geometry-aware framework that improves the mergeability of differentially private task models. DP-Merging uses a DP-compatible sharpness-aware objective to guide each private task model toward flatter loss regions, and a reference-based alignment regularizer to keep task models close to the shared pretrained initialization. We derive a merge-gap upper bound showing that reducing local curvature and reference drift tightens the bound on the loss increase induced by merging. Experiments on vision and language tasks across multiple privacy budgets show that DP-Merging consistently improves private merged-model performance while preserving the privacy guarantees of the underlying DP fine-tuning procedures.

</details>


### [225] [Simple Actors and Deep Critics for Scalable Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26659)
*Guhyeon Kang,Jaehwi Lee,Minhae Kwon*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LAC is an offline RL method with a lightweight deterministic actor and deep critic that achieves performance comparable to diffusion/flow-matching policies with 4x lower inference latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current expressive generative actors (diffusion/flow-matching) in offline RL capture multimodal behavior but require multiple denoising/integration steps per action, incurring substantial overhead at deployment. Since critics are only used during training while actors run at every decision step, allocating capacity to critics rather than actors is more favorable for inference efficiency.

Method: LAC (Light Actor, deep Critic) combines a lightweight deterministic actor with a deep critic using three key ingredients: 1) residual MLP backbone to address optimization issues, 2) n-step bootstrap targets to mitigate bootstrap-noise amplification, and 3) categorical cross-entropy loss to prevent value-range drift.

Result: On OGBench, LAC matches the performance of strongest diffusion- and flow-matching baselines while achieving up to 4x lower inference latency (comparable to one-step distilled policies without distillation). The critic recipe also transfers across different actor parametrizations.

Conclusion: LAC demonstrates that investing capacity in critics rather than actors is effective for offline RL, achieving state-of-the-art performance with significantly improved inference efficiency, and the proposed critic stabilization techniques enable scaling MLP critics in offline settings.

Abstract: Recent progress in offline reinforcement learning (RL) has been driven by expressive generative actors such as diffusion and flow-matching policies, which capture multimodal behavior in offline datasets. However, these actors require multiple denoising or integration steps per action and thus incur substantial overhead at every decision in deployment. In this work, we revisit where capacity should be invested in an offline actor--critic method. Since the critic is used only during training and is discarded at deployment while the actor runs at every decision step, allocating capacity to the critic rather than the actor is more favorable for inference-time efficiency. However, scaling MLP critics in offline RL is known to introduce several distinct instabilities that have, in practice, kept critics shallow. We identify three distinct failure modes that arise when critics are deepened in offline RL---optimization, bootstrap-noise amplification, and value-range drift---and address each with a corresponding ingredient: a residual MLP backbone, n-step bootstrap targets, and a categorical cross-entropy loss. Combining these ingredients with a lightweight deterministic actor, we propose LAC (Light Actor, deep Critic). On OGBench, LAC matches the strongest diffusion- and flow-matching baselines while achieving up to 4x lower inference latency, comparable to one-step distilled policies without distillation. Its critic recipe also transfers across actor parametrizations.

</details>


### [226] [Neural Regression with Embeddings for Numerical Attribute Prediction in Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26729)
*Rupesh Sapkota,Louis Mozart Kamdem Teyou,Moshood Yekini,Caglar Demir,Axel-Cyrille Ngonga Ngomo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LitEm is a neural regression model that enables transductive KG embedding models to predict numerical attributes, with a co-training framework that improves link prediction performance while making models "literal-aware."


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most knowledge graph embedding models neglect rich numerical attributes in real-world KGs, limiting their ability to handle diverse information and represent real-world knowledge graphs effectively.

Method: Proposes LitEm, a neural regression model for predicting numerical attributes, and a co-training framework that jointly trains state-of-the-art transductive KG embedding models with LitEm.

Result: LitEm achieves best or second-best results on most attributes across multiple datasets. Co-training improves link prediction for bilinear models and enables attribute prediction, with literal-awareness evaluation showing meaningful encoding of attribute information.

Conclusion: The approach effectively integrates numerical attributes into KG embeddings, enhancing both attribute prediction and link prediction capabilities, with demonstrated literal-awareness that goes beyond parameter addition benefits.

Abstract: In recent years, transductive knowledge graph embedding models have been applied to tasks such as link prediction and query answering. Although knowledge graphs often contain rich numerical attributes, most embedding models neglect them, limiting their ability to represent real-world knowledge graphs with diverse information. In this work, we propose a neural regression model (LitEm) that enables transductive knowledge graph embedding models to predict numerical attributes within knowledge graphs. Experimental results demonstrate that LitEm achieves the best or second-best results on most attributes across FB15K-237, YAGO15K, DB15K, and Mutagenesis. Furthermore, we propose a co-training framework that jointly trains state-of-the-art transductive knowledge graph embedding models with LitEm, which improves link prediction performance mainly for bilinear models and simultaneously enables them to predict numerical attributes. In addition, the literal-awareness evaluation demonstrates that co-training helps models to encode and exploit attribute information in a "literal-aware'' manner, suggesting that the observed gains are not merely due to additional parameters. We publicly release our implementation at https://github.com/dice-group/dice-embeddings.

</details>


### [227] [Rethinking Message Passing as Retrieval for Text-Attributed Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26732)
*Jintang Li,Yuhong Chen,Ruofan Wu,Binli Luo,Jiayi Ji,Hui Li,Rongrong Ji*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes RTA, a retrieval-augmented framework that replaces traditional GNN message passing with label-aware retrieval and propagation, showing competitive performance with improved efficiency and robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional GNNs rely on message passing between neighbors, which can be computationally expensive and sensitive to imperfect graph structures. It's unclear why neighborhood aggregation consistently outperforms simple MLPs. The authors aim to address these limitations by rethinking GNNs from a retrieval-augmented perspective.

Method: Proposes RTA (Retrieval-Augmented framework) that replaces structural message passing with label-aware retrieval and propagation. Each layer makes predictions by applying an MLP to a node representation combined with a permutation-invariant summary of retrieved graph context.

Result: Experiments on text-attributed graph benchmarks show RTA matches or outperforms strong GNN and graph LLM baselines while improving computational efficiency and robustness across diverse scenarios.

Conclusion: The retrieval-augmented view provides a novel perspective on GNNs, offering theoretical connections to attention mechanisms, demonstrating robustness to retrieval errors, and showing that MLP-based approaches with proper context retrieval can achieve state-of-the-art performance with better efficiency.

Abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are typically conceptualized as message-passing neural networks, yet it remains unclear why neighborhood aggregation reliably outperforms node-wise multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). Despite its empirical success, this paradigm can be computationally expensive and sensitive to imperfect graph structures. In this work, we present a retrieval-augmented view of GNNs: each layer makes predictions by applying an MLP to a node representation together with a permutation-invariant summary of retrieved graph context. Motivated by this perspective, we propose RTA, a simple MLP-based framework that replaces structural message passing with label-aware retrieval and propagation. We provide theoretical insights that (i) connect retrieval-based aggregation to softmax-attention message passing, and (ii) establish the robustness of retrieved-context supervision to mis-retrieved outliers. Experiments on multiple text-attributed graph benchmarks show that RTA matches or even outperforms strong GNN and graph LLM baselines while improving efficiency and robustness across diverse scenarios.

</details>


### [228] [Self-Augmented Diffusion Guidance for Physics-Informed Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26748)
*Akira Osaka,Naoya Takeishi,Takehisa Yairi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Physics-informed diffusion guidance with self-generated data augmentation ensures generated spatiotemporal signals adhere to physical laws while maintaining computational efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard diffusion models generate physically plausible spatiotemporal signals (like fluid dynamics) but don't incorporate physical constraints, leading to samples that deviate from true dynamics despite appearing visually correct.

Method: Proposes physics-informed diffusion guidance with self-generated data augmentation. Learns data distribution conditioned on deviation from physical correctness, generates samples by setting deviation condition to zero. Decouples governing equation evaluation from diffusion training/sampling, avoiding expensive equation solving during denoising.

Result: Method significantly reduces physical deviations compared to standard diffusion models, achieves further improvements when combined with existing physics-constrained diffusion methods. Enables faster sample generation and applicability to computationally expensive simulation problems.

Conclusion: The proposed approach effectively incorporates physical constraints into diffusion models for spatiotemporal signal generation while maintaining computational efficiency, enabling more accurate physical simulations without the computational burden of solving governing equations at each denoising step.

Abstract: Diffusion models can be used to generate spatiotemporal signals of physical phenomena, such as time-series images of fluid dynamics. However, a major limitation of standard diffusion models is that they do not incorporate constraints derived from the underlying physical laws. Consequently, generated samples may appear visually plausible while deviating substantially from the true dynamics. In this study, we propose a simple yet effective physics-informed approach based on diffusion guidance with self-generated data augmentation. The proposed method learns the data distribution conditioned on the degree of deviation from the physically correct dynamics and generates samples by explicitly setting the deviation condition to be zero. The method decouples the evaluation of the governing equations from the diffusion model training and sampling processes, avoiding the need to solve the governing equations at every iteration of the denoising process. This design makes the method applicable to problems requiring computationally expensive numerical simulations and enables faster sample generation. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model not only significantly reduces the deviations compared with standard diffusion models but also achieves further reductions when combined with existing physics-constrained diffusion methods.

</details>


### [229] [Safety by Design: Realized-Cost Constraints for Contextual Bandits with Continuous Actions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26755)
*Spyros Dragazis,Aldo Pacchiano*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a new safety-constrained contextual bandit framework that enforces high-probability constraints on realized costs rather than expected costs, addressing heteroscedastic settings where actions affect outcome variability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safety-constrained bandit models enforce safety by requiring expected costs to remain below thresholds, which is insufficient in heteroscedastic settings where actions affect both expected outcomes and variability. In applications like dosage selection or autonomous driving, even a single unsafe decision can have catastrophic consequences, necessitating more stringent safety guarantees.

Method: The authors propose High-Probability Constrained UCB (HPC-UCB), an optimistic-pessimistic algorithm that explores for reward while conservatively estimating the safe action set. The algorithm handles one-dimensional continuous actions with stage-wise high-probability constraints on realized costs, using a dual approach: optimistic reward estimation for exploration and pessimistic safety estimation for constraint satisfaction.

Result: For linear reward and cost models, the authors prove a tight $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\sqrt{T})$ regret bound. They extend the analysis to general function classes using the eluder dimension. Experimental results show that enforcing realized-cost safety substantially reduces violations compared with expected-cost constrained baselines.

Conclusion: The proposed high-probability constraint framework provides stronger safety guarantees than existing expected-cost approaches, particularly in heteroscedastic settings. The HPC-UCB algorithm achieves both good regret performance and substantial reduction in safety violations, making it suitable for safety-critical applications like clinical trials and autonomous systems.

Abstract: Contextual bandits are a standard framework for sequential decision-making under uncertainty, with applications in clinical trials, dosage selection, recommendation systems, and autonomous systems. Safety is central in many of these applications, since a single unsafe decision in settings such as dosage selection or autonomous driving can have catastrophic consequences. A common way to model safety in bandit problems is to associate each action with both a reward signal and a cost signal, and to optimize reward subject to constraints on cost. Most existing safety-constrained bandit models enforce safety by requiring the expected cost of each action to remain below a prescribed threshold. However, this may be insufficient in heteroscedastic settings, where the chosen action affects not only the expected reward and cost, but also the variability of the observed outcomes. We study contextual bandits with one-dimensional continuous actions and stage-wise high-probability constraints on the realized cost. We propose High-Probability Constrained UCB, an optimistic-pessimistic algorithm that explores for reward while conservatively estimating the safe action set. For linear reward and cost models, we prove a tight $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\sqrt{T})$ regret bound, and we extend the analysis to general function classes using the eluder dimension. Experiments show that enforcing realized-cost safety substantially reduces violations compared with expected-cost constrained baselines.

</details>


### [230] [Beyond Client Averaging: A Client-Independent Second-Order Stationary-Bias Component in Stochastic SCAFFOLD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26765)
*Yi-Ping Tang,Guan-Ju Peng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper provides a precise bias analysis for full-participation stochastic SCAFFOLD with one-dimensional homogeneous clients, showing that while client averaging suppresses the leading O(γ/N) bias, it doesn't remove the client-independent O(γ²) bias component.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing analyses of stochastic SCAFFOLD identify leading bias terms but don't identify first client-independent contributions at coefficient level. The paper aims to precisely quantify bias in federated learning with control variates, particularly how client averaging affects bias components.

Method: Theoretical analysis of full-participation stochastic SCAFFOLD with one-dimensional homogeneous clients, fixed local-step count H, and bounded additive gradient noise. Uses mathematical proofs to derive bias coefficients uniformly over client counts N≥2.

Result: Derived exact coefficients for stationary mean bias: leading O(γ/N) term and client-independent O(γ²) term with explicit coefficients involving f'''(x⋆), σ², and H. Shows client averaging suppresses first term but not second when coefficient is nonzero. Verified through numerical experiments.

Conclusion: Client averaging suppresses leading bias but doesn't eliminate client-independent O(γ²) bias in SCAFFOLD due to indirect mechanisms where control variates alter local trajectories and second moments, converted into bias by nonquadratic curvature. Result is limited to one-dimensional homogeneous setting.

Abstract: Existing constant-step analysis of stochastic \Scaf{} identifies a leading $O(γ/N)$ stationary mean bias and shows that higher-order bias can persist as the client count increases, but does not identify the first client-independent contribution at coefficient level. For full-participation stochastic \Scaf{} with one-dimensional homogeneous clients, fixed local-step count $H$, and bounded additive gradient noise, we prove, uniformly over $N\ge2$,
  $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}_{π_{γ,N,H}}[x]-x^\star ={}& -\frac{f'''(x^\star)σ^2}{4f''(x^\star)^2}\fracγ{N}\\ &- \frac{f'''(x^\star)σ^2}{12f''(x^\star)} \frac{(H-1)(5H-1)}{H}γ^2 +O_H\!\left(\frac{γ^2}{N}+γ^3\right). \end{aligned} $$
  Hence client averaging suppresses the leading $O(γ/N)$ bias but does not remove the client-independent $O(γ^2)$ component when its coefficient is nonzero.
  The mechanism is indirect: although the direct control contribution cancels pathwise in the linear global average, the controls still alter within-round local trajectories and their second moments. Fresh gradient noise and persistent control fluctuations therefore generate local second-moment corrections that nonquadratic curvature converts into stationary mean bias. The coefficient vanishes for quadratic objectives. Numerical experiments are consistent with the predicted coefficient, its persistence as client count increases, and the stated joint remainder. The result is restricted to the one-dimensional homogeneous fixed-$H$ setting.

</details>


### [231] [On the Indistinguishability of Human v/s AI Generated Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26797)
*Jaee Ponde,Aritra Das,Mihir More,Debayan Gupta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Analyzing how access to human writing samples enables strategic paraphrasing to make AI-generated text more human-like, with convergence guarantees and scaling analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid improvement of LLMs has created an urgent need to distinguish AI-generated text from human writing, especially as paraphrasing tools can make machine text appear more human-like. The paper aims to understand how access to human samples enables strategic manipulation of machine-generated responses.

Method: Studying a multi-sample setting with both human and machine responses to the same prompts. The approach involves repeated paraphrasing of machine-generated responses toward the human distribution. Analysis includes establishing convergence under simple mixing and stability conditions.

Result: Shows that repeated paraphrasing moves the machine distribution toward the empirical human distribution. The paper derives an explicit convergence rate, extends analysis to finite-sample settings, and characterizes how the required number of human samples and paraphrasing rounds scale with desired error.

Conclusion: Access to human writing samples enables strategic paraphrasing that can systematically make AI-generated text more human-like, with quantifiable convergence properties and practical scaling insights for detection evasion.

Abstract: The rapid improvement of LLMs has made distinguishing AI-generated text from human writing a pressing problem. This challenge is further amplified by paraphrasing tools designed to make machine-generated text appear more "human". We study how access to human writing samples can be used to strategically paraphrase machine-generated responses toward the human distribution. Under a multi-sample setting with human and machine responses to the same prompts, we show that repeated paraphrasing moves the machine distribution toward the empirical human distribution under simple mixing and stability conditions. Our results derive an explicit convergence rate, extend the analysis to a finite-sample setting, and characterize how the required number of human samples and paraphrasing rounds scale with the desired error.

</details>


### [232] [SAGE: Variate-Wise Semantic Augmentation for Vision-Language Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26829)
*Haizhao Fan,Xinyi Le*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAGE is an end-to-end CLIP-based framework for time series forecasting that combines temporal, cross-variable, textual, and visual information through dual CLIP encoders, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy without expensive LLM inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current time series forecasting models lack semantic knowledge that domain experts use, such as variable meaning and statistical behavior. Existing solutions either use expensive LLMs at inference or apply uniform textual prompts that ignore variable heterogeneity.

Method: SAGE uses CLIP text encoder with frequency-enhanced patches and variable tokens, with gated residual paths for variable-specific descriptions. In parallel, frozen CLIP vision encoder aligns rendered series with temporal representations through contrastive training. This dual CLIP approach adds semantic and visual supervision without LLMs in the forecasting loop.

Result: SAGE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across eight long-term benchmarks and the M4 dataset. Ablation studies confirm complementary gains from multimodal alignment and variable-level knowledge.

Conclusion: SAGE effectively bridges the semantic gap in time series forecasting by leveraging multimodal CLIP encoders to incorporate variable-specific knowledge and visual representations, achieving superior performance without computational overhead of LLM inference.

Abstract: Time series forecasting models operate on raw numerical sequences, lacking the semantic knowledge that domain experts implicitly leverage, such as the physical meaning of each variable, its statistical behavior, and its temporal dynamics. Recent efforts to bridge this gap fall into two camps. Some rely on large language models at inference time, which is computationally expensive. Others apply uniform textual prompts at the dataset level, ignoring the heterogeneous semantics across individual variates. We propose SAGE (Seeing and Augmenting with Grounded Encoding), an end-to-end CLIP-based framework that jointly models temporal, cross-variable, textual, and visual information. The CLIP text encoder processes frequency-enhanced patches and variable tokens, while gated residual paths inject variable-specific descriptions and statistical descriptors. In parallel, the frozen CLIP vision encoder aligns rendered series with temporal representations through a training-only contrastive objective. This dual use of CLIP adds complementary semantic and visual supervision without placing an LLM in the forecasting loop. Across eight long-term benchmarks and M4, SAGE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy. Ablations confirm complementary gains from multimodal alignment and variable-level knowledge.

</details>


### [233] [Reinforcement Learning-Based Control of CAV Platoon Joining Maneuvers in Mixed Traffic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26860)
*Biao Yin,Abderrahmane Kasmi,Nadir Farhi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A framework for testing DRL algorithms on CAV platoon joining in mixed traffic shows PPO outperforms DQN/DDQN with 98% success rate, using risk penalties or safety controllers for safety-efficiency tradeoffs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CAV platooning can improve road safety and traffic capacity, but real-world deployment faces challenges from uncertainty and heterogeneous human driving behaviors in mixed-traffic environments.

Method: Proposed a generic modeling/simulation framework using agent-based modeling with SUMO simulator to evaluate DQN, DDQN, and PPO algorithms for CAV platoon joining maneuvers, incorporating risk penalties or external safety controllers.

Result: PPO outperforms DQN and DDQN with ~98% joining success rate and <1% collision rate, but requires more decision steps. Safety controllers prevent collisions but may reduce joining efficiency, showing trade-off between safety, effectiveness, and decision efficiency.

Conclusion: Safety and efficiency must be jointly considered when designing RL-based controllers for CAV platoon joining in mixed traffic, with PPO showing best performance through risk-aware reward design.

Abstract: Connected and automated vehicle (CAV) platooning offers a promising approach to improving road safety and traffic capacity. However, platoon control in real-world traffic is challenging due to uncertainty and heterogeneous driving behaviors. Reinforcement learning (RL) has strong potential for addressing such control problems, but its practical deployment raises challenges related to safety and learning efficiency. This paper proposes a generic modeling and simulation framework for investigating CAV platoon joining maneuvers and comparing deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based control algorithms. The problem is particularly challenging in mixed-traffic environments, where CAVs coexist with human-driven vehicles exhibiting heterogeneous longitudinal and lateral behaviors. The objective is to achieve safe and efficient joining maneuvers by either incorporating penalties for risky behaviors into the learning process or using an external safety controller to constrain the learned policy. An agent-based modeling framework coupled with the Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) simulator is used to evaluate Deep Q-Network (DQN), Double Deep Q-Network (DDQN), and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Results show that PPO outperforms DQN and DDQN, achieving a joining success rate of approximately 98 % and a collision rate below 1 %, largely due to risk-related penalties incorporated into the reward function. However, this improved performance requires more decision steps to complete the maneuver, revealing a trade-off between safety, joining effectiveness, and decision efficiency. An external safety controller effectively prevents collisions, although its interventions may reduce joining efficiency. The results highlight the importance of jointly considering safety and efficiency when designing RL-based controllers for CAV platoon joining in mixed traffic.

</details>


### [234] [When Is the Sharp Covariance Envelope Tight? Feature-Only Geometry for Volume-Sampled Least Squares](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26877)
*Kihun Rhee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Establishes Loewner envelope for coefficient covariance under volume sampling with sharpness guarantees, phase transitions based on feature margins, and certificates for conservative cardinality decisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on volume sampling established identities and formulas but only at endpoint s=d. The paper aims to extend analysis to all legal budgets d <= s <= m with global sharpness guarantees and characterize exact spectral phase transitions.

Method: Uses ordinary indexed fixed-size volume sampling followed by selected unweighted least squares. Establishes Loewner envelope for centered coefficient covariance, analyzes phase transitions via feature-only margin nu_A, employs residual-augmented change of measure, and develops sound lower certificates.

Result: Obtains globally sharp Loewner envelope for coefficient covariance across all legal budgets. Identifies spectral phase transition: nu_A > 0 gives strict normalized spectral envelope for all compatible residuals, while nu_A = 0 yields spectrally tight residual. Provides one-sided quantitative slack bounds and proves attainment via support saturation.

Conclusion: The analysis provides complete characterization of coefficient covariance under volume sampling with sharpness guarantees, establishes exact spectral phase transitions via feature margins, and offers practical certificates for conservative decision-making. Claims concern conditional centered covariance in fixed-design setting, not population generalization.

Abstract: Prior analyses by Derezinski and Warmuth established all-size sampling identities, selected-OLS unbiasedness, and inverse moments for ordinary volume sampling, while their exact arbitrary-fixed-response loss and prediction-covariance formulas are at the rank-size endpoint s=d. We establish a Loewner envelope for centered coefficient covariance for every full-rank fixed pool, response, and legal budget d <= s <= m under ordinary indexed fixed-size volume sampling followed by selected unweighted least squares; its coefficient is globally sharp over the full-rank class. Global sharpness does not determine attainability on the pool in hand. Under positive loss, strict-interior budgets, and no coloops, a feature-only margin nu_A gives the exact fixed-design spectral phase: nu_A > 0 if and only if the normalized spectral envelope is strict for every compatible residual, whereas nu_A = 0 if and only if some compatible residual is spectrally tight; the same zero-margin residual is tight at every strict-interior budget. A residual-augmented change of measure supplies the response-aware mechanism and a one-sided quantitative slack bound, while support saturation proves the attainment direction. Critical equal-leverage geometry interprets the boundary, and sound lower certificates yield conservative same-primitive cardinality decisions. Frozen-feature examples show that the certificate is nonvacuous and measure the fixed-pool cost of its authorized reduction. The claims concern conditional centered, full-Gram-whitened coefficient covariance, not population generalization.

</details>


### [235] [Mitigating Strong-Modality Collapse in Multimodal Learning via Inverted Asymmetric Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26879)
*Mary Ogbuka Kenneth,Foaad Khosmood,Abbas Edalat*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper identifies "strong-modality collapse" where multimodal fusion degrades the dominant modality, proposes Inverted Asymmetric Fusion (IAF) that preserves the dominant modality while weaker modalities attend to it, and shows performance improvements over unimodal baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal fusion often fails to outperform the best unimodal baseline, with the dominant modality being degraded during integration - a phenomenon the authors term "strong-modality collapse."

Method: Proposes Inverted Asymmetric Fusion (IAF) that avoids mutual attention across modalities, preserves the dominant modality unchanged, while weaker modalities attend to it as contextual anchor. Weaker modalities are strengthened using Modality-Aware Knowledge Distillation before fusion.

Result: IAF preserves the dominant modality's internal accuracy at its unimodal ceiling across all tested configurations, while symmetric fusion degrades it by up to 18.5%. IAF improves over the strongest unimodal baseline by up to 8.25% on various benchmarks.

Conclusion: Strong-modality collapse explains why some multimodal models fail to surpass unimodal baselines, and the proposed IAF effectively addresses this issue by preserving the dominant modality while allowing weaker modalities to benefit from it through asymmetric attention.

Abstract: Fusing multiple modalities is expected to improve model performance. However, on the MultiHuSE dataset, early, late, and symmetric attention fusion often fail to outperform the best unimodal baseline (text). Pathway isolation of a symmetric attention fusion model reveals that the text-pathway accuracy drops from 74.9% to 56.4% after fusion in one such setting, indicating that the dominant modality can be degraded during integration. We term this strong-modality collapse and argue that it helps explain why some multimodal models fail to surpass unimodal baselines. We propose Inverted Asymmetric Fusion (IAF), which avoids forcing mutual attention across modalities. The dominant modality is preserved by passing through fusion unchanged, while weaker modalities attend to it as a contextual anchor. Before fusion, weaker modalities are strengthened using Modality-Aware Knowledge Distillation. We evaluate IAF on three benchmarks with different modality hierarchies: text-dominant datasets (MultiHuSE, UR-FUNNY) and an audio-visual-dominant dataset (MUStARD). Pathway isolation shows that IAF preserves the dominant modality's internal accuracy at its unimodal ceiling across all tested configurations, whereas symmetric fusion degrades it by up to 18.5% on MultiHuSE. IAF improves over the strongest unimodal baseline by up to 8.25%.

</details>


### [236] [A Layer Importance Metric for Quantization Accounting for the Speed-Quality Trade-off in Autoregressive Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26926)
*Artem Safronov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A composite metric for small LLM quantization that combines information retention and throughput gains to prioritize layers for acceleration, enabling predictable quantization without expensive inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Small language models run on devices with limited resources, but uniform quantization hurts them because they have limited redundancies and only a few layers are insensitive to lower precision. Need a method to identify which layers to quantize for optimal speed-quality trade-off.

Method: Propose a composite metric with two orthogonal criteria: information retention (measured via normalized SQNR-based coefficient) and throughput gains (modeled using roofline-based latency analysis). Profile models to find promising targets, estimate quality score via simulated quantization and speed score via roofline modeling, then combine into a composite priority coefficient to tune speed-quality trade-off.

Result: Applied to Gemma 3 1B, found Feed-Forward Network blocks and embedding matrix are most promising acceleration targets. Method achieves ~4% prediction error for accelerated speedup, allocates more resources to expressive layers compared to evolutionary search, specialized accelerators, or Shapley-value approaches, and makes sLLM quantization predictable.

Conclusion: The proposed analytical approach transforms sLLM quantization from trial-and-error into a predictable engineering task, providing a general metric that can prioritize blocks, sublayers, or entire transformer layers without requiring expensive approximate inference.

Abstract: Small language models (sLLMs) are nowadays hosted on devices with limited memory and computational budget. In an autoregressive setup, inference is memory-bandwidth bound: uniform quantization is often detrimental to such models, since their architecture has limited redundancies and only a few layers are not very sensitive to lower precision. We propose a composite metric that combines two orthogonal criteria: information retention (measured in terms of a normalized SQNR-based coefficient) and throughput gains (modeled using a roofline-based latency analysis). By profiling Gemma 3 1B, we find that Feed-Forward Network blocks and the embedding matrix are the most promising targets for acceleration. For each candidate, we estimate a normalized quality score based on simulated quantization and a normalized speed score based on roofline modeling with no actual execution needed. We combine the two scores in a composite priority coefficient, allowing us to tune the trade-off between speed and quality as needed. Our metric is general and can be used to prioritize individual blocks, their projection sublayers, or transformer layers as a whole. We evaluate our approach on several model architectures, showing that our estimates have at around 4% prediction error for the accelerated speedup. We find that our method generally allocates more resources to the most expressive layers compared to evolutionary search, specialized accelerators, or Shapley-value-based approaches that require expensive approximate inference. Our analytical approach makes sLLM quantization a predictable engineering task.

</details>


### [237] [Scaling Model-Generated Distillation Data Can Make Latent Teacher Traits More Recoverable](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26958)
*Zhichen Dong,Zhixuan Liu,Yuyu Fan,Xiangtian Li,Shuyang Zhang,Chao Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Larger off-task generated datasets surprisingly amplify subtle teacher-specific traits in student models, even when examples don't explicitly mention the traits, requiring trait-aware curation in distillation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper challenges the conventional view that scaling model-generated data always improves distillation through better coverage and noise reduction. It investigates whether larger datasets might unintentionally amplify subtle teacher-specific traits that transfer to students even in off-task data.

Method: The authors use a controlled "subliminal learning" setup where teachers are induced to express target traits, then generate restricted off-task data (e.g., number-only completions). Students are trained on varying amounts of this independent off-task data and evaluated in separate domains, with matched no-trait controls isolating target-specific transfer. They analyze LoRA updates and test across model families, trait types, multi-trait settings, and cross-model transfer.

Result: Larger independent datasets make the teacher's induced traits stand out more clearly in student behavior. When small-scale students already favor the target trait, scaling amplifies it; when they favor alternatives, more data can shift behavior toward the intended trait. These effects appear consistently across different experimental conditions.

Conclusion: Scaling generated distillation data requires trait-aware curation and evaluation even when data appears off-task or benign, as subtle teacher-specific signals become more detectable with larger datasets, potentially amplifying unintended traits.

Abstract: Scaling model-generated data is usually viewed as improving distillation: more examples should increase coverage, reduce noise, and produce stronger students. We show a second effect: larger datasets can make subtle teacher-specific signals easier to detect in the trained student, even when examples are off-task and never mention the trait. In a controlled setup inspired by subliminal learning, a teacher induced to express a target trait generates restricted off-task data, such as number-only completions. Students trained on different amounts of independent off-task data are evaluated in a separate domain, with matched no-trait controls isolating target-specific transfer. Our main finding is that larger independent datasets make the teacher's induced trait stand out more clearly in the student's later behavior. Other plausible traits may also strengthen with scale, but the target usually grows more. When the small-scale student already favors the target, scaling mainly amplifies that behavior; when it favors a related or salient alternative, more data can shift behavior toward the intended trait. Analyses of learned LoRA updates show a parallel trend. These effects appear across model families, trait types, multi-trait settings, and cross-model transfer. Our results suggest that scaling generated distillation data should be paired with trait-aware curation and evaluation, even when the data appears off-task or benign.

</details>


### [238] [Gromov-Monge Flow Matching for Equivariant Graph Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26961)
*Moritz Piening,Christian Wald*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel flow matching method for graph generation that incorporates structural awareness by using Gromov-Monge alignment in quotient spaces, improving sample quality with efficient Gromov-Wasserstein relaxations for tractable training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard permutation-equivariant architectures don't fully exploit the structural symmetries of graphs. When comparing graph pairs up to node relabeling, the natural geometry is the quotient space, but existing flow matching methods don't properly account for this structural alignment between source and target graphs.

Method: Use Gromov-Monge distance (optimal node relabeling) as Euclidean quotient metric for graph pairs. Develop tractable minibatch couplings using efficient Gromov-Wasserstein relaxations for node alignment, optionally combined with outer assignment between graphs. The approach modifies only training couplings while remaining compatible with standard permutation-equivariant architectures.

Result: The structure-aware couplings substantially improve sample quality for continuous graph and categorical molecular generation, especially at small integration budgets. Scaled-up molecular models remain competitive under conventional many-step sampling regimes.

Conclusion: Incorporating structural alignment through quotient space geometry and Gromov-Monge distances significantly enhances flow matching for graph generation, offering improved sample quality while maintaining compatibility with existing architectures and scaling effectively to larger models.

Abstract: Graphs are invariant under node permutations, motivating the use of permutation-equivariant architectures in generative models. In flow matching, however, symmetry may also enter the source--target coupling: once graph pairs are compared up to node relabeling, the natural Wasserstein geometry is that of the graph quotient space. The Euclidean quotient metric of this space coincides with the Gromov--Monge distance, obtained by optimally relabeling the nodes. We develop this perspective theoretically, showing that quotient couplings can be lifted to aligned representatives without additional cost and that symmetrization yields equivariant flow-matching minimizers, including for categorical endpoint prediction. In practice, exact Gromov--Monge alignment is intractable, so we construct minibatch couplings using efficient Gromov--Wasserstein-type relaxations and lower bounds for the inner node alignment, optionally combined with an outer assignment between graphs. The resulting procedure changes only the training coupling and is compatible with standard permutation-equivariant architectures. Across continuous graph and categorical molecular generation, these structure-aware couplings substantially improve sample quality at small integration budgets, while our scaled-up molecular models remain competitive under conventional many-step sampling.

</details>


### [239] [Packora: Systematic Design for Generative Molecular Crystal Structure Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26962)
*Nayoung Kim,Kiyoung Seong,Sungsoo Ahn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Packora is a flow-based generative model for molecular crystal structure prediction that jointly predicts atomic coordinates and lattice parameters from molecular graphs, supporting multi-component and organometallic crystals with flexible conditioning capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Molecular crystal structure prediction (CSP) is crucial in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and organic electronics because subtle differences in molecular conformation and packing can significantly impact material properties. Current methods need improvement in handling diverse crystal types and integrating multiple conditioning information.

Method: Packora uses a flow-based generative model architecture that predicts atomic coordinates and lattice jointly from molecular graphs. Key innovations include: 1) cacheable pairwise reasoning, 2) specific training objectives and numerical solver choices, 3) conditioning dropout, and 4) balanced scaling of pairwise and single representations. The method supports multi-component and organometallic crystals with flexible conditioning on molecular conformers, stereochemical labels, and space-group information.

Result: Packora outperforms baselines on both structure generation and ranking benchmarks, achieving: 1) best matched-budget coverage across all six generation benchmarks, 2) higher experimental-form recovery rates, 3) lower experimental-form ranks, and 4) faster convergence in ranking tasks. Evaluation follows CCDC CSP blind test methodology with separate generation and ranking assessments.

Conclusion: Packora represents an effective flow-based approach to molecular crystal structure prediction that handles diverse crystal types with flexible conditioning, demonstrating superior performance across multiple benchmarks through systematic architecture and training optimizations, making it a promising tool for practical CSP applications in materials science and drug development.

Abstract: Molecular crystal structure prediction (CSP) is important in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and organic electronics, where subtle differences in molecular conformation and packing can strongly affect material properties. We present Packora, a flow-based generative model for molecular CSP that jointly predicts atomic coordinates and the lattice from molecular graphs. Packora supports multi-component and organometallic crystals and can condition on any subset of molecular conformers, stereochemical labels, and space-group information within a single model. Inspired by the CCDC CSP blind test, we evaluate generation and ranking separately, using generation to isolate generator quality and ranking to measure end-to-end performance under a common relaxation and ranking pipeline. We also systematically study architecture, training, conditioning, inference, and scaling, identifying an effective design based on cacheable pairwise reasoning, training objective and numerical solver choices, conditioning dropout, and balanced scaling of pairwise and single representations. Packora outperforms the baselines on both structure generation and ranking benchmarks, achieving the best matched-budget coverage across all six generation benchmarks, as well as higher experimental-form recovery, lower experimental-form ranks, and faster convergence in ranking.

</details>


### [240] [Adversarial Training Without Input Gradients via Low-Rank Householder Expansions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26963)
*Tiana C. Johnson,Donsub Rim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Adversarial training without gradient-based inner maximization using linearized perturbations from network parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current adversarial training methods require expensive gradient computations and inner maximization loops to defend against small-norm adversarial examples. The authors aim to develop a more efficient method that avoids input differentiation while still protecting against small perturbations in the approximately linear region around inputs.

Method: The authors use a low-rank Householder expansion (LRHE) to compute adversarial examples directly from trained network parameters without input gradient iterations. This expansion captures the composed affine map of the network using activation patterns from the forward pass. They propose an adversarial training scheme that eliminates inner maximization entirely - training requires only additional forward evaluations with standard backward weight updates.

Result: The method achieves 8.7× reduction in computational cost compared to 40-step PGD adversarial training, costing only the equivalent of 2.8 PGD steps per epoch. The resulting models match or exceed standard adversarial training performance for small perturbation budgets (ε ≤ 0.02 for 3-step PGD, ε ≤ 0.012 for 40-step PGD), but performance degrades for larger perturbations beyond this linear regime.

Conclusion: The main finding is that adversarial regularization can be achieved without input differentiation or inner maximization loops. The LRHE-based method provides efficient protection against small-norm adversarial examples in the approximately linear region around inputs, demonstrating that local adversarial geometry can be obtained directly from network parameters rather than through gradient-based search.

Abstract: This work concerns adversarial training against the small-norm adversarial examples that arise from the inherent input instability of a trained deep neural network. Examples in this class are small as measured in the relative $\ell^2$-norm, and therefore lie in the neighborhood of the input on which the model acts approximately linearly, the regime in which the perturbation remains imperceptible. We first show that such examples can be computed directly from the trained network parameters, without input gradient iterations, by means of a linearization called the low-rank Householder expansion (LRHE). The expansion describes the composed affine map rather than any individual layer, and the directions it identifies are read from the activation pattern already available in the forward pass. We then propose a simple adversarial training scheme built on this construction. No differentiation with respect to the input is performed at any point: training requires only additional forward evaluations, with weight parameters updated by the standard backward pass, and the inner maximization of the usual min-max formulation is eliminated entirely. That such a regularizer exists is our main finding: the methods that dispense with the inner search all obtain their local geometry by differentiating with respect to the input, and we show this is not necessary. The regularizer costs the equivalent of $2.8$ PGD steps per epoch, an $8.7\times$ reduction relative to 40-step adversarial training on MNIST and below the cost of 3-step training. The resulting models match three-step PGD adversarial training for relative $\ell^2$ budgets $\varepsilon \le 0.02$ and 40-step training for $\varepsilon \le 0.012$, falling away beyond, consistent with the locality of the expansion.

</details>


### [241] [Graph-Based Pseudo-multimodal Contrastive Learning for 12-Lead ECG Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26964)
*Mengyu Wang,Kozo Okada,Takafumi Goto,Natsuko Jinba,Hiroki Yamaya,Kiyoshi Hibi,Tomoki Hamagami*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes Graph-CMMC: a graph-based pseudo-multimodal contrastive learning framework for 12-lead ECG analysis that uses GADF images as complementary representations and models inter-lead dependencies with graph structure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current ECG analysis methods typically focus on single-lead signals or treat leads independently, processing ECGs as 1D time-series with CNNs/RNNs. These approaches fail to capture inter-lead dependencies and global waveform patterns that are clinically essential for diagnosing coronary artery disease.

Method: Transforms ECG waveforms into Gramian Angular Difference Field (GADF) images to create complementary representations. Uses all 12 leads in a self-supervised contrastive learning framework that aligns waveform and GADF representations. Incorporates a graph-based relational module to model inter-lead dependencies and enforce structural consistency across leads during contrastive learning.

Result: The framework achieves competitive performance on multi-label coronary artery occlusion classification tasks compared to supervised learning methods. Results show effectiveness of using GADF as complementary representation and graph-based modeling of inter-lead dependencies for learning robust 12-lead ECG representations.

Conclusion: Graph-CMMC effectively addresses limitations of traditional ECG analysis by capturing inter-lead dependencies and global patterns. The graph-based pseudo-multimodal contrastive learning approach with GADF representations enables robust ECG feature learning for clinical applications like coronary artery disease diagnosis.

Abstract: 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is a standard, non-invasive examination widely used for diagnosing coronary artery disease, where clinical interpretation relies on comparing waveform patterns across multiple leads. However, most existing ECG analysis methods focus on single-lead signals or treat each lead independently, and typically process ECG signals as one-dimensional time-series data using CNNs or RNNs. While effective in modeling local waveform changes, such approaches have difficulty capturing inter-lead dependency and global waveform patterns essential for clinical diagnosis.
  To address this limitation, we propose a graph-based pseudo-multimodal contrastive learning framework called Graph-CMMC. ECG waveforms are transformed into Gramian Angular Difference Field (GADF) images to construct complementary representations of the same cardiac activity, enabling a pseudo-multimodal learning setting. Using all 12 leads, Graph-CMMC aligns waveform and GADF representations in a self-supervised manner, while a graph-based relational module is employed to model inter-lead dependency and enforce structural consistency across leads during contrastive learning.
  Experimental results on a multi-label coronary artery occlusion classification task demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance compared to supervised learning methods. These results further suggest the effectiveness of using GADF as a complementary representation and incorporating explicit graph-based modeling of inter-lead dependency for learning robust 12-lead ECG representations.

</details>


### [242] [ClusterAttention: A training-free speedup of bidirectional attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26965)
*Kasper Nordenram,Amelie Dittmann*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ClusterAttention is a training-free method that speeds up bidirectional attention layers using fast recursive clustering that adapts to key-query geometry, allowing arbitrary cluster sizes while maintaining GPU efficiency through power-of-two sizing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing sparse attention methods either rely on input structure (language order, spatial proximity) or use slow clustering processes amortized over multiple forward passes, limiting their applicability to unstructured inputs and single-forward-pass scenarios.

Method: Uses fast recursive clustering that adapts to key-query geometry in each attention head, allows arbitrary cluster sizing with power-of-two clusters for GPU efficiency, derives error expressions for sparse attention, and includes compensation for excluded clusters via centroids.

Result: Achieves 2-6x speedup on TabPFN-3 with ≥99% dense accuracy, 1.8x speedup on Wan 2.1-14B T2V video generation (better than SVOO's 1.4x), and is the first training-free method successful for unstructured inputs with single forward pass.

Conclusion: ClusterAttention provides an effective training-free speedup for attention layers that works across diverse domains (tabular data, video generation), adapts to input geometry, maintains accuracy, and outperforms domain-specific methods while being generally applicable.

Abstract: This paper introduces ClusterAttention, a general training-free speedup of bidirectional attention layers. Existing sparse attention methods either rely on structure in the input, such as order in language or spatial proximity in images, or use slow clustering processes amortized over several forward passes. ClusterAttention instead uses a fast recursive clustering method that adapts to the geometry of the keys and queries in each attention head to produce useful clusters. This method allows setting the size of the clusters arbitrarily. We utilize this by setting all clusters to be a fixed size that is a power of two, allowing the block-sparse attention to run at the same latency per query-key interaction as dense attention on GPUs. We also derive an expression for the output error in sparse attention, that explains the counterintuitive experimental finding that tight clusters can lead to larger errors than random clusters. We then derive the error when excluded clusters are compensated through their centroids, and show that this error shrinks with tighter clusters. We integrate this compensation into the method.
  On large-scale tabular data ClusterAttention speeds up TabPFN-3 arXiv:2605.13986 by two to six times, while retaining at least 99% of the dense accuracy. To our knowledge, it is the first training-free method that can be successfully applied in the setting of unstructured input and a single forward pass. For video generation with Wan 2.1-14B T2V arXiv:2503.20314 , ClusterAttention achieves output closer to dense attention and a larger speedup (1.8x versus 1.4x) compared to SVOO arXiv:2603.18636 , a leading method developed specifically for this domain, both run without offline calibration.

</details>


### [243] [TEMPLAR Wales: A georeferenced environmental and toponymic dataset of Welsh settlements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26970)
*Oktay Karakuş,Can Eyupoglu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A georeferenced dataset linking Welsh place names with environmental attributes and lexical annotations for quantitative research in toponymy and landscape studies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Place names offer valuable historical records of landscape organization, but their quantitative analysis requires systematic separation of mapped locations, lexical elements, and environmental measurements for reliable research.

Method: Created TEMPLAR Wales dataset with 3,757 settlement records linking reproducible settlement framework to deterministic lexical screening using 24 Welsh place-name elements, generating 1,350 lexical detections across 1,294 settlements. Environmental attributes include river/coastal proximity, elevation, terrain context at multiple scales, land cover, and woody cover, with parallel terrain measurements from independent elevation products.

Result: Produced a validated dataset with four relational tables, data dictionary, provenance register, and licensing metadata. Technical validation confirmed relational integrity, deterministic lexical reconstruction, documented environmental coverage, strong agreement between terrain sources, and reproducible reconstruction.

Conclusion: TEMPLAR Wales provides a reusable foundation for interdisciplinary research in toponymy, linguistic geography, historical/environmental landscape studies, and spatial analysis, while maintaining clear distinctions between computational detections and verified etymologies, and between current environmental measurements and historical reconstructions.

Abstract: Place names provide persistent records of how landscapes have been described and organised, but their quantitative reuse requires explicit separation between mapped places, lexical annotations and environmental measurements. TEMPLAR Wales is a georeferenced environmental-toponymy dataset comprising 3,757 settlement records across Wales. The resource links a reproducible settlement frame to deterministic lexical screening and settlement-level environmental attributes through stable identifiers. It contains 1,350 lexical detections across 1,294 settlements, generated from a frozen registry of 24 Welsh place-name elements, while retaining exact- and prefix-token matches and their provenance separately. Environmental attributes describe river and coastal proximity, elevation and local terrain context at multiple spatial scales, land cover and neighbourhood woody cover, with parallel terrain measurements derived from independent elevation products. The dataset is distributed as four relational tables accompanied by a field-level data dictionary, source-provenance register and licensing metadata. Technical validation confirms relational integrity, deterministic lexical reconstruction, documented environmental coverage, strong agreement between independent terrain sources and reproducible reconstruction of the frozen release. TEMPLAR Wales provides a reusable foundation for research in toponymy, linguistic geography, historical and environmental landscape studies, GIS and spatial data analysis without treating computational lexical detections as verified etymologies or contemporary environmental measurements as historical landscape reconstructions.

</details>


### [244] [Terrain signatures in Welsh settlement names](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26978)
*Oktay Karakuş,Can Eyupoglu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Welsh settlement names containing high-terrain words (bryn/mynydd) vs. low-terrain words (cwm/pant) accurately predict actual terrain elevation differences - high-terrain names occur 24m higher than low-terrain names, showing place names retain measurable environmental information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether landscape names retain measurable environmental information beyond broad geographic patterns, specifically examining Welsh settlement names for terrain-related elements.

Method: Analyzed 3,757 Welsh settlements using a frozen 24-element lexical framework with preregistered outcome-specific models. Used geographically structured validation with spatial blocking (10-, 25-, 50-km). Main comparison: 101 settlements with high-terrain elements (bryn/mynydd) vs. 139 with low-terrain elements (cwm/pant) across multiple neighborhood definitions.

Result: High-terrain names occupied locations 24.4m higher relative to 2-km surroundings (95% CI: 10.8-38.1m, p=0.00137). Association persisted across 1-, 2-, 5-km neighborhoods and independent elevation data. Adding terrain-name polarity reduced geographically held-out mean squared error by 4.63-7.30%. River-related names showed weaker evidence; woodland model was non-estimable.

Conclusion: Selected Welsh settlement-name categories retain measurable information about present-day terrain within Wales, but findings don't establish individual etymology, causal naming, historical environmental memory, or transferability to other naming systems.

Abstract: Landscapes are named, but whether names retain measurable environmental information beyond broad geographic structure is rarely tested. We analysed 3,757 Welsh settlements using a frozen, source-audited 24-element lexical framework, preregistered outcome-specific models and geographically structured validation. The central comparison contrasted 101 settlements carrying high-terrain elements (\textit{bryn} or \textit{mynydd}) with 139 carrying low-terrain elements (\textit{cwm} or \textit{pant}). High-terrain names occupied locations 24.4 m higher relative to their 2-km surroundings (95\% CI, 10.8--38.1 m; Holm-adjusted $p$ = 0.00137). The association remained positive across prespecified 1-, 2- and 5-km neighbourhood definitions and was reproduced using an independently produced elevation source (24.1 m; 95\% CI, 10.6--37.6 m). Adding terrain-name polarity to a non-lexical spatial and settlement baseline reduced geographically held-out mean squared error by 4.63\%, 6.22\% and 7.30\% under 10-, 25- and 50-km spatial blocking, respectively, although improvement varied among held-out regions. River-related names provided weaker, directionally consistent evidence, while the preregistered woodland model was non-estimable. Residual spatial structure, unresolved name language and the absence of independent external replication limit interpretation. Selected Welsh settlement-name categories therefore retain measurable information about present-day terrain within Wales, without establishing individual etymology, causal naming, historical environmental memory or transferability to other naming systems.

</details>


### [245] [Decentralized Multitask Learning over Learned Task Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26989)
*Zirui Wan,Stefan Vlaski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Decentralized multitask learning with unknown task relationships: learn graph structure from data first, then use it for cooperative learning, achieving near-optimal performance with small stepsize.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph-regularized multitask learning methods assume known task relationships, but in practical decentralized settings over networks, the underlying task dependencies are often unknown and need to be learned directly from distributed data.

Method: Two-phase decentralized strategy: 1) estimate generalized graph Laplacian from noisy non-cooperative stochastic gradient iterates using maximum likelihood estimator derived from Gaussian Markov random field prior, 2) use learned graph for cooperative multitask diffusion learning.

Result: Theoretical analysis quantifies Laplacian estimation error and its propagation to steady-state performance, introduces topology sensitivity index for network heterogeneity effects. Simulations show learned graph cooperation significantly outperforms non-cooperative learning and approaches true-graph baseline with sufficiently small estimation stepsize.

Conclusion: The proposed framework enables effective decentralized multitask learning when task relationships are unknown, with learned cooperation providing substantial performance gains over non-cooperative approaches and approaching optimal performance when estimation parameters are properly tuned.

Abstract: This paper investigates decentralized multitask learning over networks when the underlying task relationships are unknown. While existing graph-regularized multitask frameworks typically assume a known structure, practical settings often require learning inter-task dependencies directly from distributed data. We propose a decentralized two-phase strategy that first estimates a generalized graph Laplacian from noisy non-cooperative stochastic gradient iterates, and subsequently exploits the learned graph to enable cooperative multitask diffusion learning. This framework is motivated by a Gaussian Markov random field prior, which gives rise to a decentralized maximum likelihood estimator for the graph Laplacian. The analysis quantifies the Laplacian estimation error and its propagation to the steady-state performance of the multitask diffusion recursion, and introduces a topology sensitivity index to capture the effect of network heterogeneity. Simulation results corroborate the theoretical findings and demonstrate that cooperation enabled by the learned task graph significantly improves performance over non-cooperative learning, while approaching the true-graph baseline when the estimation stepsize is sufficiently small.

</details>


### [246] [Benchmarking_Fast_Domain_Adaptation_for_Unsupervised_Speech_Units](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26992)
*Robin San Roman,Manel Khentout,Tu Anh Nguyen,Paul Michel,Yossi Adi,Emmanuel Dupoux*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ABX-Accent benchmark evaluates representation learning models on accented speech adaptation, showing 23.6% improvement with adaptive domain normalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Limited understanding of how representation learning methods handle out-of-domain speech, particularly important for accented speech where there's a long tail of accents diverging from standard ones. Need to evaluate adaptation to new domains with few-shot learning.

Method: Introduces ABX-Accent benchmark based on AESRC dataset with 10 English accents, each with small (<10 hours) unlabelled training sets. Uses adaptive domain normalization to fine-tune pretrained Contrastive Predictive Coding models on accents, first developed on LibriSpeech with male/female split.

Result: Proposed adaptive domain normalization method achieves 23.6% relative improvement on average across-speaker ABX scores compared to non-adapted models when applied to the new benchmark.

Conclusion: The ABX-Accent benchmark enables evaluation of representation learning on accented speech adaptation, demonstrating significant improvements with adaptive domain normalization for few-shot adaptation to new accents.

Abstract: Representation learning has attracted great atten- tion and managed to reach good performances as a pretraining method for downstream tasks or as a first step towards unsu- pervised speech modeling. Yet, little is known about how such methods deal with out-of-domain speech and how could they be adapted in a few shot to new domains. This is important especially for accented speech where one observes a long tail of accents that diverge from the standard ones. We introduce ABX- Accent, a benchmark based on the AESRC dataset that features 10 different accents of English. It includes a small (< 10 hours) unlabelled training set in each of the accents and adaptations of the Zero Resources Challenge ABX evaluation metrics to each of the accents. We illustrate this benchmark with a baseline model that uses adaptive domain normalization to fine tune a pretrained Contrastive Predictive Coding model on the accents. This method is first developed on LibriSpeech using a male/female split. When applied to the new benchmark, the proposed method yields a relative improvement of 23.6% on across-speaker ABX scores on average compared to non adapted models. The data and metrics will be open sourced upon paper acceptance

</details>


### [247] [Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27032)
*Ivan Kruzhilov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DPO's β coefficient is problematic because it conflates preference-noise scale with optimization dynamics, causing non-monotonic policy changes and making loss values incomparable across β values.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper identifies that Direct Preference Optimization's β parameter, commonly interpreted as controlling KL constraint, actually entangles two distinct roles: it governs inverse preference-noise scale and rescales optimization dynamics simultaneously, causing issues with interpretation and optimization.

Method: Proposes a centered-softplus reformulation that is argmin-equivalent to DPO for β>0, making inverse preference-noise-scale and learning-rate effects explicit and independently tunable. The normalized version also admits a continuous β→0 endpoint reducing to a linear preference-margin objective.

Result: Shows that standard DPO has problematic behavior: policy deviation is non-monotone in β (vanishes at small β, peaks at intermediate values, decreases at large β), and loss values are not comparable across β values.

Conclusion: The entanglement in DPO's β parameter obscures its role, increases sensitivity to hyperparameters, and complicates learning-rate scheduling. The proposed centered-softplus formulation resolves these issues by making the effects explicit and independently tunable.

Abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a widely used objective for aligning language models from preference data, with the coefficient $β$ commonly interpreted as controlling the KL constraint to a reference policy. We show that $β$ entangles two distinct roles: it governs the effective inverse preference-noise scale and simultaneously rescales the optimization dynamics, coupling this scale with the effective step size. As a consequence, at a fixed learning rate the achieved policy deviation is non-monotone in $β$: it vanishes in a dead zone at small $β$, reaches a peak at an intermediate value, and decreases again for larger $β$. Moreover, standard DPO loss values are not comparable across $β$: runs with nearly identical loss curves can differ several-fold in KL divergence from the reference model. This entanglement obscures the role of $β$, increases sensitivity to hyperparameter choices, and complicates learning-rate scheduling. We propose a centered-softplus reformulation that is argmin-equivalent to DPO for $β>0$, while making the inverse preference-noise-scale and learning-rate effects explicit and independently tunable. The normalized centered-softplus objective also admits a continuous $β\to0$ endpoint that reduces to a linear preference-margin objective.

</details>


### [248] [Performance Foundations of Parallel & Distributed Reasoning Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27046)
*Maciej Besta,Leonard Schmidt,Lara Nonino,Robert Gerstenberger,Pierre Pang,Patrik Okanovic,Ales Kubicek,Tiancheng Chen,Baraq Lipshitz,Torsten Hoefler*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper systematizes the RL-for-LLM paradigm, analyzes computational challenges in training Reasoning Language Models (RLMs), develops a taxonomy of parallelism strategies, and provides practical guidelines for building scalable and cost-effective RLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL-for-LLM paradigms like RLVR can significantly improve LLM reasoning capabilities, but training state-of-the-art Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) requires massive computational resources (millions of GPU-hours) and complex multi-model pipelines that stress modern hardware beyond classical supervised training, making RLM training a major parallel/distributed systems challenge.

Method: 1) Systematize the RL-for-LLM paradigm and provide compute-centric analysis of prominent post-training frameworks (PPO, GRPO, and variants). 2) Develop a taxonomy of intra- and inter-model parallelism strategies covering traditional techniques and novel forms for multi-model RLM training. 3) Use the work-depth model of parallel computing to make taxonomy rigorous and portable. 4) Analyze existing RLM frameworks to distill practical guidelines.

Result: The paper provides a comprehensive systematization of RL-for-LLM training, develops a rigorous taxonomy of parallelism strategies using work-depth model, analyzes computational characteristics of different post-training frameworks, and identifies practical guidelines for scalable RLM development.

Conclusion: RLM training is both an algorithmic and distributed systems challenge requiring novel parallelism approaches; the paper provides foundational systematization, computational analysis, and practical guidance for building high-performance, scalable, and cost-effective Reasoning Language Models.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) and other RL-style post-training paradigms have been used for aligning large language models (LLMs) with reasoning standards. The resulting recent Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) such as DeepSeek-R1, o3, and Kimi k1.5 show that such RL-style post-training ("RL-for-LLMs") can substantially improve chain-of-thought reasoning, long-horizon planning, and self-correction. However, the computational footprint of these systems is massive: state-of-the-art RLM training requires millions of GPU-hours and tightly coupled multi-model pipelines that stress modern hardware far beyond classical supervised LLM training. This makes RLM training as much a parallel and distributed systems problem as an algorithmic one. In this work, to facilitate developing RLMs that are simultaneously high-performance, scalable, and cost-effective, we first systematize the RL-for-LLM paradigm and provide a compute-centric analysis of prominent post-training algorithmic frameworks: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), as well as their variants. Second, we develop a taxonomy of intra- and inter-model parallelism strategies for RL-for-LLMs, covering both traditional techniques (data, tensor, pipeline, sequence, context, and expert parallelism) as well as novel forms of parallelism and optimization techniques for multi-model RLM training, for example disaggregated placement, stage fusion, hybrid parallelism, and asynchronous execution. We harness the work-depth model of parallel computing to make our taxonomy and its insights rigorous and portable. Finally, we analyze existing RLM frameworks and we distill practical guidelines and outline open research directions for building scalable, fast, and cost-effective RLMs.

</details>


### [249] [Soft Active Electromyography Interface for Machine Learning-Enabled Silent Speech Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27048)
*Yuta Kurotaki,Shusuke Yamakoshi,Reitaro Yoshida,Yutaka Isoda,Tamami Takano,Yuji Isano,Yusuke Miyake,Kentaro Kuribayashi,Hiroki Ota*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A soft wearable EMG interface on the fingertip enables accurate silent speech recognition through machine learning for privacy-sensitive environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current silent speech recognition systems have limitations: they require constant facial attachment (which is inconvenient), raise privacy concerns, and suffer from unstable signal acquisition. There's a need for more practical, privacy-preserving, and reliable alternatives.

Method: Developed a soft, active EMG interface worn on the hand with a fingertip electrode that can be positioned near lips when needed. The device integrates liquid metal interconnects, transparent flexible printed circuit electrodes, and elastomer encapsulation for mechanical stability during finger motion. A deep neural network was trained on these stable EMG signals.

Result: The system achieved a mean accuracy of 97.2 ± 1.3% across three subjects in classifying a 30-word vocabulary. Real-time drone control demonstrated practical application in noisy and privacy-sensitive environments where conventional voice recognition fails.
