Our framework therefore enables efficient label spreading on large-scale image datasets and produces accurate labels even when only a few labeled samples are available.

</details>


### [275] [Privacy Without Regret: Differentially Private Inference-Time Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26324)
*Ishi Jain,Nandini Bhattad,Sayak Ray Chowdhury*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BoN sampling suffers from reward hacking and privacy issues; adding calibrated noise to rewards solves both, enabling differentially private alignment that matches optimal regularization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Best-of-N sampling has two major problems: reward hacking (exploiting reward model errors) and lack of privacy protection for the sensitive human preference data used to train reward models. These issues limit the practical deployment of inference-time alignment strategies.

Method: Two methods: 1) PrivBoN adds Gumbel noise to reward scores before selection, providing both ε-differential privacy and KL-regularized alignment. 2) PrivITP combines χ²-regularized rejection sampling with a two-phase Gaussian mechanism, achieving ex-post (ε,δ)-DP with privacy cost independent of n.

Result: When privacy budget exceeds critical threshold ε*, the privacy-mandated noise is regret-optimal regularization, imposing zero additional alignment cost. PrivITP decouples regularization from privacy parameters and achieves skyline performance up to noise inflation. Experiments show both methods are scaling-monotonic (unlike BoN), with PrivITP matching or outperforming PrivBoN.

Conclusion: Adding calibrated noise to reward scores resolves both reward hacking and privacy issues in BoN sampling, enabling differentially private inference-time alignment that matches the information-theoretic optimal regularization, making alignment strategies more practical and robust.

Abstract: Best-of-N (BoN) sampling is the simplest and most widely deployed inference-time alignment strategy, but it suffers from two distinct problems: reward hacking, in which the selected response exploits errors in the proxy reward model, and the absence of any privacy protection for the sensitive human preference data used to train that reward model. We show that a single intervention-adding calibrated noise to reward scores before selection-resolves both. Our first result, Private Best-of-N (PrivBoN), establishes that Gumbel noise at an appropriate scale simultaneously provides $ε$-differential privacy and implements KL-regularized alignment. Whenever the privacy budget exceeds a critical threshold $ε^*$, the privacy-mandated noise is the regret-optimal regularization, and privacy imposes zero additional alignment cost-matching the information-theoretic skyline of Huang et al. (2025). Because $ε^*$ depends on an unknown coverage coefficient, we introduce Private Inference-Time Pessimism (PrivITP), which combines $χ^2$-regularized rejection sampling with a two-phase Gaussian mechanism. PrivITP achieves ex-post $(ε,δ)$-DP with a privacy cost independent of the number of responses $n$, cleanly decouples the regularization parameter from the privacy parameter, and attains the skyline up to a noise-inflation term. Experiments across several language models, datasets, and reward models confirm our results: PrivBoN and PrivITP are scaling-monotonic (unlike BoN, which degrades past a critical $n$), and PrivITP matches or outperforms PrivBoN at equivalent privacy levels, with the largest gains in the strong-privacy regime.

</details>


### [276] [Beyond Capability Benchmarks: Learning Operational Fingerprints of LLM Cloud Services from Production Incident Metadata](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26332)
*Meiwei Zhang,Eduardo Miranda,Bruce Baynes,Suvigya Jain,Wanlong Chen,Tao He,Sergey Borodavkin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OpEmbed learns operational fingerprints of LLM cloud services from structured support-case metadata without text, enabling better model selection and operational forecasting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM service selection relies on capability benchmarks that don't reveal operational behavior after deployment, leaving a gap between pre-deployment evaluation and real-world performance.

Method: Framework aggregates model-time windows into 8-channel operational signatures and learns low-dimensional representations using temporal contrastive learning, cross-view reconstruction, and generational-ordinality regularization from structured support-case metadata.

Result: On 33k+ production support cases across 7 LLM families over 26 months, OpEmbed recovers interpretable family/version structure, improves operational forecasting over baselines, works with limited early data, and supports cross-model fault-type transfer.

Conclusion: OpEmbed provides practical operational insights for model onboarding, support readiness assessment, and monitoring, bridging the gap between capability benchmarks and real-world service behavior.

Abstract: Managed LLM services are now part of real production systems, but model selection and service planning still rely heavily on capability benchmarks that reveal little about operational behavior after deployment. We present Operational Embedding (OpEmbed), a framework for learning compact operational fingerprints of LLM cloud services from structured, privacy-preserving support-case metadata, without using case text. OpEmbed aggregates model--time windows into an eight-channel operational signature and learns a low-dimensional representation via temporal contrastive learning, cross-view reconstruction, and generational-ordinality regularization. Evaluated on more than 33,000 production support cases spanning seven LLM families over 26 months at Google Cloud, OpEmbed recovers interpretable family- and version-level structure, improves leave-one-model-out operational forecasting over non-learned baselines, remains useful under limited early-window data, and supports cross-model fault-type transfer. We report the practical lessons learned from building and evaluating this tool for model onboarding, support readiness assessment, and operational monitoring.

</details>


### [277] [CG4AI: A Column Generation Framework for Training AI Models Under Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26375)
*Youcef Magnouche,Abderrahmane Driouch,Sébastien Martin,Pierre Bauguion*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CG4AI is a framework that builds convex combinations of AI models while enforcing linear constraints on outputs via a master linear program and pricing subproblem, achieving guaranteed feasibility and improved accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard ML training doesn't guarantee that models will satisfy predefined rules or constraints on outputs, which is essential in real-world applications like autonomous systems and network routing.

Method: Uses a master linear program to determine optimal mixture weights for convex combination of models, with a pricing subproblem that generates new models guided by LP dual variables (focusing on most violated constraints). Includes cutting-plane procedure to extend feasibility guarantees beyond training set.

Result: Applied to digit classification on MNIST and multi-commodity flow problems. Experiments show CG4AI reliably produces feasible predictors while achieving better accuracy than single-model baselines on both MNIST and SNDLIB benchmark networks.

Conclusion: CG4AI successfully provides a framework for building AI models that guarantee constraint satisfaction while maintaining or improving accuracy, addressing a critical gap in standard ML training approaches.

Abstract: Standard machine-learning training minimizes a loss function over a dataset, but does not guarantee that the resulting model will satisfy predefined rules or constraints on its outputs. In many real-world applications, ranging from autonomous systems to network routing, such guarantees are essential. We propose CG4AI, a framework that builds a convex combination of AI models while enforcing linear constraints on the combined output. A master linear program (LP) determines the optimal mixture weights, while a pricing subproblem generates new models guided by LP dual variables, focusing attention on the most violated constraints. A cutting-plane procedure extends feasibility guarantees beyond the training set. We apply CG4AI to two problems: (i) digit classification on MNIST, where we demonstrate four distinct uses of constraints, learning from constraints alone, improving adversarial robustness, correcting misclassified examples, and enforcing output relabeling; and (ii) the multi-commodity flow problem, where link capacity constraints are enforced on neural-network routing predictors. Experiments on MNIST and standard SNDLIB benchmark networks show that CG4AI reliably produces feasible predictors while achieving better accuracy than single-model baselines.

</details>


### [278] [The Latent Diagnostic Taxonomy: A Framework for Constructing Classifiers and Diagnosing Their Decisions, Applied to Prompt Injection Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26423)
*Jaturong Kongmanee,Smile Thanapattheerakul*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A framework for creating trustworthy classifiers with diagnostic capabilities to identify which confident decisions can be trusted, using dimensionality-optimized classifiers and latent support vectors to detect brittle failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current classifiers often make confident decisions that may not be robust - they can be easily manipulated by minor input changes or contain hidden biases. There's a need for safeguards that can identify which confident predictions are truly trustworthy versus those that are brittle or exploitable.

Method: Latent Diagnostic Taxonomy framework: (1) Build dimensionality-optimized classifier with embedding dimensionality selected via cross-validation, (2) Identify latent support vectors (~29% of training examples) that represent influential prompts, (3) Use tokens and attack magnitudes to construct diagnostic taxonomy for classifying prompts into different risk categories.

Result: Applied to a classifier on public prompt injection dataset, found ~77% of confident decisions are not robust to single token removal. Identified two distinct failure patterns: confidence calibration failure and genuinely exploitable shortcuts. Created taxonomy that categorizes prompts into: Safe to rely on classifier, Heuristic Bias, Heuristic Override, and Insufficient Context requiring human review.

Conclusion: The proposed Latent Diagnostic Taxonomy provides an end-to-end framework for building safer classifiers with built-in diagnostics. It enables systematic identification of trustworthy vs. brittle decisions, offers remediation strategies for problematic prompts, and helps deploy classifiers more safely by routing uncertain cases for human review.

Abstract: This paper proposes a framework for constructing a classifier as a safeguard layer, and for developing a complementary diagnostic that identifies which of the classifier's confident decisions can be trusted. This framework, the Latent Diagnostic Taxonomy, consists of (i) constructing a dimensionality-optimized classifier, in which the embedding dimensionality is empirically selected via cross-validated performance rather than fixed a priori, (ii) locating a relatively small set of latent support vectors (~ 29% of total training examples) representing influential prompts for identifying tokens that alter the classifier's predicted labels, and (iii) utilizing such tokens and their associated attack magnitudes for constructing a diagnostic taxonomy. This diagnostic taxonomy provides an end-to-end guideline for flagging prompts that require different treatments: rely Safely on the classifier's decision; flag Heuristic Bias and Heuristic Override cases; route Insufficient Context cases for further human/safety review. Applying the framework to a classifier trained on a public prompt injection dataset, we find that a substantial fraction of its confident decisions (~ 77%) are not robust to removing a single token, and that this brittleness separates into two distinct failure patterns: a confidence calibration failure and a genuinely exploitable shortcut. For each zone of the taxonomy, we also recommend strategies for remediating diagnosed prompts. We illustrate the framework as a series of steps, demonstrating how each step operates.

</details>


### [279] [FedCMAPSS: A Benchmark for Federated Learning in Remaining Useful Life Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26433)
*Amelia Sorrenti,Matteo Pennisi,Concetto Spampinato,Simone Palazzo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FedCMAPSS introduces a standardized benchmark for federated remaining useful life (RUL) estimation using NASA C-MAPSS data to evaluate federated learning algorithms under realistic industrial scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The development of robust RUL estimation models is limited by scarcity of run-to-failure data. While federated learning offers promise for collaborative training without sharing sensitive sensor data, there's currently no common evaluation framework for comparing different approaches in predictive maintenance applications.

Method: Created FedCMAPSS benchmark based on NASA C-MAPSS dataset with five standardized tasks simulating real-world industrial challenges. Conducted systematic evaluation of state-of-the-art federated optimization algorithms across multiple neural architectures, ensuring reproducibility through public code and data splits.

Result: Established reproducible baselines for federated RUL estimation that can serve as a standard foundation for developing and comparing federated predictive maintenance solutions. The benchmark covers scenarios ranging from ideal IID settings to extreme statistical heterogeneity.

Conclusion: FedCMAPSS fills a critical gap in federated learning for predictive maintenance by providing the first standardized evaluation framework, enabling fair comparison of federated optimization algorithms and accelerating progress in data-driven prognostics and health management for Industry 4.0.

Abstract: Data-driven prognostics and health management has emerged as a key enabler for Industry 4.0, yet the development of robust remaining useful life (RUL) estimation models is often limited by the scarcity of run-to-failure data. While federated learning offers a promising paradigm to collaboratively train predictive models without sharing sensor data, research efforts have operated so far in the absence of a common evaluation framework. To address this gap, this paper introduces FedCMAPSS, a benchmark for federated RUL estimation based on the commonly-used NASA C-MAPSS dataset. We define a set of five standardized tasks designed to simulate real-world industrial challenges, ranging from ideal IID settings to extreme statistical heterogeneity, and conduct a systematic evaluation of state-of-the-art federated optimization algorithms across multiple neural architectures. By establishing reproducible baselines and making the source code and data splits publicly available, this work aims to provide a standard foundation for developing and comparing federated predictive maintenance solutions.

</details>


### [280] [NeoTriFuse: Reliability-Aware Multimodal Fusion under Missingness Heterogeneity for Neonatal Mortality Risk Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26436)
*Jiyuan Tian,Qincheng Shen,Ye Lin,Yu Gao,Haohui Lu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NeoTriFuse: A reliability-aware multimodal fusion framework for neonatal mortality prediction that treats missing data as reliability signals to dynamically adjust modality contributions, achieving high performance despite extreme class imbalance and data missingness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neonatal mortality prediction from bedside monitoring data faces several challenges: extreme class imbalance, heterogeneous clinical risk factors, multi-scale temporal dynamics, and substantial missing data. Conventional approaches treat missingness as a preprocessing problem rather than leveraging it as valuable information.

Method: Proposes NeoTriFuse, a reliability-aware multimodal fusion framework that models missingness as explicit reliability signals that dynamically modulate modality contributions during fusion. The framework integrates static perinatal variables, local-global temporal encoders, and patient-level statistical summaries through reliability-guided gating mechanisms, while jointly optimizing mortality prediction and an auxiliary length-of-stay objective.

Result: Achieves competitive performance with an F1 score of 0.6736 +/- 0.0216 and an AUROC of 0.9454 +/- 0.0056. Ablation studies show that local-global temporal architecture and patient-level summary branch contribute most to predictive performance, while reliability-aware gating provides additional improvements on threshold-dependent metrics under heterogeneous observation completeness. Performance remains stable across nearby hyperparameter settings.

Conclusion: Reliability-aware multimodal fusion is a practical approach for neonatal mortality prediction under realistic clinical missingness conditions. Treating missingness as reliability signals rather than just a preprocessing problem allows the model to dynamically adjust modality contributions, leading to improved performance in challenging clinical scenarios.

Abstract: Neonatal mortality risk prediction from bedside monitoring data remains challenging due to extreme class imbalance, heterogeneous clinical risk factors, multi-scale temporal dynamics, and substantial missingness. We propose NeoTriFuse, a reliability-aware multimodal fusion framework for missingness-heterogeneous neonatal monitoring data. Unlike conventional multimodal approaches that treat missingness primarily as a preprocessing issue, NeoTriFuse models missingness as an explicit reliability signal that dynamically modulates modality contributions during fusion. The framework integrates static perinatal variables, local-global temporal encoders, and patient-level statistical summaries through reliability-guided gating mechanisms, while jointly optimizing mortality prediction and an auxiliary length-of-stay objective. NeoTriFuse achieves competitive performance, with an F1 score of 0.6736 +/- 0.0216 and an AUROC of 0.9454 +/- 0.0056. Ablation studies indicate that the local-global temporal architecture and patient-level summary branch contribute most substantially to predictive performance, while reliability-aware gating provides additional improvements on threshold-dependent metrics under heterogeneous observation completeness. Sensitivity analyses further suggest stable performance across nearby hyperparameter settings. Overall, the findings support reliability-aware multimodal fusion as a practical approach for neonatal mortality prediction under realistic clinical missingness conditions.

</details>


### [281] [Subgraph Filtering for Fair Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26437)
*Haohui Lu,jiyuan Tian,Fangyu Zhou,Shahadat Uddin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SF-GNN is a lightweight framework that filters bias-prone edges during GNN message-passing to mitigate structural fairness issues while maintaining predictive performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing fairness-aware GNN methods only constrain representations or predictions globally without controlling local structural pathways where biased information propagates during aggregation.

Method: Proposes Subgraph Filtering for Fair Graph Neural Networks (SF-GNN) that identifies bias-prone edges using sensitive homophily with structural propagation amplifiers (hub participation and triadic closure), then incorporates stochastic edge filtering in each message-passing step to downweight/remove these edges while preserving remaining graph structure, with statistical-parity regularization and warm-up schedule.

Result: Experiments on five benchmark datasets show SF-GNN achieves consistent fairness improvements while maintaining competitive predictive performance, leading to better fairness-accuracy trade-off than recent fairness-aware GNN baselines.

Conclusion: SF-GNN effectively mitigates structural bias at its source through local edge filtering during message passing, offering a lightweight and architecture-agnostic solution for fair GNNs with improved fairness-accuracy trade-offs.

Abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) can exhibit unfair behavior even when sensitive attributes are excluded from node features, because graph topology and message passing propagate group-correlated signals under sensitive homophily. Existing fairness-aware GNN methods mainly constrain representations or prediction distributions at a global level, without explicitly controlling the local structural pathways through which biased information propagates during aggregation. We propose Subgraph Filtering for Fair Graph Neural Networks (SF-GNN), a lightweight and architecture-agnostic framework that mitigates structural bias at its source. SF-GNN identifies bias-prone edges by combining sensitive homophily with structural propagation amplifiers, including hub participation and triadic closure. It then incorporates stochastic edge filtering into each message-passing step to selectively downweight or remove these edges while preserving the remaining graph structure. Training further incorporates a statistical-parity regularizer with a warm-up schedule to stabilize optimization. Experiments on five benchmark datasets show that SF-GNN achieves consistent fairness improvements while maintaining competitive predictive performance, leading to a better fairness--accuracy trade-off than recent fairness-aware GNN baselines.

</details>


### [282] [Toward Equitable Low-Carbon Mobility: Fairness-Aware Demand Prediction for Expanding Bike-Sharing Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26451)
*Man Luo,Yixuan Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FairGIN is a fairness-aware graph neural network that addresses cold-start prediction challenges and reduces income-based disparities in bike-sharing system expansion while maintaining high accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bike-sharing system expansion faces two main challenges: 1) cold-start prediction problems for newly deployed stations lacking historical ridership data, causing distribution gaps between training and inference; and 2) existing models trained on historical data may reinforce structural inequalities, as lower ridership in low-income areas may reflect limited infrastructure access rather than actual weak demand.

Method: FairGIN integrates three components: 1) Expansion-Simulated Increment Training (stochastically simulates network expansion during training to reduce cold-start distribution gap), 2) Attention-Based Knowledge Transfer (uses station-adaptive temperature scaling with orthogonal embedding alignment to transfer representations from existing to new stations), and 3) Fairness-Aware Optimization (introduces income-stratified regularization and equity-calibrated deployment score for more inclusive station placement).

Result: Experiments on NYC and Seattle datasets demonstrate that FairGIN achieves state-of-the-art predictive accuracy across diverse expansion scenarios while substantially reducing income-based disparities without compromising overall system efficiency.

Conclusion: FairGIN successfully addresses both the cold-start prediction challenge in bike-sharing system expansion and mitigates fairness issues by reducing income-based disparities, providing a comprehensive solution for equitable urban mobility planning.

Abstract: Bike-sharing systems are an important component of low-carbon urban mobility, but continued expansion creates challenges in both cold-start prediction and equitable resource allocation. Newly deployed stations lack historical ridership records, causing a mismatch between training and inference for graph-based models on evolving networks. Historical demand may also encode structural inequalities, as lower ridership in low-income neighborhoods can reflect limited infrastructure access rather than weak latent demand. Models trained directly on such data may therefore reinforce existing mobility disparities. We propose FairGIN, a fairness-aware graph neural network for demand prediction in expanding bike-sharing systems. FairGIN integrates three components. Expansion-Simulated Increment Training stochastically simulates network expansion during training to reduce the cold-start distribution gap. Attention-Based Knowledge Transfer combines station-adaptive temperature scaling with orthogonal embedding alignment to transfer representations from data-rich existing stations to data-sparse new stations. Fairness-Aware Optimization introduces income-stratified regularization and an equity-calibrated deployment score to support more inclusive station placement. Experiments on NYC and Seattle demonstrate that FairGIN achieves state-of-the-art predictive accuracy across diverse expansion scenarios while substantially reducing income-based disparities without compromising overall system efficiency.

</details>


### [283] [Distributed Training using an Intelligent Network](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26453)
*Nihar Shah,Ben Blier*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Distributed WAN training improved by making networks active participants using multicast/FGPA technologies and optimized synchronization schedules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Distributed training across WANs faces bandwidth, latency, and topology constraints that limit parameter exchange between compute islands, creating bottlenecks compared to colocated training.

Method: Two-pronged approach: (1) Systems - use multicast for outbound traffic replication and in-line FPGAs for inbound traffic aggregation, extending data center technologies to WAN; (2) Algorithms - optimization framework generating rotating clique synchronization schedules around network topology and technologies.

Result: The approach is demonstrated on a nine-city topology modeled on DoubleZero network, showing how optimal schedules adapt to network capabilities, narrowing the gap to colocated training.

Conclusion: Making networks active participants with appropriate hardware technologies and algorithmic scheduling can significantly improve distributed WAN training performance.

Abstract: Distributed training across a wide area network (WAN) is challenging, as continuous parameter exchange by islands of compute is constrained by limited bandwidth, high latency, and uneven topology. We propose making the network an active participant in training. On the systems side, such networks should leverage (i) multicast technology to replicate outbound traffic and (ii) in-line FPGAs to aggregate inbound traffic, to ease egress and ingress bottlenecks. These technologies are used for training across workers within a data center, but this paper extends them to the WAN. On the algorithms side, we develop an optimization framework that produces rich synchronization schedules (namely, rotating cliques of islands) around the underlying network topology and these technologies, to maximize information exchange. Finally, we illustrate this on a nine-city topology modeled on the DoubleZero network, a live programmable WAN equipped with both technologies, and show how the optimal schedules shift with the network's capabilities. Together, these can narrow the gap to the gold standard of colocated training.

</details>


### [284] [Diff Mining: Logit Differences Reveal Finetuning Objectives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26462)
*Greg Kocher,Robert West,Clément Dumas,Julian Minder*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Diff Mining is a framework that identifies what a finetuned model has learned by comparing its output logits to the base model's, extracting amplified tokens as a fingerprint of training without needing model internals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Finetuning is widely used but opaque - it's unclear exactly which behaviors emerge, and unwanted behaviors may arise. As models become more capable, understanding finetuning better is increasingly important for safety and interpretability.

Method: Two-stage framework: (1) extract per-context logit differences between finetuned and base models on a reference corpus, (2) aggregate signals using either Top-K frequency method or Non-negative Matrix Factorization to construct interpretable token sets representing the finetune.

Result: Outperforms state-of-the-art model diffing methods in finetune domain detection, both in identifying relevant tokens and downstream performance when an interpretability agent uses extracted tokens. Identifies over one third of injected biases without targeted probing.

Conclusion: Diff Mining is an effective, scalable framework that shows promise for developing auditing tools to detect finetuning objectives by analyzing output logit differences, requiring only black-box access to models.

Abstract: Finetuning has become the gold standard for refining existing behaviors and inducing new ones in language models, yet it often remains unclear exactly which behaviors emerge during this process. As models grow ever more capable, understanding finetuning better becomes increasingly important, particularly since unwanted behaviors may arise during finetuning. In this paper, we introduce Diff Mining, a simple yet effective framework for identifying what a finetuned model has learned by comparing its logits to those of its base model. Diff Mining effectively surfaces salient tokens that are amplified in the finetuned model, serving as a fingerprint of its training -- even on text unrelated to the finetuning domain. Unlike many existing model diffing methods which require model internals, Diff Mining only needs access to output logits and scales to large models. The framework consists of two modular stages: (i) extracting per-context logit differences between the finetuned and base models on a reference corpus, and (ii) aggregating the resulting signals to construct an interpretable token set representing the finetune. For aggregation, we explore both a simple Top-K frequency method and a Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF)-based approach for disentangling multiple finetuning objectives into distinct token clusters. Empirically, Diff Mining succeeds across diverse settings: on finetune domain detection, it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art model diffing methods both in identifying relevant tokens and in downstream performance when an interpretability agent is given access to the extracted token set; on models with injected biases, it identifies more than one third of the biases without targeted probing. Overall, our framework shows promise in developing auditing tools to detect finetuning objectives.

</details>


### [285] [Active Curriculum Refinement for Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26469)
*Zhenya Liu,Yuxin Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PATH is a curriculum learning framework that actively learns over directed acyclic curriculum graphs in reinforcement learning, sampling diverse paths first and then reallocating training to unmastered regions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many RL environments have prerequisite relations (difficulty-increasing edits or parameter increments) forming curriculum DAGs, but this structure is often only implicitly exploited rather than explicitly modeled for better training.

Method: PATH performs active learning over curriculum graphs by first expanding coverage through sampling diverse curriculum paths, then reallocating training toward regions that remain unmastered.

Result: Experiments across diverse environments show that PATH explicitly leverages graph structure to achieve strong robustness and generalization compared to implicit approaches.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling curriculum graph structure through active learning (PATH framework) significantly improves RL training by better leveraging prerequisite relations between environments.

Abstract: In many reinforcement learning (RL) domains, environments are connected by prerequisite relations, such as difficulty-increasing edits or parameter increments, which induce a directed acyclic curriculum graph (DAG). Although this structure is often exploited only implicitly, explicitly modeling it can improve training. We introduce PATH, a curriculum-learning framework that performs active learning over the curriculum graph. PATH first expands coverage by sampling diverse curriculum paths and then reallocates training toward regions that remain unmastered. Experiments across diverse environments show that PATH explicitly leverages the graph structure to achieve strong robustness and generalization.

</details>


### [286] [Shared Actors Need Not Share Critics: Effects of Value Mismatch in Parallel Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26481)
*Zhenya Liu,Yang Meng,Zhuokai Zhao,Xuefeng Liu,Yuxin Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A critic trained across multiple environments without environment information suffers from value mismatch, systematically biasing policy updates; conditioning the critic on environment index improves learning stability and performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When training a single policy in parallel across multiple environments (procedurally generated levels, randomized dynamics, or curricula), implementations commonly use one critic across all environments. However, different environments can assign different expected returns to the same input visible to the critic, creating value mismatch that systematically biases policy updates within individual environments.

Method: 1) Theoretical analysis using illustrative bandit models with multiple environments and a common optimal arm to characterize how value mismatch redistributes sampled policy updates. 2) Minimal intervention: give only a logged environment index to the critic so it can separate value targets. 3) Experiments in Controlled CartPole, MuJoCo, BipedalWalker, and Procgen to validate predictions.

Result: 1) Value mismatch causes systematic shifts in sampled advantages, reinforcing unhelpful actions while attenuating or reversing useful ones. 2) Controlled experiments confirm predicted shifted values, advantages, and performance gaps. 3) In BipedalWalker and Procgen, environment-index conditioning yields more stable learning and higher returns. 4) Across all 16 Procgen games, multihead conditional critic improves aggregate normalized return on 600 unseen levels per game by 40.8%.

Conclusion: Value mismatch is a direct mechanism through which critic sharing can degrade stochastic learning dynamics (not captured by scalar estimator variance alone). Conditioning the critic on an environment index is broadly effective in parallel reinforcement learning, improving performance and stability across diverse environments.

Abstract: When a single policy is trained in parallel across multiple environments of the same task, such as procedurally generated levels, randomized dynamics, or curricula, implementations commonly use one critic across all sampled environments. Yet different environments can assign different expected returns to the same input visible to the critic. A critic without environment information must then reconcile distinct value targets, systematically shifting the sampled advantages within individual environments. Using illustrative bandit models with multiple environments and a common optimal arm, we characterize how this value mismatch redistributes sampled policy updates, reinforcing unhelpful actions while attenuating or even reversing useful ones. The oracle processes using no baseline, the shared value, or the value specific to the sampled environment have the same mean logit update at a fixed policy and converge to the same optimal policy, yet their realized learning paths can differ sharply. The analysis motivates a minimal intervention: give only a logged environment index to the critic so that it can separate the value targets. Controlled CartPole and MuJoCo experiments expose the predicted shifted values, advantages, and performance gaps. In the more complex BipedalWalker and Procgen settings, the same intervention yields more stable learning and higher returns. Across all $16$ Procgen games, the multihead conditional critic improves aggregate normalized return on $600$ unseen levels per game by $40.8\%$. In conclusion, the theory identifies value mismatch as a direct mechanism through which critic sharing can degrade stochastic learning dynamics, not captured by scalar estimator variance alone, and the experiments show that conditioning on an index is broadly effective in parallel reinforcement learning.

</details>


### [287] [Bayesian methods and Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms for curve reconstruction and point cloud data analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26490)
*Asir Intesar Tushar,Ioannis Sgouralis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Bayesian framework for reconstructing closed curves from noisy point-cloud data with uncertainty quantification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Point-cloud data from imaging/sensor technologies has issues: large volumes, localization noise, missing information. Existing pipelines only provide single best-fit reconstruction without uncertainty quantification, limiting reliability assessments.

Method: Fully Bayesian framework modeling observed points as noisy perturbations of latent locations constrained to underlying curve, regularized by non-parametric prior. Uses Markov chain Monte Carlo samplers tailored to point-cloud characteristics for posterior inference.

Result: Numerical experiments (synthetic examples and real-world LiDAR datasets) demonstrate accurate reconstructions with quantified uncertainty over recovered curves.

Conclusion: The Bayesian approach successfully addresses limitations of existing point-cloud reconstruction methods by providing uncertainty quantification alongside accurate curve reconstructions, making results more reliable for applications.

Abstract: Point-cloud data routinely captured by modern imaging and sensor technologies provide detailed geometric descriptions of objects and environments, but their analysis is hindered by large data volumes, localization noise, and missing information. In addition, existing point-cloud reconstruction pipelines typically return a single best-fit structure without uncertainty quantification. We introduce a fully Bayesian framework for representing point-cloud data and reconstructing closed curves, in which observed points are modeled as noisy perturbations of latent locations constrained to lie on the underlying curve that is regularized by a non-parametric prior. Posterior inference in our framework is carried out using a series of Markov chain Monte Carlo samplers tailored to point-cloud characteristics. Numerical experiments, including synthetic examples and real-world LiDAR datasets, show accurate reconstructions and quantified uncertainty over the recovered curves.

</details>


### [288] [A Unified Framework for Fair and Personalized Decentralized Learning under Communication Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26493)
*Krishnendu S. Tharakan,Carlo Fischione*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Decentralized multi-task learning algorithm (DMFL-SQ) combines personalization, fairness, and communication efficiency through sparsification, quantization, and event-triggered communication, achieving good convergence and fairness results with reduced communication overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Decentralized learning systems improve scalability, privacy, and robustness but face challenges with statistical heterogeneity across clients, fairness in client-level performance, and stringent communication constraints. The paper asks: how fair can decentralized learning be under limited communication?

Method: Proposed DMFL-SQ algorithm: a decentralized multi-task learning approach that combines graph-based personalization, agnostic mixture fairness objective, and compressed event-triggered communication using sparsification and quantization. The framework unifies personalization, fairness, and communication efficiency in one system.

Result: Theoretical: Achieves O(T^{-1/2}) convergence rate for non-convex objectives despite sparse, quantized communication; provides PAC-Bayes generalization guarantees. Empirical: On CIFAR-10 and MUSMET EEG datasets, DMFL-SQ substantially reduces communication while maintaining predictive performance and improving fairness across clients.

Conclusion: Personalization, fairness, and communication efficiency can be jointly achieved in decentralized learning while preserving convergence rates. DMFL-SQ demonstrates practical effectiveness in both synthetic and real-world heterogeneous settings with significant communication reduction.

Abstract: Decentralized learning systems aim to collaboratively train models across multiple clients without relying on a central coordinator. While decentralization improves scalability, privacy, and robustness, it also exacerbates three fundamental challenges: statistical heterogeneity across clients, fairness in client-level performance, and stringent communication constraints. This raises a natural question: \emph{how fair can decentralized learning be under limited communication?} We address this question by presenting a unified framework for decentralized learning under communication constraints, bringing together graph-based personalization, agnostic fairness, and compressed event-triggered communication. Specifically, we propose a new algorithm DMFL-SQ, a decentralized multi-task learning algorithm that couples personalized model training over a communication graph with an agnostic mixture fairness objective, while reducing communication through sparsification, quantization, and event-triggered synchronization. We establish convergence guarantees for general non-convex objectives and show that DMFL-SQ achieves an $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2})$ rate in expected squared Moreau-envelope stationarity despite sparse, quantized, and event-triggered communication. We further derive PAC-Bayes generalization guarantees for the fairness-aware mixture objective. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and the real heterogeneous MUSMET EEG dataset demonstrate that DMFL-SQ substantially reduces communication while maintaining predictive performance and improving fairness across clients. Together, our theoretical and empirical results show that personalization, fairness, and communication efficiency can be jointly achieved in decentralized learning while preserving the dominant convergence rate.

</details>


### [289] [A Single Suffix to Break Them All: Basin-Aware Jailbreaks for Merged Model Families](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26506)
*Yu Zhe,Yixin Tan,Junhao Wei,Wang Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Model merging can create safety risks even with individually safe models due to vulnerabilities in the pretrained foundation, leading to transferable jailbreak attacks that work across different merged models sharing the same backbone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work assumes model merging risks come from unsafe constituent models, but this paper shows merging reveals hidden jailbreak vulnerabilities rooted in the pretrained foundation model, even when all constituent models are individually safety-aligned.

Method: The paper introduces Basin-Aware Jailbreak (BAJ), which formulates jailbreak generation as min-max optimization over the merging space to produce transferable adversarial suffixes that work across merged model families sharing the same pretrained backbone.

Result: Experiments across diverse backbones and merging settings show BAJ achieves consistently high transfer success rates and remains effective under existing safety defenses.

Conclusion: Model merging poses significant safety risks beyond just unsafe constituent models, revealing hidden vulnerabilities from the pretrained foundation, requiring new safety considerations and defenses for merged models.

Abstract: Model merging enables combining multiple fine-tuned models without additional training, but its safety implications remain poorly understood. Prior work primarily attributes merging risks to unsafe constituent models, implicitly assuming that merging individually aligned models preserves safety. In contrast, we show that model merging reveals a previously overlooked jailbreak risk rooted in the pretrained foundation model, even when all constituent models are individually safety-aligned. Motivated by this observation, we study a new threat setting where an attacker constructs jailbreak prompts that generalize across merged models sharing the same pretrained backbone, without access to the exact merging coefficients or constituent checkpoints. To exploit this phenomenon, we propose \textbf{Basin-Aware Jailbreak (BAJ)}, which formulates jailbreak generation as a min--max optimization over the merging space to produce transferable adversarial suffixes across merged model families. Experiments across diverse backbones and merging settings show that BAJ achieves consistently high transfer success rates and remains effective under existing defenses.

</details>


### [290] [Algorithmic Principles For Multiclass Learning Are Hard To Come By: Limits of Regularization and Proper Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26516)
*Julian Asilis,Shaddin Dughmi,Vatsal Sharan,Alec Sun,Shang-Hua Teng,Chang Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Multiclass learning cannot be reduced to proper learning, proper learning requires sublinear training errors, and regularization frameworks have fundamental limitations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand whether learning reduces to proper learning (even with enlarged hypothesis classes), whether proper learning can be captured by regularization frameworks, and to resolve open problems about the limitations of proper learning and regularization in multiclass learning.

Method: Constructive impossibility proofs: exhibiting specific multiclass problems that demonstrate the limitations of proper learning and regularization frameworks, complemented by positive results characterizing sufficient conditions for SRM learnability and representability.

Result: 1. A learnable multiclass problem cannot be embedded in any properly learnable class (learning ≠ proper learning even with class enlargement). 2. Proper learning requires training error: every properly learnable class admits proper learner with o(m) errors, but every sublinear scale a_m=o(m) is necessary for some problem. 3. Regularization limitations: a properly learnable class not learnable by SRM, and a learnable class not learnable by local regularizers.

Conclusion: Proper learning and regularization have fundamental limitations in multiclass learning theory; learning cannot be reduced to proper learning, proper learning inherently requires sublinear training errors, and standard regularization frameworks like SRM cannot capture all learnable classes.

Abstract: Two of the most fundamental questions in statistical learning theory are the following: which prediction problems are learnable, and how should they be learned? For the former, elegant answers often take the form of combinatorial dimensions. The latter question, however, has proved considerably more elusive: all known general-purpose multiclass learners rely on intricate orientations of exponentially large one-inclusion structures, and familiar algorithmic principles such as proper learning and regularization remain poorly understood. Motivated by prior work, we ask whether learning reduces to proper learning---possibly over a larger hypothesis class---and whether proper or improper multiclass learning can ultimately be captured by suitable regularizers.
  Our primary results answer both questions negatively, resolving three open problems from prior work. First, we exhibit a learnable multiclass problem that cannot be embedded in any properly learnable class, meaning learning cannot be reduced to proper learning by enlarging the hypothesis class. Second, we demonstrate that proper learning can require training error and characterize this phenomenon precisely: every properly learnable class admits a proper learner making $o(m)$ errors on samples of size $m$, but every prescribed sublinear scale $a_m=o(m)$ is necessary for some properly learnable problem. Third, regularization is not a general learner: we exhibit a properly learnable class that cannot be learned by any Structural Risk Minimization (SRM) learner, and a learnable class that cannot be learned by any local regularizer. We complement these impossibility results with a positive theory that gives two sufficient conditions for SRM learnability and characterizes SRM representability through integrability of revealed preferences.

</details>


### [291] [High Probability Derivative Bounds for Random tanh Neural Networks on a Hypercube](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26526)
*Josef Dick,Michael Feischl,Fabian Zehetgruber*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Paper establishes high-probability bounds for mixed derivatives of wide random tanh networks, showing polynomial rather than exponential dependence on depth for sufficiently wide networks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior deterministic analysis using Euclidean operator norms yields derivative bounds that grow exponentially with network depth, which is undesirable for understanding network regularity and applications like quasi-Monte Carlo integration.

Method: Analyzes wide random neural networks with Gaussian weights and Xavier initialization, isolating the linear term in highest-order derivatives and controlling corresponding tangent directions using measurable finite nets. Specifically studies tanh networks with scalar output.

Result: For sufficiently wide networks, proves derivative bounds where first-order derivatives are depth-independent, and higher-order mixed derivatives grow polynomially as L^{|u|-1} rather than exponentially. Provides high-probability bounds for Euclidean Lipschitz constants and weighted Sobolev norms.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate that wide random neural networks exhibit better regularity than suggested by worst-case deterministic analysis, with implications for quasi-Monte Carlo integration and QMC-based training methods.

Abstract: We establish high-probability bounds for mixed input derivatives of wide random neural networks whose activation derivatives satisfy a factorial growth bound. Our main result specializes these estimates to $\tanh$ networks with Xavier initialization. A direct deterministic analysis based on Euclidean operator norms of the weight matrices yields derivative bounds that generally grow exponentially with the depth. We show that this growth can be substantially improved for sufficiently wide Gaussian networks by isolating the term that is linear in the highest-order derivative and controlling the corresponding tangent directions by measurable finite nets.
  For scalar-output $\tanh$ networks with Gaussian weights and Xavier initialization, we prove that there exist constants $C,C_0,C_1>0$ such that, whenever the common hidden width satisfies $n \geq C\left(L^3n_0^2(1+\log n_0)+L^2\left(1+\log(L/η)\right)\right)$, then, with probability at least $1-η$, the estimate $\left|D^u\mathcal{R}_{Φ^{(L)}}(x)\right| \leq C_0 |u|! (C_1L)^{|u|-1}\prod_{j\in u}β_j(η,n_0)$ holds simultaneously for every non-empty $u\subseteq[n_0]$ and every $x\in[0,1]^{n_0}$. Thus, the first-order derivative bound is independent of the depth, while a square-free mixed derivative of order $|u|$ grows at most polynomially as $L^{|u|-1}$, apart from the coordinate factors. As consequences, we obtain high-probability bounds for the Euclidean Lipschitz constant and for weighted Sobolev norms of the network realization. The latter connect the derivative estimates to quasi-Monte Carlo integration and indicate how such regularity can enter the analysis of QMC-based training.

</details>


### [292] [Predicting Quantifiability from Primary Screens to Prioritize Dose-Response Profiling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26538)
*Sean Lim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a framework for predicting quantifiability in drug screening - whether follow-up testing will yield usable potency estimates - as a distinct objective from biological activity detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current drug screening strategies focus on identifying biologically active compounds, but confirmed activity doesn't guarantee quantifiable potency estimates. Many active compounds fail to produce usable dose-response data in follow-up testing, wasting expensive dose-response profiling capacity.

Method: The authors developed a framework to model quantifiability as a separate triage objective from biological activity. They analyzed screening data to predict whether compounds would yield reportable dose-response estimates, finding that screening features (especially response characteristics) provided most predictive information rather than molecular structure.

Result: Quantifiability was strongly predictable from initial screening data. Response-based predictors maintained robustness across unseen chemical scaffolds and generalized across different assay-mechanism families. The probability of successful quantification varied significantly with response amplitude and assay context.

Conclusion: Experimental measurability is a predictable property distinct from biological activity. Quantifiability-aware triage can optimize the allocation of costly dose-response profiling resources in drug discovery pipelines.

Abstract: High-throughput drug screening relies on low-cost primary assays to prioritize compounds for more expensive dose-response profiling, where potency is ultimately quantified. Current screening strategies largely focus on identifying compounds that will confirm biological activity on follow-up, implicitly assuming that confirmed activity will also yield a usable potency estimate. However, confirmed biological activity in screening does not necessarily translate into a quantifiable potency, because active compounds can still fail to produce a reportable dose-response estimate. We therefore present a framework for modeling quantifiability, whether follow-up testing will yield a usable potency estimate, as a distinct triage objective from biological activity. Quantifiability was strongly predictable from the preceding low-cost screen, with most predictive information arising from the observed screening features rather than molecular structure. Response-based predictors remained robust on previously unseen chemical scaffolds and generalized across held-out assay-mechanism families, while the probability of successful quantification varied strongly with response amplitude and assay context. These findings establish experimental measurability, distinct from biological activity, as a predictable property of screening outcomes and show that quantifiability-aware triage can improve the allocation of costly dose-response profiling capacity.

</details>


### [293] [Chart2SVG: Editable SVG Generation from Raster Chart Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26544)
*Jinning Cui,Lu Chen,Haoyan Shi,Yue He,Chenglong Wang,Mengyu Zhou,Weidong Huang,Yunhai Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Chart2SVG: A multimodal LLM that converts raster charts to structured SVGs with semantic tokens, enabling programmatic editing through a Chart Structure Graph.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Need to convert static raster charts (pixel-based images) into structured, editable SVG formats that maintain semantic meaning and support programmatic manipulation for interactive visualization tools.

Method: Multimodal large language model with chart-specific semantic tokens; uses Beagle+ dataset (33K canonicalized chart samples); combines specialized training objectives with rendering-aware post-training; constructs Chart Structure Graph (CSG) for visual dependencies.

Result: Chart2SVG substantially outperforms baselines in reconstruction fidelity and downstream editing utility; produces SVGs that are both visually accurate and structurally consistent.

Conclusion: The approach advances development of intelligent and interactive visualization tools by enabling raster-to-SVG conversion with semantic understanding and programmatic editing capabilities.

Abstract: We present Chart2SVG, a multimodal large language model that converts static raster charts into structurally organized, semantically enriched SVGs that support programmatic editing. By incorporating chart-specific semantic tokens into a vision-language model, Chart2SVG captures both geometric primitives and their functional roles. To support robust structural recovery, we introduce Beagle+, a dataset of 33K canonicalized and structurally distilled chart samples. Our approach combines specialized training objectives with a rendering-aware post-training phase, producing SVGs that are both visually accurate and structurally consistent. To facilitate higher-level manipulations, we construct a Chart Structure Graph (CSG) that exposes visual dependencies, enabling tasks such as interactive exploration, chart repurposing, and layout reuse. Experiments show that Chart2SVG substantially outperforms baselines in reconstruction fidelity and downstream editing utility, advancing the development of intelligent and interactive visualization tools.

</details>


### [294] [Arrive and Survive: Scaling Safe Goal-Conditioned Policy Learning from One-Bit Failure Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26571)
*Guopeng Li,Yiyang Duan,Yiru Jiao,Chengcheng Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Safe-CRL fixes systematic bias in contrastive reinforcement learning for failure-prone environments by weighting samples by survival probability, improving safety and goal-reaching performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing contrastive RL methods have a theoretical flaw in failure-terminated MDPs: they ignore the probability mass removed by failure termination when constructing positive samples, causing systematic overestimation bias in goal-reaching values and unsafe policy learning.

Method: Introduces Safe-CRL with two minimal corrections: 1) mass-weighted InfoNCE to correct overweighting of short surviving futures in critic learning, and 2) log-survival-mass score to restore missing survival mass in policy optimization. Only requires the one-bit failure termination signal.

Result: Across twelve failure-prone robot navigation and locomotion tasks, Safe-CRL consistently improves survival and substantially outperforms the Scaling-CRL baseline in goal-reaching performance. Deep Safe-CRL policies exhibit complex failure-avoidance behaviors.

Conclusion: The study completes CRL theory under failure termination and provides a scalable safe RL framework. The method successfully addresses catastrophic failure bootstrapping issues while maintaining scalability and only requiring minimal failure signal.

Abstract: Contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL) scales effectively in goal-conditioned tasks by casting policy learning into a self-supervised contrastive objective. However, in a failure-terminated Markov decision process, established CRL considers pre-failure future goals only when constructing positive samples, without accounting for the probability mass removed by failure termination. Our theoretical analysis shows that this omission induces a systematic overestimation bias in goal-reaching values. Consequently, near-failure trajectories provide disproportionately strong supervision of success despite retaining little future occupancy. Unsafe actions can thereby be reinforced through catastrophic failure bootstrapping, leading to failed policy learning and unsustainable goal-reaching behaviours. To address this problem, we introduce two minimal yet strong corrections: mass-weighted InfoNCE corrects the overweighting of short surviving futures in critic learning, and a log-survival-mass score restores the missing survival mass in policy optimization. The resulting method, Safe Contrastive Reinforcement Learning (Safe-CRL), requires only the one-bit signal provided by failure termination to scale safe goal-conditioned policy learning. Across twelve failure-prone robot navigation and locomotion tasks, Safe-CRL consistently improves survival and substantially outperforms the Scaling-CRL baseline in goal-reaching performance. Additionally, deep Safe-CRL policies exhibit complex failure-avoidance behaviours. This study completes the CRL theory under failure termination and provides a scalable safe RL framework. The code is available via https://github.com/RomainLITUD/safe-crl.

</details>


### [295] [Activation Outliers Matter: Robust Recovery for Quantized Multimodal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26581)
*Tanzila Rahman,Mehran Taghian Jazi,Yunke Peng,Zhuang Ma,Anandharaju Durai Raju,Yao Wang,Xing Huang,Hei Yi Mak,Shadan Golestan,Hoang Le,Yonghan Dong,Wei Guo,Yaoyuan Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RFQ (Residual Fallback Quantization) is a lightweight activation reconstruction framework that significantly improves ultra-low-bit (4-bit) quantization performance for MLLMs by adding a quantized residual pathway to compensate for activation quantization errors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ultra-low-bit quantization (4-bit formats like MXFP4 and HiF4) causes significant performance degradation in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), despite hardware support making it attractive for efficient training and deployment. The paper identifies activation quantization as the primary bottleneck.

Method: Proposed Residual Fallback Quantization (RFQ) - a lightweight activation reconstruction framework that supplements the primary ultra-low-bit activation representation with an auxiliary quantized residual pathway to explicitly model and compensate for quantization errors.

Result: RFQ consistently recovers substantial performance lost under MXFP4 and HiF4 quantization on Wan2.2 and Qwen3-VL models, significantly narrowing the gap to BF16 baselines across both generation and reasoning benchmarks. MXFP8 achieves near-lossless performance while 4-bit quantization causes significant degradation.

Conclusion: Activation quantization is the dominant bottleneck in ultra-low-bit MLLMs, and residual-based activation reconstruction (RFQ) provides an effective, practical strategy for robust 4-bit deployment with no architectural modifications and negligible computational overhead.

Abstract: Low-bit quantization offers a promising avenue for reducing the computational and memory demands of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Recent hardware support for low-precision formats, ranging from MXFP8 to ultra-low-bit formats such as MXFP4 and HiF4, has accelerated research into efficient MLLM training and deployment. In this work, we present a systematic study of these quantization schemes in representative MLLMs that span both video generation and reasoning tasks. Our analysis shows that MXFP8 achieves near-lossless performance, whereas aggressive 4-bit quantization leads to significant degradation. Through extensive ablations, we identify activation quantization as the primary source of this performance loss, contributing substantially more than weight quantization. Motivated by this observation, we propose Residual Fallback Quantization (RFQ), a lightweight activation reconstruction framework that supplements the primary ulta-low-bit activation representation with an auxiliary quantized residual pathway. By explicitly modeling and compensating for quantization errors, RFQ improves activation fidelity while preserving the efficiency advantages of ultra-low-bit computation. RFQ requires no architectural modifications and incurs negligible computational overhead. Extensive experiments on Wan2.2 and Qwen3-VL demonstrate that RFQ consistently recovers a substantial portion of the performance lost under the quantization of MXFP4 and HiF4, significantly narrowing the gap to BF16 baselines across both generation and 4 reasoning benchmarks. Our findings establish activation quantization as the dominant bottleneck in ultra-low-bit MLLMs and highlight residual-based activation reconstruction as an effective and practical strategy for robust 4-bit deployment.

</details>


### [296] [J-Zero: Unified Challenger--Solver--Judge Co-Evolution from Zero Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26582)
*Gyouk Chu,Myeongho Jeon,Eunho Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: J-Zero is a unified Challenger-Solver-Judge co-evolution framework that enables self-improving language models in both verifiable and unverifiable domains through adversarial task generation and known-preference training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While self-evolving language models show promise for reducing human supervision costs, most progress has been limited to verifiable domains. There's a significant gap in enabling self-evolution in unverifiable domains where ground truth verification is challenging.

Method: Proposes a Challenger-Solver-Judge co-evolution framework where: (1) Challenger generates increasingly difficult tasks, (2) Solver learns to produce better responses, (3) Judge co-adapts using preference pairs with known ordering derived from how responses were produced (Solver's answer over Challenger's, decomposed/recombined answer over one-shot answer), rather than from the Judge's own scores.

Result: J-Zero outperforms baselines by average 4.2 points on verifiable domains and 8.0 points on unverifiable domains. It continues improving through at least ten iterations while baselines degrade after only two iterations.

Conclusion: The J-Zero framework successfully enables sustainable self-evolution in both verifiable and unverifiable domains through its three-component co-adaptation approach with known-preference training, demonstrating robust iterative improvement beyond baseline methods.

Abstract: Self-evolving language models have recently emerged as a promising path toward superintelligence, with the advantage of reducing the cost of human supervision. While considerable progress has been made in verifiable domains, self-evolution in unverifiable domains remains substantially less explored. We propose Judge co-adaptation from Zero data (J-Zero), a unified Challenger--Solver--Judge co-evolution framework that supports self-improvement across both domains. The Challenger and Solver co-evolve through an adversarial interaction: the Challenger generates increasingly difficult tasks, while the Solver learns to produce higher-quality responses to them. In parallel, the Judge co-adapts using preference pairs whose ordering is known in advance from how each response was produced, i.e., the Solver's answer over the Challenger's, and its decomposed-and-recombined answer over its one-shot answer, rather than from the Judge's own scores. J-Zero outperforms the baselines by an average of 4.2 points on verifiable and 8.0 points on unverifiable domains, and continues to improve through at least ten iterations, whereas the baselines degrade after two.

</details>


### [297] [GRAS: Guided Reduced-Variance Proposals and Adaptive Selection for Training-Free Reward Alignment in Discrete Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26585)
*Kwanyoung Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GRAS (Guided Reduced-variance proposals and Adaptive Selection) improves training-free steering of discrete diffusion models by reducing gradient variance with Rao-Blackwellized reveal and leave-one-out baselines, and introducing adaptive resampling temperature via group-relative advantage standardization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Discrete diffusion models are powerful generators for sequence data, but steering them toward downstream rewards at inference time without retraining remains challenging. Existing training-free steering methods (gradient guidance, search, or their combination) have weaknesses: gradient guidance uses single noisy samples leading to high variance, and search methods use fixed temperature resampling that ignores reward distribution across denoising steps.

Method: GRAS introduces two key improvements: 1) For gradient guidance, reduces variance using Rao-Blackwellized reveal for differentiable rewards and leave-one-out baselines for non-differentiable rewards; 2) For search, standardizes per-step values into group-relative advantage, which mathematically collapses to an adaptive resampling temperature. The method requires no additional denoiser cost.

Result: Across regulatory DNA and protein design tasks, GRAS achieves the best training-free reward performance, outperforming prior training-free methods and matching or surpassing reward-fine-tuned models. It remains effective even for non-differentiable rewards.

Conclusion: GRAS provides a simple yet effective solution to training-free steering of discrete diffusion models by addressing both gradient variance and fixed-temperature search weaknesses, achieving state-of-the-art performance across biological sequence design domains while maintaining computational efficiency.

Abstract: Discrete diffusion models have become a strong, widely adopted class of generators for sequence data, and steering them toward a downstream reward at inference time, without any retraining, is increasingly important. Such training-free steering is done by gradient guidance, by search, or by combining the two. We study the combined regime and identify two weaknesses in how it is usually run: the guided proposal estimates its gradient from a single noisy sample, and the search then resamples particles at a fixed temperature that ignores how rewards spread across each denoising step. We address both with a small set of changes that add no denoiser cost. For the proposal, we lower the estimator variance with a Rao-Blackwellized reveal for differentiable rewards and a leave-one-out baseline for non-differentiable ones; for the search, we standardize the per-step values into a group-relative advantage and prove it collapses to a single active ingredient, an adaptive resampling temperature. We call the resulting method Guided Reduced-variance proposals and Adaptive Selection (GRAS). GRAS is simple yet effective: across regulatory DNA and protein design it attains the best training-free reward, outperforming prior training-free methods and matching or surpassing a reward-fine-tuned model, and it remains effective even for non-differentiable rewards.

</details>


### [298] [SimCast-S2S: An Efficient Generative Model for Subseasonal Precipitation Forecasting via Transfer Learning from Climate Simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26594)
*Hiep V. Dang,Antonios Mamalakis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SimCast-S2S: A latent diffusion model for probabilistic subseasonal-to-seasonal precipitation forecasting that combines variational autoencoders, transfer learning, and efficient ensemble generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: S2S precipitation forecasting is crucial but challenging due to weak predictive signals, high uncertainty, and computational constraints of operational systems. Current data-driven approaches lack proper uncertainty quantification and struggle with limited observational data.

Method: A generative latent-diffusion framework that uses variational autoencoders to operate in compact latent space, employs diffusion-based generative pipeline for probabilistic forecasting, and applies transfer learning via low-rank adaptation (LoRA) pretrained on climate simulations then fine-tuned on reanalysis data.

Result: Outperforms deep learning baselines (CNNs, U-Nets) and remains competitive with state-of-the-art operational systems like ECMWF-S2S baseline, despite using fewer atmospheric variables and no post-processing, bias correction, or calibration.

Conclusion: Latent generative modeling combined with simulation-to-reanalysis transfer learning offers an efficient and scalable approach for data-driven probabilistic S2S precipitation forecasting.

Abstract: Subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) precipitation forecasting has substantial financial and societal impact, yet remains challenging because of weak predictive signals, high associated uncertainty, and the computational cost of operational systems, which constrains simulation fidelity. We introduce SimCast-S2S, a generative latent-diffusion framework for probabilistic S2S precipitation forecasting that addresses three major bottlenecks in data-driven prediction. First, because S2S prediction requires uncertainty quantification rather than only deterministic point forecasts, SimCast-S2S is the first data-driven system that uses a diffusion-based generative pipeline for S2S prediction, enabling effective sampling from the underlying conditional distribution. Second, since generating large probabilistic ensembles is computationally costly in physical space, SimCast-S2S instead operates in a compact latent space learned by variational autoencoders, enabling efficient large-ensemble generation. Third, diffusion models typically require large training datasets; SimCast-S2S overcomes this via transfer learning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), pretraining on large ensembles of climate simulations before fine-tuning on limited reanalysis data. On reanalysis data, SimCast-S2S outperforms deep learning baselines, including convolutional neural networks and U-Net architectures. Notably, despite using only a subset of atmospheric input variables and no post-processing, bias correction, or calibration, SimCast-S2S remains competitive with, and in many cases outperforms, state-of-the-art operational systems such as the ECMWF-S2S baseline. These results indicate that latent generative modeling combined with simulation-to-reanalysis transfer learning offers an efficient and scalable path toward data-driven probabilistic S2S precipitation forecasting.

</details>


### [299] [Technical Comparative Benchmarking Study: Advanced AI Hybrid Methods for Renewable Energy Farm Optimization and Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26613)
*Majid Masoumi,Asghar Dashtiy,Mohammad Dehghan,Mina Rajabi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper benchmarks various ML approaches for renewable energy forecasting, finding that Extra Trees ensemble performs best for structured wind farm layout data, while RF-BiLSTM hybrid achieves the overall best accuracy for spatiotemporal forecasting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide comprehensive benchmarking of different machine learning architectures (conventional ML, ensembles, deep learning, Transformers, graph models, and hybrids) for renewable energy forecasting scenarios, determining which approaches work best under different data conditions.

Method: Evaluated multiple ML approaches across three datasets: large-scale WEC dataset, 16 WEC dataset, and 10-minute SCADA measurements from Penmanshiel wind farm. Tested conventional ML, ensemble learning, deep neural networks, recurrent architectures, Transformers, graph-based models (STGCN), and hybrid ensemble-deep learning approaches under complementary renewable energy scenarios.

Result: Extra Trees ensemble showed clear advantage for structured WEC layout data with 63.7% MAE reduction compared to MLP baseline. STGCN achieved MAE of 167.0 kW and R=0.93 by learning spatial-temporal interactions. RF-BiLSTM hybrid achieved best overall accuracy with MAE=150.5 kW, representing 75% reduction vs standalone LSTM and 10% improvement over STGCN.

Conclusion: No single AI architecture is universally optimal - randomized/boosted ensembles work best for structured WEC surrogate modeling, graph networks excel when spatial interactions dominate, and ensemble-recurrent hybrids provide strongest balance when tabular relationships and temporal dynamics coexist.

Abstract: This study provides a comprehensive benchmarking of conventional machine learning (ML), ensemble learning, deep neural networks, recurrent architectures, Transformers, graph based models, and hybrid ensemble deep learning approaches under complementary renewable energy scenarios. Three datasets are considered: a large scale WEC dataset, a 16 WEC dataset, and operational 10 min SCADA measurements at the Penmanshiel wind farm. For structured WEC layout data, tree ensembles exhibited a clear advantage over conventional ML and neural predictors because randomized partitioning and boosting efficiently captured nonlinear layout power interactions without requiring explicit feature representation learning. The Extra Trees was the strongest model, achieving considerable results. Relative to the MLP baseline, this corresponds to an approximately 63.7% reduction in MAE, demonstrating the suitability of randomized tree ensembles for high dimensional structured WEC data. Also, STGCN reduced the MAE to approximately 167.0 kW and achieved R = 0.93 by explicitly learning spatial and temporal turbine interactions. The best overall forecasting accuracy was obtained by the RF BiLSTM hybrid, with an MAE=150.5 kW. Compared with standalone LSTM, this represents an approximately 75% reduction in MAE, while improving on STGCN by approximately 10.0%. Finally, the experiments reveal that no single AI architecture is universally optimal: randomized and boosted ensembles are particularly effective for structured WEC surrogate modeling, graph networks become advantageous when explicit spatial interactions dominate, and ensemble recurrent hybrids provide the strongest balance when nonlinear tabular relationships and temporal dynamics coexist.

</details>


### [300] [Robust Neural Stimulation Response Modeling Through Meta-Learning and Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26649)
*Matthew J Bryan,Daniel C Muir,Felix Schwock,Azadeh Yazdan-Shahmorad,Rajesh P N Rao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Meta-learning and pretraining significantly improve neural stimulation forecasting models, reducing catastrophic failures and calibration requirements by 50-90%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model-based closed-loop neural stimulation faces two major obstacles: catastrophic forecast failures in many sessions and impractical per-session calibration requirements that conflict with clinical constraints.

Method: Extended temporal basis function models with cross-session pretraining using a novel architecture and algorithm based on model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML), evaluated on 40 sessions of optogenetic stimulation in primary sensorimotor cortex of two non-human primates.

Result: Meta-learning dramatically reduces catastrophic forecast failure (sessions with test R-squared < 0.05 dropped from 16/40 to 1/40 for 1k calibration set), narrows prediction intervals significantly (p < 0.05), and reduces calibration requirements by 50-90% at matched accuracy.

Conclusion: Cross-session structure in stimulation responses is consistent enough to support pretraining, providing first empirical evidence that meta-learning approaches are viable for neural stimulation, addressing key obstacles to deploying model-based stimulation controllers.
