Abstract: Objective: Model-based closed-loop neural stimulation holds promise for therapeutic applications ranging from Parkinson's disease to sensory restoration, but deployment has been limited by two obstacles: 1) forecasting models for predicting the consequences of stimulation fail catastrophically on a meaningful fraction of sessions, and 2) per-session calibration requirements are often incompatible with clinical constraints. We address both by demonstrating, for the first time, that meta-learning and pretraining can be applied to neural stimulation response modeling. Methods: Temporal basis function models (TBFMs) forecast state-dependent neural responses to stimulation. We extend TBFMs with cross-session pretraining using a novel architecture and algorithm based on model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML), evaluating them on 40 sessions of optogenetic stimulation in primary sensorimotor cortex of two non-human primates. Results: Meta-learning substantially reduces catastrophic forecast failure: for a 1k calibration set size, sessions with test R-squared < 0.05 drop from 16 of 40 (single-session training) to 1 (MAML-pretrained), and prediction intervals become significantly narrower (p < 0.05). Calibration requirements are reduced by 50-90% at matched accuracy, enabling experiments otherwise infeasible within clinical session-time constraints. Conclusion: Our results demonstrate that cross-session structure in stimulation responses is consistent enough to support pretraining, providing the first empirical evidence that meta-learning approaches are viable for neural stimulation. Significance: The robustness and sample efficiency gains directly address known obstacles to deploying model-based stimulation controllers. Our results motivate community efforts to assemble standardized multi-site stimulation datasets and to further explore meta-learning for robust closed-loop stimulation.

</details>


### [301] [When Privacy Hurts Mergeability: Geometry-Aware Model Merging under Differential Privacy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26655)
*Jin Liu,Junkang Liu,Ning Xi,Yinbin Miao,Dawei Wei,Ke Cheng,Jianfeng Ma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DP-Merging is a geometry-aware framework that improves the merging of differentially private fine-tuned models by addressing local sharpness and reference drift issues, enabling better multi-task performance while preserving privacy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model merging enables multi-task models without centralizing task data, but differentially private (DP) fine-tuned models are difficult to merge effectively due to geometric challenges, and the impact of DP on merging is not well understood.

Method: DP-Merging uses two techniques: 1) DP-compatible sharpness-aware objective to guide private task models toward flatter loss regions (addressing local sharpness), and 2) reference-based alignment regularizer to keep task models close to shared pretrained initialization (addressing reference drift).

Result: Experiments on vision and language tasks across multiple privacy budgets show that DP-Merging consistently improves private merged-model performance while preserving the privacy guarantees of underlying DP fine-tuning procedures.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that addressing geometric obstacles (local sharpness and reference drift) enables effective merging of differentially private models, with DP-Merging providing both theoretical bounds and empirical improvements for privacy-preserving multi-task learning.

Abstract: Model merging promises to construct a single multi-task model from independently fine-tuned task models without accessing the original task data. This makes it attractive when task data cannot be centralized, but released task models may still leak private fine-tuning data. Differential privacy (DP) provides a principled mechanism for limiting such leakage, yet its effect on model merging remains poorly understood. In this paper, we study the geometry of differentially private model merging and identify two geometric obstacles that make private task models difficult to merge: \emph{local sharpness}, which makes task losses sensitive to the parameter displacement induced by merging, and \emph{reference drift}, which measures the displacement of private task models from the shared pretrained initialization and amplifies cross-task interference. Based on these observations, we propose \textbf{DP-Merging}, a geometry-aware framework that improves the mergeability of differentially private task models. DP-Merging uses a DP-compatible sharpness-aware objective to guide each private task model toward flatter loss regions, and a reference-based alignment regularizer to keep task models close to the shared pretrained initialization. We derive a merge-gap upper bound showing that reducing local curvature and reference drift tightens the bound on the loss increase induced by merging. Experiments on vision and language tasks across multiple privacy budgets show that DP-Merging consistently improves private merged-model performance while preserving the privacy guarantees of the underlying DP fine-tuning procedures.

</details>


### [302] [Simple Actors and Deep Critics for Scalable Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26659)
*Guhyeon Kang,Jaehwi Lee,Minhae Kwon*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LAC (Light Actor, deep Critic) is an offline RL approach that shifts capacity from computationally expensive actors (like diffusion/flow-matching policies) to deep critics, achieving similar performance with 4x lower inference latency by addressing instability issues in deep critics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current offline RL methods use expressive generative actors (diffusion/flow-matching) that require multiple steps per action, creating substantial inference overhead. Since critics are discarded at deployment while actors run at every step, it's more efficient to allocate capacity to critics rather than actors, but scaling MLP critics causes instability issues.

Method: Proposes LAC with: 1) Residual MLP backbone to address optimization issues, 2) n-step bootstrap targets to reduce bootstrap-noise amplification, 3) Categorical cross-entropy loss to prevent value-range drift, combined with a lightweight deterministic actor.

Result: On OGBench, LAC matches the performance of strongest diffusion and flow-matching baselines while achieving up to 4x lower inference latency, comparable to one-step distilled policies but without requiring distillation. The critic recipe also transfers across different actor parametrizations.

Conclusion: Shifting capacity from actors to critics is an effective strategy for offline RL, balancing performance and inference efficiency. By addressing specific failure modes in deep critics, LAC demonstrates that lightweight actors with deep critics can achieve state-of-the-art performance with significantly improved inference speed.

Abstract: Recent progress in offline reinforcement learning (RL) has been driven by expressive generative actors such as diffusion and flow-matching policies, which capture multimodal behavior in offline datasets. However, these actors require multiple denoising or integration steps per action and thus incur substantial overhead at every decision in deployment. In this work, we revisit where capacity should be invested in an offline actor--critic method. Since the critic is used only during training and is discarded at deployment while the actor runs at every decision step, allocating capacity to the critic rather than the actor is more favorable for inference-time efficiency. However, scaling MLP critics in offline RL is known to introduce several distinct instabilities that have, in practice, kept critics shallow. We identify three distinct failure modes that arise when critics are deepened in offline RL---optimization, bootstrap-noise amplification, and value-range drift---and address each with a corresponding ingredient: a residual MLP backbone, n-step bootstrap targets, and a categorical cross-entropy loss. Combining these ingredients with a lightweight deterministic actor, we propose LAC (Light Actor, deep Critic). On OGBench, LAC matches the strongest diffusion- and flow-matching baselines while achieving up to 4x lower inference latency, comparable to one-step distilled policies without distillation. Its critic recipe also transfers across actor parametrizations.

</details>


### [303] [Neural Regression with Embeddings for Numerical Attribute Prediction in Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26729)
*Rupesh Sapkota,Louis Mozart Kamdem Teyou,Moshood Yekini,Caglar Demir,Axel-Cyrille Ngonga Ngomo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LitEm enhances transductive KG embedding models to predict numerical attributes via neural regression, and a co-training framework improves link prediction while enabling attribute prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most transductive knowledge graph embedding models ignore rich numerical attributes present in knowledge graphs, limiting their ability to represent real-world knowledge graphs with diverse information.

Method: Proposes LitEm (neural regression model) for numerical attribute prediction, and a co-training framework that jointly trains state-of-the-art transductive KG embedding models with LitEm.

Result: LitEm achieves best or second-best results on most attributes across FB15K-237, YAGO15K, DB15K, and Mutagenesis. Co-training improves link prediction performance (mainly for bilinear models) while enabling numerical attribute prediction.

Conclusion: The co-training framework helps models encode and exploit attribute information in a "literal-aware" manner, with gains not merely due to additional parameters, enabling better representation of real-world knowledge graphs.

Abstract: In recent years, transductive knowledge graph embedding models have been applied to tasks such as link prediction and query answering. Although knowledge graphs often contain rich numerical attributes, most embedding models neglect them, limiting their ability to represent real-world knowledge graphs with diverse information. In this work, we propose a neural regression model (LitEm) that enables transductive knowledge graph embedding models to predict numerical attributes within knowledge graphs. Experimental results demonstrate that LitEm achieves the best or second-best results on most attributes across FB15K-237, YAGO15K, DB15K, and Mutagenesis. Furthermore, we propose a co-training framework that jointly trains state-of-the-art transductive knowledge graph embedding models with LitEm, which improves link prediction performance mainly for bilinear models and simultaneously enables them to predict numerical attributes. In addition, the literal-awareness evaluation demonstrates that co-training helps models to encode and exploit attribute information in a "literal-aware'' manner, suggesting that the observed gains are not merely due to additional parameters. We publicly release our implementation at https://github.com/dice-group/dice-embeddings.

</details>


### [304] [Rethinking Message Passing as Retrieval for Text-Attributed Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26732)
*Jintang Li,Yuhong Chen,Ruofan Wu,Binli Luo,Jiayi Ji,Hui Li,Rongrong Ji*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A retrieval-augmented framework (RTA) replaces traditional GNN message passing with label-aware retrieval and propagation, achieving comparable performance to GNNs with improved efficiency and robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional GNNs as message-passing networks have unclear advantages over simple MLPs, are computationally expensive, and sensitive to imperfect graph structures. The authors question why neighborhood aggregation outperforms node-wise MLPs despite these drawbacks.

Method: Proposes RTA, an MLP-based framework that replaces structural message passing with label-aware retrieval and propagation. Each layer applies an MLP to node representations combined with permutation-invariant summaries of retrieved graph context. Theoretically connects retrieval-based aggregation to softmax-attention message passing.

Result: Experiments on text-attributed graph benchmarks show RTA matches or outperforms strong GNN and graph LLM baselines while improving computational efficiency and robustness across diverse scenarios.

Conclusion: The retrieval-augmented view of GNNs provides a viable alternative to traditional message passing, offering comparable performance with better efficiency and robustness, while establishing theoretical connections between retrieval mechanisms and attention-based message passing.

Abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are typically conceptualized as message-passing neural networks, yet it remains unclear why neighborhood aggregation reliably outperforms node-wise multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). Despite its empirical success, this paradigm can be computationally expensive and sensitive to imperfect graph structures. In this work, we present a retrieval-augmented view of GNNs: each layer makes predictions by applying an MLP to a node representation together with a permutation-invariant summary of retrieved graph context. Motivated by this perspective, we propose RTA, a simple MLP-based framework that replaces structural message passing with label-aware retrieval and propagation. We provide theoretical insights that (i) connect retrieval-based aggregation to softmax-attention message passing, and (ii) establish the robustness of retrieved-context supervision to mis-retrieved outliers. Experiments on multiple text-attributed graph benchmarks show that RTA matches or even outperforms strong GNN and graph LLM baselines while improving efficiency and robustness across diverse scenarios.

</details>


### [305] [Self-Augmented Diffusion Guidance for Physics-Informed Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26748)
*Akira Osaka,Naoya Takeishi,Takehisa Yairi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A physics-informed diffusion model that generates physically-consistent spatiotemporal data by learning the data distribution conditioned on deviation from physical laws, enabling faster generation without solving governing equations at each denoising step.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard diffusion models can generate visually plausible spatiotemporal signals of physical phenomena but often deviate from true physical dynamics since they don't incorporate constraints from underlying physical laws. This limits their practical utility for scientific applications requiring physically accurate simulations.

Method: Proposes a physics-informed diffusion guidance approach with self-generated data augmentation. The method learns the data distribution conditioned on the degree of deviation from physically correct dynamics, then generates samples by explicitly setting the deviation condition to zero. It decouples governing equation evaluation from diffusion model training and sampling, avoiding computationally expensive numerical simulations at every denoising iteration.

Result: The proposed model significantly reduces physical deviations compared to standard diffusion models. When combined with existing physics-constrained diffusion methods, it achieves even further reductions in deviations. The method enables faster sample generation while maintaining physical accuracy.

Conclusion: The proposed physics-informed diffusion guidance approach effectively incorporates physical constraints into diffusion models for spatiotemporal data generation, achieving better physical consistency than standard methods while being computationally efficient and compatible with existing physics-constrained techniques.

Abstract: Diffusion models can be used to generate spatiotemporal signals of physical phenomena, such as time-series images of fluid dynamics. However, a major limitation of standard diffusion models is that they do not incorporate constraints derived from the underlying physical laws. Consequently, generated samples may appear visually plausible while deviating substantially from the true dynamics. In this study, we propose a simple yet effective physics-informed approach based on diffusion guidance with self-generated data augmentation. The proposed method learns the data distribution conditioned on the degree of deviation from the physically correct dynamics and generates samples by explicitly setting the deviation condition to be zero. The method decouples the evaluation of the governing equations from the diffusion model training and sampling processes, avoiding the need to solve the governing equations at every iteration of the denoising process. This design makes the method applicable to problems requiring computationally expensive numerical simulations and enables faster sample generation. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model not only significantly reduces the deviations compared with standard diffusion models but also achieves further reductions when combined with existing physics-constrained diffusion methods.

</details>


### [306] [Safety by Design: Realized-Cost Constraints for Contextual Bandits with Continuous Actions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26755)
*Spyros Dragazis,Aldo Pacchiano*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes High-Probability Constrained UCB, an optimistic-pessimistic algorithm for contextual bandits with continuous actions that enforces stage-wise high-probability constraints on realized costs, addressing limitations of expected-cost constraints in heteroscedastic settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safety-constrained bandit models only constrain expected costs, which is insufficient in heteroscedastic settings where actions affect outcome variability. Many applications (clinical trials, dosage selection, autonomous systems) require safety guarantees on realized costs, not just expectations, since single unsafe decisions can have catastrophic consequences.

Method: High-Probability Constrained UCB (HPC-UCB), an optimistic-pessimistic algorithm that explores for reward while conservatively estimating the safe action set using upper confidence bounds for reward (optimistic) and lower confidence bounds for cost (pessimistic) to ensure safety constraints are met with high probability.

Result: For linear reward and cost models, the algorithm achieves tight $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\sqrt{T})$ regret bound, where d is dimension and T is time horizon. Analysis extends to general function classes using eluder dimension. Experiments show substantial reduction in safety violations compared to expected-cost constrained baselines.

Conclusion: Enforcing high-probability constraints on realized costs provides stronger safety guarantees than expected-cost constraints, particularly in heteroscedastic settings. The proposed algorithm achieves optimal regret while significantly reducing safety violations.

Abstract: Contextual bandits are a standard framework for sequential decision-making under uncertainty, with applications in clinical trials, dosage selection, recommendation systems, and autonomous systems. Safety is central in many of these applications, since a single unsafe decision in settings such as dosage selection or autonomous driving can have catastrophic consequences. A common way to model safety in bandit problems is to associate each action with both a reward signal and a cost signal, and to optimize reward subject to constraints on cost. Most existing safety-constrained bandit models enforce safety by requiring the expected cost of each action to remain below a prescribed threshold. However, this may be insufficient in heteroscedastic settings, where the chosen action affects not only the expected reward and cost, but also the variability of the observed outcomes. We study contextual bandits with one-dimensional continuous actions and stage-wise high-probability constraints on the realized cost. We propose High-Probability Constrained UCB, an optimistic-pessimistic algorithm that explores for reward while conservatively estimating the safe action set. For linear reward and cost models, we prove a tight $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\sqrt{T})$ regret bound, and we extend the analysis to general function classes using the eluder dimension. Experiments show that enforcing realized-cost safety substantially reduces violations compared with expected-cost constrained baselines.

</details>


### [307] [Beyond Client Averaging: A Client-Independent Second-Order Stationary-Bias Component in Stochastic SCAFFOLD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26765)
*Yi-Ping Tang,Guan-Ju Peng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: For one-dimensional homogeneous federated learning with SCaffold algorithm, client averaging suppresses leading O(γ/N) bias but cannot eliminate client-independent O(γ²) bias, which arises from control fluctuations interacting with nonquadratic curvature.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous analysis of stochastic SCaffold identified O(γ/N) stationary mean bias but didn't characterize the first client-independent bias contribution. The paper aims to precisely quantify these bias components to understand fundamental limitations of client averaging in federated optimization.

Method: Analytical proof for full-participation stochastic SCaffold with one-dimensional homogeneous clients, fixed local-step count H, and bounded additive gradient noise. Uses mathematical analysis uniformly over N ≥ 2 to derive exact bias coefficients.

Result: The stationary mean bias has two main components: 1) O(γ/N) term with coefficient -f'''(x⋆)σ²/[4f''(x⋆)²], 2) O(γ²) term with coefficient -f'''(x⋆)σ²/[12f''(x⋆)] × (H-1)(5H-1)/H. The O(γ²) term persists even as N increases.

Conclusion: Client averaging suppresses O(γ/N) bias but cannot remove client-independent O(γ²) bias when its coefficient is nonzero. This bias arises indirectly from control fluctuations interacting with nonquadratic curvature, and vanishes for quadratic objectives. The analysis provides precise characterization of federated optimization bias tradeoffs.

Abstract: Existing constant-step analysis of stochastic \Scaf{} identifies a leading $O(γ/N)$ stationary mean bias and shows that higher-order bias can persist as the client count increases, but does not identify the first client-independent contribution at coefficient level. For full-participation stochastic \Scaf{} with one-dimensional homogeneous clients, fixed local-step count $H$, and bounded additive gradient noise, we prove, uniformly over $N\ge2$,
  $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}_{π_{γ,N,H}}[x]-x^\star ={}& -\frac{f'''(x^\star)σ^2}{4f''(x^\star)^2}\fracγ{N}\\ &- \frac{f'''(x^\star)σ^2}{12f''(x^\star)} \frac{(H-1)(5H-1)}{H}γ^2 +O_H\!\left(\frac{γ^2}{N}+γ^3\right). \end{aligned} $$
  Hence client averaging suppresses the leading $O(γ/N)$ bias but does not remove the client-independent $O(γ^2)$ component when its coefficient is nonzero.
  The mechanism is indirect: although the direct control contribution cancels pathwise in the linear global average, the controls still alter within-round local trajectories and their second moments. Fresh gradient noise and persistent control fluctuations therefore generate local second-moment corrections that nonquadratic curvature converts into stationary mean bias. The coefficient vanishes for quadratic objectives. Numerical experiments are consistent with the predicted coefficient, its persistence as client count increases, and the stated joint remainder. The result is restricted to the one-dimensional homogeneous fixed-$H$ setting.

</details>


### [308] [On the Indistinguishability of Human v/s AI Generated Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26797)
*Jaee Ponde,Aritra Das,Mihir More,Debayan Gupta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper shows that strategically paraphrasing AI-generated text using human writing samples can make it converge to the human distribution with explicit convergence rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs rapidly improve, distinguishing AI-generated text from human writing becomes crucial. This problem is exacerbated by paraphrasing tools that make machine text appear more human-like, creating a need for understanding how to strategically use human samples to paraphrase AI text toward human distribution.

Method: Under a multi-sample setting with both human and machine responses to the same prompts, the study shows that repeated paraphrasing moves the machine distribution toward the empirical human distribution. The analysis establishes simple mixing and stability conditions and extends to finite-sample settings.

Result: The results derive an explicit convergence rate and characterize how the required number of human samples and paraphrasing rounds scale with desired error. This provides quantitative understanding of how strategic paraphrasing using human samples can transform AI-generated text toward human-like distributions.

Conclusion: Strategic paraphrasing with access to human writing samples can effectively move AI-generated text toward human distribution with quantifiable convergence rates, offering insights for both improving AI text detection and making AI text more human-like.

Abstract: The rapid improvement of LLMs has made distinguishing AI-generated text from human writing a pressing problem. This challenge is further amplified by paraphrasing tools designed to make machine-generated text appear more "human". We study how access to human writing samples can be used to strategically paraphrase machine-generated responses toward the human distribution. Under a multi-sample setting with human and machine responses to the same prompts, we show that repeated paraphrasing moves the machine distribution toward the empirical human distribution under simple mixing and stability conditions. Our results derive an explicit convergence rate, extend the analysis to a finite-sample setting, and characterize how the required number of human samples and paraphrasing rounds scale with the desired error.

</details>


### [309] [SAGE: Variate-Wise Semantic Augmentation for Vision-Language Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26829)
*Haizhao Fan,Xinyi Le*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAGE is a CLIP-based framework for time series forecasting that combines temporal, textual, and visual information without using large language models at inference time, achieving state-of-the-art results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional time series forecasting models operate on raw numerical sequences without semantic knowledge that domain experts use. Existing approaches either use computationally expensive LLMs at inference time or apply uniform textual prompts ignoring variable-specific semantics.

Method: SAGE uses a dual CLIP architecture: text encoder processes frequency-enhanced patches and variable tokens with gated residual paths for variable-specific descriptions, while frozen vision encoder aligns rendered series with temporal representations via contrastive learning.

Result: Achieved state-of-the-art accuracy across eight long-term benchmarks and M4 dataset. Ablations confirmed complementary gains from multimodal alignment and variable-level knowledge.

Conclusion: SAGE demonstrates that integrating multimodal semantic supervision (textual descriptions and visual representations) without expensive LLM inference can significantly improve time series forecasting by capturing variable-specific semantics and temporal dynamics.

Abstract: Time series forecasting models operate on raw numerical sequences, lacking the semantic knowledge that domain experts implicitly leverage, such as the physical meaning of each variable, its statistical behavior, and its temporal dynamics. Recent efforts to bridge this gap fall into two camps. Some rely on large language models at inference time, which is computationally expensive. Others apply uniform textual prompts at the dataset level, ignoring the heterogeneous semantics across individual variates. We propose SAGE (Seeing and Augmenting with Grounded Encoding), an end-to-end CLIP-based framework that jointly models temporal, cross-variable, textual, and visual information. The CLIP text encoder processes frequency-enhanced patches and variable tokens, while gated residual paths inject variable-specific descriptions and statistical descriptors. In parallel, the frozen CLIP vision encoder aligns rendered series with temporal representations through a training-only contrastive objective. This dual use of CLIP adds complementary semantic and visual supervision without placing an LLM in the forecasting loop. Across eight long-term benchmarks and M4, SAGE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy. Ablations confirm complementary gains from multimodal alignment and variable-level knowledge.

</details>


### [310] [Reinforcement Learning-Based Control of CAV Platoon Joining Maneuvers in Mixed Traffic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26860)
*Biao Yin,Abderrahmane Kasmi,Nadir Farhi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a simulation framework to evaluate deep reinforcement learning algorithms for CAV platoon joining in mixed traffic, finding PPO with risk penalties achieves high success rates but requires more decision steps, revealing safety-efficiency trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CAV platooning can improve road safety and traffic capacity, but real-world platoon control faces challenges from uncertainty and heterogeneous driving behaviors in mixed traffic environments with human-driven vehicles. While RL has potential for such control problems, practical deployment raises safety and learning efficiency concerns.

Method: The paper develops an agent-based modeling framework coupled with SUMO simulator to evaluate DRL-based control algorithms (DQN, DDQN, PPO) for CAV platoon joining. Two safety approaches are examined: incorporating risk penalties in the reward function during learning, and using an external safety controller to constrain learned policies.

Result: PPO outperforms DQN and DDQN, achieving ~98% joining success rate and <1% collision rate when risk penalties are included in rewards. However, this improved performance requires more decision steps. External safety controllers effectively prevent collisions but may reduce joining efficiency.

Conclusion: The study reveals trade-offs between safety, joining effectiveness, and decision efficiency in RL-based CAV platoon control. Results emphasize the importance of jointly considering safety and efficiency when designing RL controllers for mixed traffic environments.

Abstract: Connected and automated vehicle (CAV) platooning offers a promising approach to improving road safety and traffic capacity. However, platoon control in real-world traffic is challenging due to uncertainty and heterogeneous driving behaviors. Reinforcement learning (RL) has strong potential for addressing such control problems, but its practical deployment raises challenges related to safety and learning efficiency. This paper proposes a generic modeling and simulation framework for investigating CAV platoon joining maneuvers and comparing deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based control algorithms. The problem is particularly challenging in mixed-traffic environments, where CAVs coexist with human-driven vehicles exhibiting heterogeneous longitudinal and lateral behaviors. The objective is to achieve safe and efficient joining maneuvers by either incorporating penalties for risky behaviors into the learning process or using an external safety controller to constrain the learned policy. An agent-based modeling framework coupled with the Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) simulator is used to evaluate Deep Q-Network (DQN), Double Deep Q-Network (DDQN), and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Results show that PPO outperforms DQN and DDQN, achieving a joining success rate of approximately 98 % and a collision rate below 1 %, largely due to risk-related penalties incorporated into the reward function. However, this improved performance requires more decision steps to complete the maneuver, revealing a trade-off between safety, joining effectiveness, and decision efficiency. An external safety controller effectively prevents collisions, although its interventions may reduce joining efficiency. The results highlight the importance of jointly considering safety and efficiency when designing RL-based controllers for CAV platoon joining in mixed traffic.

</details>


### [311] [When Is the Sharp Covariance Envelope Tight? Feature-Only Geometry for Volume-Sampled Least Squares](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26877)
*Kihun Rhee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Analysis of volume sampling's coefficient covariance under fixed-design settings, establishing a Loewner envelope that is globally sharp, with phase transitions based on feature margin and leverage geometry.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on volume sampling established properties like unbiasedness and inverse moments, but left gaps in understanding exact loss and covariance formulas beyond the special case where sample size equals dimension (s=d). The paper aims to provide a complete characterization of coefficient covariance under ordinary volume sampling for all legal budget sizes.

Method: Establishes a Loewner envelope for centered coefficient covariance under ordinary indexed fixed-size volume sampling followed by selected unweighted least squares. Uses feature-only margin analysis to determine spectral phase transitions, residual-augmented change of measure for response-aware mechanisms, and leverage geometry interpretation for boundary cases.

Result: Provides globally sharp Loewner envelope for coefficient covariance across all full-rank pools, responses, and legal budgets (d <= s <= m). Identifies spectral phase transitions based on feature margin ν_A: ν_A > 0 gives strict envelope for all compatible residuals, ν_A = 0 allows spectral tightness. Shows the same zero-margin residual is tight at every strict-interior budget and provides conservative cardinality decisions via lower certificates.

Conclusion: The analysis completes the understanding of volume sampling's coefficient covariance properties, establishing exact conditions for spectral tightness and providing practical tools for conservative decision-making under fixed-design settings. The results are specific to conditional centered, full-Gram-whitened coefficient covariance rather than population generalization.

Abstract: Prior analyses by Derezinski and Warmuth established all-size sampling identities, selected-OLS unbiasedness, and inverse moments for ordinary volume sampling, while their exact arbitrary-fixed-response loss and prediction-covariance formulas are at the rank-size endpoint s=d. We establish a Loewner envelope for centered coefficient covariance for every full-rank fixed pool, response, and legal budget d <= s <= m under ordinary indexed fixed-size volume sampling followed by selected unweighted least squares; its coefficient is globally sharp over the full-rank class. Global sharpness does not determine attainability on the pool in hand. Under positive loss, strict-interior budgets, and no coloops, a feature-only margin nu_A gives the exact fixed-design spectral phase: nu_A > 0 if and only if the normalized spectral envelope is strict for every compatible residual, whereas nu_A = 0 if and only if some compatible residual is spectrally tight; the same zero-margin residual is tight at every strict-interior budget. A residual-augmented change of measure supplies the response-aware mechanism and a one-sided quantitative slack bound, while support saturation proves the attainment direction. Critical equal-leverage geometry interprets the boundary, and sound lower certificates yield conservative same-primitive cardinality decisions. Frozen-feature examples show that the certificate is nonvacuous and measure the fixed-pool cost of its authorized reduction. The claims concern conditional centered, full-Gram-whitened coefficient covariance, not population generalization.

</details>


### [312] [Mitigating Strong-Modality Collapse in Multimodal Learning via Inverted Asymmetric Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26879)
*Mary Ogbuka Kenneth,Foaad Khosmood,Abbas Edalat*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Inverted Asymmetric Fusion (IAF) to address "strong-modality collapse" in multimodal models, where dominant modalities degrade during fusion. IAF preserves dominant modalities unchanged while weaker modalities attend to them, combined with Modality-Aware Knowledge Distillation, improving over unimodal baselines by up to 8.25%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors observed that despite expectations, multimodal fusion (early, late, symmetric attention) often fails to outperform the best unimodal baseline on datasets like MultiHuSE. They identified "strong-modality collapse" - where the dominant modality's performance degrades during fusion (e.g., text accuracy dropping from 74.9% to 56.4%). This phenomenon helps explain why some multimodal models underperform compared to single-modality approaches.

Method: Proposed Inverted Asymmetric Fusion (IAF) that avoids forcing mutual attention across modalities. The dominant modality passes through fusion unchanged, while weaker modalities attend to it as a contextual anchor. Before fusion, weaker modalities are strengthened using Modality-Aware Knowledge Distillation. The approach was evaluated on three benchmarks with different modality hierarchies: text-dominant datasets (MultiHuSE, UR-FUNNY) and audio-visual-dominant dataset (MUStARD).

Result: Pathway isolation analysis shows that IAF preserves the dominant modality's internal accuracy at its unimodal ceiling across all tested configurations, while symmetric fusion degrades it by up to 18.5% on MultiHuSE. IAF improves over the strongest unimodal baseline by up to 8.25%, successfully overcoming the strong-modality collapse problem.

Conclusion: Strong-modality collapse is a key reason why multimodal fusion sometimes underperforms unimodal baselines. The proposed Inverted Asymmetric Fusion approach effectively addresses this by preserving dominant modalities while allowing weaker modalities to benefit from them as contextual anchors, combined with knowledge distillation to strengthen weaker modalities before fusion.

Abstract: Fusing multiple modalities is expected to improve model performance. However, on the MultiHuSE dataset, early, late, and symmetric attention fusion often fail to outperform the best unimodal baseline (text). Pathway isolation of a symmetric attention fusion model reveals that the text-pathway accuracy drops from 74.9% to 56.4% after fusion in one such setting, indicating that the dominant modality can be degraded during integration. We term this strong-modality collapse and argue that it helps explain why some multimodal models fail to surpass unimodal baselines. We propose Inverted Asymmetric Fusion (IAF), which avoids forcing mutual attention across modalities. The dominant modality is preserved by passing through fusion unchanged, while weaker modalities attend to it as a contextual anchor. Before fusion, weaker modalities are strengthened using Modality-Aware Knowledge Distillation. We evaluate IAF on three benchmarks with different modality hierarchies: text-dominant datasets (MultiHuSE, UR-FUNNY) and an audio-visual-dominant dataset (MUStARD). Pathway isolation shows that IAF preserves the dominant modality's internal accuracy at its unimodal ceiling across all tested configurations, whereas symmetric fusion degrades it by up to 18.5% on MultiHuSE. IAF improves over the strongest unimodal baseline by up to 8.25%.

</details>


### [313] [A Layer Importance Metric for Quantization Accounting for the Speed-Quality Trade-off in Autoregressive Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26926)
*Artem Safronov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a composite metric combining information retention and throughput gains to intelligently identify which layers in small language models should be quantized for optimal speed-quality trade-off, requiring no actual execution for analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Small language models (sLLMs) run on devices with limited memory and computational resources. Inference is memory-bandwidth bound, but uniform quantization often hurts performance because sLLMs have limited redundancies and only a few layers are not sensitive to lower precision. Existing methods for selective quantization require expensive approximate inference.

Method: Proposes a composite metric with two orthogonal criteria: 1) Information retention measured via normalized SQNR-based coefficient, and 2) Throughput gains modeled using roofline-based latency analysis. The method profiles models (like Gemma 3 1B) to identify promising targets (Feed-Forward Network blocks and embedding matrix), estimates quality scores via simulated quantization and speed scores via roofline modeling, then combines them into a composite priority coefficient that allows tuning the speed-quality trade-off.

Result: Evaluation on several model architectures shows around 4% prediction error for accelerated speedup. The method generally allocates more resources to the most expressive layers compared to evolutionary search, specialized accelerators, or Shapley-value-based approaches that require expensive approximate inference.

Conclusion: The analytical approach makes sLLM quantization a predictable engineering task by providing a general metric that can prioritize individual blocks, projection sublayers, or transformer layers without requiring actual execution, enabling intelligent resource allocation based on the specific speed-quality trade-off needed.

Abstract: Small language models (sLLMs) are nowadays hosted on devices with limited memory and computational budget. In an autoregressive setup, inference is memory-bandwidth bound: uniform quantization is often detrimental to such models, since their architecture has limited redundancies and only a few layers are not very sensitive to lower precision. We propose a composite metric that combines two orthogonal criteria: information retention (measured in terms of a normalized SQNR-based coefficient) and throughput gains (modeled using a roofline-based latency analysis). By profiling Gemma 3 1B, we find that Feed-Forward Network blocks and the embedding matrix are the most promising targets for acceleration. For each candidate, we estimate a normalized quality score based on simulated quantization and a normalized speed score based on roofline modeling with no actual execution needed. We combine the two scores in a composite priority coefficient, allowing us to tune the trade-off between speed and quality as needed. Our metric is general and can be used to prioritize individual blocks, their projection sublayers, or transformer layers as a whole. We evaluate our approach on several model architectures, showing that our estimates have at around 4% prediction error for the accelerated speedup. We find that our method generally allocates more resources to the most expressive layers compared to evolutionary search, specialized accelerators, or Shapley-value-based approaches that require expensive approximate inference. Our analytical approach makes sLLM quantization a predictable engineering task.

</details>


### [314] [Scaling Model-Generated Distillation Data Can Make Latent Teacher Traits More Recoverable](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26958)
*Zhichen Dong,Zhixuan Liu,Yuyu Fan,Xiangtian Li,Shuyang Zhang,Chao Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Scaling generated data can amplify subtle teacher-specific traits in students even when training on off-task data, requiring careful trait-aware curation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper challenges the conventional view that scaling model-generated data always improves distillation through better coverage and reduced noise. It investigates how larger datasets can unexpectedly amplify teacher-specific traits in students, even when the training data appears off-task or benign.

Method: Uses a controlled setup inspired by subliminal learning: teachers induced to express target traits generate restricted off-task data (e.g., number-only completions). Students are trained on varying amounts of independent off-task data and evaluated in separate domains. Matched no-trait controls isolate target-specific transfer. The approach includes analysis of learned LoRA updates and tests across model families, trait types, multi-trait settings, and cross-model transfer.

Result: Larger independent datasets make the teacher's induced trait stand out more clearly in student behavior. When small-scale students already favor the target trait, scaling amplifies that behavior; when they favor alternatives, more data can shift behavior toward the intended trait. These effects appear consistently across different experimental conditions.

Conclusion: Scaling generated distillation data should be paired with trait-aware curation and evaluation, as larger datasets can unexpectedly amplify subtle teacher-specific signals even in off-task data, potentially causing unintended behavioral transfers.

Abstract: Scaling model-generated data is usually viewed as improving distillation: more examples should increase coverage, reduce noise, and produce stronger students. We show a second effect: larger datasets can make subtle teacher-specific signals easier to detect in the trained student, even when examples are off-task and never mention the trait. In a controlled setup inspired by subliminal learning, a teacher induced to express a target trait generates restricted off-task data, such as number-only completions. Students trained on different amounts of independent off-task data are evaluated in a separate domain, with matched no-trait controls isolating target-specific transfer. Our main finding is that larger independent datasets make the teacher's induced trait stand out more clearly in the student's later behavior. Other plausible traits may also strengthen with scale, but the target usually grows more. When the small-scale student already favors the target, scaling mainly amplifies that behavior; when it favors a related or salient alternative, more data can shift behavior toward the intended trait. Analyses of learned LoRA updates show a parallel trend. These effects appear across model families, trait types, multi-trait settings, and cross-model transfer. Our results suggest that scaling generated distillation data should be paired with trait-aware curation and evaluation, even when the data appears off-task or benign.

</details>


### [315] [Gromov-Monge Flow Matching for Equivariant Graph Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26961)
*Moritz Piening,Christian Wald*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Equivariant graph generative models using quotient space couplings that incorporate symmetry-aware alignments between source-target graph pairs via efficient Gromov-Wasserstein approximations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current graph generative models leverage permutation-equivariant architectures but don't account for symmetry in source-target couplings during flow matching. When comparing graph pairs up to node relabeling, the natural geometry is the graph quotient space, which hasn't been properly exploited in generative modeling.

Method: 1) Theoretical development showing quotient couplings can be lifted to aligned representatives without cost and symmetrization yields equivariant flow-matching minimizers. 2) Practical implementation using efficient Gromov-Wasserstein-type relaxations for minibatch couplings (inner node alignment) combined with optional outer assignment between graphs. 3) Compatible with standard permutation-equivariant architectures, changing only the training coupling.

Result: Substantial improvement in sample quality at small integration budgets across continuous graph and categorical molecular generation tasks. Scaled-up molecular models remain competitive under conventional many-step sampling.

Conclusion: Incorporating symmetry-aware couplings through quotient space geometry and efficient Gromov-Wasserstein approximations significantly enhances graph generative models, particularly for sampling efficiency, while maintaining compatibility with existing equivariant architectures.

Abstract: Graphs are invariant under node permutations, motivating the use of permutation-equivariant architectures in generative models. In flow matching, however, symmetry may also enter the source--target coupling: once graph pairs are compared up to node relabeling, the natural Wasserstein geometry is that of the graph quotient space. The Euclidean quotient metric of this space coincides with the Gromov--Monge distance, obtained by optimally relabeling the nodes. We develop this perspective theoretically, showing that quotient couplings can be lifted to aligned representatives without additional cost and that symmetrization yields equivariant flow-matching minimizers, including for categorical endpoint prediction. In practice, exact Gromov--Monge alignment is intractable, so we construct minibatch couplings using efficient Gromov--Wasserstein-type relaxations and lower bounds for the inner node alignment, optionally combined with an outer assignment between graphs. The resulting procedure changes only the training coupling and is compatible with standard permutation-equivariant architectures. Across continuous graph and categorical molecular generation, these structure-aware couplings substantially improve sample quality at small integration budgets, while our scaled-up molecular models remain competitive under conventional many-step sampling.

</details>


### [316] [Packora: Systematic Design for Generative Molecular Crystal Structure Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26962)
*Nayoung Kim,Kiyoung Seong,Sungsoo Ahn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Packora is a flow-based generative model for molecular crystal structure prediction that jointly predicts atomic coordinates and lattice from molecular graphs, supporting multi-component/organometallic crystals with flexible conditioning, outperforming baselines in generation and ranking tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Molecular crystal structure prediction is crucial in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and organic electronics because subtle differences in molecular conformation and packing significantly impact material properties. Current approaches need improvement in handling multi-component systems, flexible conditioning, and overall performance.

Method: Packora uses a flow-based generative model architecture that jointly predicts atomic coordinates and lattice parameters from molecular graphs. Key innovations include: cacheable pairwise reasoning, optimized training objectives and numerical solvers, conditioning dropout for flexible input handling, and balanced scaling of pairwise and single representations. It supports multi-component and organometallic crystals and can condition on molecular conformers, stereochemical labels, and space-group information.

Result: Packora outperforms baselines on both structure generation and ranking benchmarks: achieves best matched-budget coverage across all six generation benchmarks, higher experimental-form recovery rates, lower experimental-form ranks, and faster convergence in ranking tasks.

Conclusion: Packora represents a significant advance in molecular crystal structure prediction, demonstrating superior performance through its flow-based generative architecture with flexible conditioning capabilities. The systematic study of architecture, training, and scaling choices provides valuable insights for future CSP model development.

Abstract: Molecular crystal structure prediction (CSP) is important in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and organic electronics, where subtle differences in molecular conformation and packing can strongly affect material properties. We present Packora, a flow-based generative model for molecular CSP that jointly predicts atomic coordinates and the lattice from molecular graphs. Packora supports multi-component and organometallic crystals and can condition on any subset of molecular conformers, stereochemical labels, and space-group information within a single model. Inspired by the CCDC CSP blind test, we evaluate generation and ranking separately, using generation to isolate generator quality and ranking to measure end-to-end performance under a common relaxation and ranking pipeline. We also systematically study architecture, training, conditioning, inference, and scaling, identifying an effective design based on cacheable pairwise reasoning, training objective and numerical solver choices, conditioning dropout, and balanced scaling of pairwise and single representations. Packora outperforms the baselines on both structure generation and ranking benchmarks, achieving the best matched-budget coverage across all six generation benchmarks, as well as higher experimental-form recovery, lower experimental-form ranks, and faster convergence in ranking.

</details>


### [317] [Adversarial Training Without Input Gradients via Low-Rank Householder Expansions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26963)
*Tiana C. Johnson,Donsub Rim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Adversarial training without input gradient computation using low-rank Householder expansion, achieving competitive defense with significantly lower computational cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing adversarial training methods require expensive input gradient computations and iterative inner maximization. There's a need for more efficient methods that can defend against small-norm adversarial examples while reducing computational overhead.

Method: Proposes LRHE (low-rank Householder expansion) to compute adversarial examples directly from network parameters without input gradient iterations. Uses this to create an adversarial training scheme that eliminates inner maximization, requiring only additional forward evaluations and standard backward passes for weight updates.

Result: Method achieves 8.7× reduction in computational cost compared to 40-step PGD training on MNIST. Matches 3-step PGD training for ε ≤ 0.02 and 40-step training for ε ≤ 0.012, with performance dropping beyond these budgets due to expansion locality.

Conclusion: Input differentiation is not necessary for effective adversarial training against small-norm attacks. LRHE-based training provides efficient defense with minimal computational overhead, demonstrating that adversarial examples can be computed directly from network parameters.

Abstract: This work concerns adversarial training against the small-norm adversarial examples that arise from the inherent input instability of a trained deep neural network. Examples in this class are small as measured in the relative $\ell^2$-norm, and therefore lie in the neighborhood of the input on which the model acts approximately linearly, the regime in which the perturbation remains imperceptible. We first show that such examples can be computed directly from the trained network parameters, without input gradient iterations, by means of a linearization called the low-rank Householder expansion (LRHE). The expansion describes the composed affine map rather than any individual layer, and the directions it identifies are read from the activation pattern already available in the forward pass. We then propose a simple adversarial training scheme built on this construction. No differentiation with respect to the input is performed at any point: training requires only additional forward evaluations, with weight parameters updated by the standard backward pass, and the inner maximization of the usual min-max formulation is eliminated entirely. That such a regularizer exists is our main finding: the methods that dispense with the inner search all obtain their local geometry by differentiating with respect to the input, and we show this is not necessary. The regularizer costs the equivalent of $2.8$ PGD steps per epoch, an $8.7\times$ reduction relative to 40-step adversarial training on MNIST and below the cost of 3-step training. The resulting models match three-step PGD adversarial training for relative $\ell^2$ budgets $\varepsilon \le 0.02$ and 40-step training for $\varepsilon \le 0.012$, falling away beyond, consistent with the locality of the expansion.

</details>


### [318] [Graph-Based Pseudo-multimodal Contrastive Learning for 12-Lead ECG Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26964)
*Mengyu Wang,Kozo Okada,Takafumi Goto,Natsuko Jinba,Hiroki Yamaya,Kiyoshi Hibi,Tomoki Hamagami*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Graph-CMMC: A graph-based pseudo-multimodal contrastive learning framework that transforms 12-lead ECG signals into GADF images to learn inter-lead dependencies and robust representations for coronary artery disease diagnosis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most existing ECG analysis methods focus on single-lead signals or treat leads independently, using 1D time-series processing that fails to capture inter-lead dependencies and global waveform patterns essential for clinical diagnosis of coronary artery disease.

Method: Proposes Graph-CMMC framework that transforms ECG waveforms into Gramian Angular Difference Field (GADF) images to create complementary representations. Uses all 12 leads with a graph-based relational module to model inter-lead dependency and align waveform/GADF representations via self-supervised contrastive learning.

Result: Achieves competitive performance on multi-label coronary artery occlusion classification compared to supervised learning methods, demonstrating effectiveness of GADF as complementary representation and graph-based modeling of inter-lead dependencies.

Conclusion: The proposed Graph-CMMC framework successfully addresses limitations of existing ECG analysis methods by incorporating inter-lead dependencies through graph-based modeling and pseudo-multimodal contrastive learning with GADF representations, enabling more robust 12-lead ECG analysis for clinical applications.

Abstract: 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is a standard, non-invasive examination widely used for diagnosing coronary artery disease, where clinical interpretation relies on comparing waveform patterns across multiple leads. However, most existing ECG analysis methods focus on single-lead signals or treat each lead independently, and typically process ECG signals as one-dimensional time-series data using CNNs or RNNs. While effective in modeling local waveform changes, such approaches have difficulty capturing inter-lead dependency and global waveform patterns essential for clinical diagnosis.
  To address this limitation, we propose a graph-based pseudo-multimodal contrastive learning framework called Graph-CMMC. ECG waveforms are transformed into Gramian Angular Difference Field (GADF) images to construct complementary representations of the same cardiac activity, enabling a pseudo-multimodal learning setting. Using all 12 leads, Graph-CMMC aligns waveform and GADF representations in a self-supervised manner, while a graph-based relational module is employed to model inter-lead dependency and enforce structural consistency across leads during contrastive learning.
  Experimental results on a multi-label coronary artery occlusion classification task demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance compared to supervised learning methods. These results further suggest the effectiveness of using GADF as a complementary representation and incorporating explicit graph-based modeling of inter-lead dependency for learning robust 12-lead ECG representations.

</details>


### [319] [ClusterAttention: A training-free speedup of bidirectional attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26965)
*Kasper Nordenram,Amelie Dittmann*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ClusterAttention is a training-free method that speeds up bidirectional attention layers using fast recursive clustering that adapts to key/query geometry, allowing block-sparse attention to run at the same latency as dense attention while maintaining high accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing sparse attention methods either rely on input structure (language order, spatial proximity) or use slow clustering processes amortized over multiple forward passes, limiting their applicability to unstructured input and single forward pass scenarios.

Method: Uses fast recursive clustering that adapts to the geometry of keys and queries in each attention head, producing clusters of arbitrary size. Sets clusters to fixed power-of-two sizes to enable block-sparse attention to run at the same latency as dense attention on GPUs. Includes error compensation through centroids for excluded clusters.

Result: On tabular data, speeds up TabPFN-3 by 2-6x while retaining ≥99% accuracy. For video generation with Wan 2.1-14B T2V, achieves 1.8x speedup (vs 1.4x for SVOO) and output closer to dense attention. First training-free method successfully applicable to unstructured input with single forward pass.

Conclusion: ClusterAttention provides an effective training-free solution for speeding up bidirectional attention across diverse domains (tabular data, video generation) while maintaining accuracy, overcoming limitations of existing sparse attention methods that rely on input structure or multi-pass clustering.

Abstract: This paper introduces ClusterAttention, a general training-free speedup of bidirectional attention layers. Existing sparse attention methods either rely on structure in the input, such as order in language or spatial proximity in images, or use slow clustering processes amortized over several forward passes. ClusterAttention instead uses a fast recursive clustering method that adapts to the geometry of the keys and queries in each attention head to produce useful clusters. This method allows setting the size of the clusters arbitrarily. We utilize this by setting all clusters to be a fixed size that is a power of two, allowing the block-sparse attention to run at the same latency per query-key interaction as dense attention on GPUs. We also derive an expression for the output error in sparse attention, that explains the counterintuitive experimental finding that tight clusters can lead to larger errors than random clusters. We then derive the error when excluded clusters are compensated through their centroids, and show that this error shrinks with tighter clusters. We integrate this compensation into the method.
  On large-scale tabular data ClusterAttention speeds up TabPFN-3 arXiv:2605.13986 by two to six times, while retaining at least 99% of the dense accuracy. To our knowledge, it is the first training-free method that can be successfully applied in the setting of unstructured input and a single forward pass. For video generation with Wan 2.1-14B T2V arXiv:2503.20314 , ClusterAttention achieves output closer to dense attention and a larger speedup (1.8x versus 1.4x) compared to SVOO arXiv:2603.18636 , a leading method developed specifically for this domain, both run without offline calibration.

</details>


### [320] [TEMPLAR Wales: A georeferenced environmental and toponymic dataset of Welsh settlements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26970)
*Oktay Karakuş,Can Eyupoglu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TEMPLAR Wales is a georeferenced environmental-toponymy dataset linking 3,757 Welsh settlements to deterministic lexical detections and environmental attributes, providing a reusable foundation for toponymy and landscape research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Place names contain historical landscape information, but quantitative reuse requires explicit separation between mapped places, lexical annotations, and environmental measurements. Existing resources often lack this explicit separation, making systematic analysis difficult.

Method: Created a reproducible settlement frame with deterministic lexical screening using a frozen registry of 24 Welsh place-name elements, generating 1,350 lexical detections across 1,294 settlements. Linked settlements to environmental attributes including river/coastal proximity, elevation, terrain context, land cover, and woody cover at multiple spatial scales, with parallel terrain measurements from independent elevation products.

Result: The TEMPLAR Wales dataset contains 3,757 settlement records with 1,350 lexical detections, structured as four relational tables with data dictionary, source-provenance register, and licensing metadata. Technical validation confirms relational integrity, deterministic lexical reconstruction, strong agreement between terrain sources, and reproducible reconstruction.

Conclusion: TEMPLAR Wales provides a reusable foundation for toponymy, linguistic geography, historical/environmental landscape studies, GIS and spatial data analysis, while maintaining clear boundaries between computational lexical detections and verified etymologies, and between contemporary environmental measurements and historical landscape reconstructions.

Abstract: Place names provide persistent records of how landscapes have been described and organised, but their quantitative reuse requires explicit separation between mapped places, lexical annotations and environmental measurements. TEMPLAR Wales is a georeferenced environmental-toponymy dataset comprising 3,757 settlement records across Wales. The resource links a reproducible settlement frame to deterministic lexical screening and settlement-level environmental attributes through stable identifiers. It contains 1,350 lexical detections across 1,294 settlements, generated from a frozen registry of 24 Welsh place-name elements, while retaining exact- and prefix-token matches and their provenance separately. Environmental attributes describe river and coastal proximity, elevation and local terrain context at multiple spatial scales, land cover and neighbourhood woody cover, with parallel terrain measurements derived from independent elevation products. The dataset is distributed as four relational tables accompanied by a field-level data dictionary, source-provenance register and licensing metadata. Technical validation confirms relational integrity, deterministic lexical reconstruction, documented environmental coverage, strong agreement between independent terrain sources and reproducible reconstruction of the frozen release. TEMPLAR Wales provides a reusable foundation for research in toponymy, linguistic geography, historical and environmental landscape studies, GIS and spatial data analysis without treating computational lexical detections as verified etymologies or contemporary environmental measurements as historical landscape reconstructions.

</details>


### [321] [Terrain signatures in Welsh settlement names](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26978)
*Oktay Karakuş,Can Eyupoglu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Welsh settlement names with terrain-related elements (like bryn/mynydd for high terrain vs cwm/pant for low terrain) contain measurable environmental information about present-day elevation differences, with high-terrain names located about 24 meters higher than low-terrain names in their local surroundings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether landscape names retain measurable environmental information beyond broad geographic structure, specifically examining whether Welsh settlement names with terrain-related elements actually correspond to measurable elevation differences in the present-day landscape.

Method: Analyzed 3,757 Welsh settlements using a frozen, source-audited 24-element lexical framework with preregistered outcome-specific models and geographically structured validation. Compared 101 settlements with high-terrain elements (bryn/mynydd) against 139 settlements with low-terrain elements (cwm/pant) using multiple spatial scales (1-, 2-, and 5-km neighborhood definitions). Used geographically held-out validation with spatial blocking (10-, 25-, and 50-km blocks).

Result: High-terrain names occupied locations 24.4 m higher relative to their 2-km surroundings (95% CI: 10.8-38.1 m; statistically significant). The association was consistent across different neighborhood definitions and reproduced with independent elevation data. Adding terrain-name polarity to spatial models reduced geographically held-out mean squared error by 4.63-7.30% across different spatial blocking schemes. River-related names showed weaker evidence, while woodland model was non-estimable.

Conclusion: Selected Welsh settlement-name categories retain measurable information about present-day terrain within Wales, but this doesn't establish individual etymology, causal naming, historical environmental memory, or transferability to other naming systems. Limitations include residual spatial structure, unresolved name language, and absence of independent external replication.

Abstract: Landscapes are named, but whether names retain measurable environmental information beyond broad geographic structure is rarely tested. We analysed 3,757 Welsh settlements using a frozen, source-audited 24-element lexical framework, preregistered outcome-specific models and geographically structured validation. The central comparison contrasted 101 settlements carrying high-terrain elements (\textit{bryn} or \textit{mynydd}) with 139 carrying low-terrain elements (\textit{cwm} or \textit{pant}). High-terrain names occupied locations 24.4 m higher relative to their 2-km surroundings (95\% CI, 10.8--38.1 m; Holm-adjusted $p$ = 0.00137). The association remained positive across prespecified 1-, 2- and 5-km neighbourhood definitions and was reproduced using an independently produced elevation source (24.1 m; 95\% CI, 10.6--37.6 m). Adding terrain-name polarity to a non-lexical spatial and settlement baseline reduced geographically held-out mean squared error by 4.63\%, 6.22\% and 7.30\% under 10-, 25- and 50-km spatial blocking, respectively, although improvement varied among held-out regions. River-related names provided weaker, directionally consistent evidence, while the preregistered woodland model was non-estimable. Residual spatial structure, unresolved name language and the absence of independent external replication limit interpretation. Selected Welsh settlement-name categories therefore retain measurable information about present-day terrain within Wales, without establishing individual etymology, causal naming, historical environmental memory or transferability to other naming systems.

</details>


### [322] [Decentralized Multitask Learning over Learned Task Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26989)
*Zirui Wan,Stefan Vlaski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Decentralized two-phase multitask learning that first estimates task relationships from noisy gradients, then uses learned graph for cooperative diffusion learning without requiring prior knowledge of task dependencies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph-regularized multitask learning assumes known task relationships, but practical decentralized settings require learning inter-task dependencies from distributed data without prior structural knowledge.

Method: Two-phase approach: 1) Estimate generalized graph Laplacian from noisy non-cooperative stochastic gradient iterates using decentralized maximum likelihood estimator derived from Gaussian Markov random field prior; 2) Use learned graph for cooperative multitask diffusion learning.

Result: Theoretical analysis quantifies Laplacian estimation error and its propagation to steady-state performance, introduces topology sensitivity index for network heterogeneity. Simulations show learned-graph cooperation significantly outperforms non-cooperative learning and approaches true-graph baseline with small estimation stepsize.

Conclusion: Decentralized two-phase approach effectively learns task relationships from distributed data and enables cooperative learning that achieves performance close to known-structure baselines, addressing practical limitations of existing methods.

Abstract: This paper investigates decentralized multitask learning over networks when the underlying task relationships are unknown. While existing graph-regularized multitask frameworks typically assume a known structure, practical settings often require learning inter-task dependencies directly from distributed data. We propose a decentralized two-phase strategy that first estimates a generalized graph Laplacian from noisy non-cooperative stochastic gradient iterates, and subsequently exploits the learned graph to enable cooperative multitask diffusion learning. This framework is motivated by a Gaussian Markov random field prior, which gives rise to a decentralized maximum likelihood estimator for the graph Laplacian. The analysis quantifies the Laplacian estimation error and its propagation to the steady-state performance of the multitask diffusion recursion, and introduces a topology sensitivity index to capture the effect of network heterogeneity. Simulation results corroborate the theoretical findings and demonstrate that cooperation enabled by the learned task graph significantly improves performance over non-cooperative learning, while approaching the true-graph baseline when the estimation stepsize is sufficiently small.

</details>


### [323] [Benchmarking_Fast_Domain_Adaptation_for_Unsupervised_Speech_Units](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26992)
*Robin San Roman,Manel Khentout,Tu Anh Nguyen,Paul Michel,Yossi Adi,Emmanuel Dupoux*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces ABX-Accent, a benchmark for evaluating speech representation learning on accented English, and demonstrates that adaptive domain normalization of pretrained CPC models yields 23.6% relative improvement on accented speech.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current speech representation learning methods lack evaluation on out-of-domain speech and few-shot adaptation to new domains, particularly for accented speech where there's a long tail of accents diverging from standard ones.

Method: 1) Created ABX-Accent benchmark using AESRC dataset with 10 English accents, each with small unlabelled training sets and adapted ABX evaluation metrics. 2) Developed baseline model using adaptive domain normalization to fine-tune pretrained Contrastive Predictive Coding (CPC) models on accents. 3) First validated method on LibriSpeech using male/female split, then applied to ABX-Accent benchmark.

Result: The proposed adaptive domain normalization method achieved a relative improvement of 23.6% on average across-speaker ABX scores compared to non-adapted models when applied to the ABX-Accent benchmark.

Conclusion: Adaptive domain normalization effectively improves speech representation learning for accented speech in few-shot scenarios, and the ABX-Accent benchmark provides a valuable tool for evaluating such methods on diverse English accents.

Abstract: Representation learning has attracted great atten- tion and managed to reach good performances as a pretraining method for downstream tasks or as a first step towards unsu- pervised speech modeling. Yet, little is known about how such methods deal with out-of-domain speech and how could they be adapted in a few shot to new domains. This is important especially for accented speech where one observes a long tail of accents that diverge from the standard ones. We introduce ABX- Accent, a benchmark based on the AESRC dataset that features 10 different accents of English. It includes a small (< 10 hours) unlabelled training set in each of the accents and adaptations of the Zero Resources Challenge ABX evaluation metrics to each of the accents. We illustrate this benchmark with a baseline model that uses adaptive domain normalization to fine tune a pretrained Contrastive Predictive Coding model on the accents. This method is first developed on LibriSpeech using a male/female split. When applied to the new benchmark, the proposed method yields a relative improvement of 23.6% on across-speaker ABX scores on average compared to non adapted models. The data and metrics will be open sourced upon paper acceptance

</details>


### [324] [Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27032)
*Ivan Kruzhilov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DPO's β parameter has hidden dual roles that cause optimization issues, and a centered-softplus reformulation solves these problems by decoupling the noise scale from learning rate effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper identifies problems with the standard DPO objective where the β parameter has two entangled roles: controlling inverse preference-noise scale and rescaling optimization dynamics. This entanglement causes issues like non-monotonic policy deviation with β, incomparable loss values across β settings, increased hyperparameter sensitivity, and complicated learning-rate scheduling.

Method: The authors propose a centered-softplus reformulation of DPO that maintains argmin-equivalence for β>0 while making the inverse preference-noise scale and learning-rate effects explicit and independently tunable. This normalized version also admits a continuous β→0 endpoint that reduces to a linear preference-margin objective.

Result: The analysis reveals that at fixed learning rates, policy deviation is non-monotonic in β: vanishing in a "dead zone" at small β, peaking at intermediate values, then decreasing again for larger β. Also, standard DPO loss values aren't comparable across β settings - runs with similar loss curves can have several-fold differences in KL divergence from reference models.

Conclusion: The centered-softplus reformulation successfully decouples the problematic dual roles of β in standard DPO, making optimization dynamics clearer, hyperparameters more robust, and providing a continuous endpoint at β→0 for better interpretability and control.

Abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a widely used objective for aligning language models from preference data, with the coefficient $β$ commonly interpreted as controlling the KL constraint to a reference policy. We show that $β$ entangles two distinct roles: it governs the effective inverse preference-noise scale and simultaneously rescales the optimization dynamics, coupling this scale with the effective step size. As a consequence, at a fixed learning rate the achieved policy deviation is non-monotone in $β$: it vanishes in a dead zone at small $β$, reaches a peak at an intermediate value, and decreases again for larger $β$. Moreover, standard DPO loss values are not comparable across $β$: runs with nearly identical loss curves can differ several-fold in KL divergence from the reference model. This entanglement obscures the role of $β$, increases sensitivity to hyperparameter choices, and complicates learning-rate scheduling. We propose a centered-softplus reformulation that is argmin-equivalent to DPO for $β>0$, while making the inverse preference-noise-scale and learning-rate effects explicit and independently tunable. The normalized centered-softplus objective also admits a continuous $β\to0$ endpoint that reduces to a linear preference-margin objective.
