</details>


### [325] [Performance Foundations of Parallel & Distributed Reasoning Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27046)
*Maciej Besta,Leonard Schmidt,Lara Nonino,Robert Gerstenberger,Pierre Pang,Patrik Okanovic,Ales Kubicek,Tiancheng Chen,Baraq Lipshitz,Torsten Hoefler*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper systematizes the RL-for-LLM paradigm for reasoning language models, provides compute-centric analysis of post-training algorithms, develops a taxonomy of parallelism strategies for multi-model training, and offers practical guidelines for building scalable and cost-effective RLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL-for-LLM post-training substantially improves reasoning capabilities but has massive computational requirements (millions of GPU-hours) and complex multi-model pipelines that stress modern hardware beyond classical LLM training, making RLM training a significant parallel/distributed systems challenge.

Method: 1) Systematizing RL-for-LLM paradigm with compute-centric analysis of PPO, GRPO and variants; 2) Developing taxonomy of intra- and inter-model parallelism strategies covering traditional techniques and novel optimizations for multi-model RLM training; 3) Using work-depth model of parallel computing for rigorous analysis; 4) Analyzing existing RLM frameworks.

Result: Provides comprehensive taxonomy of parallelism strategies, practical guidelines for scalable RLM training, and outlines open research directions. The work-depth model offers rigorous and portable analysis framework.

Conclusion: To develop high-performance, scalable, and cost-effective Reasoning Language Models, researchers need systematic approaches to parallel/distributed systems challenges, combining algorithmic analysis with novel parallelism strategies and practical implementation guidelines.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) and other RL-style post-training paradigms have been used for aligning large language models (LLMs) with reasoning standards. The resulting recent Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) such as DeepSeek-R1, o3, and Kimi k1.5 show that such RL-style post-training ("RL-for-LLMs") can substantially improve chain-of-thought reasoning, long-horizon planning, and self-correction. However, the computational footprint of these systems is massive: state-of-the-art RLM training requires millions of GPU-hours and tightly coupled multi-model pipelines that stress modern hardware far beyond classical supervised LLM training. This makes RLM training as much a parallel and distributed systems problem as an algorithmic one. In this work, to facilitate developing RLMs that are simultaneously high-performance, scalable, and cost-effective, we first systematize the RL-for-LLM paradigm and provide a compute-centric analysis of prominent post-training algorithmic frameworks: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), as well as their variants. Second, we develop a taxonomy of intra- and inter-model parallelism strategies for RL-for-LLMs, covering both traditional techniques (data, tensor, pipeline, sequence, context, and expert parallelism) as well as novel forms of parallelism and optimization techniques for multi-model RLM training, for example disaggregated placement, stage fusion, hybrid parallelism, and asynchronous execution. We harness the work-depth model of parallel computing to make our taxonomy and its insights rigorous and portable. Finally, we analyze existing RLM frameworks and we distill practical guidelines and outline open research directions for building scalable, fast, and cost-effective RLMs.

</details>


### [326] [Soft Active Electromyography Interface for Machine Learning-Enabled Silent Speech Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27048)
*Yuta Kurotaki,Shusuke Yamakoshi,Reitaro Yoshida,Yutaka Isoda,Tamami Takano,Yuji Isano,Yusuke Miyake,Kentaro Kuribayashi,Hiroki Ota*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A soft, wearable EMG interface on the fingertip enables silent speech recognition by detecting muscle signals near lips when needed, achieving high accuracy with machine learning and validating real-time drone control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current silent speech recognition systems have limitations: they require constant facial attachment (uncomfortable), raise privacy concerns, and suffer from unstable signal acquisition. There's a need for more practical, secure, and user-friendly alternatives to conventional voice recognition, especially in noisy or privacy-sensitive environments.

Method: Developed a soft, active electromyography (EMG) interface worn on the hand with a fingertip electrode positioned near lips to acquire EMG signals only when needed. The device integrates liquid metal interconnects, transparent flexible printed circuit electrodes, and elastomer encapsulation for mechanical stability during finger motion. Used a deep neural network trained on these stable signals for word-level classification.

Result: Achieved mean accuracy of 97.2 ± 1.3% across three subjects in classifying a 30-word vocabulary, demonstrating robust linguistic discrimination. Successfully validated real-time drone control, showing practicality in noisy and privacy-sensitive environments where conventional voice recognition fails.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that soft, wearable EMG systems can serve as secure and intuitive human-machine interfaces, overcoming limitations of traditional silent speech recognition approaches and enabling applications in challenging environments.

Abstract: Silent speech recognition (SSR) provides an alternative communication pathway in the absence of audible speech. However, conventional approaches are limited by the need for constant facial attachment, privacy concerns, and unstable signal acquisition. Here, we propose a soft, active electromyography (EMG) interface that enables word-level SSR using machine learning. Worn on the hand, the device uses a fingertip electrode that can be positioned near the lips to acquire EMG signals only when needed. The interface integrates liquid metal (LM) interconnects, transparent flexible printed circuit (FPC) electrodes, and elastomer encapsulation to ensure high mechanical stability during finger motion. A deep neural network trained on these stable signals achieved a mean accuracy of 97.2 $\pm$ 1.3% across three subjects in classifying a 30-word vocabulary, demonstrating robust linguistic discrimination. Furthermore, real-time drone control validates the practicality of this approach in noisy and privacy-sensitive environments where conventional voice recognition fails. This study highlights the potential of soft, wearable EMG systems as secure and intuitive human-machine interfaces.

</details>


### [327] [Unifying Detection and Adaptation in Task-Free Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27070)
*Dezheng Han,Anbang Zhang,Zhihao Zhu,Shuaishuai Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FiUni: A Fisher-guided unified framework for batch-level task detection and parameter-efficient continual adaptation in LLMs without requiring explicit task boundaries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing continual learning methods for LLMs rely on explicit task boundaries during training, limiting applicability to realistic task-free scenarios where tasks arrive without clear boundaries.

Method: Leverages Fisher information matrix (FIM) of pre-trained models, specifically the orthogonality among principal subspaces of K-FAC approximation, to detect task similarity. Uses FIM-derived frozen subspaces to guide low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and matches Fisher principal subspaces of incoming batches with historical ones to dynamically decide whether to reuse, expand, or create new subspaces.

Result: FiUni effectively infers latent batch-level task affiliations and achieves competitive performance against advanced task-aware CL methods with fewer trainable parameters.

Conclusion: The proposed framework successfully addresses catastrophic forgetting in task-free continual learning scenarios by dynamically balancing knowledge sharing and task isolation through Fisher information-guided adaptation.

Abstract: To mitigate catastrophic forgetting in downstream continual learning (CL) for large language models (LLMs), existing methods typically constrain parameter updates or introduce task-specific adaptation modules. However, these methods often rely on explicit task boundaries during training, limiting their applicability to realistic task-free scenarios. In this paper, we propose a \textbf{Fi}sher-guided \textbf{uni}fied (\textbf{FiUni}) framework for batch-level task detection and parameter-efficient continual adaptation. FiUni is motivated by a key observation about the Fisher information matrix (FIM) of pre-trained models: the orthogonality among the principal subspaces of its Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (K-FAC) approximation, estimated from a small number of downstream task samples, can reflect the similarity between different tasks. Based on this observation, FiUni constructs FIM-derived frozen subspaces to guide low-rank adaptation (LoRA), while matching the Fisher principal subspace of each incoming batch window with historical subspaces. This enables FiUni to adaptively determine whether to reuse existing knowledge, expand a related subspace, or create a new subspace, dynamically balancing knowledge sharing and task isolation. Experiments show that FiUni can effectively infer latent batch-level task affiliations and achieve competitive performance against advanced task-aware CL methods with fewer trainable parameters.

</details>


### [328] [Emotional Preferences as Goal-Priority Regulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27072)
*Shiqi Liu,Yihua Tan,Hu Fu,Guanyu Qi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Emotional preferences can autonomously regulate competing objective priorities through reinforcement learning, with an inner controller providing preference-conditioned behaviors and an outer generator learning state-dependent preferences from high-level goals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In decision-making for agents, determining relative priorities of competing lower-level objectives typically requires external specification. However, emotional preferences that emerge autonomously from higher-level goals could provide adaptive regulation under changing environments and internal states, inspired by goal-directed theory of emotion.

Method: Proposes a computational framework with multi-objective reinforcement learning inner controller and outer preference generator. The inner controller learns preference-conditioned behaviors, while the outer generator learns state-dependent objective preferences through RL on high-level goals. The approach characterizes policy space and provides optimality gap analysis.

Result: Experiments in multi-objective exploration environments show learned preference functions exhibit contextual priority switching, graded trade-offs, and temporal persistence. The approach outperforms fixed-preference and handcrafted-preference strategies, with theoretical analysis showing optimality gap vanishes when optimal policy is representable.

Conclusion: Emotional preferences can be computationally realized as state-dependent regulation of goal priorities that emerges through optimization, providing adaptive decision-making superior to prespecified preferences, with theoretical guarantees on performance when behavioral repertoire is sufficient.

Abstract: A core question in decision-making for agents is whether the relative priorities of competing lower-level objectives can be determined by emotional preferences autonomously generated by higher-level goals, rather than being externally prespecified. Under changing external environments and evolving internal states, emotions play an important functional role in regulating the relative priorities of competing goals. Inspired by the goal-directed theory of emotion, this paper studies how such preference regulation can be computationally realized through reinforcement learning. We first propose a conception of emergent emotional preference: a high-level goal autonomously induces state-dependent preferences over competing lower-level objectives. This conception is built upon a framework consisting of a multi-objective reinforcement learning inner controller and an outer preference generator. The inner controller provides a repertoire of preference-conditioned goal-directed behaviors, while the outer preference generator learns a mapping from the current state to objective preferences through reinforcement learning on a high-level goal. We operationalize emotional preference as a state-dependent regulation of relative goal priorities that emerges through optimization. Furthermore, we characterize the policy space induced by preference regulation and derive an upper bound on the optimality gap in terms of the representation error of the inner behavioral repertoire. We show that the gap vanishes when the optimal policy can be represented by the available preference-conditioned policies. Experiments in self-constructed multi-objective exploration environments show that the learned preference function exhibits contextual priority switching, graded trade-offs, and temporal persistence, and outperforms the evaluated fixed-preference and handcrafted-preference strategies.

</details>


### [329] [Tabular Deep Learning for Algorithmic Trading: Cross-Regime Bayesian Optimisation for Equity Signal Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27076)
*Joshua Le Grice*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Regime-robust hyperparameter optimization for equity prediction models enables consistent out-of-sample performance across different market conditions, with a Hybrid XGBoost+TabNet ensemble achieving 51.26% annual returns and statistical alpha.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Algorithmic trading represents a $20B+ market where marginal gains in signal robustness yield significant economic returns. Existing equity prediction models fail to explicitly target regime robustness during hyperparameter selection, limiting their effectiveness across different market conditions.

Method: Trained five model classes on 300 large-cap US stocks over 11 years using daily data. Implemented Bayesian optimization targeting trading performance across three statistically different market regimes. Developed a Hybrid ensemble combining XGBoost and TabNet via rank aggregation.

Result: Regime-robust hyperparameter selection showed strong out-of-sample generalization with signal precision above random baseline across all test quarters. The Hybrid ensemble achieved 51.26% annualized return, 2.44 Sharpe ratio, and statistically significant CAPM alpha of 0.423 (p=0.011) with near-zero beta. Alternative data had secondary importance after technical/fundamental features and contributed more to short positions.

Conclusion: Regime-aware hyperparameter optimization is crucial for robust equity prediction models. Gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost) outperform individual deep learning architectures, but combining them with TabNet via rank aggregation creates superior performance. The approach generates market-neutral alpha through stock selection rather than market exposure.

Abstract: Algorithmic trading now represents a market exceeding $20 billion, where even marginal gains in signal robustness can translate into economically significant returns. Existing evaluations of equity prediction models do not explicitly target regime robustness during hyperparameter selection. Five model classes are trained on daily observations from approximately 300 large-cap US equities over eleven years, with Bayesian optimisation configured to target trading performance across three statistically different market regimes. Regime-robust hyperparameter selection is associated with out-of-sample generalisation, as signal precision remains above the random baseline across all four quarters of the test period, and portfolio performance slowly degrades under simulated input noise before collapsing beyond a defined threshold. No individual tabular deep learning architecture outperforms gradient-boosted trees, but combining XGBoost and TabNet using rank aggregation produces a Hybrid ensemble with an annualised return of 51.26%, a Sharpe ratio of 2.44, and a statistically significant CAPM alpha of 0.423 (p = 0.011). A near-zero beta indicates this outperformance is driven by stock selection, not market exposure. Alternative data plays a secondary role once technical and fundamental features are accounted for, as well as contributing more strongly on the short side than the long, and varies by model class. An interactive application makes these results explorable in real time, with live data integration the remaining step toward practical deployment.

</details>


### [330] [Cone Extended Rayleigh Quotients for Directed Graph Learning: Minimax Spectral Certificates, Sensitivity, and Adaptive Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27122)
*Yavdat Sh. Il'yasov,Nur F. Valeev*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A framework for spectral analysis and control of directed graph learning operators using two-sided cone Rayleigh quotients, enabling spectral certification, sensitivity analysis, and trainable graph interventions without symmetry or cone-preservation assumptions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Directed graph learning produces nonsymmetric propagation operators with distinct right/left spectral structures, requiring analysis tools that don't rely on symmetry, nonnegativity, or cone preservation assumptions typical in undirected graph spectral analysis.

Method: Two-sided cone Rayleigh framework for generalized pencils [Bθ-λG] with computable cone bounds, smooth soft-min/max surrogates preserving rigorous one-sided bounds, and first-order optimal graph interventions using right-left sensitivity analysis Dλ_C(B)[H]=v_C^T H u_C.

Result: Demonstrates applicability beyond cone-preserving operators, reveals transitions from interior eigenpairs to boundary complementary quasi-pairs under signed perturbations, shows symmetrization can remove direction-based predictive information, and achieves 21.5% spectral level reduction with only 0.5% edge-weight budget on Cora citation network.

Conclusion: The learning-oriented spectral certification framework enables effective analysis and control of directed graph learning operators, providing practical tools for spectral sensitivity analysis, trainable graph interventions, and adaptive spectral control without restrictive structural assumptions.

Abstract: Directed graph learning naturally leads to trainable nonsymmetric propagation operators with distinct right and left spectral structures. Building on the two-sided cone Rayleigh framework for generalized pencils \[ B_θ-λG, \] we develop a learning-oriented methodology for spectral certification, sensitivity analysis, and control without requiring symmetry, nonnegativity, or cone preservation. In the positive-orthant setting, computable lower and upper cone bounds provide an a posteriori enclosure of a distinguished cone level, while smooth soft-min/max surrogates preserve rigorous one-sided bounds with explicit approximation errors and remain differentiable with respect to the trainable parameters.
  For a simple interior level, the right and left modes satisfy \[ Dλ_C(B)[H]=v_C^T H u_C, \] yielding first-order optimal graph-supported interventions under prescribed perturbation budgets and motivating adaptive spectral control. Numerical experiments demonstrate the applicability of the approach beyond cone-preserving operators and in directed learning settings. Signed nonsymmetric perturbations reveal a transition from interior eigenpairs to boundary complementary quasi-pairs, including non-spectral cone levels, while controlled experiments show that symmetrization can remove predictive information carried solely by edge direction.
  On the directed Cora citation network, adaptive recomputation of the right--left sensitivity reduces the distinguished spectral level by approximately $21.5\%$ under a cumulative edge-weight reduction budget of $0.5\%$, with no observed change in test accuracy for the trained model and data split considered.

</details>


### [331] [TRACE-CRC: Trajectory-Adaptive Conformal Risk Control for Multi-Step Channel State Information Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27124)
*Kiarash Rezaei,Mehdi Sattari,Javad Aliakbari,Tommy Svensson,Paolo Monti,Carlos Natalino*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TRACE-CRC is a trajectory-aware uncertainty quantification method for multi-step CSI prediction that controls the risk of having any uncovered future frame using conformal risk control with trajectory-adaptive calibration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern deep learning-based CSI predictors only provide point predictions without calibrated uncertainty estimates, which is problematic for multi-step CSI prediction where downstream decisions like beamforming or scheduling may fail if any part of the predicted trajectory is unreliable.

Method: TRACE-CRC constructs Frobenius-norm uncertainty balls around predicted CSI matrices and controls the risk that at least one future frame is uncovered. It combines future-step-dependent error profiling, trajectory difficulty stratification, and learn-then-test (LTT) risk control instead of calibrating each future step independently.

Result: TRACE-CRC achieves reliable trajectory-level coverage with substantially smaller uncertainty balls than conservative multi-step corrections, while avoiding the trajectory undercoverage of compact stepwise and adaptive conformal baselines.

Conclusion: TRACE-CRC provides an effective method for trajectory-aware uncertainty quantification in multi-step CSI prediction, addressing the limitations of existing approaches and enabling more reliable downstream decisions in wireless communication systems.

Abstract: Reliable prediction of time-varying channel state information (CSI) is essential for efficient wireless communication. Each CSI frame is a matrix-valued representation of the wireless channel response, and a sequence of CSI frames forms a temporal channel trajectory. Modern deep learning-based CSI predictors, however, often provide only point predictions and lack calibrated uncertainty estimates. This limitation is particularly problematic in multi-step CSI prediction, where the target is a sequence of future CSI matrices, and downstream decisions such as beamforming or scheduling may fail if any part of the predicted trajectory is unreliable. We propose trajectory-adaptive calibration and error profiling with conformal risk control (TRACE-CRC), a method for trajectory-aware uncertainty quantification in multi-step CSI prediction. TRACE-CRC constructs Frobenius-norm uncertainty balls around predicted CSI matrices and controls the risk that at least one future frame is uncovered. Instead of calibrating each future step independently, TRACE-CRC combines future-step-dependent error profiling, trajectory difficulty stratification, and learn-then-test (LTT) risk control. Empirically, TRACE-CRC achieves reliable trajectory-level coverage with substantially smaller uncertainty balls than conservative multi-step corrections, while avoiding the trajectory undercoverage of compact stepwise and adaptive conformal baselines.

</details>


### [332] [Ultra Low-Power, Lightweight, Probabilistic RSS-Based Path Reconstruction: A System for Landscape-Scale Bee Tracking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27152)
*Christopher J. Noroozi,Joseph L. Woodgate,Michael Mangan,Michael T. Smith*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel RSS-based localization method using rotating high-gain transmitters and probabilistic modeling achieves 15m accuracy for ultra-lightweight (38mg) receivers while consuming less than 180uW, enabling tracking of flying insects like bumblebees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a need for low-power localization systems for small, power-constrained devices (like in movement ecology, IoT, robotics) that cannot use GNSS. Existing RSS-based methods have limitations in range and require too many power-intensive measurements for accurate AoA inference.

Method: Uses minimal RSS measurements from simple rotating high-gain transmitters (300m range) with probabilistic modeling to infer AoA. The receiver's movement path is modeled using a Gaussian process and reconstructed using doubly stochastic variational inference.

Result: Achieves approximately 15m accuracy tracking of 38mg receivers (including power source) over scalable landscape range while consuming less than 180uW. Accuracy improves to about 10m with less than 600uW by taking more RSS measurements. Successfully demonstrated by tracking Bombus terrestris (bumblebee) nest return flights.

Conclusion: This novel RSS-based localization method provides a practical solution for low-power tracking of ultra-lightweight moving devices, with promising applications in behavioral studies of flying insect species and other fields requiring small, power-efficient localization systems.

Abstract: Applications in fields such as movement ecology, Internet of Things or robotics share the need for systems that localize devices that are too small and power constrained to implement GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite Systems). Alternative low-power localization methods often rely on only measurements of RSS (Received Signal Strength) to infer the AoA (Angle of Arrival) of a transmitted radio frequency signal, but are limited by range and the power demand of the large number of RSS measurements required to infer an accurate AoA. In this paper we address these issues with a novel RSS-based method for tracking ultra lightweight and low-power moving receivers across a complex landscape, achieved by using a minimal number of RSS measurements from simple rotating high-gain transmitters with a range of 300m, and applying probabilistic modelling to infer their AoA. The receiver's movement path is then modelled using a Gaussian process and reconstructed using doubly stochastic variational inference, resulting in approximately 15m accuracy tracking of receivers weighing 38mg (including power source) over a scalable landscape range while consuming less than 180uW, increased to approximately 10m accuracy at less than 600uW by taking more RSS measurements. We anticipate that this method will support fields such as the behavioural study of flying insect species, which we demonstrate by applying the system to track Bombus terrestris nest return flights.

</details>


### [333] [Inductive Correlation Clustering with Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27153)
*Francesco Paolo Nerini,Francesco Bonchi,Arijit Khan,André Panisson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a GNN-based framework for Inductive Correlation Clustering that can generalize to unseen graphs, achieving up to 5 orders of magnitude faster inference while maintaining competitive approximation ratios compared to standard transductive CC algorithms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Correlation Clustering (CC) has significant scalability issues and is inherently transductive, requiring algorithms to be executed from scratch for each new problem instance. There's a need for inductive approaches that can generalize to unseen graphs with minimal computational overhead.

Method: The authors use Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to learn structural patterns and node features during training, enabling generalization to new graphs from the same distribution. The framework serves as an inductive approach to Correlation Clustering.

Result: The framework reduces inference time by up to 5 orders of magnitude while maintaining approximation ratios within ~10% of the best baseline. It also achieves competitive results on standard CC benchmarks and serves as an effective learnable pooling mechanism for graph classification, enhancing hierarchical structure capture.

Conclusion: GNNs provide an effective solution to the scalability and transductive limitations of Correlation Clustering, enabling fast inductive generalization while maintaining solution quality. The framework also demonstrates utility as a learnable pooling layer for graph classification tasks.

Abstract: Correlation Clustering (CC) is a natural formulation of clustering in combinatorial optimization, which uses a graph representation of the input and does not require a pre-specified number of clusters. Given $n$ objects and a pairwise similarity function, the goal is to cluster the objects so that similar objects are put in the same cluster and dissimilar objects are put in different clusters. Despite its versatility, existing CC algorithms suffer from significant scalability issues and are inherently transductive: i.e., the algorithm must be executed from scratch for any new problem instance.
  In this work, we bridge this gap by leveraging Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to solve Inductive Correlation Clustering, a novel generalization of the CC problem designed to handle unseen graph instances. By learning to exploit common structural patterns and node features during training, our framework generalizes to new graphs drawn from the same distribution with minimal computational overhead with respect to standard algorithms. We demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of our approach through extensive experiments. Our framework not only excels in the inductive setting, e.g., lowering the inference time up to $5$ order of magnitude, while maintaining an approximation ratio within $~10\%$ of the best baseline solution, but also achieves competitive results on standard (transductive) CC benchmarks. Finally, we showcase a practical application of our framework as a learnable pooling mechanism for graph classification. Our results indicate that our method serves as an efficient pooling layer, enhancing the ability of GNNs to capture hierarchical structural information in networks.

</details>


### [334] [Diffusion Policies for Short-Horizon Planning in Robot Crowd Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27158)
*Wendong Li,Jochen Garcke*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PDPO is an offline-to-online RL framework using diffusion policies to generate short-horizon action chunks for safer crowd navigation, addressing evaluation artifacts with boundary constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL methods for robot crowd navigation output only single reactive actions per timestep, limiting representation of diverse short-term avoidance strategies in dense, dynamic, multimodal human-robot interactions.

Method: Proposes Planning Diffusion Policy Optimization (PDPO): pretrains diffusion policy on collision-avoidance demonstrations, then fine-tunes online with PPO by treating denoising as internal decision process. Generates five-step action chunks applied receding-horizon. Introduces modified benchmark where boundary violations count as collisions.

Result: PDPO achieves improved success rate over strong baselines. Ablations show action chunks are especially important for the modified bounded benchmark that prevents agents from bypassing dense crowds by leaving valid domain.

Conclusion: Diffusion policies with action chunking enhance crowd navigation safety and performance, particularly when addressing evaluation artifacts through proper boundary constraints that reflect real-world navigation requirements.

Abstract: Robot crowd navigation requires safe and efficient decision-making under dense, dynamic, and multimodal human--robot interactions. Existing reinforcement-learning methods typically output a single reactive action at each timestep, which limits their ability to represent diverse short-term avoidance strategies. We propose Planning Diffusion Policy Optimization (PDPO), an offline-to-online reinforcement-learning framework that uses a diffusion policy to generate short-horizon action chunks for crowd navigation. PDPO is first pretrained on collision-avoidance demonstrations and then fine-tuned online with PPO by treating the denoising process as an internal decision process. During execution, the policy generates a five-step action chunk and applies it in a receding-horizon manner. Furthermore, we observe an evaluation artifact in common crowd-navigation benchmarks: without explicit boundary constraints, learned agents may leave the valid domain and bypass dense crowds. To address this, we introduce a setting in which boundary violations are treated as collisions. Experiments show that PDPO obtains an improved success rate over strong baselines, and ablations demonstrate that action chunks are especially important for the modified bounded benchmark.

</details>


### [335] [TraceBench: Controlled Evaluation of LLM Agents for Time-Series Root-Cause Attribution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27182)
*Tommaso Bendinelli,Artur Dox,Christian Holz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TraceBench is a simulation framework that generates controlled root-cause attribution tasks for evaluating LLM agents on time-series anomaly detection, revealing insights about agent performance across different system conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents are increasingly being used for anomaly detection and root-cause analysis in time-series data from real-world systems, but their performance hasn't been systematically evaluated under controlled conditions. There's a need for a standardized framework to assess how well these agents can identify parameter changes in dynamical systems.

Method: The authors introduce TraceBench, a simulation-based framework that generates controlled root-cause attribution tasks. They simulate three interpretable mechanical systems, create tasks where agents must determine if system parameters were altered and identify which one, and systematically evaluate four LLM agents across controlled experimental conditions.

Result: The evaluation reveals several key findings: 1) Agents benefit substantially from domain context, 2) They primarily explore data through numerical console output rather than visualizations, 3) Agents perform worse when required to produce Python scripts mapping time-series to predictions compared to submitting predictions directly.

Conclusion: TraceBench provides a valuable framework for systematically evaluating LLM agents on time-series root-cause analysis tasks. The study yields new insights into how these agents analyze dynamical system observations and establishes benchmarks for future research, with all datasets, agent trajectories, results, and a leaderboard publicly available.

Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly applied to anomaly detection and root-cause analysis in time-series observations collected from real-world systems; however, their performance on these tasks has not been systematically evaluated under controlled conditions. We introduce TraceBench, a simulation-based framework for generating controlled root-cause attribution tasks. In each generated task, an agent receives time-series observations produced by simulating a physical dynamical system and must determine whether a system parameter was altered during the simulation and, if so, which one. Using TraceBench, we generate tasks from three interpretable mechanical systems and systematically evaluate four LLM agents across controlled experimental conditions, yielding new insights into how these agents analyze time-series observations from dynamical systems. Our results show that agents benefit substantially from domain context and explore data primarily through numerical console output rather than visualizations. We also find that agents generally perform worse when required to produce a Python script that maps each time-series sample to a predicted root-cause label than when they submit predictions directly. We release our datasets, agent trajectories, experimental results, and a leaderboard on our website, tracebench.github.io.

</details>


### [336] [When Interference Graphs Evolve: Doubly Robust Estimation of Dynamic Peer Effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27187)
*Xiaojing Du*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A framework for estimating peer effects in dynamic social networks that separates pre-assignment history, dynamic peer exposure, and post-assignment network evolution using controlled contrasts and introduces a doubly robust estimator.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Peer effects are challenging to estimate in evolving social networks because network history, dynamic peer exposure, and post-assignment network changes have distinct causal roles but are often conflated in existing methods.

Method: Introduces a controlled contrast framework indexing outcomes by own treatment, temporally aggregated peer exposure, and post-assignment evolution summary. Develops Dynamic Network Doubly Robust (DynaNet-DR) estimator combining temporally factorized propensity with normalized augmentation, plus representative-score prediction, fixed clipping, and finite-sample stabilization.

Result: The estimator is consistent under specified conditions when either outcome regression or propensity estimator is consistent. Semi-synthetic benchmarks on real temporal graph sequences show favorable estimation accuracy for full-profile methods, with MathOverflow study as observational illustration.

Conclusion: The framework successfully disentangles distinct causal components in dynamic network peer effect estimation and provides a robust estimator that performs well in practical applications while addressing the unique challenges of evolving interaction graphs.

Abstract: Peer effects are difficult to estimate when interaction graphs evolve because pre-assignment network history, dynamic peer exposure, and post-assignment network change have distinct causal roles. We introduce a controlled contrast framework that indexes potential outcomes by own treatment, temporally aggregated peer exposure, and a post-assignment evolution summary. Differences between the resulting means define own-treatment, peer-exposure, controlled network-evolution, and joint controlled contrasts rather than a mediation decomposition. We develop the Dynamic Network Doubly Robust estimator, DynaNet-DR, which combines a temporally factorized propensity with normalized augmentation. Under consistency, summary sufficiency, sequential exchangeability, positivity, nuisance convergence, and weak dependence, its canonical estimator is consistent when either the outcome regression or the propensity estimator is consistent. The reported implementation adds representative-score prediction, fixed clipping, and finite-sample stabilization. Semi-synthetic benchmarks on fixed real temporal graph sequences show favorable estimation accuracy among methods targeting the full profile. These benchmarks assess summary-indexed contrasts rather than counterfactual edge generation, and the MathOverflow study is an observational illustration under the stated assumptions.

</details>


### [337] [Common Geodesics Do Not Guarantee Fisher Consistency of the Structured SVM: Minimal Counterexamples and a Tree-Metric Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27203)
*Jintao Fei,Jiangying Luo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper shows that the common-geodesic condition is insufficient for Fisher consistency of structured SVM with argmax decoder, provides counterexamples for branching trees, and establishes minimal sizes for counterexamples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous work established that a necessary condition for Fisher consistency of structured SVM requires the task loss to be a metric where every output triple has a common geodesic point. The motivation is to determine whether this condition is also sufficient, which would complete the characterization of Fisher consistency for this important machine learning framework.

Method: The authors use combinatorial and geometric analysis of metric spaces, particularly focusing on tree metrics and graph structures. They construct explicit counterexamples (like the four-output unit star) and use primal-dual certificates to prove optimality claims. They classify positively weighted tree metrics and analyze specific graph families like $K_{m,n}$ bipartite graphs.

Result: 1. The common-geodesic condition is insufficient for Fisher consistency with argmax decoder.
2. A four-output unit star provides a minimal counterexample among metrics satisfying the condition.
3. For tree metrics: argmax consistency holds iff the tree is a path (linear).
4. Branching trees fail only at boundary distributions; all trees maintain argmax property at full-support distributions.
5. Among metrics satisfying the condition, five outputs are necessary and sufficient for full-support counterexamples; $K_{2,3}$ is the smallest such example.
6. A full-support counterexample exists for the 3D Hamming cube.

Conclusion: The paper reveals a decoder gap in structured prediction: even when a calibrated link function exists (ensuring Fisher consistency), the specific argmax decoder may not be validated on all surrogate-risk minimizers. This has implications for decoder design in structured SVM and understanding the relationship between surrogate losses and inference procedures.

Abstract: A known necessary condition for Fisher consistency of the structured support vector machine requires the task loss to be a metric for which every output triple has a common geodesic point. We show that this condition is not sufficient for the canonical coordinate-wise argmax decoder. A four-output unit star admits an exactly optimal score vector whose maximizers are all strictly non-Bayes, and four outputs are minimal among metrics satisfying the condition. We then completely classify positively weighted tree metrics whose vertex set is the output space: argmax consistency holds if and only if the tree is a path. The failure on branching trees is confined to boundary distributions; every tree retains the argmax property at every full-support distribution. Among metrics satisfying the common-geodesic condition, five outputs are necessary and sufficient for a full-support counterexample; $K_{2,3}$ is the smallest member of an infinite $K_{m,n}$ family. We additionally give a full-support counterexample for the three-dimensional Hamming cube. All optimality claims have exact primal-dual certificates. The counterexamples expose a concrete decoder gap: in this polyhedral setting, an embedding can guarantee the existence of a calibrated link without validating a prescribed argmax link on every surrogate-risk minimizer.

</details>


### [338] [Profit based evaluation of machine learning for nitrogen recommendations in winter wheat](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27205)
*Xulong Wang,Po Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Machine learning fails as a direct replacement for standard nitrogen rate advice but works as a profit-scored correction that reduces losses by 25-43%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current UK nitrogen rate advice for winter wheat doesn't respond to price fluctuations, and recent price swings significantly affect optimal rates. While machine learning is often proposed as a solution, it's typically evaluated on prediction accuracy rather than actual profit impact.

Method: The authors developed a test bench using 892 yield response curves from two long-term UK experiments. They evaluated nitrogen advice by directly measuring the profit it forgoes on measured yield curves, sweeping nitrogen-to-grain price ratios to cover all price scenarios. They tested machine learning models and a simple correction step applied after modeling.

Result: Machine learning failed as a predictor - no model could recover the best rate within farm tolerance. At normal prices, all models performed worse than standard advice on profit. However, a simple correction step applied after modeling cut profit losses by 25%, and this same frozen correction reduced losses by 43% at a second site without retraining. A hybrid approach combining standard advice with damped correction removed bias and trimmed large losses.

Conclusion: Machine learning pays off not as a replacement for standard nitrogen rate advice, but as a profit-scored correction to it. The price sweep approach also provides a way to price emission cuts, showing costs comparable to current carbon prices.

Abstract: Nitrogen rates for winter wheat are set before the season, under unknown prices and weather. The standard UK advice does not respond to prices, yet recent price swings moved the most profitable rate by tens of kilograms per hectare. Machine learning is often proposed as the fix. However, it is usually judged on prediction accuracy, and accurate prediction does not by itself make the recommended rate more profitable. Our insight is to score nitrogen advice directly by the profit it forgoes on measured yield response curves. We build a test bench on 892 such curves from two long running UK experiments, and sweep the nitrogen to grain price ratio to cover all price scenarios. On this bench, machine learning fails as a predictor. No model recovers the best rate within farm tolerance, and the benchmark noise shows none can. At normal prices, every model also loses to the standard advice on profit. The gain sits elsewhere. A simple correction step applied after the model cuts profit losses by a quarter, while better models and extra features give no gain. The same frozen correction cuts losses by 43% at the second site without any retraining. A hybrid of standard advice plus a damped correction removes bias and trims rare large losses. The same price sweep also prices emission cuts, at a cost comparable to current carbon prices. Machine learning therefore pays as a profit scored correction to standard advice, not as its replacement.

</details>


### [339] [HALO: A Heterogeneity-Aware Language-Aligned IMU Foundation Model for Open-Set Human Activity Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27233)
*Zihan Ding,Liyu Zhang,Xiaomin Ouyang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HALO is a heterogeneity-aware language-aligned IMU foundation model for human activity recognition that addresses sensing heterogeneity and poor generalization through two-stage training: heterogeneity-aware self-supervised pretraining followed by text encoder alignment for open-set recognition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current HAR lacks unified models that generalize across subjects, devices, and activities due to sensing heterogeneity (different sampling rates, channel configurations, sensor placements) and poor generalization to unseen activities and label vocabularies.

Method: Two-stage training: 1) Heterogeneity-aware self-supervised pretraining with adaptive-pooling tokenization, channel-independent feature extraction, and contextualized sensor conditioning using natural-language descriptions. 2) Alignment of IMU encoder with text embeddings via synonym-aware soft contrastive learning for open-set recognition via cosine-similarity retrieval.

Result: HALO outperforms 5 SOTA baselines on all 8 aggregate metrics across 7 held-out datasets, improves zero-shot open-set accuracy by 13.7 percentage points using only 35M parameters (10x fewer than MOMENT), but fails on datasets with severe distribution shift.

Conclusion: HALO successfully addresses sensing heterogeneity and enables open-set recognition through language alignment, demonstrating superior performance with fewer parameters, though challenges remain for severe distribution shifts.

Abstract: Human Activity Recognition (HAR) using inertial measurement units (IMUs) enables a wide range of applications, yet the field still lacks a unified model that can generalize across diverse subjects, devices, and activities. Training such a model is difficult due to two key challenges: sensing heterogeneity -- differences in sampling rates, channel configurations, and sensor placements -- and poor generalization to unseen activities and label vocabularies. We introduce HALO (Heterogeneity-Aware Language-aligned Open-set model), a domain-specific IMU foundation model that addresses both challenges through a two-stage training framework. Stage 1 pretrains the IMU encoder with heterogeneity-aware self-supervised learning, including adaptive-pooling tokenization, channel-independent feature extraction, and contextualized sensor conditioning that injects natural-language sensor descriptions into each channel embedding. Stage 2 aligns this IMU encoder with text embeddings via synonym-aware soft contrastive learning, enabling open-set recognition via cosine-similarity retrieval without per-dataset classifiers. Trained on 10 public HAR datasets and evaluated on 7 held-out datasets, HALO outperforms five state-of-the-art baselines on all 8 aggregate metrics, and still leads on 3 of 4 settings under baseline-matched inputs. Despite using only ~35M trainable parameters -- 10x fewer than the latest foundation model MOMENT (341.2M) -- HALO improves zero-shot open-set accuracy, measured over all 87 training labels, by 13.7 percentage points. On two further datasets with severe distribution shift, every model including HALO collapses zero-shot. A video demonstration of HALO's performance in real world is available at https://youtu.be/rooVKragtFU

</details>


### [340] [Importance Scoring of Transformer Attention Heads in Learning Tabular Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27241)
*Ahmad Jad Allah,Kazi F. Akhter,Md. Kamrozzaman Bhuiyan,Manar D. Samad*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel importance-scoring metric is proposed to interpret multi-head transformer models for tabular data, showing which attention heads are most/least important for model performance across diverse datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformers have been extensively studied in vision and NLP domains, but their application to tabular data remains underexplored. Deep learning models are computationally demanding and opaque, making it important to understand how they transform data for better optimization and interpretation.

Method: Proposes an importance-scoring metric to interpret multi-head transformer models on tabular data. Experiments conducted on 40 diverse tabular datasets with head dropping techniques based on the importance scores to analyze model resilience and performance impact.

Result: In 72.5% of experiments, models were most resilient when heads with lowest importance scores were gradually removed. Removing the most important heads first caused the greatest performance reduction. Important heads were scattered across layers without consistent patterns, and head importance varied considerably across different tabular datasets.

Conclusion: The proposed importance score provides valuable insights for interpreting transformer models on tabular data, differs from patterns observed in vision/NLP domains, can improve architectural efficiency by identifying redundant heads, and the source code is made publicly available.

Abstract: Computationally demanding and opaque deep learning models can be better understood and optimized by analyzing how they transform data. While deep transformers have been widely studied in computer vision and natural language processing, their application in tabular data remains relatively underexplored. This paper presents one of the first applications of an importance-scoring metric to interpret multi-head transformer models in learning from tabular data. Experiments conducted on 40 diverse tabular datasets demonstrate robustness to head drops based on the proposed head importance score. In 72.5\% of experimental examples, the model remains most resilient to performance drops when heads with the lowest importance scores are gradually removed. In contrast, removing the most important attention head first results in the greatest reduction in classification performance. A closer look at individual head importance scores across six attention layers reveals that important heads are scattered across layers, with no consistent layer-specific trends. In contrast to the image and language domains, the importance of individual attention heads varies considerably across tabular datasets with different schemas and feature spaces. The proposed importance score can improve efficiency and redundancy within transformer architectures. We make the source code for measuring the importance of individual attention heads publicly available.

</details>


### [341] [Circuit Condensation: Post-Training that Concentrates a Behavior's Causal Circuit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27254)
*Sai Adith Senthil Kumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Circuit Condensation: A method to post-train neural networks to concentrate interpretable behaviors into smaller causal circuits by pruning low-attribution edges and training low-rank adapters, achieving 8.1× average circuit size reduction while preserving task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current mechanistic interpretability approaches using frozen discovery often return hundreds of circuit edges, making them hard to inspect, compare, or verify exhaustively. There's a need for methods to create more compact, interpretable circuits while preserving model behavior.

Method: Circuit Condensation post-trains models to concentrate behaviors into smaller causal graphs through iterative rounds: prune low-attribution edges, train a low-rank adapter to match original behavior through remaining edges, and retain cuts only if task performance and general capabilities survive. The method tests every subset of circuits to identify reducible and non-reducible components.

Result: Across four behaviors and eight models, condensed circuits are smaller than strongest frozen baseline in 30 of 32 settings (8.1× average reduction, up to 316×). Weight updates rather than search alone drive reduction. On indirect object identification, condensation isolates 24 heads (17 with documented roles) vs. 61 heads (36 undocumented) for matched frozen circuit, creating a sufficient sub-circuit rather than full reconstruction.

Conclusion: Circuit Condensation successfully creates more compact, interpretable circuits while preserving model behavior, revealing dependencies between edges that cannot be understood independently. The method produces sufficient sub-circuits of mechanisms rather than reconstructions, enabling better inspection, comparison, and verification in mechanistic interpretability.

Abstract: One approach to mechanistic interpretability explains behavior through circuits: the components and connections that carry it. Frozen discovery often returns hundreds of edges, making them hard to inspect, compare, or verify exhaustively. We introduce Circuit Condensation, which post-trains models to concentrate behaviors into smaller causal graphs. Each round prunes low-attribution edges and trains a low-rank adapter to match the original through what remains, retaining the cut only if task performance and general capability survive. Across four behaviors and eight models, condensed circuits are smaller than the strongest frozen baseline in 30 of 32 settings, by $8.1\times$ on average and up to $316\times$. Repeating the search without weight updates produces larger circuits in 29 of 32 settings, showing that weight updates, rather than search alone, drive the reduction. Testing every subset of 19 circuits finds 11 that cannot be reduced and reveals removable edges in the rest. Pair ablations expose dependencies between edges, showing that their effects cannot be understood independently. On indirect object identification, condensation isolates 24 heads, 17 of them with documented roles, against 61 heads and 36 undocumented ones for the matched frozen circuit: a sufficient sub-circuit of the published mechanism rather than a reconstruction of it. The resulting circuit tracks the original model's next-token distribution and predicts its errors.

</details>


### [342] [Making Latent Evolution Explicit: Operator-Structured Transitions for World Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27259)
*Xiaoxiao Lu,Yunlong Dong,Jiahao Shi,Ye Yuan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LEON introduces a novel architecture for latent transition prediction in World Action Models that uses learned operators for state evolution rather than transformer-based token interaction, improving robot policy performance and robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current World Action Models (WAMs) use Transformer-based predictors for latent transition prediction, but these are designed for token interaction rather than temporal evolution, creating a mismatch with the actual dynamics of scene states.

Method: The Latent Evolution Operator Network (LEON) models latent evolution through context-modulated operator-based propagation and additive forcing, grounded in the controlled Koopman generator theory. It organizes transitions around a shared evolution-operator structure with complementary additive change.

Result: LEON improves closed-loop performance and robustness across two different WAM formulations, while remaining effective under full transition replacement. Controlled dynamical systems verify the architecture's inductive bias and the complementary roles of operator propagation and forcing.

Conclusion: Transition realization is a consequential architectural choice in latent WAMs, and the evolution-specific inductive bias of LEON provides superior performance compared to transformer-based approaches for modeling temporal evolution.

Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) augment robot policies by predicting how task-relevant scene states may evolve under interaction. Recent WAMs increasingly perform such prediction in latent representation spaces, avoiding full appearance-level generation while preserving control-relevant information. Yet latent transitions are commonly realized with Transformer-based predictors whose inductive structure is centered on token interaction rather than temporal evolution. We study transition realization as an architectural choice distinct from predictive representation and prediction-policy coupling. We introduce the Latent Evolution Operator Network (LEON), which models latent evolution in a learned observable space through context-modulated operator-based propagation and additive forcing. Grounded in the controlled Koopman generator view of evolution, LEON organizes context-dependent transition variation around a shared evolution-operator structure while retaining a complementary path for additive change. Controlled dynamical systems verify the resulting evolution-specific inductive bias and the complementary roles of operator propagation and forcing. Across two WAM formulations that integrate latent prediction into the policy differently, LEON improves closed-loop performance and robustness while remaining effective under full transition replacement. These results establish transition realization as a consequential architectural choice in latent WAMs.

</details>


### [343] [MM-Spectrum: Multimodal Multi-spectral Molecular Structural Elucidation with a Stable MoE Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27286)
*Hai-tao Yu,Nan Min,Zheng Fang,Hongyu Zhan,Yusen Tan,Yuhan Wang,Jun Xia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MM-Spectrum is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts framework for molecular structure elucidation from multimodal spectroscopic data, addressing performance degradation from direct concatenation of heterogeneous signals through modality-aware routing and specialized expert design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Direct concatenation of multimodal spectroscopic measurements for molecular structure inference suffers from anomalous performance degradation due to pronounced heterogeneity and multimodal imbalance across different spectral modalities.

Method: Proposes MM-Spectrum, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts framework with: 1) explicit modality-aware routing mechanism that exposes spectral identity to routers, 2) shared and interaction experts for extracting modality-unique and cross-modal synergistic information, and 3) heterogeneous expert capacities to suppress noise-induced interference.

Result: Achieves consistent and substantial improvements across full-modality, bimodal, and missing-modality settings on molecular structural elucidation tasks, supported by ablation studies and interpretability analyses.

Conclusion: The proposed MM-Spectrum framework effectively addresses the limitations of direct concatenation for multimodal spectroscopic data by better matching information characteristics under multispectral imbalance, enabling more robust molecular structure elucidation.

Abstract: Inferring molecular structures from multimodal spectroscopic measurements requires integrating complementary yet highly heterogeneous signals. However, the common paradigm of directly concatenating multispectral sequences can exhibit anomalous performance degradation, primarily due to pronounced heterogeneity and the resulting multimodal imbalance across modalities. As a remedy, we propose MM-Spectrum, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts framework tailored for multimodal multispectral spectra-to-structure elucidation. To better match the information characteristics under multispectral imbalance, MM-Spectrum introduces an explicit modality-aware routing mechanism that exposes spectral identity to the router in addition to token content representations. Moreover, it incorporates shared and interaction experts, together with heterogeneous expert capacities, to extract multispectral modality-unique and cross-modal synergistic information while suppressing noise-induced interference. Across full-modality, bimodal, and missing-modality settings on molecular structural elucidation, MM-Spectrum achieves consistent and substantial improvements, supported by ablation studies and interpretability analyses.

</details>


### [344] [QuantumBoostNet: A Hybrid Classical-Quantum Architecture for Enhanced Accuracy in Cardiac Ultrasound View Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27302)
*Mihai Udrescu-Milosav,Stefan-Alexandru Jura,Mihai Udrescu,Gerhard-Paul Diller*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QuantumBoostNet is a hybrid classical-quantum architecture that combines classical CNN with quantum circuits to improve cardiac ultrasound view identification, outperforming classical and other hybrid models while showing robustness to noise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate cardiac ultrasound view identification is critical for precise anatomical interpretation and reducing clinical errors. Classical computer vision models often underperform on medical imaging due to high noise levels, creating a need for better specialized approaches.

Method: QuantumBoostNet uses a hybrid architecture with a classical backbone and two heads: one classical and one quantum (implemented as a 10-qubit parametrized quantum circuit). It employs two-stage training with adaptive transition between heads using a mixing parameter that monitors loss dynamics.

Result: QuantumBoostNet consistently outperforms state-of-the-art classical and hybrid models in cardiac ultrasound view identification, achieving relative improvement over best competitors. It also shows superior performance on established image classification benchmarks and exhibits robustness to noise.

Conclusion: Hybrid classical-quantum models like QuantumBoostNet are promising for specialized medical imaging applications, offering better performance than purely classical approaches despite current limitations in quantum hardware simulation.

Abstract: Accurate identification of the correct view or angle in cardiac ultrasound (echocardiogram) is a critical component of cardiologic imaging. This step is essential for precise anatomical interpretation, reliable measurement, and the reduction of clinical errors. Although computer vision has advanced significantly, most state-of-the-art models perform well on standard benchmarks but often yield suboptimal results in specialized medical imaging tasks due to the high level of noise present in the data. QuantumBoostNet, a hybrid classical-quantum architecture, is introduced to address these challenges. This model integrates a classical backbone with two heads: one classical and one quantum, with the quantum head implemented as a parametrized 10-qubit quantum circuit. Training occurs in two stages, with an adaptive transition between heads governed by a mixing parameter that monitors loss dynamics. Extensive experiments indicate that, despite the limited number of qubits that can be simulated, QuantumBoostNet consistently outperforms state-of-the-art classical and hybrid classical-quantum models in cardiac ultrasound view identification, achieving a relative improvement over the best competitor. QuantumBoostNet also demonstrates superior performance on established image classification benchmarks and exhibits robustness to noise. These findings support the continued development of hybrid classical-quantum models for specialized medical imaging applications.

</details>


### [345] [Beyond Parallel Blindness: Information Floors and Model Gaps in Block Drafting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27339)
*Xinwei Qiang,Xiang Fang,Chang Chen,Yue Guan,Yufei Ding*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Block drafters have two rejection sources: missing within-block info and imperfect modeling; an "information floor" separates them, showing current drafters far above floor limits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current block drafting methods generate multiple tokens in parallel before earlier tokens are known, leading to rejections that mix two different types of losses: missing information about future tokens within the block and imperfect modeling of observable information. Existing metrics like accepted length cannot distinguish between these two sources of error.

Method: The authors introduce an "information floor" concept - the minimum expected rejection at a specified conditioning order. Rejection above this floor is the "model gap." They estimate both using target rollouts across four domains, four open-weight targets, and a frontier API target to separate the two types of losses.

Result: Three key findings: 1) All-parallel floor reaches 0.286 at final slot on Qwen3-4B, limiting best proposals to 71% per-slot acceptance; 2) One realized token removes 86-100% of this floor; 3) Current drafters (DFlash, DSpark) remain far above their floors, with model gaps accounting for 43-64% of DFlash rejection and 85-92% of DSpark's oracle-conditioned rejection.

Conclusion: The information floor separates the value of short-range conditioning from proposal quality. Current drafters have significant room for improvement as most rejection comes from the model gap rather than fundamental information limits. Short-range conditioning dramatically reduces the information floor, showing locality in language modeling.

Abstract: Block drafters propose several tokens in one forward pass, before earlier target tokens are realised. Their rejection mixes two losses: missing within-block path information and imperfect modelling of observable information. Accepted length cannot distinguish them. We separate the two with an information floor, the minimum expected rejection at a specified conditioning order; rejection above this floor is the model gap. Estimating both from target rollouts across four domains, four open-weight targets, and a frontier API target yields three findings. First, the all-parallel floor reaches $0.286$ at the final slot on Qwen3-4B, limiting even the best proposal to $71\%$ per-slot acceptance. Second, one realised token removes $86$--$100\%$ of this floor, a locality also recovered by an independent mutual-information analysis. Third, current drafters remain far above their floors: the final-slot model gap accounts for $43$--$64\%$ of DFlash rejection and $85$--$92\%$ of DSpark's oracle-conditioned rejection. These findings separate the value of short-range conditioning from proposal quality.

</details>


### [346] [Understanding Evolution Strategies for LLM Reasoning: Broader Reasoning Coverage than GRPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27351)
*Yunpeng Ba,Zhi Zheng,Yue Xie,Jiaqing Li,Xialiang Tong,Tao Zhong,Mingxuan Yuan,Zhichao Lu,Xuyang Wu,Zhenkun Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ES (Evolution Strategies) is a memory-efficient LLM reasoning method that achieves broader reasoning coverage than GRPO, leading to better Pass@K performance. The paper identifies functional sparsity in ES updates and proposes a hybrid GRPO-ES strategy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To better understand ES optimization behavior and define its advantages over mainstream post-training paradigms like GRPO for LLM reasoning, as ES's optimization mechanisms remain understudied despite its memory efficiency.

Method: Systematically investigate ES dynamics through theoretical analysis and empirical studies. Theoretically analyze verifier-projected Jensen-Shannon diversity; empirically compare ES vs GRPO performance, identify functional sparsity in updates, study hyperparameter effects, and develop a sequential GRPO-ES training strategy.

Result: 1) ES shows performance advantage over GRPO with broader reasoning coverage and better Pass@K; 2) ES updates are functionally sparse despite large parameter drift; 3) ES requires smaller population size in larger LLMs; 4) Hybrid GRPO-ES combines GRPO's Pass@1 strength with ES's Pass@K gains.

Conclusion: ES is a distinct reasoning post-training paradigm rather than just a memory-efficient alternative to GRPO, offering unique advantages in reasoning coverage and sparse functional updates without catastrophic forgetting.

Abstract: Evolution Strategies (ES) have recently emerged as a memory-efficient post-training paradigm for LLM reasoning. However, the optimization behavior of ES remains understudied, making it hard to define its advantage scope compared to mainstream post-training paradigms (e.g., Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)). By systematically investigating ES dynamics and mechanisms, this paper first identifies a performance advantage of ES over GRPO, theoretically and empirically showing that ES can lead to broader reasoning coverage, thereby better exploiting the reasoning capabilities of pretrained LLMs. Theoretically, we show that verifier-projected Jensen-Shannon diversity across the ES population is helpful to higher Pass@K performances. Empirically, unlike GRPO, which exhibits entropy collapse, ES improves Pass@1 while attaining higher Pass@K than GRPO. We further develop a sequential GRPO-ES training strategy that combines GRPO's strength in Pass@1 with ES's gains in Pass@K. Second, we find that despite substantial whole-model parameter drift, the task-performance gains of ES are only contributed to a sparse subset of larger-magnitude updates. This functional sparsity suggests that large parameter movement need not imply widespread functional change, and held-out evaluations further show that it does not necessarily lead to catastrophic forgetting. Finally, we study how hyperparameter design affects the effectiveness of ES, demonstrating that ES requires a smaller population size in a larger LLM. These findings position ES as a distinct reasoning post-training paradigm rather than a less effective, memory-efficient alternative to GRPO.

</details>
