### [347] [Zero-Shot Self-Orchestration with Ledger-Based Control for Improved LLM Coding Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26480)
*Victor Gao,Vida Khosrowshahi,Ali Khosrowshahi,Xihao Sun,Juhyun Lee,Simon,Lee*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: Multi-agent manager-worker systems can improve coding performance over single-model baselines, but benefits are conditional on model type and reasoning settings, offering cost-effective accuracy improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems are widely reported to beat single-model baselines, but evidence is mixed and comparisons are confounded due to simultaneous changes in token budgets, tool calls, and prompts, making it unclear what actually contributes to performance gains.

Method: Investigates the manager-worker scaffold over a shared filesystem workspace with no training and no per-benchmark tuning, comparing against the same model answering in a single pass. Tests across nine models (five open-weight, four frontier closed models) on 100 latest hard LiveCodeBench problems, analyzing performance with and without reasoning enabled.

Result: Scaffold benefit is real but conditional: significant gains for some models (Qwen3.8-27B +23.4%, GPT-5.6-Luna +10.6%, GPT-5.6-Terra +8.0%, Kimi-K3 +30.4%, Minimax-M3 +11.0%) but null or negative for others (Qwen3.6-35B -1 to -9%). Manager roughly triples token cost but buys accuracy more cheaply than moving to larger models (GPT-5.6-Terra with manager nearly matches Fable 5's accuracy at 1/5 the price).

Conclusion: Multi-agent manager-worker systems can provide cost-effective performance improvements for coding tasks, particularly through context management and problem decomposition mechanisms, but benefits vary significantly by model type and reasoning settings.

Abstract: Multi-agent large language model systems are widely reported to beat single-model baselines, but the evidence is mixed, and comparisons are usually confounded: pipelines change token budgets, tool calls, and prompts simultaneously, so an aggregate gain rarely reveals what actually helped. We investigate the effect of introducing the manager-worker scaffold over a shared filesystem workspace, with no training and no per-benchmark tuning, measured against the same model answering in a single pass. Across nine models -- five open-weight, spanning 9B to ~2.8T parameters, and four frontier closed models -- on the 100 latest hard LiveCodeBench problems, the scaffold's benefit is real but conditional: large and statistically significant for some (Qwen3.8-27B +23.4, GPT-5.6-Luna +10.6 and GPT-5.6-Terra +8.0, each over five paired passes; Kimi-K3 +30.4 and Minimax-M3 +11.0 over five paired passes with reasoning off, both at $p < 10^{-4}$, and +42 and +12 in a single pass at a 128k cap) and null or negative for others (Qwen3.6-35B -1 to -9 with reasoning off). With the manager, Opus-5 achieves the highest score in the study at 91% in one pass. Running a manager roughly triples the token bill, but it buys accuracy more cheaply than moving to a larger model does: GPT-5.6-Terra with a manager nearly matches Fable 5's single-call accuracy (85.0 against 87.4, $p = 0.59$) at a fifth of the price (\$11.71 against \$61.11 per 100-problem pass, $p < 10^{-4}$), and the Qwen-27B arm does it for \$51.75 on weights anyone can self-host. Our transcript analysis finds several mechanisms behind the gains, of which two recur: context management, in which short worker calls and shared notes organize state and reduce truncation, and problem decomposition. Improvements are modest for large models with reasoning enabled, but larger for some models with reasoning disabled and for smaller models with reasoning enabled.

</details>


### [348] [Risks and Controls for Multi-Agent Systems: an analytical framework for deployment of AI agents across organisational boundaries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26626)
*Alistair Reid,Simon O'Callaghan,Dustin Venini,Liam Carroll,Tiberio Caetano*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: A framework for analyzing AI agent interaction risks across organizational boundaries, identifying governance tiers and control mechanisms for risk mitigation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As organizations increasingly deploy AI agents that interact with each other across organizational boundaries, new risks emerge from these interactions. Once interactions cross organizational perimeters, no single organization can fully observe, control, or govern them, creating systemic vulnerabilities.

Method: The paper introduces three deployment tiers based on governance structures: 1) Singular governance (single organization controls all agents), 2) Federated governance (multiple organizations under agreed rules), and 3) Open environments (no central authority). For each tier, the framework examines risk factors, failure modes, available controls, and identifies responsible actors.

Result: The framework provides a structured approach to reason about AI agent interaction risks, identifies who can apply controls in different governance scenarios, and highlights governance gaps where collective action is required to address systemic risks.

Conclusion: A systematic governance framework is needed to address the emerging risks of AI agent interactions, particularly as these interactions cross organizational boundaries. The proposed tiered approach helps organizations, policymakers, and researchers understand where governance can be applied and where collective action is needed to manage systemic risks.

Abstract: This report presents a framework to help organisations, policymakers and researchers reason about the risks that emerge when AI agents interact with each other, how those risks change as interactions cross organisational boundaries, and the controls that may help address them.
  As organisations deploy AI agents, those agents will increasingly interact with each other: inside the organisation, with the agents of partners, customers and suppliers, and with unknown counterparties on the open internet. Failures can emerge from the interactions themselves, and once those interactions cross an organisation's perimeter, no single organisation can fully see, control or govern them.
  The report introduces three deployment tiers, defined by the minimum common governance binding any two interacting agents: singular governance, where one organisation governs every agent; federated governance, where multiple organisations deploy into a shared environment under agreed rules; and open environments, where agents operate with no central authority and shared standards are adopted voluntarily if at all.
  Within each tier, the report examines risk factors, failure modes and available controls. It identifies who is positioned to apply the controls, and where no actor is positioned to act, it characterises the gap and the collective action required to close it.

</details>


### [349] [Fixed-Haven Reservation for Online Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery in Dense Warehouses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26759)
*Taisei Hirayama,Kohei Yoshida,Hiroki Sakaji,Itsuki Noda*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: SHARP introduces fixed Safe Haven reservation for online MAPD in dense warehouses, proving task completion guarantees under Haven-Reachability without needing extra waiting endpoints or biconnected topology.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense warehouses with single-lane aisles, dead ends, and tree-like guidepaths have limited space for idle agents. Existing MAPD guarantees rely on extra waiting endpoints or biconnected topology assumptions that fail in such layouts.

Method: Fixed-Haven reservation where each agent owns a Safe Haven (usually its start cell) that only the owner may occupy. SHARP (Safe-Haven Retreat Planner) keeps busy or retreating agents on collision-free reserved routes ending at their Havens under Haven-Reachability assumptions.

Result: SHARP achieves 100% success rate on all tested configurations in robustness sweep, while TP, PIBT, and PIBTTP-TA baselines fail. Fixed return mechanism proves central to robustness in tree-like layouts. Disabling mid-retreat reassignment worsens service time by 1.89x and makespan by 1.53x.

Conclusion: Fixed-Haven reservation provides robust guarantees for online MAPD in challenging warehouse layouts without requiring extra infrastructure or biconnected topology, with SHARP demonstrating superior reliability despite higher centralized planning costs.

Abstract: Dense warehouses often contain single-lane aisles, dead ends, and tree-like guidepaths that leave little room for idle agents to wait without blocking others. Existing Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery (MAPD) guarantees for completing all finitely released tasks typically rely on extra waiting endpoints that planned paths can avoid, or on biconnected topology; these assumptions may fail in such layouts. We study fixed-Haven reservation for online MAPD, where pickup-delivery tasks are released over time. Each agent owns a fixed Safe Haven (Haven for short), usually its start cell, that only the owner may occupy and that other agents treat as blocked. For finite task releases, we prove that this fixed-Haven contract completes all released tasks under Haven-Reachability and explicit planning/progress assumptions. We implement the contract in SHARP, a Safe-Haven Retreat Planner that keeps every busy or retreating agent on a collision-free reserved route ending at its Haven. We compare SHARP with representative TP and PIBT-family MAPD baselines: Token Passing (TP), Priority Inheritance with Backtracking (PIBT), and PIBT with Temporary Priority and Temporary Avoidance (PIBTTP-TA) for biconnected main areas with attached trees. In the robustness sweep, SHARP is the only method with 100% success on all tested configurations, at substantially higher centralized planning cost on tree-like layouts. A TP-style fixed-home-return counterfactual with full-route validation also recovers robustness on tested tree-like layouts, suggesting that fixed return is a central robustness mechanism there. A no-overwrite variant shows that disabling mid-retreat reassignment worsens service time (release-to-delivery latency) by 1.89 times and makespan by 1.53 times in the tested high-load tree condition.

</details>


### [350] [Dynamic Haven Selection for Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery in Constrained Warehouses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26939)
*Taisei Hirayama,Kohei Yoshida,Hiroki Sakaji,Itsuki Noda*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: A-sharp (Adaptive SHARP) is an improved multi-agent planning algorithm that allows robots to adaptively change their retreat havens during task assignment, reducing makespan by 16.7% compared to fixed-haven approaches in warehouse environments with constrained layouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Space-efficient warehouse layouts with single-agent-width aisles and dead-end workstations create bottlenecks where robots have limited waiting spots without blocking others. Fixed-haven approaches like SHARP can send robots to distant havens after deliveries, reducing efficiency in Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery (MAPD) tasks.

Method: A-sharp extends SHARP by allowing agents to adaptively change their retreat haven at task assignment time instead of using fixed havens. It prevents conflicts through: 1) an availability test for candidate havens to ensure no two agents rely on the same location, and 2) a pending-release rule that keeps the previous haven protected until the agent departs, preventing occupied/reserved location conflicts.

Result: Both algorithms completed all 14,400 runs across 72,000 total runs. A-sharp showed significantly better makespan in 107 out of 138 configurations and was never significantly worse than SHARP. On tree maps, A-sharp achieved a median makespan reduction of 16.7%.

Conclusion: A-sharp successfully addresses the limitations of fixed-haven approaches by enabling adaptive haven selection while maintaining safety guarantees. The algorithm preserves invariants and ensures finite-release completeness, significantly improving efficiency in constrained warehouse environments without sacrificing reliability.

Abstract: Space-efficient warehouse layouts often contain single-agent-width aisles and dead-end workstations where robots have few places to wait without blocking others. In Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery (MAPD) on such constrained layouts, robots must accept online pickup-delivery tasks while preserving protected waiting locations called Havens. The Safe HAven Retreat Planner (SHARP) introduced a mechanism that extends each committed task path with a validated retreat to the agent's dedicated initial Haven, but fixed-Haven commitments can send agents toward distant Havens after deliveries. We present A-sharp (Adaptive SHARP), which changes an agent's retreat target at task assignment time. A naive switch can cause two agents to rely on the same waiting location or let another committed path pass through a location that is still occupied or reserved. A-sharp prevents these failures with an availability test for candidate Havens and a pending-release rule that keeps the previous Haven protected until the agent departs. Under explicit Haven-structure and Safe Interval Path Planning (SIPP) assumptions, we prove invariant preservation and finite-release completeness: every task in any finite release sequence is delivered in finite time. Across 72,000 runs on 14,400 paired map-agent-count-rate-seed cases over four maps, both SHARP and A-sharp complete their respective 14,400 runs. For makespan (final delivery time), a prespecified paired comparison with Holm correction over all 138 configurations with more Havens than agents finds A-sharp significantly better in 107 configurations and never significantly worse than SHARP; on the tested tree map, the median reduction is 16.7%.

</details>


### [351] [One Model, Many Minds: Unlocking Multi-Agent Synergy in a Single Agent via Mixture of Roles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27338)
*Zhichen Zeng,Huiyuan Chen,Jingru Cheng,Juan Zha,Ming Liu,Ying Chen,Xiyuan Yang,Chaosheng Dong,Haiyang Zhang,Hanghang Tong*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: MoRe (Mixture of Roles) enables multi-perspective specialization in LLMs through dynamic role composition in a single-agent, single-turn inference, matching multi-agent system performance with 20x lower token cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current approaches for LLM specialization have limitations: single-agent methods with fixed personas can't adapt to diverse queries, while multi-agent systems require costly multi-turn interactions to fuse specializations. There's a need for efficient single-turn inference that can handle multiple perspectives.

Method: MoRe learns a codebook of steering vectors encoding latent roles, then uses a query-aware router to dynamically fuse multiple roles into a single steering vector. This composed vector steers a frozen backbone LLM, enabling multi-perspective specialization in single-turn inference. Training uses three-stage SFT curriculum and GRPO post-training.

Result: MoRe outperforms single-agent baselines by 2.2% on average across reasoning and personality benchmarks, achieves performance on par with multi-agent systems while reducing token cost by 20x.

Conclusion: MoRe successfully bridges the gap between single-agent efficiency and multi-agent system versatility, providing an effective solution for dynamic multi-perspective problem solving with significantly reduced computational overhead.

Abstract: Specializing Large Language Models (LLMs) toward distinct abilities underpins successes ranging from personalized assistants to multi-agent systems (MAS). Single-agent paradigms rely on pre-defined personas or steering vectors to induce specialization, yet they impose a single fixed specialization that fails to adapt to diverse queries. Conversely, MAS achieves dynamic multi-perspective problem solving by orchestrating agents with distinct text-based roles, but fusing these specializations requires multi-turn interactions that inflate context length and inference cost. To address these limitations, we propose Mixture of Roles (MoRe), which adaptively composes multiple specializations into a single steering vector for single-turn inference. Specifically, MoRe learns a diversified codeboox of steering vectors, each of which encodes a latent role. A query-aware router dynamically fuses the codebook into a steering vector that encompasses multiple roles. By steering the backbone LLM with the composed vector, MoRe enables multi-perspective specialization in a single-agent, single-turn inference process. The proposed MoRe can be efficiently trained via a three-stage SFT curriculum and GRPO post-training, while the backbone LLM remains frozen. Experiments across reasoning and personality benchmarks show that MoRe outperforms single-agent baselines by 2.2% on average, and achieves performance on par with MAS while reducing token cost by 20x.

</details>


### [352] [Zero-Shot Self-Orchestration with Ledger-Based Control for Improved LLM Coding Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26480)
*Victor Gao,Vida Khosrowshahi,Ali Khosrowshahi,Xihao Sun,Juhyun Lee,Simon,Lee*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: Multi-agent LLM systems with manager-worker scaffolds can improve coding performance on hard LiveCodeBench problems, but benefits are conditional on model size and reasoning settings, offering cost-effective accuracy gains compared to simply using larger models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There's mixed evidence about multi-agent LLM systems beating single-model baselines, with confounding factors like token budgets, tool calls, and prompt changes making it unclear what actually helps. The paper aims to isolate the effect of introducing a manager-worker scaffold over a shared filesystem workspace without training or per-benchmark tuning.

Method: The study tests nine models (five open-weight spanning 9B to ~2.8T parameters, and four frontier closed models) on 100 latest hard LiveCodeBench problems. It compares a manager-worker scaffold over shared filesystem workspace against the same model answering in a single pass, with no training or per-benchmark tuning. Analysis includes both reasoning-enabled and disabled settings, with transcript analysis to identify mechanisms behind gains.

Result: The scaffold's benefit is real but conditional: statistically significant for some models (Qwen3.8-27B +23.4%, GPT-5.6-Luna +10.6%, GPT-5.6-Terra +8.0%, Kimi-K3 +30.4%, Minimax-M3 +11.0%) and null or negative for others (Qwen3.6-35B -1 to -9% with reasoning off). With manager, Opus-5 achieves highest score at 91%. Manager roughly triples token costs but buys accuracy more cheaply than moving to larger models - GPT-5.6-Terra with manager nearly matches Fable 5's single-call accuracy at a fifth of the price.

Conclusion: Multi-agent manager-worker scaffolds can provide cost-effective performance improvements for LLMs on coding tasks, but benefits depend on model characteristics. Key mechanisms include context management and problem decomposition. For some models, the scaffold offers cheaper accuracy gains than simply scaling up model size, making it a practical alternative especially for smaller models with reasoning enabled or larger models with reasoning disabled.

Abstract: Multi-agent large language model systems are widely reported to beat single-model baselines, but the evidence is mixed, and comparisons are usually confounded: pipelines change token budgets, tool calls, and prompts simultaneously, so an aggregate gain rarely reveals what actually helped. We investigate the effect of introducing the manager-worker scaffold over a shared filesystem workspace, with no training and no per-benchmark tuning, measured against the same model answering in a single pass. Across nine models -- five open-weight, spanning 9B to ~2.8T parameters, and four frontier closed models -- on the 100 latest hard LiveCodeBench problems, the scaffold's benefit is real but conditional: large and statistically significant for some (Qwen3.8-27B +23.4, GPT-5.6-Luna +10.6 and GPT-5.6-Terra +8.0, each over five paired passes; Kimi-K3 +30.4 and Minimax-M3 +11.0 over five paired passes with reasoning off, both at $p < 10^{-4}$, and +42 and +12 in a single pass at a 128k cap) and null or negative for others (Qwen3.6-35B -1 to -9 with reasoning off). With the manager, Opus-5 achieves the highest score in the study at 91% in one pass. Running a manager roughly triples the token bill, but it buys accuracy more cheaply than moving to a larger model does: GPT-5.6-Terra with a manager nearly matches Fable 5's single-call accuracy (85.0 against 87.4, $p = 0.59$) at a fifth of the price (\$11.71 against \$61.11 per 100-problem pass, $p < 10^{-4}$), and the Qwen-27B arm does it for \$51.75 on weights anyone can self-host. Our transcript analysis finds several mechanisms behind the gains, of which two recur: context management, in which short worker calls and shared notes organize state and reduce truncation, and problem decomposition. Improvements are modest for large models with reasoning enabled, but larger for some models with reasoning disabled and for smaller models with reasoning enabled.

</details>


### [353] [Risks and Controls for Multi-Agent Systems: an analytical framework for deployment of AI agents across organisational boundaries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26626)
*Alistair Reid,Simon O'Callaghan,Dustin Venini,Liam Carroll,Tiberio Caetano*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: A framework to analyze risks from AI agent interactions across organizational boundaries, categorizing governance structures into three tiers and identifying control gaps requiring collective action.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As organizations increasingly deploy AI agents that interact across organizational boundaries, failures can emerge from these interactions themselves, and no single organization can fully see, control or govern interactions that cross their perimeter, creating systemic risks.

Method: The report develops a framework with three deployment tiers based on governance structures (singular governance, federated governance, open environments), within which it examines risk factors, failure modes, available controls, and identifies responsible actors or governance gaps requiring collective action.

Result: The framework identifies three governance tiers for AI agent interactions, analyzes specific risk factors and failure modes within each tier, determines which actors can apply controls, and highlights governance gaps where collective action is needed.

Conclusion: The report concludes that addressing AI agent interaction risks requires collaborative governance frameworks and collective action, especially when interactions cross organizational boundaries where no single entity has full visibility or control.

Abstract: This report presents a framework to help organisations, policymakers and researchers reason about the risks that emerge when AI agents interact with each other, how those risks change as interactions cross organisational boundaries, and the controls that may help address them.
  As organisations deploy AI agents, those agents will increasingly interact with each other: inside the organisation, with the agents of partners, customers and suppliers, and with unknown counterparties on the open internet. Failures can emerge from the interactions themselves, and once those interactions cross an organisation's perimeter, no single organisation can fully see, control or govern them.
  The report introduces three deployment tiers, defined by the minimum common governance binding any two interacting agents: singular governance, where one organisation governs every agent; federated governance, where multiple organisations deploy into a shared environment under agreed rules; and open environments, where agents operate with no central authority and shared standards are adopted voluntarily if at all.
  Within each tier, the report examines risk factors, failure modes and available controls. It identifies who is positioned to apply the controls, and where no actor is positioned to act, it characterises the gap and the collective action required to close it.

</details>


### [354] [Fixed-Haven Reservation for Online Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery in Dense Warehouses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26759)
*Taisei Hirayama,Kohei Yoshida,Hiroki Sakaji,Itsuki Noda*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: A Safe Haven Retreat Planner (SHARP) uses fixed Safe Havens for agents in dense warehouse MAPD problems, achieving 100% success rate where other methods fail on tree-like layouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MAPD methods rely on assumptions like extra waiting endpoints or biconnected topology that fail in dense warehouse layouts with single-lane aisles, dead ends, and tree-like guidepaths where agents can't wait without blocking others.

Method: Fixed-Haven reservation where each agent owns a fixed Safe Haven (usually its start cell) that only the owner may occupy. SHARP keeps busy or retreating agents on collision-free reserved routes ending at their Havens, with explicit planning/progress assumptions.

Result: SHARP achieves 100% success on all tested configurations, outperforming TP, PIBT, and PIBTTP-TA. Fixed return is identified as a central robustness mechanism, and disabling mid-retreat reassignment worsens service time by 1.89x and makespan by 1.53x.

Conclusion: Fixed-Haven reservation with the SHARP planner provides robust completion guarantees for MAPD in challenging dense warehouse layouts where traditional methods fail, though at higher centralized planning cost for tree-like layouts.

Abstract: Dense warehouses often contain single-lane aisles, dead ends, and tree-like guidepaths that leave little room for idle agents to wait without blocking others. Existing Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery (MAPD) guarantees for completing all finitely released tasks typically rely on extra waiting endpoints that planned paths can avoid, or on biconnected topology; these assumptions may fail in such layouts. We study fixed-Haven reservation for online MAPD, where pickup-delivery tasks are released over time. Each agent owns a fixed Safe Haven (Haven for short), usually its start cell, that only the owner may occupy and that other agents treat as blocked. For finite task releases, we prove that this fixed-Haven contract completes all released tasks under Haven-Reachability and explicit planning/progress assumptions. We implement the contract in SHARP, a Safe-Haven Retreat Planner that keeps every busy or retreating agent on a collision-free reserved route ending at its Haven. We compare SHARP with representative TP and PIBT-family MAPD baselines: Token Passing (TP), Priority Inheritance with Backtracking (PIBT), and PIBT with Temporary Priority and Temporary Avoidance (PIBTTP-TA) for biconnected main areas with attached trees. In the robustness sweep, SHARP is the only method with 100% success on all tested configurations, at substantially higher centralized planning cost on tree-like layouts. A TP-style fixed-home-return counterfactual with full-route validation also recovers robustness on tested tree-like layouts, suggesting that fixed return is a central robustness mechanism there. A no-overwrite variant shows that disabling mid-retreat reassignment worsens service time (release-to-delivery latency) by 1.89 times and makespan by 1.53 times in the tested high-load tree condition.

</details>


### [355] [Dynamic Haven Selection for Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery in Constrained Warehouses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26939)
*Taisei Hirayama,Kohei Yoshida,Hiroki Sakaji,Itsuki Noda*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: A-sharp (Adaptive SHARP) improves multi-agent pickup-delivery in constrained warehouses by dynamically changing agents' retreat targets to havens at task assignment time, reducing makespan compared to fixed-haven SHARP approach.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In space-efficient warehouse layouts with single-agent-width aisles and dead-end workstations, robots have limited waiting spots without blocking others. Existing MAPD solutions with fixed-haven commitments can send agents to distant havens after deliveries, reducing efficiency.

Method: A-sharp extends the SHARP framework by allowing agents to change their retreat haven targets at task assignment time. It prevents conflicts through: 1) availability test for candidate havens, and 2) pending-release rule that keeps previous haven protected until agent departs.

Result: Across 72,000 runs on 14,400 test cases, A-sharp significantly outperforms SHARP in makespan: better in 107 out of 138 configurations, never worse, with median reduction of 16.7% on tree maps. Both approaches maintain 100% completion rates.

Conclusion: A-sharp provides adaptive haven selection that improves efficiency while maintaining safety guarantees. The approach preserves invariants and ensures finite-release completeness while achieving substantial makespan reductions in constrained warehouse environments.

Abstract: Space-efficient warehouse layouts often contain single-agent-width aisles and dead-end workstations where robots have few places to wait without blocking others. In Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery (MAPD) on such constrained layouts, robots must accept online pickup-delivery tasks while preserving protected waiting locations called Havens. The Safe HAven Retreat Planner (SHARP) introduced a mechanism that extends each committed task path with a validated retreat to the agent's dedicated initial Haven, but fixed-Haven commitments can send agents toward distant Havens after deliveries. We present A-sharp (Adaptive SHARP), which changes an agent's retreat target at task assignment time. A naive switch can cause two agents to rely on the same waiting location or let another committed path pass through a location that is still occupied or reserved. A-sharp prevents these failures with an availability test for candidate Havens and a pending-release rule that keeps the previous Haven protected until the agent departs. Under explicit Haven-structure and Safe Interval Path Planning (SIPP) assumptions, we prove invariant preservation and finite-release completeness: every task in any finite release sequence is delivered in finite time. Across 72,000 runs on 14,400 paired map-agent-count-rate-seed cases over four maps, both SHARP and A-sharp complete their respective 14,400 runs. For makespan (final delivery time), a prespecified paired comparison with Holm correction over all 138 configurations with more Havens than agents finds A-sharp significantly better in 107 configurations and never significantly worse than SHARP; on the tested tree map, the median reduction is 16.7%.

</details>


### [356] [One Model, Many Minds: Unlocking Multi-Agent Synergy in a Single Agent via Mixture of Roles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27338)
*Zhichen Zeng,Huiyuan Chen,Jingru Cheng,Juan Zha,Ming Liu,Ying Chen,Xiyuan Yang,Chaosheng Dong,Haiyang Zhang,Hanghang Tong*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: MoRe enables single-agent LLMs to dynamically combine multiple specialized roles in single-turn inference, matching multi-agent system performance while reducing token cost by 20x.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current single-agent LLMs use fixed specializations that can't adapt to diverse queries, while multi-agent systems require multi-turn interactions that increase context length and inference costs. There's a need for dynamic multi-perspective problem solving in a single-agent framework.

Method: Mixture of Roles (MoRe) learns a diversified codebook of steering vectors encoding latent roles. A query-aware router dynamically fuses multiple codebook vectors into a single steering vector that encompasses multiple roles. This composed vector steers the frozen backbone LLM, enabling multi-perspective specialization in single-turn inference. The system is trained via three-stage supervised fine-tuning curriculum and GRPO post-training.

Result: MoRe outperforms single-agent baselines by 2.2% on average across reasoning and personality benchmarks. It achieves performance on par with multi-agent systems while reducing token cost by 20x.

Conclusion: MoRe successfully bridges the gap between static single-agent specialization and dynamic multi-agent collaboration, providing efficient multi-perspective problem solving through adaptive role composition in single-turn inference.

Abstract: Specializing Large Language Models (LLMs) toward distinct abilities underpins successes ranging from personalized assistants to multi-agent systems (MAS). Single-agent paradigms rely on pre-defined personas or steering vectors to induce specialization, yet they impose a single fixed specialization that fails to adapt to diverse queries. Conversely, MAS achieves dynamic multi-perspective problem solving by orchestrating agents with distinct text-based roles, but fusing these specializations requires multi-turn interactions that inflate context length and inference cost. To address these limitations, we propose Mixture of Roles (MoRe), which adaptively composes multiple specializations into a single steering vector for single-turn inference. Specifically, MoRe learns a diversified codeboox of steering vectors, each of which encodes a latent role. A query-aware router dynamically fuses the codebook into a steering vector that encompasses multiple roles. By steering the backbone LLM with the composed vector, MoRe enables multi-perspective specialization in a single-agent, single-turn inference process. The proposed MoRe can be efficiently trained via a three-stage SFT curriculum and GRPO post-training, while the backbone LLM remains frozen. Experiments across reasoning and personality benchmarks show that MoRe outperforms single-agent baselines by 2.2% on average, and achieves performance on par with MAS while reducing token cost by 20x.

</details>
